Whiten the local coordinates by $Q^{-1/2}$, write $H$ for the largest whitened jump length, and let $A$ be a positive local $C^2$ function with $A(0)=1$ giving the scalar multipliers at the neighbors. If its Hessian operator norm on the whitened one-step ball is bounded by $B$ and $BH^2\le101/30000$, then $K\le-101\lambda/(1250\ell^2)$. No bound on its gradient is required.

The local lift requires the values of the common two-step polynomials used below to be consistent at physical vertices reached by two jumps. A globally translation-invariant graph is unnecessary. In particular, shrinking-jump families with $\inf\lambda>0$ in either class cannot satisfy a common finite lower bound, even when their exit rates diverge.

*Frozen defect divided by the correct moment.* Let $L_0$ be the translation stencil in whitened coordinates. Reuse $s,a_s$ for its jump vectors and unchanged physical-time rates. Then
$$
\sum_s a_s ss^{\mathsf T}=2I_4,\qquad M_j=\sum_s a_s|s|^j,\qquad M_2=8 .
\tag{I.3p.1}
$$
Set $q(x)=|x|^2$ and $f(x)=q(x)-q(x)^2/(100H^2)$. The covariance transformation preserves the jump generator and its curvature test under pullback by the local lift. On the two-step ball this polynomial gives the same directed second-difference computation (I.3o.2)–(I.3o.4), which requires only the covariance, finite rates and the maximum jump length. In particular, with $c_0=101/1250$,
$$
\Gamma_{2,0}(f)(0)-\tfrac14(L_0 f(0))^2
\le -c_0 M_4/H^2,\qquad
0<\Gamma_0(f)(0)=\tfrac12\sum_s a_s f(s)^2\le M_4/2 .
\tag{I.3p.2}
$$
The strict positivity follows since $f(s)\ge(99/100)|s|^2$ on a jump and the covariance is nonsingular. The upper bound follows from $f(s)\le|s|^2$. Dividing (I.3p.2) by the actual $\Gamma_0(f)(0)$ gives $K\le-2c_0/H^2$. This argument does not bound $M_4$ away from zero. It uses the same positive fourth moment in the curvature defect and the denominator. Since $H\le\ell/\sqrt\lambda$, it proves the first assertion even when that moment tends to zero and the total exit rate tends to infinity.

*Symmetric stencil with a local scalar time change.* At the marked vertex and its one-step neighbors let $L=A L_0$. The corresponding carré du champ is $\Gamma=A\Gamma_0$ at those rows. At the origin $L f=L_0 f$ and $\Gamma(f)=\Gamma_0(f)$. For $\Gamma_2(f)=\tfrac12 L\Gamma(f)-\Gamma(f,Lf)$ the exact change is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma_2(f)(0)-\Gamma_{2,0}(f)(0)
&=\tfrac12\sum_s a_s(A(s)-1)D_f(s),\\
D_f(s)&=\Gamma_0(f)(s)-f(s)L_0 f(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3p.3}
$$
Indeed the first term of $\Gamma_2$ changes by $\tfrac12\sum_s a_s(A(s)-1)\Gamma_0(f)(s)$. The second term changes by $-\tfrac12\sum_s a_s f(s)(A(s)-1)L_0f(s)$, since $f(0)=0$ and $A(0)=1$. Only the two-step data enter this identity.

The polynomial is even, and symmetry of the frozen rates makes both $\Gamma_0(f)$ and $L_0f$ even. Hence $D_f(s)=D_f(-s)$. Taylor's theorem on the line from $-s$ to $s$ gives
$$
|A(s)+A(-s)-2|\le B|s|^2.
$$
Pairing the equal rates in (I.3p.3) bounds its absolute value by
$$
\frac B4\sum_s a_s |s|^2 |D_f(s)|.
\tag{I.3p.4}
$$
This is the cancellation that removes a gradient or total exit-rate condition.

For $|x|\le H$ and any jump $t$, the radial map $u\mapsto u-u^2/(100H^2)$ has derivative in $[0,1]$ on $0\le u\le4H^2$. Therefore
$$
|f(x+t)-f(x)|\le 2|x||t|+|t|^2,\qquad
\Gamma_0(f)(x)\le 32|x|^2+M_4 .
$$
The second bound follows by squaring with $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ and using $M_2=8$. The radial and tangential eigenvalues of the Hessian of $f$ are $2-12|x|^2/(100H^2)$ and $2-4|x|^2/(100H^2)$, respectively. They lie in $[0,2]$ throughout the two-step ball. Pair the symmetric jumps and use the centered second-difference bound to get
$$
|L_0 f(x)|
\le \tfrac12\sum_t a_t\,2|t|^2
=8 .
$$
As $|f(x)|\le |x|^2$, it follows that $|D_f(s)|\le M_4+40|s|^2$. Inserting this in (I.3p.4) gives the uniform bound $12 B M_4$, without a lower bound on $M_4$ or an upper bound on the number or total rate of jumps.

If $BH^2\le101/30000$, then $12 B M_4\le(c_0/2)M_4/H^2$. The actual defect is at most $-(c_0/2)M_4/H^2$ by (I.3p.2), while $\Gamma(f)(0)=\Gamma_0(f)(0)\le M_4/2$ stays positive. Dividing gives $K\le-c_0/H^2$, proving the second assertion and the stated physical-length bound. All curvatures use the original physical time of the base row; only spatial coordinates were whitened. The test is an all-function test because the local polynomial can be extended to a function on the rest of the finite graph. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3q"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3q-dimension-doubling-obstruction-for-inhomogeneous-periodic-product-jump-laws"></a>**Proposition I.3q (Dimension Doubling Obstruction for Inhomogeneous Periodic Product Jump Laws).** Let $L$ be the generator of a Cartesian product of $d$ finite cycles, each of length at least five, with positive nearest-neighbor left and right rates in physical time. In each coordinate its rates may vary arbitrarily around its cycle and may be directed. Its generator is the sum of the coordinate generators, with each summand acting on its own coordinate. Let $\rho$ be the minimum of all these positive rates. If an all-function curvature-dimension bound $\mathrm{BE}(K,D)$ holds at every vertex for some $0<D<2d$, then
$$
K\le-\left(\frac{2d}{D}-1\right)\rho .
\tag{I.3q.1}
$$
For homogeneous cycles with equal left and right rates on each factor, $\mathrm{BE}(0,2d)$ holds on the product, so the dimension $2d$ is sharp for a nonnegative lower bound within this class. In particular every four-dimensional product of these cycles with $\rho\ge\kappa h^{-2}$ for a fixed $\kappa>0$ fails the uniform exact dimension-four gate of Definition I.3h as $h\downarrow0$. This allows nonscalar rate inhomogeneity, unbounded rate ratios, and no approximation by frozen rows.

The separate qualified varying-stencil family of Corollary C.6c.7.1 also fails the exact finite gate: in its actual physical time $K_n\le-101n/(625\tau_*)$, and in its metric-normalized form $K_n\le-101n/(625\ell_*^2)$.

*Local two-step test in one factor.* Use the convention $\Gamma_2(f)=\tfrac12L\Gamma(f)-\Gamma(f,Lf)$. At vertex $i$ write $a_i$ for its left rate and $b_i$ for its right rate. Put $f(i)=0$, let $m=f(i-1)$ and $p=f(i+1)$, and let the two second-neighbor values be $u=f(i-2)$ and $v=f(i+2)$. A cycle of length at least five makes these five sites distinct, so the values can be assigned freely. Direct substitution into $\Gamma_2$ and completion of the two squares give
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Gamma_2(f)(i)-\tfrac12(Lf(i))^2\\
&=\frac{a_i}{4}\bigl(3b_{i-1}-a_{i-1}-a_i-b_i\bigr)m^2
 +\frac{b_i}{4}\bigl(3a_{i+1}-b_{i+1}-a_i-b_i\bigr)p^2\\
&\quad+\frac{a_i a_{i-1}}{4}(u-2m)^2
      +\frac{b_i b_{i+1}}{4}(v-2p)^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3q.2}
$$
To obtain the coefficients, the two inward rates are $b_{i-1}$ and $a_{i+1}$, and the two outward rates are $a_{i-1}$ and $b_{i+1}$. For example, the outward terms involving $u$ are $(a_i a_{i-1}/4)(u-m)^2-(a_i a_{i-1}/2)m(u-m)$, which give the displayed square and the term $-a_i a_{i-1}m^2/4$. The inward terms give $3a_i b_{i-1}m^2/4$. The base-row terms after subtracting $(Lf)^2/2$ contribute $-a_i(a_i+b_i)m^2/4$. The right-hand contributions are obtained by reversing left and right. This proves (I.3q.2) with no stationarity or reversibility hypothesis.

Write $A_i$ and $B_i$ for the parentheses in the first and second coefficients. Periodic summation gives
$$
\sum_i A_i=2\sum_i(b_i-a_i),\qquad
\sum_i B_i=2\sum_i(a_i-b_i).
\tag{I.3q.3}
$$
Their total is zero. Consequently some vertex has a direction whose coefficient is nonpositive. At that vertex let $r$ be the rate in that direction. Set the increment in the chosen direction to $1/r$, the other increment to zero, and the second-neighbor values to twice their respective increments. Extend the five values to the remaining sites. Then
$$
Lf(i)=1,\qquad \Gamma(f)(i)=\frac1{2r},\qquad
\Gamma_2(f)(i)\le\frac12.
\tag{I.3q.4}
$$

*Product and curvature bound.* Apply (I.3q.4) independently to the $d$ factors, take the product of the chosen vertices, and use the sum $F$ of the corresponding single-coordinate test functions. Its first and second carré du champ quantities are the sums of those in the factors. For the second this follows directly because each $\Gamma(f_i)$ and $L_i f_i$ depends only on coordinate $i$, and the off-coordinate differences of those terms vanish. At the chosen vertex,
$$
LF=d,\qquad
\Gamma(F)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d r_j^{-1},\qquad
\Gamma_2(F)\le d/2.
$$
Thus the assumed inequality forces
$$
K\le
-\frac{d(2d/D-1)}{\sum_{j=1}^d r_j^{-1}}
\le-\rho(2d/D-1).
\tag{I.3q.5}
$$
The last step uses $r_j\ge\rho$ and the positive factor $2d/D-1$. This proves (I.3q.1).

For homogeneous symmetric factors the base and inward/outward rates are equal in (I.3q.2), so the two first coefficients vanish. Hence each factor has $\Gamma_2\ge (Lf)^2/2$. On the product, all mixed-coordinate contributions to $\Gamma_2$ are nonnegative: pairing commuting jumps in two distinct coordinates gives a nonnegative multiple of the squared mixed second difference. Equivalently, the translation identity (I.3o.2) splits into its same-coordinate and mixed-coordinate sums. Apply the one-factor bound to each coordinate slice and use $\sum_j(L_jF)^2/2\ge(\sum_jL_jF)^2/(2d)$. This proves $\mathrm{BE}(0,2d)$ and the sharpness assertion.

*Application to the existing qualified source.* For Corollary C.6c.7.1 the operator $L_n/\tau_*$ is the actual transfer logarithm in its physical time by (C.6c.7.5). Its physical jump displacement is $(\ell_*/n)s$ for the stencil element $s$ and its rates are $a_n(s)/\tau_*$ by (C.6c.7.6). Symmetry under sign changes and coordinate permutations gives $\sum_{s\in S_m}ss^{\mathsf T}=(Q_m/4)I_4$. Together with the separate nearest-neighbor term of (C.6c.7.3) this yields
$$
Q=\tfrac12\sum_s\frac{a_n(s)}{\tau_*}
       \frac{\ell_*^2}{n^2}ss^{\mathsf T}
  =\frac{\ell_*^2}{\tau_*}I_4,\qquad
\ell=\frac{\ell_*}{\sqrt n}.
\tag{I.3q.6}
$$
All two-step lifts exist on the stated nested stages, since two jumps have lattice length at most $2\sqrt n<n/2$. The first clause of Proposition I.3p now gives $K_n\le-101n/(625\tau_*)$. Multiplying the generator by $\tau_*/\ell_*^2$ multiplies its curvature lower-bound parameter by the same scalar, giving the asserted metric-normalized version. This is the exact all-function test on the actual source generator. The smooth-core curvature and RCD limit of Corollary C.6c.7.1 remain valid under their own tested convention. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3r"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3r-exact-two-hop-curvature-test-and-triangle-spread-obstruction"></a>**Proposition I.3r (Exact Two-Hop Curvature Test and Triangle-Spread Obstruction).** Let $L f(x)=\sum_y a_{xy}(f(y)-f(x))$ be a finite jump generator with no self-loop rates and symmetric support, so $a_{xy}>0$ exactly when $a_{yx}>0$. The rates need not be symmetric. Write $d_x=\sum_y a_{xy}$ and work at a nonisolated vertex $x$. Let $S_1(x)$ and $S_2(x)$ be its first and second support spheres. Define the two-step backtrack, total and triangular weights
$$
R_x=\sum_{y\in S_1(x)}a_{xy}a_{yx},\qquad
J_x=\sum_{y\in S_1(x)}a_{xy}d_y,\qquad
T_x=\sum_{\substack{y,z\in S_1(x)}}a_{xy}a_{yz}.
\tag{I.3r.1}
$$
For every dimension parameter $D>0$, an all-function $\mathrm{BE}(K,D)$ bound at $x$ forces
$$
K\le
\frac{(1-4/D)d_x^2+4R_x-J_x+T_x}{2d_x}.
\tag{I.3r.2}
$$
There is also the exact finite quadratic test below, which retains the overlaps of all two-hop paths.

In particular, if every row's largest jump probability is at most $\beta$, and $T_x\le\theta J_x$ with $4\beta+\theta<1$, then any common $\mathrm{BE}(K,4)$ lower bound satisfies $K\le-(1-4\beta-\theta)d_{\min}/2$, where $d_{\min}$ is the minimum exit rate on the support component in question. The same conclusion holds locally at a vertex using the bounds on its immediate neighbor rows and their exit rates. These conditions need no coordinate product, frozen-row approximation, or upper bound on the exit rates. A triangle-free graph has $T_x=0$ even if its support has many squares.

*Exact elimination of the second sphere.* Set $f(x)=0$, $m_y=f(y)$ for $y\in S_1(x)$, and use the abbreviations
$$
S=\sum_y a_{xy}m_y,\quad P=\sum_y a_{xy}m_y^2,\quad
w_{yz}=a_{xy}a_{yz},\quad
W_z=\sum_{y\in S_1(x)}w_{yz}\quad(z\in S_2(x)).
$$
Thus $Lf(x)=S$ and $2\Gamma(f)(x)=P$. Substituting $\Gamma_2(f)=\tfrac12L\Gamma(f)-\Gamma(f,Lf)$ gives
$$
4\Gamma_2(f)(x)
=2S^2-d_xP+
\sum_{y\in S_1(x)}\sum_{z}w_{yz}
     \bigl((f(z)-2m_y)^2-m_y^2\bigr).
\tag{I.3r.3}
$$
Indeed the first term of $4\Gamma_2$ gives $\sum_{y,z}w_{yz}(f(z)-m_y)^2-d_x P$, and the mixed term subtracts $2\sum_{y,z}w_{yz}m_y(f(z)-m_y)$ and adds $2S^2$. Completing the square gives (I.3r.3). The inner sum ranges over neighbors of $y$, so its terms reach only $x$, $S_1(x)$ and $S_2(x)$.

Each $z\in S_2(x)$ is a free variable and $W_z>0$. For fixed first-sphere values its minimizing value is
$$
f(z)=2\frac{\sum_y w_{yz}m_y}{W_z}.
$$
The minimized quadratic expression for $4[\Gamma_2(f)(x)-(Lf(x))^2/D]$ is therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal Q_{x,D}(m)
={}&(2-4/D)S^2-d_xP\\
 &+\sum_y 3w_{yx}m_y^2
   +\sum_{y,z\in S_1(x)}
      w_{yz}\bigl((m_z-2m_y)^2-m_y^2\bigr)\\
 &+\sum_{z\in S_2(x)}
   \left(3\sum_y w_{yz}m_y^2
       -4\frac{(\sum_y w_{yz}m_y)^2}{W_z}\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3r.4}
$$
No branches with shared second-sphere vertices were separated in this minimization. In particular their rank-one terms use the sum over all routes to the same vertex. The exact pointwise test is $\mathcal Q_{x,D}(m)\ge 2K P$ for every real vector $m$. It is necessary by taking the displayed minimizing values and sufficient because every other second-sphere assignment increases the quadratic expression. Thus its smallest generalized eigenvalue relative to the form $2P$ gives the optimal local lower bound.

For a second explicit necessary estimate, take independent uniformly signed $m_y\in\{-1,1\}$ in (I.3r.4) and average. Since no term $a_{yy}$ occurs, the ordered triangle term has expectation $4T_x$. The first term has expectation $(2-4/D)\sum_y a_{xy}^2-d_x^2$. The second-sphere term retains only its diagonal numerator after averaging. This gives
$$
K\le \frac{(2-4/D)\sum_y a_{xy}^2-d_x^2+
             3J_x+T_x-
             4\displaystyle\sum_{z\in S_2(x)}
                     \frac{\sum_y w_{yz}^2}{W_z}}
            {2d_x}.
\tag{I.3r.5}
$$
It is valid with arbitrary overlapping squares and triangles. It can be used together with (I.3r.2) or with the full quadratic test.

*Radial and stationary consequences.* In (I.3r.3) take $m_y=1$ for every neighbor and $f(z)=2$ on $S_2(x)$. This already minimizes all second-sphere terms. The terms of the inner sum at $x$, $S_1(x)$ and $S_2(x)$ contribute respectively $3R_x$, zero, and $-(J_x-R_x-T_x)$. With $S=P=d_x$, this proves (I.3r.2). If a stationary probability $\mu$ is supplied, summing the same inequality weighted by $\mu_x$ gives
$$
K\le
\frac{-(4/D)\sum_x\mu_x d_x^2+
       4\sum_x\mu_x R_x+\sum_x\mu_xT_x}
     {2\sum_x\mu_x d_x}.
\tag{I.3r.6}
$$
Here stationarity gives $\sum_x\mu_xJ_x=\sum_x\mu_x d_x^2$. In the symmetric-rate case, one may use uniform $\mu$, and $\sum_x R_x=\sum_{x,y}a_{xy}^2$. At $D=4$ this exposes the backtrack and triangle mass needed to compensate the total squared exit. For the local spread condition, $a_{yx}\le\beta d_y$ gives $R_x\le\beta J_x$. With $T_x\le\theta J_x$, (I.3r.2) at $D=4$ gives $K\le-(1-4\beta-\theta)J_x/(2d_x)$. Since $J_x/d_x$ is the outgoing-rate-weighted mean of the neighbor exits, the claimed bound follows.

*An actual reversible nonscalar family.* For even $n\ge10$ take the physical four-torus with vertices $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^4$, spacing $h=\ell_*/n$, and descriptors
$$
\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_4,\ \pm(e_1+2e_2)\}.
$$
Every descriptor changes the parity of the coordinate sum. Hence this graph is bipartite and $T_x=0$ at every vertex. At $x$ let the rates of the two $e_1$ edges be $h^{-2}\bigl(1+(-1)^{x_2}/4\bigr)$ and let every other edge rate be $h^{-2}$. The $e_1$ rate is the same when read from either endpoint because those edges keep $x_2$ fixed. Thus all rates are symmetric, with uniform reversible measure. The rows vary by a fixed fraction in one directional pair as $x_2$ changes by one, while the other directional pairs remain fixed. The additional descriptor has two nonzero coordinates, so this is not a Cartesian nearest-neighbor product with the given physical coordinates. The maximum displacement is $\sqrt5 h$, and the axial rates alone give a uniformly positive physical covariance. The ten rates at each vertex lie between $3h^{-2}/4$ and $5h^{-2}/4$. Consequently $d_{\min}\ge(15/2)h^{-2}$ and $\beta\le1/6$. The exact test gives
$$
K\le-\frac{5}{4h^2}.
\tag{I.3r.7}
$$
This example may be implemented with the rational descriptor-weighted endpoint compiler of Theorem C.6c.7 by taking dimensionless rates $n^2$ times these listed relative weights, node probability $n^{-4}$, period $n^{-4}$ and microscopic length $\ell_*/n$. The maximum dimensionless exit is at most $(25/2)n^2$, so its product with the period is at most $1/8$ for the stated $n$. Its physical generator is the transfer logarithm divided by the physical period, with rates $n^2/\tau_*$ times the same relative weights. Thus its corresponding exact finite curvature bound in physical time is $K\le-5n^2/(4\tau_*)$. The qualified compiler and curvature estimate require no assertion about the Mosco limit or cosmological stress of these inhomogeneous rows. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3s"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3s-averaged-dimension-four-obstruction-for-varying-centered-stencils"></a>**Proposition I.3s (Averaged Dimension-Four Obstruction for Varying Centered Stencils).** Consider a finite reversible jump network on a flat four-dimensional physical torus with positive reversible probability $\mu$. Use a consistent Euclidean lift of every two-hop neighborhood, with reverse displacements opposite and two-hop displacements additive. Suppose each vertex has an antipodally symmetric displacement law in its own lifted coordinates, and each row has the same positive definite covariance
$$
Q=\tfrac12\sum_s a_x(s)ss^{\mathsf T}.
$$
The rows may have different supports, different higher moments, and arbitrarily large exit rates. Let $\ell$ be the largest physical jump length and $\lambda$ the least eigenvalue of $Q$. Every common all-function dimension-four lower bound obeys
$$
K\le -\frac{428\lambda}{1225\ell^2}.
\tag{I.3s.1}
$$
Thus no uniform finite bound exists on shrinking uniformly elliptic families in this class. The result does not require the rows to approach a common translation stencil.

*Common coordinates and averaging.* Whiten all displacement vectors by the same $Q^{-1/2}$. Write $H$ for the largest whitened length and retain the rates in physical time. At every row the displacement covariance is now $2I_4$. For a first displacement $s$ from $x$ to $y$, and a second displacement $t$ from $y$, write
$$
A=|s|^2,\qquad B=|t|^2,\qquad c=s\cdot t,\qquad
m_j(x)=\sum_s a_x(s)|s|^j .
$$
Thus $m_2(x)=8$. Angle brackets below mean averaging over $x$ with $\mu_x$, and $\mathbb E_2$ denotes the unnormalized two-step rate sum $\sum_{x,s,t}\mu_x a_x(s)a_y(t)$ applied to its integrand. Reversibility gives $\mu_xa_x(s)=\mu_ya_y(-s)$ on an edge and also gives stationarity. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_2[B^k-A^k]=0,\qquad
\mathbb E_2[A^kB]=8\langle m_{2k}\rangle,\qquad
\mathbb E_2[AB^k]=8\langle m_{2k}\rangle .
\tag{I.3s.2}
$$
The first identity follows by detailed balance on the first displacement and the incoming-rate identity at its endpoint, as detailed below. For the second sum over $t$ at $y$ using $m_2(y)=8$. For the third reverse the first edge and sum its squared lengths at $y$. All products are finite at each stage.

At each $x$ separately let $q(\xi)=|\xi|^2$, $u(\xi)=|\xi|^4$ in the coordinates centered at $x$. These can be used as vertex test functions on the two-hop lift and extended to the remaining vertices. Let $\mathcal D_x(f,g)=\Gamma_2(f,g)(x)-Lf(x)Lg(x)/4$. Polarization of (I.3r.3), for $f(x)=g(x)=0$, gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
4\mathcal D_x(f,g)
={}&Lf(x)Lg(x)
-d_x\sum_s a_x(s)f(s)g(s)\\
&+\sum_{s,t} a_x(s)a_y(t)
\bigl[(f(s+t)-2f(s))(g(s+t)-2g(s))-f(s)g(s)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3s.3}
$$
Here $d_x=\sum_s a_x(s)$. The exit term uses $d_x$, whereas a two-step sum over a first-displacement function uses the second-row exit $d_y$. These give the same average by reversibility. For any such function $g_0(A)$,
$$
\mathbb E_2[g_0(A)]-\left\langle d_x\sum_s a_x(s)g_0(|s|^2)\right\rangle
=\sum_{x,y}\mu_xa_{xy}(d_y-d_x)g_0(|s|^2)=0.
\tag{I.3s.4}
$$
The last equality pairs the two orientations of each physical edge. Also $\mathbb E_2[B^k]=\langle d_xm_{2k}(x)\rangle$ by stationarity, which is the explicit form of the first cancellation in (I.3s.2).

*Quadratic and crossed defects.* In the sum in (I.3s.3), odd powers of $c$ vanish under $t\mapsto-t$ at the row of $y$. For $(f,g)=(q,q)$ its even polynomial is
$$
-2AB+B^2+4c^2.
$$
Here $Lq(x)=8$, $\mathbb E_2[AB]=64$, and $\mathbb E_2[c^2]=16$: at a fixed first step the second covariance gives $\sum_t a_y(t)c^2=2A$. The pure $B^2$ term cancels the base exit term by stationarity. Therefore $\langle\mathcal D_x(q,q)\rangle=0$.

For $(f,g)=(q,u)$ the even polynomial in the same sum is
$$
-3A^2B+AB^2+4Ac^2+B^3+12Bc^2.
\tag{I.3s.5}
$$
Now $Lu(x)=m_4(x)$. The two mixed powers average to $8\langle m_4\rangle$ each by (I.3s.2), and the pure $B^3$ term cancels the exit term. The covariance immediately gives $\mathbb E_2[Ac^2]=2\langle m_4\rangle$. For the other cross square reverse the first edge using detailed balance. The first step is then an outgoing step from $y$ of length $|s|$, and its covariance gives $\sum_s a_y(s)(s\cdot t)^2=2B$ for fixed $t$. Hence $\mathbb E_2[Bc^2]=2\langle m_4\rangle$ as well. Combining with the base term $8\langle m_4\rangle$ in (I.3s.3) gives
$$
\langle\mathcal D_x(q,u)\rangle
=\frac14(8-24+8+8+24)\langle m_4\rangle
=6\langle m_4\rangle .
\tag{I.3s.6}
$$

*Quartic upper bound and the all-function test.* For $(f,g)=(u,u)$ the even polynomial is
$$
-4A^3B+2A^2B^2+8A^2c^2+4AB^3
 +48ABc^2+B^4+24B^2c^2+16c^4 .
$$
Cancel $B^4$ in the average against the base exit term. Use $c^2\le AB$ and drop the negative term to bound the remaining polynomial by $8A^3B+66A^2B^2+28AB^3$. Each of these three mixed monomials has average at most $8H^2\langle m_4\rangle$: for the first and last use (I.3s.2) and $m_6\le H^2m_4$, and for the middle use $B^2\le H^2B$. Also $\langle(Lu)^2\rangle=\langle m_4^2\rangle\le8H^2\langle m_4\rangle$ since $m_4\le H^2m_2$. With the factor $1/4$ in (I.3s.3), this gives
$$
\langle\mathcal D_x(u,u)\rangle
\le 206H^2\langle m_4\rangle .
\tag{I.3s.7}
$$

Use at each vertex the test $f_x=q-u/(35H^2)$. Its averaged defect, by (I.3s.6)–(I.3s.7), satisfies
$$
\left\langle\mathcal D_x(f_x,f_x)\right\rangle
\le-\left(\frac{12}{35}-\frac{206}{35^2}\right)
       \frac{\langle m_4\rangle}{H^2}
=-\frac{214}{1225}\frac{\langle m_4\rangle}{H^2}.
\tag{I.3s.8}
$$
On every one-step neighbor $f_x(s)=A(1-A/(35H^2))$ lies in $[(34/35)A,A]$. Consequently $0<\langle\Gamma(f_x)(x)\rangle\le\langle m_4\rangle/2$. If the all-function lower bound holds, it can be tested with a different $f_x$ at each vertex and then averaged, giving
$$
K\le-\frac{428}{1225H^2}.
\tag{I.3s.9}
$$
Finally $H\le\ell/\sqrt\lambda$. This proves (I.3s.1).

The admissible condition includes genuinely different reversible stencils even on the same metric grid. For instance, on an even four-torus keep nearest-neighbor symmetric rates and add positive length-two symmetric jumps in direction $e_1$, allowing their rates to vary arbitrarily with the second coordinate. Compensate their second moment by varying the two length-one $e_1$ rates, keeping all rates positive. Each varying rate is constant along its own $e_1$ lines, so the edge rates are reversible with uniform $\mu$. The other direction rates are fixed. This preserves the entire covariance, while the fourth moments may alternate by a fixed fraction across neighboring lines. The uniform obstruction (I.3s.9) applies to every such calibration. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3t"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3t-moment-obstruction-with-unequal-covariance"></a>**Proposition I.3t (Moment Obstruction with Unequal Covariance).** Use the reversible flat four-dimensional torus and consistent local two-hop lifts of Proposition I.3s. Keep the antipodal symmetry of each row, and allow its physical covariance $Q_x$ to vary freely with the vertex. Put
$$
\lambda_x=\tfrac14\operatorname{tr}Q_x,\qquad
A_x=Q_x-\lambda_x I,\qquad
Q_x=\tfrac12\sum_s a_x(s)ss^{\mathsf T},\qquad
M_{4,x}=\sum_s a_x(s)|s|^2ss^{\mathsf T},
\qquad m_4(x)=\operatorname{tr}M_{4,x}.
\tag{I.3t.1}
$$
Write $\ell>0$ for the largest physical jump length, $\lambda_-=\min_x\lambda_x$, and $\lambda_+=\max_x\lambda_x$. Let angle brackets denote the reversible probability average. If $Q_x=\lambda_x I$ and $\lambda_->0$, every common all-function dimension-four curvature lower bound satisfies
$$
K\le-\frac{36\lambda_-^2}{103\lambda_+\ell^2}.
\tag{I.3t.2}
$$
The same calculation gives the necessary anisotropy bound below. In particular (I.3t.2) excludes a uniform finite bound for shrinking reversible conformal stencils with uniformly positive $\lambda_-$ and bounded $\lambda_+$, even with full contrast between neighboring rows.

*Exact averaged defects.* At each $x$ center the physical lift there and use $q(\xi)=|\xi|^2$, $u(\xi)=|\xi|^4$. Let $\mathcal D_x(f,g)=\Gamma_2(f,g)(x)-Lf(x)Lg(x)/4$. Write $A=|s|^2$, $B=|t|^2$, $c=s\cdot t$ on a first step $s$ from $x$ to $y$ and second step $t$ from $y$. Denote the two-step rate sum with initial weight $\mu_x$ by $\mathbb E_2$. Also set $m_j(x)=\sum_s a_x(s)|s|^j$ and $d_x=\sum_s a_x(s)$. Then $m_2=8\lambda$ and
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_2[B^k]&=\langle d_xm_{2k}(x)\rangle,\\
\mathbb E_2[A^kB]&=\mathbb E_2[AB^k]=\langle m_{2k}m_2\rangle,\\
\mathbb E_2[c^2]&=4\langle\operatorname{tr} Q_x^2\rangle,\qquad
\mathbb E_2[Ac^2]=\mathbb E_2[Bc^2]=2\langle\operatorname{tr}(Q_xM_{4,x})\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3t.3}
$$
The first line uses the incoming-rate identity $\sum_x\mu_x a_{xy}=\mu_y d_y$. For $AB^k$ and $Bc^2$, reverse the first edge by detailed balance. Both displacements then have the same departure vertex $y$, with the first displacement replaced by its negative. This also evaluates $c^2$ by contracting the two second-moment matrices. For $A^kB$ and $Ac^2$, summing the second displacement first gives the needed second moment at $y$. Reversing the first edge moves the first-displacement moment to that same vertex.

In (I.3s.3) the two-step polynomials for $(q,q)$ and $(q,u)$, after removing the terms odd in the second displacement by antipodal symmetry, are respectively
$$
-2AB+B^2+4c^2,\qquad
-3A^2B+AB^2+4Ac^2+B^3+12Bc^2.
$$
The pure $B^2$ and $B^3$ terms cancel the exit terms in the averaged (I.3s.3). Substituting $Lq=m_2$ and $Lu=m_4$, and using (I.3t.3), gives the exact identities
$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\mathcal D_x(q,q)\rangle
 &=4\langle\operatorname{tr} Q_x^2\rangle-\tfrac14\langle m_2^2\rangle
 =4\langle\|A_x\|_F^2\rangle,\\
\langle\mathcal D_x(q,u)\rangle
 &=8\langle\operatorname{tr}(Q_xM_{4,x})\rangle-\tfrac14\langle m_2m_4\rangle
 =\langle6\lambda_xm_4(x)+8\operatorname{tr}(A_xM_{4,x})\rangle .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3t.4}
$$

*Quartic bound and the curvature denominator.* For $(u,u)$ the even two-step polynomial in (I.3s.3) is
$$
-4A^3B+2A^2B^2+8A^2c^2+4AB^3+48ABc^2+B^4+24B^2c^2+16c^4 .
$$
The pure $B^4$ term cancels the exit term. Dropping $-4A^3B$ and using $c^2\le AB$ bounds the remaining polynomial by $8A^3B+66A^2B^2+28AB^3$. Each mixed monomial has averaged sum at most $8\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle$ by (I.3t.3), $m_6\le\ell^2m_4$ and $B^2\le\ell^2B$. Also $m_4^2\le8\lambda_+\ell^2m_4$. Including the base term $(Lu)^2$ and dividing by four gives
$$
\langle\mathcal D_x(u,u)\rangle\le
\frac{8(8+66+28)+8}{4}\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle
=206\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle .
\tag{I.3t.5}
$$

Test at each vertex with $f_x=q-\varepsilon u/\ell^2$, where $0\le\varepsilon<1$. On a one-hop step, $f_x(s)=A(1-\varepsilon A/\ell^2)$, so
$$
0<\tfrac12(1-\varepsilon)^2\langle m_4\rangle
\le\langle\Gamma(f_x)(x)\rangle\le\tfrac12\langle m_4\rangle
\tag{I.3t.6}
$$
whenever the network has a nonzero jump. Each centered polynomial is a separate admissible all-function test using its local lift. For conformal rows, (I.3t.4) and (I.3t.5) give
$$
\langle\mathcal D_x(f_x,f_x)\rangle
\le \frac{-12\varepsilon\lambda_-+206\varepsilon^2\lambda_+}{\ell^2}
      \langle m_4\rangle.
$$
Choose $\varepsilon=6\lambda_-/(206\lambda_+)<1$. The right side is $-36\lambda_-^2\langle m_4\rangle/(206\lambda_+\ell^2)$. The common lower bound implies $K\langle\Gamma(f_x)(x)\rangle\le\langle\mathcal D_x(f_x,f_x)\rangle$. The upper bound on the positive denominator in (I.3t.6) gives (I.3t.2).

For arbitrary rows, write $b=(6-8\alpha)\lambda_-$ if $\|A_x\|_{\rm op}\le\alpha\lambda_x$ with $0\le\alpha<3/4$. The positive semidefinite $M_{4,x}$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(A_xM_{4,x})\ge-\alpha\lambda_x m_4(x)$, so the mixed defect in (I.3t.4) is at least $b\langle m_4\rangle$. If an all-function lower bound is at least $-K_0$ with $K_0\ge0$, the same test at $\varepsilon=b/(206\lambda_+)$ implies
$$
4\langle\|A_x\|_F^2\rangle\ge
\left(\frac{b^2}{206\lambda_+\ell^2}-\frac{K_0}{2}\right)\langle m_4\rangle .
\tag{I.3t.7}
$$
In particular, asymptotically isotropic rows in this operator-norm sense with $\langle m_4\rangle/\ell^2$ bounded below cannot sustain a bounded lower curvature parameter when $\lambda_-$ stays positive and $\lambda_+$ stays bounded. The exact identities apply without this small-anisotropy premise.

*Reversible witness with full contrast.* On an even four-torus $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^4$ with $n\ge12$ and side $\ell_*$, give all coordinate $\pm1$ jumps dimensionless rate $n^2$ and coordinate $\pm2$ jumps rate $n^2 b_x$, where $b_x=1/16$ or $3/16$ according to the parity of the coordinate sum. The length-two jumps preserve parity and the length-one rate is constant, so the rates are symmetric with uniform reversible probability. Each row is antipodal. The actual physical generator of the descriptor-weighted endpoint compiler of Theorem C.6c.7 divides these rates by its time unit $\tau_*$, and the physical jump lengths are $\ell_*/n$ and $2\ell_*/n$. Thus
$$
Q_x=\frac{\ell_*^2}{\tau_*}(1+4b_x)I,\qquad
\lambda_-=\frac{5\ell_*^2}{4\tau_*},\qquad
\lambda_+=\frac{7\ell_*^2}{4\tau_*}.
$$
The two-step lift is consistent since its coordinate radius is at most four. The rates and node probabilities are rational in the compiler's units, and its period $n^{-4}$ times the maximal dimensionless exit is at most $(19/2)n^{-2}<1/8$. This realizes the same generator on the paid source clock. At neighboring vertices the covariance and the relative length-one to length-two rates change by fixed factors. The exact bound (I.3t.2) gives $K\le-225 n^2/(2884\tau_*)$ in physical time. This example supplies the curvature obstruction on the actual endpoint generator. The remaining stress, continuum and cosmological comparison maps require their own inputs. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3u"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3u-dimension-four-obstruction-with-reversible-drift"></a>**Proposition I.3u (Dimension-Four Obstruction with Reversible Drift).** Use a finite reversible jump network on a flat physical four-torus with the consistent two-hop lifts of Proposition I.3s. The rows may have nonzero displacement means and need not be antipodal. Use $Q_x,\lambda_x,A_x,M_{4,x},m_4(x),\ell$ and the averaging conventions of Proposition I.3t. Suppose $\lambda_+=\max_x\lambda_x>0$. Define
$$
v_3(x)=\sum_s a_x(s)|s|^2s,\qquad T_3(x)=\sum_s a_x(s)s^{\otimes3}.
$$
For the same vertex-centered radial polynomials $q$ and $u$, the exact averaged defects and a quartic upper bound are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\mathcal D_x(q,q)\rangle&=4\langle\|A_x\|_F^2\rangle,\\
\langle\mathcal D_x(q,u)\rangle
&=\left\langle
6\lambda_xm_4(x)+8\operatorname{tr}(A_xM_{4,x})
-|v_3(x)|^2-2\|T_3(x)\|_F^2
\right\rangle,\\
\langle\mathcal D_x(u,u)\rangle&\le398\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3u.1}
$$
When $Q_x=\lambda_x I$ and $\lambda_-=\min_x\lambda_x>0$, suppose that the paired submeasure with rates $\min\{a_x(s),a_x(-s)\}$ retains at least a fixed fraction $\eta>0$ of each row's fourth moment. Here an absent displacement has rate zero. Then every common exact all-function dimension-four lower bound satisfies
$$
K\le-\frac{36\eta^2\lambda_-^2}{199\lambda_+\ell^2}.
\tag{I.3u.2}
$$
In place of the pairing condition, one can use the quantitative least-squares residual test below. The bound can hold even if the norms of the row means diverge as the maximum jump length shrinks.

*Odd terms after detailed balance.* Keep $A=|s|^2$, $B=|t|^2$, $c=s\cdot t$ for successive steps, and $\mathbb E_2$ for the averaged two-step rate sum. Reversing the first edge turns that sum into a same-row sum over two independent outgoing steps, with its first displacement negated. The remaining same-row sum is symmetric under interchange of these steps. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_2[A^iB^j c^k]=\mathbb E_2[A^jB^i c^k]
\tag{I.3u.3}
$$
for nonnegative integers $i,j,k$. For odd $k$, each sum has the negative of the sign of its same-row outgoing product. The identities (I.3t.3) for the even moment sums need no antipodal hypothesis.

The pointwise polarization (I.3s.3) has the same even parts as in Proposition I.3t. Its odd parts for $(q,q)$ and $(q,u)$ are respectively
$$
-4Ac+4Bc,\qquad
-6A^2c+4ABc+6B^2c+8c^3 .
$$
This follows by expanding the first-step factors $B-A+2c$ for $q$ and $(A+B+2c)^2-2A^2$ for $u$, then subtracting the first-step product. Equation (I.3u.3) cancels the first odd polynomial and the terms $-6A^2c+6B^2c$ of the second. The reverse-edge same-row sums give $\mathbb E_2[ABc]=-\langle |v_3|^2\rangle$ and $\mathbb E_2[c^3]=-\langle\|T_3\|_F^2\rangle$. Including the factor $1/4$ in the polarization proves the first two lines of (I.3u.1).

For $(u,u)$ the odd polynomial is
$$
-8A^3c+8A^2Bc+24AB^2c+32Ac^3+8B^3c+32Bc^3 .
$$
By (I.3u.3) its sum is $32\mathbb E_2[A^2Bc]+64\mathbb E_2[Ac^3]$. Pointwise both $|A^2Bc|$ and $|Ac^3|$ are at most $A^{5/2}B^{3/2}\le(A^3B+A^2B^2)/2$. The same even-moment estimate as in (I.3t.5) bounds the latter average by $8\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle$. Including the factor $1/4$, the odd terms contribute at most $192\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle$. Adding the bound $206\lambda_+\ell^2\langle m_4\rangle$ for the even terms proves the last line of (I.3u.1). The base terms and stationary cancellations are the same as in Proposition I.3t because $Lq=m_2$ and $Lu=m_4$ at the center regardless of row mean.

*Residual test and curvature.* For a conformal row define two least-squares residuals
$$
\begin{aligned}
R_0(x)&=\inf_{b\in\mathbb R^4}\sum_s a_x(s)(|s|^2-b\cdot s)^2,\\
R_2(x)&=\inf_{B_0}\sum_s a_x(s)\|s\otimes s-B_0s\|_F^2 ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.3u.4}
$$
where $B_0$ ranges over linear maps from vectors to real $4$ by $4$ matrices. The Gram matrix of the linear displacement features is $2\lambda_x I$. Thus
$$
R_0(x)=m_4(x)-\frac{|v_3(x)|^2}{2\lambda_x},\qquad
R_2(x)=m_4(x)-\frac{\|T_3(x)\|_F^2}{2\lambda_x}.
\tag{I.3u.5}
$$
The mixed defect in (I.3u.1) is therefore $\langle2\lambda R_0+4\lambda R_2\rangle$. For the paired submeasure the even target features are orthogonal to every linear feature, by pairing $s$ and $-s$. Its least-squares residual is its fourth moment for either target. Minimizing over the entire row cannot lower either residual below the infimum over this submeasure. The pairing premise hence gives $R_0,R_2\ge\eta m_4$, and the mixed defect is at least $b\langle m_4\rangle$ for $b=6\eta\lambda_-$. More generally the same proof applies whenever the measured residuals give $\langle2\lambda R_0+4\lambda R_2\rangle\ge b\langle m_4\rangle$ for a fixed $b>0$.

Take $\varepsilon=b/(398\lambda_+)$ and $f_x=q-\varepsilon u/\ell^2$. One can take $b\le6\lambda_+$ since both residuals are at most $m_4$, so $0<\varepsilon<1$. The first line of (I.3u.1) vanishes on conformal rows. The tested average curvature defect is at most $-b^2\langle m_4\rangle/(398\lambda_+\ell^2)$. As in (I.3t.6), its positive averaged carré du champ lies between $(1-\varepsilon)^2\langle m_4\rangle/2$ and $\langle m_4\rangle/2$. Testing the common all-function bound with a separately centered $f_x$ at every vertex and averaging gives
$$
K\le-\frac{b^2}{199\lambda_+\ell^2}.
\tag{I.3u.6}
$$
This gives (I.3u.2) and the residual version. For nonconformal rows the first term in (I.3u.1) remains, and the displayed identities give the corresponding necessary anisotropy inequality.

*Paid reversible example with diverging row drift.* On an even torus of side $\ell_*$ and grid spacing $h=\ell_*/n$, $n\ge12$, write $p_x=(-1)^{x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4}$. For each coordinate $j$ use dimensionless rates $n^2(1+p_x/4)$ to $x+e_j$ and $n^2(1-p_x/4)$ to $x-e_j$. Use rates $n^2 b_x$ to each $x\pm2e_j$, where $b_x=1/16$ when $p_x=1$ and $b_x=3/16$ otherwise. Reversibility for uniform mass follows because length-one moves reverse $p_x$ and swap the orientation, while length-two moves preserve $p_x$. The rational descriptor-weighted compiler of Theorem C.6c.7 applies with period $n^{-4}$: the maximal exit-period product is $(19/2)n^{-2}<1/8$, and its clock divides the rates by $\tau_*$. The two-step lifts have coordinate radius at most four. The physical covariances and the row means are respectively
$$
Q_x=\frac{\ell_*^2}{\tau_*}(1+4b_x)I,\qquad
\sum_s a_x(s)s=\frac{p_x n\ell_*}{2\tau_*}\sum_{j=1}^4 e_j .
$$
The full contrast between the row means is of inverse mesh order. The ratio of the paired to total fourth moment is $(3/2+32b_x)/(2+32b_x)\ge7/8$. With $\ell=2\ell_*/n$, (I.3u.2) gives the exact physical-clock bound $K\le-1575n^2/(50944\tau_*)$. The example uses the same retained paid source generator for the curvature test. The continuum and cosmological maps have their separate gates. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3v"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3v-zero-fourth-moment-residual-and-a-positive-two-dimensional-limit"></a>**Proposition I.3v (Zero Fourth-Moment Residual and a Positive Two-Dimensional Limit).** Use the consistent two-hop physical lifts of Proposition I.3u. Suppose the reversible jump generator has conformal positive covariance at each vertex and $R_2(x)=0$ everywhere, with $R_2$ in (I.3u.4). Assume also a common positive rate $r$ on every directed edge of the symmetric support. Each row then consists of four mutually orthogonal outgoing displacements. For each vertex form the graph on its four outgoing directions whose edges are the pairs lacking a shared second neighbor. The exact pointwise dimension-four curvature is
$$
K_4(x)=r\min\{0,\,2-\lambda_{\max}(\mathsf L_{\mathrm{miss},x})\},
\tag{I.3v.1}
$$
where $\mathsf L_{\mathrm{miss},x}$ is the ordinary unweighted graph Laplacian of this missing-pair graph. In particular $\mathrm{BE}(0,4)$ at $x$ holds exactly when its missing pairs form a matching, including the empty matching. If they do not form a matching, $K_4(x)\le-r$. The rate and covariance assumptions permit an actual paid sequence with $\mathrm{BE}(0,4)$ and a noncollapsed two-dimensional metric and energy limit, as constructed below.

*Rigidity of a zero residual row.* Since the row is finite, $R_2(x)=0$ means a linear map $B_0$ satisfies $s\otimes s=B_0s$ for every retained nonzero displacement $s$. The positive covariance implies that the displacement vectors span $\mathbb R^4$. Choose four independent support vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_4$ and write any other support vector as $s=\sum_j c_jv_j$. Linearity gives $s\otimes s=\sum_j c_jv_j\otimes v_j$. Comparing its coefficients in the tensor basis $v_i\otimes v_j$ yields $c_i c_j=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $c_j^2=c_j$ for each $j$. Thus every nonzero support vector equals one of the four chosen vectors. The vectors $\sqrt{a_x(v_j)}v_j$ form the columns of a square matrix whose product with its transpose is $2\lambda_x I$. They are therefore orthogonal with squared norms $2\lambda_x$. A consistent local lift makes the four distinct outgoing displacements four distinct neighbors. Under a common rate their lengths at a fixed vertex are equal.

There are no triangles: at $x$ a triangle would use two orthogonal displacement vectors $v_i,v_j$, while at $x+v_i$ the two triangle legs $-v_i$ and $v_j-v_i$ have nonzero dot product. A second neighbor shared by the directions $i,j$ is necessarily the fourth vertex of their Euclidean rectangle. Indeed writing its lift $z$ relative to $x$ as $v_i+v_j+w$, the right angles at the two immediate neighbors give $w\perp v_i,v_j$. At $z$ the two incident legs are orthogonal, with inner product $|w|^2$, so $w=0$. This proves uniqueness of the common vertex for a pair. No second neighbor can be shared by three directions, because it would have to equal $v_i+v_j$ and $v_i+v_k$ for distinct $j,k$. These statements use reverse and additive displacements in the same two-hop lift, including on the torus.

*Exact local curvature.* Set $f(x)=0$ and write $m_j=f(x+v_j)$. The four backtracking weights in (I.3r.4) are $r^2$, there are no triangle terms, and each neighbor has three forward two-step routes. The second-sphere terms can be evaluated relative to the case where all those routes end at separate vertices. A single route from direction $i$ then contributes $-r^2m_i^2$. Merging two routes from $i,j$ into their shared second neighbor increases this quadratic expression by $2r^2(m_i-m_j)^2$, directly from the last line of (I.3r.4) with $W_z=2r^2$. In the all-separate case the backtrack term cancels the three forward terms from each neighbor. At $D=4$, $S=r\sum_i m_i$, $P=r\sum_i m_i^2$ and $d_x=4r$. Hence the minimized form is
$$
\mathcal Q_{x,4}(m)
=r^2\left[\left(\sum_i m_i\right)^2-4\sum_i m_i^2
   +2\sum_{\{i,j\}\ \mathrm{shared}}(m_i-m_j)^2\right].
$$
Using $\sum_{i<j}(m_i-m_j)^2=4\sum_i m_i^2-(\sum_i m_i)^2$ gives
$$
\mathcal Q_{x,4}(m)
=r^2\left[4\sum_i m_i^2-\left(\sum_i m_i\right)^2
 -2\sum_{\{i,j\}\ \mathrm{missing}}(m_i-m_j)^2\right].
\tag{I.3v.2}
$$
This form vanishes on constants. On the orthogonal complement of constants its smallest eigenvalue divided by $2r$ is $r(2-\lambda_{\max}(\mathsf L_{\mathrm{miss},x}))$. Because the latter is nonpositive whenever there is any missing pair and is positive if none are missing, the full-space smallest eigenvalue must include the constant value zero. Taking the minimum with the constant mode gives (I.3v.1). For a matching the missing Laplacian has largest eigenvalue zero or two. If two missing edges meet, the missing graph contains the three-vertex path, whose largest Laplacian eigenvalue is three. Extending its eigenvector by zero on the fourth vertex and adding the other nonnegative edge forms gives $\lambda_{\max}\ge3$. This proves the asserted exact sign test and the negative gap. In particular when $r$ diverges, any fixed finite lower curvature bound forces a matching at every vertex at sufficiently fine stages.

*Paid positive example and its limits.* Fix $\ell_*>0$, set $h=\ell_*/n$ for even $n\ge12$, and work first on the physical two-torus of side $\ell_*$. Embed the cycle of length $2n$ by the successive lifted vertices
$$
(jh,jh),\quad ((j+1)h,jh),\quad ((j+1)h,(j+1)h),
\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z ,
$$
where the last vertex of one pair starts the next. Take the product of two such cycles in the two disjoint coordinate planes of the four-torus. Every vertex has four mutually orthogonal steps of length $h$, one signed step in each ambient coordinate. Give all edges the dimensionless rate $n^2$. The uniform vertex law is reversible, the physical generator is $L_n/\tau_*$, and every row has physical covariance $Q_x=(\ell_*^2/(2\tau_*))I_4$. Its $R_2(x)$ is zero, since the four step tensors prescribe a linear map on the displacement basis. The two directions of the same cycle factor have no shared second neighbor because that cycle has length greater than four. Directions from different factors always complete a rectangle. Thus the missing pairs are a matching of size two, and (I.3v.1) gives exact $K_4(x)=0$ everywhere.

This is a source of Theorem C.6c.7 with integer coordinate edge descriptors $\pm e_j$, positive rational rates $n^2$, uniform node probability $(2n)^{-2}$ and period $n^{-4}$. Its exit-period product is $4n^{-2}<1/8$, and the descriptor length is $h$. Each supported two-hop lift is consistent since $4h<\ell_*$. The compiler uses the graph's actual descriptor path metric and clock. In particular the metric is not the restriction of the ambient four-torus distance. Its transfer logarithm yields the physical generator just used in the all-function test.

Write each cycle coordinate as its arc-length parameter $t$ of period $2\ell_*$. In these coordinates the discrete path metric is the restriction of the sum of the two circular distances. The grids have Hausdorff error at most $h$ in this metric, and their uniform node laws converge to normalized Haar measure. For $h\le R\le\ell_*/2$, the number of mesh points in a ball of radius $R$ is between the cardinalities of an inscribed square of coordinate radius $R/2$ and a circumscribed square of coordinate radius $R$, so the normalized mass is between fixed positive multiples of $(R/\ell_*)^2$, independent of $n$. Thus the measured metric limit has two-dimensional noncollapse and fails the four-dimensional scaling of (I.3h.1).

The physical graph forms have a quadratic Mosco limit on the same arc-length parameter torus. In discrete normalized Fourier coordinates their eigenvalues for $-L_n/\tau_*$ are
$$
\frac{4n^2}{\tau_*}
\left[\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k_1}{2n}\right)+
      \sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k_2}{2n}\right)\right],
\qquad k_i\in\mathbb Z/(2n)\mathbb Z .
\tag{I.3v.3}
$$
Choose frequency representatives $-n,\ldots,n-1$ and use the isometric embedding into the corresponding continuum trigonometric modes with normalized Haar measure. For each fixed frequency the eigenvalue tends to $\pi^2(k_1^2+k_2^2)/\tau_*$. For the lower bound under weak $L^2$ convergence, first restrict the nonnegative energy sum to finitely many fixed modes, pass to their limiting coefficients and eigenvalues, then exhaust all modes. For the recovery sequence truncate the continuum Fourier series to these frequency boxes. Its $L^2$ tail tends to zero and its energies converge by dominated convergence on the weighted square sum, since $\sin^2 z\le z^2$. For infinite limiting energy the recovery inequality is automatic. This proves Mosco convergence to the form $(\ell_*^2/\tau_*)\int(|\partial_{t_1}f|^2+|\partial_{t_2}f|^2)\,d\mu$.

The last form is the quadratic Riemannian energy in the arc-length coordinates. The actual path metric is their $\ell^1$ product, whose local dual norm is $\ell^\infty$, so that quadratic form is not its Cheeger energy. Thus the example passes the exact finite curvature test, while its capacity-volume exponent and metric-energy identification do not pass the four-dimensional bridge. The curvature test alone supplies neither. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3w"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3w-global-matching-rigidity-and-the-capacity-volume-obstruction"></a>**Proposition I.3w (Global Matching Rigidity and the Capacity-Volume Obstruction).** Use the equal-rate reversible conformal zero-residual class of Proposition I.3v. Suppose the network is connected and its four incident edges at every vertex have consistent undirected labels $1,\ldots,4$, one edge of each label. Require that each geometric rectangle has the same labels on its opposite sides. This holds in particular for a globally axis-aligned physical embedding, with each label the unsigned ambient axis of the edge. Give each edge its positive physical length and use the corresponding shortest-path metric. If the exact all-function dimension-four curvature lower bound is greater than $-r$, where $r$ is the common physical jump rate, then the missing-pair graph is one fixed matching throughout the network. The measured network cannot have four-dimensional noncollapse over an unbounded ratio of retained scales on a sequence of such stages.

More precisely, at each such stage the network is a length-preserving quotient in the following sense. There is a product of at most two weighted cycles and at most four two-point factors, with the sum of their factor metrics, and a surjective map to the network that maps each metric ball onto the metric ball of the same radius centered at its image. The factors and lengths are induced by its actual labeled moves. Every ball of radius $R$ in the network can consequently be covered by at most
$$
16\left(1+8R/\rho\right)^2
\tag{I.3w.1}
$$
balls of radius $\rho$ for $0<\rho\le R$. No global lower bound on the edge lengths is required for the cover.

*Labeled moves and the invariant matching.* The move $T_i$ taking a vertex along its label-$i$ edge is a fixed-point-free involution. For $i\ne j$ a shared second neighbor is necessarily the vertex of the Euclidean rectangle of Proposition I.3v. Because opposite labels agree, the pair is shared at $x$ exactly when
$$
T_iT_j x=T_jT_i x .
\tag{I.3w.2}
$$
Conversely this equality gives a shared second neighbor because the two first neighbors differ and the support has no triangles. The shared condition at $T_i x$ is $T_iT_jT_i x=T_jT_iT_i x=T_jx$. Applying $T_i$ to both sides gives exactly the shared condition at $x$, and the calculation is reversible. Exchanging $i$ and $j$ gives the same equivalence at $T_jx$. Thus each of the shared and missing conditions persists under either of its two labels.

By (I.3v.1) the curvature hypothesis forces the missing-pair graph at every vertex to be a matching. Suppose $\{i,j\}$ is missing at $x$ and $k$ is different from $i,j$. Then $\{i,k\}$ and $\{j,k\}$ are shared at $x$ and at both $T_i x,T_j x$, because the missing pair persists at those vertices. If $\{i,j\}$ were shared at $T_kx$, the shared equalities would give
$$
T_kT_iT_jx
=T_iT_kT_jx
=T_iT_jT_kx
=T_jT_iT_kx
=T_jT_kT_ix
=T_kT_jT_ix .
\tag{I.3w.3}
$$
The first equality uses the pair $\{i,k\}$ at $T_jx$, the middle swap uses the assumed shared pair at $T_kx$, and the last equality uses $\{j,k\}$ at $T_ix$. The remaining swaps use the pairs at $x$. Since $T_k$ is injective this contradicts the missing pair at $x$. Thus the same missing pair persists across every label. Connectedness shows that any missing pair is missing everywhere, and all the remaining pairs are shared everywhere.

*Actual factor lengths and ball quotient.* Partition the four labels into the two-element blocks of the fixed missing matching and its remaining singleton labels. Moves from distinct blocks commute on every vertex. Fix a base vertex $x_0$. For each block let its factor be the orbit of $x_0$ under just that block's moves, with its corresponding labeled edges. A singleton gives a two-point factor. A two-label factor is a finite connected graph with exactly one distinct edge of each of its two labels at every vertex. It is an alternating even cycle. Its length metric uses the actual lengths of its edges in the original physical network.

For a tuple of factor vertices choose for each a word of its block moves taking $x_0$ to that vertex. Apply the product of these words to $x_0$ to define the map to the network. It is independent of the chosen words: for a change in one block, commute all other blocks to its left and then use equality of the endpoints at $x_0$. Every network vertex is an endpoint of a word in all four labels, and commuting across blocks regroups that word to show surjectivity. The map sends each labeled factor edge to a network edge of the same length. Indeed moving that edge across any generator of a different block gives its opposite side in a shared Euclidean rectangle, so the length is preserved under transport by any word in the other blocks. It follows that paths in the product map to paths of the same length. Conversely every network path lifts from any chosen factor tuple over its starting point by using its sequence of labels in the product. Each edge has the same length there, and the lifted endpoint maps to the original endpoint. This proves the ball statement, including shortest-path distances and any periodic identifications. No injectivity of the product map is needed.

In a weighted cycle, the vertices of any metric ball of radius $R$ lie on the two arcs of length $R$ in the associated metric circle. The same is true when the arcs overlap, and if the circle has circumference at most $2R$ they cover it. Each arc can be divided into at most $1+4R/\rho$ subarcs of length at most $\rho/4$. For each nonempty subarc choose a vertex, so every vertex in the subarc is at cycle distance at most $\rho/4$ from that center. For each of the at most two cycle factors this gives at most $2(1+4R/\rho)$ choices. In singleton factors simply use all the vertices, with at most $2^{4-2j}$ choices when there are $j$ cycle factors. A product ball projects into the radius-$R$ ball of each factor. The product of the chosen centers covers it by balls of radius at most $j\rho/4\le\rho$, since the singleton coordinates match exactly. The resulting number is at most $2^{4-j}(1+4R/\rho)^j$ with $j\le2$, bounded by (I.3w.1). The ball quotient carries the cover to the network. This proof uses physical edge lengths, rather than graph distance or a chosen coordinate volume.

*Four-dimensional capacity-volume exclusion.* Suppose a sequence in this class has $r_n\to\infty$ in the fixed physical clock and a common finite exact curvature lower bound. Proposition I.3v forces the matching condition at every vertex for all sufficiently fine stages, so the same covering estimate holds at each of those stages. Suppose also that its capacity measure satisfies the uniform bounds
$$
v_-s^4\le m_n(B_s(x))\le v_+s^4
\tag{I.3w.4}
$$
on every retained vertex and retained local scale, with fixed $v_-,v_+>0$. Pick two retained scales $\rho\le R$ on the same stage. The cover yields
$$
v_-R^4
\le 16 v_+(1+8R/\rho)^2\rho^4
\le1296 v_+ R^2\rho^2.
\tag{I.3w.5}
$$
Thus $R/\rho\le36\sqrt{v_+/v_-}$. Any scale-bridge family with retained local scale ratios diverging violates this inequality. In particular the globally axis-aligned, connected, equal-rate zero-residual class cannot meet both exact finite curvature and four-dimensional capacity-volume noncollapse of Definition I.3h on an expanding local scale window. The argument permits arbitrary periodic quotients and physical cycle lengths. It does not assume that an available quotient has a continuum limit. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3x"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3x-intrinsic-axis-transport-and-stable-global-volume-obstruction"></a>**Proposition I.3x (Intrinsic Axis Transport and Stable Global Volume Obstruction).** Use a connected finite jump network on the flat physical four-torus with the consistent two-hop lifts of Proposition I.3v. Suppose that every row has positive conformal covariance and zero fourth-moment tensor residual $R_2(x)$. No global axes or edge labels are supplied. Assume the actual rates on the symmetric support lie in $[(1-\delta)r,(1+\delta)r]$ for one physical rate $r>0$ and $0\le\delta\le1/500$. If a common exact all-function dimension-four curvature lower bound exceeds $-r/3$, then every row's four unsigned physical axes are the same throughout the network. The edges have a canonical consistent labeling by those four axes up to one common permutation, and the hypotheses for the global matching and ball-cover proof of Proposition I.3w follow. In the equal-rate case the same conclusion holds under the weaker curvature threshold $K>-r$.

Consequently no shrinking sequence of this class with $r_n\to\infty$ in physical time and a common finite exact dimension-four curvature lower bound can have the four-dimensional capacity-volume law of Definition I.3h on expanding retained local scale windows. This includes initially rotating local frames. The obstruction uses only the unsigned axes forced by the actual rectangles.

*Support rigidity and curvature margin.* The zero-residual linear algebra of Proposition I.3v does not use equal rates. It gives four mutually orthogonal outgoing displacements per vertex, no triangles, at most one shared second neighbor for each pair of outgoing directions, and no second neighbor shared by three directions. Each shared second neighbor completes the corresponding Euclidean rectangle. These facts apply to the actual support even when the rates vary.

At a fixed vertex, freeze all local rates on that support to one for the purpose of computing a comparison quadratic form. If its missing-pair graph is not a matching, it contains a path with two missing edges. Set the corresponding first-neighbor values to $-1,2,-1$ along this path, and the fourth value to zero. Put $f(x)=0$ and choose each second-neighbor value to be twice the average of the first-neighbor values reaching it. These are the minimizing values for the frozen test of (I.3r.4). The chosen first-neighbor vector has squared norm six and sum zero. The two missing edges already contribute $18$ to its missing-pair Laplacian form. Thus (I.3v.2) gives
$$
4\bigl[\Gamma_{2,\mathrm{fr}}(f)(x)-(L_{\mathrm{fr}}f(x))^2/4\bigr]\le-12 .
\tag{I.3x.1}
$$
Use the same test values for the actual generator divided by $r$. Denote its base exit by $d$, its first weighted sum by $S$, and its first weighted squared sum by $P$, as in Proposition I.3r. The dimension-four expression of (I.3r.3) has base term $S^2-dP$. The normalized rates differ from one by at most $\delta$, so
$$
|S|\le4\delta,\qquad |P-6|\le6\delta,\qquad |d-4|\le4\delta.
$$
Consequently the absolute change of the base term from its frozen value is at most $48\delta+40\delta^2$. There are sixteen ordered two-step routes, including the backtracks. Their test brackets $(f(z)-2f(y))^2-f(y)^2$ have absolute value at most $64$, since $|f(z)|\le4$ and $|f(y)|\le2$. The product of their two normalized rates differs from one by at most $2\delta+\delta^2$. Therefore the absolute change of the full expression (I.3x.1) is bounded by
$$
48\delta+40\delta^2+16\cdot64(2\delta+\delta^2)
=2096\delta+1064\delta^2<6
\tag{I.3x.2}
$$
on the stated range. The actual normalized defect is at most $-6/4$ and its positive carré du champ is $P/2\le3(1+\delta)$. Thus the normalized curvature lower bound is at most $-1/[2(1+\delta)]\le-1/3$. Multiplying the generator by $r$ multiplies its curvature parameter by $r$, giving the claimed exclusion at a nonmatching vertex. This local comparison uses no bounds on changes of rates across an edge beyond the displayed common rate interval. In the exact equal-rate case (I.3v.1) gives the stated sharper threshold directly.

*Transport forced by physical rectangles.* The curvature premise now makes the missing-pair graph a matching everywhere. Let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent, and write $s$ for their physical displacement from $x$ to $y$. At $y$ the reverse displacement is $-s$, so the traversed unsigned axis is the same. Of the three other outgoing directions at $x$, at most one fails to share a rectangle with $s$, because the missing pairs form a matching. Each shared rectangle supplies at $y$ the same physical transverse displacement as at $x$, using the equality of opposite sides in the Euclidean lift. Thus at least two further distinct unsigned axes at $x$ occur at $y$. If only two further axes have been obtained, the fourth is their common one-dimensional orthogonal complement together with the traversed axis. It is uniquely the fourth axis at both vertices. Therefore the unordered set of four orthogonal lines is identical across each edge.

The physical tangent axes are compared in the common flat torus coordinates. Reverse and additive displacements in the local lifts make this comparison independent of the chosen period representatives. Connectedness propagates the same four lines to the entire graph. Give them labels $1,\ldots,4$ at any one vertex. The same labels now apply everywhere, each edge has the same label at both ends, and opposite sides of every rectangle have the same label. There is no further labeling ambiguity along a closed path because the labels are assigned to the actual fixed physical lines. No sign coherence is needed.

*Volume consequence.* The proof of Proposition I.3w from its matching hypothesis onward uses only the involutive labeled moves, rectangle length transport and connectedness, so it applies here independently of rate variation. It yields its weighted cycle-factor quotient and the ball cover by at most $16(1+8R/\rho)^2$ radius-$\rho$ balls. If the same capacity measure obeys $v_-s^4\le m(B_s)\le v_+s^4$ on both retained radii $\rho,R$ at every vertex, the cover implies
$$
R/\rho\le36\sqrt{v_+/v_-}.
\tag{I.3x.3}
$$
A fixed common finite lower curvature bound exceeds $-r_n/3$ at all sufficiently fine stages when $r_n\to\infty$. Equation (I.3x.3) then rules out a four-dimensional noncollapse window with diverging retained scale ratio. This conclusion does not presuppose convergence of the network metric or its energy. It excludes this curvature and volume combination before the continuum, stress and observable gates. $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3y"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3y-exact-schur-gap-and-curvature-with-arbitrary-row-clocks"></a>**Proposition I.3y (Exact Schur Gap and Curvature with Arbitrary Row Clocks).** On the reversible flat four-dimensional jump networks of Proposition I.3u with conformal covariance, the exact all-function curvature bound satisfies the averaged Schur-gap inequality below, without a rate contrast or antipodal assumption. On the zero tensor residual subclass with one common physical edge length, the local curvature is given by an exact weighted missing-rectangle matrix for arbitrary positive vertex rates. If this subclass has connected vertex-transitive support and increasing average physical rate, no common finite exact curvature lower bound and four-dimensional capacity-volume law can coexist on expanding retained scale windows.

*The general reversible Schur gap.* At each vertex $x$ use the physical quadratic $q_x(z)=|z-x|^2$ in its two-hop lift. For $z\in S_2(x)$ let $w_{yz}=a_{xy}a_{yz}$ and $W_z=\sum_{y\in S_1(x)}w_{yz}$ as in Proposition I.3r. Set
$$
G_x=\frac14\sum_{z\in S_2(x)}W_z
 \left(q_x(z)-2\frac{\sum_{y\in S_1(x)}w_{yz}q_x(y)}{W_z}\right)^2 .
\tag{I.3y.1}
$$
Let $\widetilde q_x$ keep the value of $q_x$ at $x$ and on the first sphere, and assign its minimizing value from (I.3r.4) at every second-sphere vertex. The completed square in (I.3r.3) gives
$$
\mathcal D_x(\widetilde q_x,\widetilde q_x)
=\mathcal D_x(q_x,q_x)-G_x,\qquad
\Gamma(\widetilde q_x)(x)=\Gamma(q_x)(x)=m_4(x)/2 .
$$
The first identity of (I.3u.1) gives $\langle\mathcal D_x(q_x,q_x)\rangle=0$ for conformal rows, even when their drift and covariance scales vary. Thus any common $\mathrm{BE}(K,4)$ bound satisfies
$$
K\le -\,\frac{2\langle G_x\rangle}{\langle m_4\rangle}.
\tag{I.3y.2}
$$
The positive covariance guarantees the denominator is positive. In particular a uniform lower bound $K\ge-K_0$ with $K_0\ge0$ requires $\langle G_x\rangle\le K_0\langle m_4\rangle/2$. If $K\ge0$, then $G_x=0$ at every vertex with positive reversible mass.

For the zero residual support geometry of Proposition I.3v, (I.3y.1) has two explicit kinds of terms. At an unshared second neighbor reached by $s$ followed by $t$, the two steps are orthogonal at the intermediate vertex. Its contribution to $G_x$ is $a_x(s)a_{x+s}(t)(|t|^2-|s|^2)^2/4$. At a shared second neighbor over directions $i,j$, write $A_i=|s_i|^2$, $A_j=|s_j|^2$ and $y_i=x+s_i$, $y_j=x+s_j$. Conformality and zero residual give $a_x(s_i)A_i=2\lambda_x$, and the same relation at the neighbors. The rectangle weights are $4\lambda_x\lambda_{y_i}/(A_iA_j)$ and $4\lambda_x\lambda_{y_j}/(A_iA_j)$. The shared term is consequently
$$
\frac{\lambda_x(\lambda_{y_i}-\lambda_{y_j})^2}
     {A_iA_j(\lambda_{y_i}+\lambda_{y_j})}(A_i-A_j)^2.
\tag{I.3y.3}
$$
Thus exact nonnegative curvature in this class forces length equality along every unshared two-step turn and equal neighbor covariances at every rectangle with unequal side lengths. The inequality (I.3y.2) quantifies the average condition without a pointwise curvature sign premise.

*Exact matrix on a common physical edge length.* Suppose now that every physical edge has length $h>0$ and the tensor residual is zero. At each $x$ the four displacements are orthogonal by Proposition I.3v. Its four directional rates are all $r_x=2\lambda_x/h^2$, but the row clock $r_x$ may vary arbitrarily. Conversely, these positive scalar row clocks have reversible law proportional to $1/r_x$ on a connected finite support. The supports have no triangles, and the only shared second neighbors are the unique rectangles for their direction pairs.

At $x$ write $y_i$ for its four neighbors and $m_i$ for the test values there relative to $f(x)=0$. In (I.3r.4), first give each of the three forward routes out of each $y_i$ a separate second neighbor. The three forward terms then cancel the corresponding backtrack term, since all the second-step rates from $y_i$ are $r_{y_i}$. The base terms leave
$$
r_x^2\bigl[(\sum_i m_i)^2-4\sum_i m_i^2\bigr].
$$
For a shared pair $\{i,j\}$, the routes have weights $r_xr_{y_i}$ and $r_xr_{y_j}$. Merging their endpoints increases the minimized form by
$$
r_x\,\frac{4r_{y_i}r_{y_j}}{r_{y_i}+r_{y_j}}(m_i-m_j)^2 .
$$
This follows by taking the weighted variance of the two preferred second-neighbor values $2m_i$ and $2m_j$. Write $\mathsf L_{ij}$ for the Laplacian of one edge between coordinates $i,j$ of the four-dimensional first-neighbor vector, and $\mathsf L_{K_4}=\sum_{i<j}\mathsf L_{ij}$. Thus the exact local lower-bound test is
$$
\mathsf M_x(r):=
\sum_{\{i,j\}\ {\rm shared}}
 \frac{4r_{y_i}r_{y_j}}{r_{y_i}+r_{y_j}}\mathsf L_{ij}
 -r_x\mathsf L_{K_4}
 \succeq 2K I.
\tag{I.3y.4}
$$
Indeed (I.3r.4) gives the minimized defect multiplied by four as $r_xm^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M_x(r)m$, while $2P=2r_x\|m\|^2$. Equivalently the optimal local $K_4(x)$ is half the least eigenvalue of this matrix, including its constant null mode. This is a necessary and sufficient test on the supplied actual finite rates, with no comparison to equal rates needed.

*Arbitrary contrast on transitive supports.* The function $H(u,v)=4uv/(u+v)$ is jointly concave on positive pairs. Its Hessian is
$$
-\frac8{(u+v)^3}
\begin{pmatrix}v^2&-uv\\-uv&u^2\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Each $\mathsf L_{ij}$ is positive semidefinite, and the base term of (I.3y.4) is linear in $r_x$. Thus $\mathsf M_x$ is Loewner-concave in the row clocks with the support fixed. A support automorphism permutes vertices and the local coordinate labels, and transports the shared pairs because they are defined by the second-neighbor relation. Therefore any common curvature bound for the actual rate assignment also holds for each assignment transported by a support automorphism. It holds for their average by concavity of (I.3y.4) at every vertex. If the support is vertex-transitive, that average assignment is constant at the arithmetic mean $\bar r$ of the actual vertex clocks. No automorphism of the physical embedding is required, since this step uses only the combinatorial test (I.3y.4) on the same support and its fixed physical edge length.

If a vertex has a nonmatching missing graph, Proposition I.3v gives $K_4(x)\le-\bar r$ for this constant comparison assignment. Hence the original assignment could only have a common lower bound $K\le-\bar r$. On a sequence with $\bar r\to\infty$ in its actual physical clock and a common finite lower bound, the missing graph must therefore be a matching everywhere at sufficiently fine stages, regardless of the contrast between row clocks. The geometric transport in Proposition I.3x from its matching conclusion onward applies independently of the rates. It forces common unsigned physical axes and the ball-cover estimate of Proposition I.3w, which bounds every pair of retained local scales by $R/\rho\le36\sqrt{v_+/v_-}$ under the four-dimensional capacity-volume law. This contradicts an expanding scale window. Neither averaging the clocks nor the constant-clock comparison is used to replace the physical source or its volume law. They establish a necessary inequality for the actual curvature. General nontransitive supports and unequal edge lengths retain the exact tests (I.3y.2) and, where applicable, (I.3y.4). $\square$

<a id="proposition-i3z"></a>

<a id="proposition-i3z-opposite-edge-clock-separation-on-nontransitive-supports"></a>**Proposition I.3z (Opposite-Edge Clock Separation on Nontransitive Supports).** Use the connected flat conformal zero tensor residual class of Proposition I.3y with one common positive physical edge length. The rates $r_x$ may vary arbitrarily across vertices, and no support automorphisms are required. Call an edge weak if it lies in at most one geometric rectangle. If an edge $xy$ lies in none, every common exact all-function dimension-four curvature lower bound satisfies
$$
K\le-2\max\{r_x,r_y\}.
\tag{I.3z.1}
$$
If it lies in exactly one rectangle, write its opposite edge as $zw$ with $x$ adjacent to $z$ and $y$ adjacent to $w$, and put
$$
R_{xy}=\sqrt{\frac{r_zr_w}{r_xr_y}},\qquad r_{xy}=\min\{r_x,r_y\}.
$$
Whenever $R_{xy}<3$, one has
$$
K\le -\,\frac{2(3-R_{xy})}{3(1+R_{xy})}\,r_{xy}.
\tag{I.3z.2}
$$
In particular a rectangle with two weak opposite edges forces $K\le-2r_{\min}/3$, where $r_{\min}$ is the smallest row rate in the network. A common lower bound $K\ge-K_0$ with $K_0\ge0$ requires every weak edge with $r_{xy}>K_0/2$ to have a rectangle and satisfy
$$
R_{xy}\ge \frac{3-\tfrac{3K_0}{2r_{xy}}}
                    {1+\tfrac{3K_0}{2r_{xy}}}.
\tag{I.3z.3}
$$

Suppose a sequence of these networks has $r_{\min}\to\infty$ in physical time and admits a common finite exact curvature lower bound. If all unique-rectangle weak edges satisfy a common upper bound $R_{xy}\le R_0<3$, then every sufficiently fine stage has no weak edges. The intrinsic frame and global volume proofs of Propositions I.3x and I.3w then exclude a four-dimensional capacity-volume law on expanding retained scale windows. This criterion bounds relative geometric means across the particular weak-edge rectangles, while permitting arbitrarily large individual rate contrasts. Alternatively, if every stage with any weak edge has a weak edge with no rectangle or a rectangle with two opposite weak edges, the same exclusion follows without any clock balance assumption.

*Endpoint tests.* The row rates are scalar on the four directions since conformality and zero tensor residual give $a_x(s)|s|^2=2\lambda_x$, and the edge length is common. Thus Proposition I.3y supplies the exact matrix (I.3y.4). Let $i$ be the direction from $x$ to $y$, and choose the first-neighbor test vector
$$
m=e_i-\tfrac14\mathbf 1 .
$$
Its squared norm is $3/4$. Its differences vanish on every pair not involving $i$, and have squared value one on the three pairs involving $i$. Hence (I.3y.4) implies
$$
\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\ {\rm shared}}
  H(r_y,r_{y_j})-3r_x\ge\tfrac32 K,\qquad H(u,v)=\frac{4uv}{u+v}.
\tag{I.3z.4}
$$
The same argument at $y$ uses the reverse direction of the same physical edge. The geometric support result of Proposition I.3v identifies the shared pairs with the actual rectangles containing that edge, independently of rates. With none, (I.3z.4) gives $K\le-2r_x$ and $K\le-2r_y$, proving (I.3z.1). With one rectangle, the two inequalities are
$$
\frac{H(r_y,r_z)}{r_x}\ge 3+\frac{3K}{2r_x},\qquad
\frac{H(r_x,r_w)}{r_y}\ge 3+\frac{3K}{2r_y}.
\tag{I.3z.5}
$$

*Exact product and the clock ratio.* Write $a=r_x$, $b=r_y$, $c=r_z$, and $d=r_w$. The product of the two left sides of (I.3z.5) is
$$
\frac{16cd}{(b+c)(a+d)}
\le \frac{16cd}{(\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd})^2}
=\left(\frac{4R_{xy}}{1+R_{xy}}\right)^2.
\tag{I.3z.6}
$$
The inequality is the arithmetic–geometric mean bound $bd+ac\ge2\sqrt{abcd}$. Set $r_*=r_{xy}$ and $R=R_{xy}$. If $R<3$ and $K$ were greater than the right side of (I.3z.2), then each right side of (I.3z.5) would be strictly greater than
$$
3-\frac{3-R}{1+R}=\frac{4R}{1+R}>0.
$$
This uses $a,b\ge r_*$, and holds also if $K$ is nonnegative. Multiplying gives a contradiction to (I.3z.6), proving (I.3z.2). If $K\ge-K_0$ and $r_*>K_0/2$, then each right side of (I.3z.5) is at least $3-3K_0/(2r_*)>0$. Combining with (I.3z.6) and solving for $R$ gives (I.3z.3). The case of no rectangle has already been excluded by (I.3z.1) under these hypotheses.

If both opposite edges of a rectangle are weak, both have that unique rectangle. Their ratios are reciprocals, so at least one is at most one. The coefficient in (I.3z.2) is then at least $2/3$. This proves the rate-independent consequence for their topology. More generally any persistent weak edge on a fine sequence with bounded lower curvature must have its unique opposite edge nonweak, and (I.3z.3) makes the required opposite-edge geometric mean approach at least three times its own. This is a necessary constraint on actual rates and edge incidence, irrespective of how the vertex clocks were selected.

*Capacity-volume consequence.* At a fixed vertex a direction with at least two missing pairs has at most one shared pair, since there are three other directions. Thus a nonmatching missing graph is equivalent to at least one incident weak edge. The common lower bound and $r_{\min}\to\infty$ exclude every zero-rectangle edge by (I.3z.1). Under $R_{xy}\le R_0<3$, (I.3z.2) likewise excludes every remaining weak edge at sufficiently fine stages. Under the stated alternative topological premise, (I.3z.1) and the opposite-weak-edge consequence give the same conclusion. Then every missing graph is a matching. Intrinsic unsigned axes are forced by the physical rectangle transport of Proposition I.3x, and the ball-cover proof of Proposition I.3w applies with no rate comparison. If the same retained capacity measure obeys the four-dimensional volume bounds on scales $0<\rho\le R$, it gives $R/\rho\le36\sqrt{v_+/v_-}$. Diverging retained scale ratios are therefore impossible. The criterion leaves open nontransitive supports with weak edges whose unique opposite edges are nonweak and sufficiently faster. It makes no replacement of the actual endpoint generator or capacity measure. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i3aa"></a>

<a id="theorem-i3aa-selected-native-stress-and-backreaction-on-one-operational-slab"></a>**Theorem I.3aa (Selected Native Stress and Backreaction on One Operational Slab).** On the supplied native finite interaction class and the fixed four-field material action of Theorem I.3l, there is a sequence of finite source stages carrying a common selected metric, paid propagation and capacity records, actual metric-source and rate instruments, a material event clock, and the finite Neumann reconstruction of the expansion on $D=[1,2]\times\mathbb T^3$. The finite-stage comparison uses a declared capital and formation tariff. The source, moment and elliptic errors converge to zero in the normalized coordinates specified below. The limiting normalized four-dimensional backreaction is strictly positive. The sequence has the direct smooth noncollapsed RCD and graph-form limit stated below.

*One indexed source and its selection.* Write $B_*=\log t+t\cos x/100$. On the retained slab use the candidate metrics $g_B=\ell^2[-dt^2+e^{2B}d\mathbf x^2]$. The positive material coefficient functions $F,V$ are fixed once by the action of Theorem I.3l. The finite candidate bank consists of $B=B_*+\psi(t)Q(t-1,x)$, with $\psi$ a fixed smooth endpoint cutoff, $Q$ in the finite Bernstein–Fourier coefficient grid in the [native source construction](../related/calculation_companions/appendix_i/i3aa-selected-native-source.md), and a uniform sixth-derivative envelope. The bank is centered on the declared material solution. The criterion tests the actual fixed-action equations and the actual consistency-controller force, with certified derivatives and native history residuals. In particular the controller's cancellation of a sampled trajectory residual does not remove that residual from the comparison. The zero coefficient word is a strict witness at sufficiently fine stages. The bank also has nonzero shape-admitted candidates.

The literal finite native inventory at geometry index $k$ uses $R=80\cdot2^k$, $N=8\cdot10^{28}R^3$, $V_0=N^4$ qualified vertices and $E=V_0((2R+1)^4-1)$ directed edges. Put $\rho=R/N$, $\ell=\delta_{\rm prop}/\rho$ at the fixed physical receipt length $\delta_{\rm prop}$, and $\eta=\hbar\kappa/\ell^2$. A scalar grid of dyadic side count $J\mid N$ receives the vertices by the actual spatial cell map. Four material modes per cell each have the full $8^d$-level native encoding. The geometry consumes the same candidate's positive density $\mu=e^{3B}$ and its installed smooth length receipts. A qualified vertex has flagged retained capacity $q_v\ln4$, with $q_v=e^{3B(v)}/27$, so the calibrated capacity masses yield the same measure used in the half-form. Its held clock and material bodies, qualification factors, trained private archives, directed-edge stocks, programs, addresses, pointers and all native padding remain in the one physical census.

At a fixed stage, the initial joint entropy of the native source is
$$
S_0=3V_0\ln8+\sum_v h_2(q_v),
\qquad
\mathcal C_{\rm stage}=E_{\rm initial}
+T_{\rm form}\bigl(m_{\rm total}\ln8-S_0\bigr),
\tag{I.3aa.1}
$$
where $h_2$ is binary entropy and $T_{\rm form}>0$ is the stated formation price. The first term in $S_0$ is the joint entropy of the correlated qualifier outputs. The coherent material preparation and the named controller, clock and auxiliary ready stocks have the prepared states of the construction. All supplied artifacts remain, with zero reusable-return credit in this tariff. A fixed stage freezes the shared inventory envelope, common controller-force envelope, scale and admission tolerances before comparing prices. Each candidate keeps its own physical state, controller coefficients and history within this stage. Refining a price enclosure leaves those data fixed. The least upper endpoint among complete price intervals of width at most $\varepsilon_{\rm price}$ selects a candidate within $\varepsilon_{\rm price}$ of the least actual price among the stage-certified candidates. This follows by comparing its upper endpoint to the upper endpoint of an actual minimizer of that finite set.

For every selected candidate the actual fixed-action scalar equation has the transport residual $\overline E_0$. Its positive material coefficient yields
$$
\|B-B_*\|_\infty
\leq e^6\bigl(\|B(1)-B_*(1)\|_\infty+2\|\overline E_0\|_\infty\bigr).
\tag{I.3aa.2}
$$
Indeed subtract the scalar equations, move the transport term to the left and use the common bounds on the material coefficients and $|B|\leq\log3$. The remaining growth coefficient along characteristics is bounded by $6$, and the coefficient multiplying the residual is at most $2$. The torus has no inflow boundary, so Gronwall gives (I.3aa.2). The common higher-derivative envelope upgrades uniform convergence to $C^2$ convergence. The supplied positive witness and the scalar-grid, geometry and interval dovetail give eventual finite certification with shrinking tolerances. The search tests the actual finite equations and history. It permits arbitrary precision refinement of their exact matrix entries, including the interval arithmetic remainder for time evolution.
