If $n\le1$, $\varphi_n$ decreases from $\varphi_n(0)=1$, so $h_\chi'\ge1$, with equality only when $A_G=0$. If $n>1$, $\varphi_n$ increases on $(0,u_*)$ and decreases afterward, with $u_*=(n-1)/n$ and maximum $M_n=n\,e^{-(n-1)/n}$, and $M_n>1$ because $\log n>1-1/n$ for $n>1$. Hence $\inf h_\chi'=1-A_G(M_n-1)$, attained at $y_*=u_*^{-1/n}$, and only there when $A_G>0$. For $A_G<A_{\mathrm{crit}}$, $h_\chi'>0$; for $A_G=A_{\mathrm{crit}}$, $h_\chi'\ge0$ with a single zero, so $h_\chi$ is still strictly increasing; for $A_G>A_{\mathrm{crit}}$, $h_\chi'<0$ near $y_*$ while $h_\chi'\to1+A_G>0$ as $y\downarrow0$, so $h_\chi$ is not monotone. Evaluating (I.13c.5.2) at $n=3/2$ gives the displayed value.

Item 2. Since $y\le h_\chi(y)\le(1+A_G)y$ and $h_\chi$ is continuous and strictly increasing, $h_\chi$ is a bijection of $(0,\infty)$, and $k_\chi$ is continuous and strictly increasing with $x/(1+A_G)\le k_\chi(x)\le x$. Integration gives (I.13c.5.3). As $F'=k_\chi$ is strictly increasing, $F$ is strictly convex and strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$; for $\xi\ne\xi'$ and $0<t<1$, $|t\xi+(1-t)\xi'|\le t|\xi|+(1-t)|\xi'|$, with strict inequality when $|\xi|=|\xi'|$, so $\mathcal F$ is strictly convex. Its gradient $\nabla_\xi\mathcal F(\xi)=\mu(|\xi|/a_\chi)\xi$ tends to zero as $\xi\to0$ because $k_\chi(x)\le x$, so $\mathcal F\in C^1(\mathbb R^3)$. For $x=h_\chi(y)$, $\mu(x)=k_\chi(x)/x=y/h_\chi(y)=1/\nu_\chi(y)$, and the limits follow from $\nu_\chi(y)\to1$ as $y\to\infty$ and $\nu_\chi(y)\to1+A_G$ as $y\downarrow0$. The Euler-Lagrange equation is the computation of Proposition I.5b with $g_\Lambda$ replaced by $a_\chi$. With $p=2$, the bounds (I.13c.5.3) and $|\nabla_\xi\mathcal F(\xi)|\le|\xi|$ supply the growth hypotheses of Theorem I.6.

Item 3. With $y=g_N/a_\chi$ and $|\nabla\Phi|=a_\chi h_\chi(y)$, item 2 gives $\mu(h_\chi(y))\,a_\chi h_\chi(y)=a_\chi y=g_N$. Both fields are radial and outward, so $\mu(|\nabla\Phi|/a_\chi)\nabla\Phi=\nabla\Phi_b$, whose divergence is $4\pi G\rho_b$ by Gauss's law; (I.13c.5.5) is $h_\chi(y)=y\,\nu_\chi(y)$. In an exterior region $M_b$ is constant and $y^{-n}=(a_\chi R^2/(GM_b))^n=(R/L_0)^{2n}$, which gives Equation I.4 with the stated parameters for every $M_b$. For the sheet, planar symmetry and the flux jump $4\pi G\Sigma_b$ across the sheet give $\mu(|\Phi'|/a_\chi)\Phi'=2\pi G\Sigma_b\operatorname{sgn}z$, and the same inversion gives the planar field. There $\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=(a_\chi/(2\pi G\Sigma_b))^n$ equals $1$ exactly at $\Sigma_\times$, and $L_0(M_b)^2=GM_b/a_\chi=M_b/(2\pi\Sigma_\times)$.

Item 4. Since $\nabla_\xi\mathcal F(\xi)=\mu(|\xi|/a_\chi)\xi$, one has $\partial_i[\mathcal F(\nabla\Phi)]=\mu\,\partial_k\Phi\,\partial_i\partial_k\Phi$. Differentiating (I.13c.5.7), this term cancels the term $\mu\,\partial_j\Phi\,\partial_j\partial_i\Phi$ from the product rule, leaving $\partial_jT^{\Phi}_{ij}=(4\pi G)^{-1}\partial_i\Phi\,\partial_j(\mu\,\partial_j\Phi)=\rho_b\,\partial_i\Phi$. For compactly supported $\rho_b$, the divergence theorem on a ball of radius $r$ containing the support gives $\int\rho_b\,\partial_i\Phi\,d^3x=\oint_{|x|=r}T^{\Phi}_{ij}n_j\,dS$, which tends to zero along the stated sequence.

Item 5. By Gauss's law, a flux-normalized spherical solution obeys $F'(|\nabla\Phi|/a_\chi)=g_N/a_\chi$, because $\mu(x)x=F'(x)$. Requiring (I.13c.5.5) for all spherical sources gives $F'(h_\chi(y))=y$ for every $y>0$, since every $y>0$ is attained by some source and radius. For $A_G>A_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)$, item 1 shows that the continuous function $h_\chi$ is not monotone and hence not injective, so $F'$ would take two values at one point.

Item 6. Let $\mathcal T$ satisfy $\mathcal T[\lambda\rho]=\lambda\mathcal T[\rho]$ for $\lambda>0$, and suppose a spherical source $\rho$ of mass $M_b$ and its rescaling $\lambda\rho$, $\lambda\ne1$, both obey the exterior law at an exterior radius $R$. Homogeneity gives $|\mathcal T[\lambda\rho](R)|=\lambda|\mathcal T[\rho](R)|$; inserting the exterior law for both sources and dividing by $\lambda GM_b/R^2$ gives $e^{-(R/L_0(\lambda M_b))^{2n}}=e^{-(R/L_0(M_b))^{2n}}$ when $A_G>0$, hence $L_0(\lambda M_b)=L_0(M_b)$, contradicting $L_0(\lambda M_b)=\sqrt\lambda\,L_0(M_b)$. The response of Theorem I.13h is linear in its source coordinate, $o_y=Ry$. ∎

<a id="theorem-i13c6-exactness-and-vacuum-geometry-of-the-spatial-clock-field"></a>**Theorem I.13c.6 (Exactness and Vacuum Geometry of the Spatial-Clock Field).** Fix $a_\chi>0$, $n>0$ and $A_G\ge0$, and let $\nu_\chi$ be (I.13c.5.1), extended by $\nu_\chi(0)=1+A_G$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be connected and open, let $u:=\Phi_b\in C^2(\Omega)$, and define
$$
V_u:=\nu_\chi\!\left(\frac{|\nabla u|}{a_\chi}\right)\nabla u,
\qquad
\mathcal R_u:=\{x\in\Omega:\nabla u(x)\ne0\}.
\tag{I.13c.6.1}
$$
For $A_G>0$, the following statements hold.

1. **Exactness on an arbitrary domain.** The field $V_u$ is $C^1$ on all of $\Omega$. A potential $\Phi\in C^2(\Omega)$ with $\nabla\Phi=V_u$ exists exactly when
$$
d|\nabla u|\wedge du=0\quad\hbox{on }\mathcal R_u,
\qquad
\oint_\gamma V_u\cdot dx=0
\quad\hbox{for every closed piecewise }C^1\hbox{ curve }\gamma\subset\Omega.
\tag{I.13c.6.2}
$$
The differential condition makes $V_u\cdot dx$ closed on all of $\Omega$, including every critical point. The period condition follows on a simply connected domain; more generally, it suffices to check generators of first real homology when such generators are supplied. The potential is unique up to an additive constant.

2. **Local distance foliation.** If $u\in C^3(\Omega)$, the differential condition in (I.13c.6.2) holds near a regular point exactly when, on a sufficiently small neighborhood,
$$
u=f(d),\qquad f'\ne0,
\tag{I.13c.6.3}
$$
where $d$ is signed distance to a regular level-surface patch. The orientation can be chosen with $f'>0$. For a Poisson source, its local density obeys $4\pi G\rho_b=f''(d)+f'(d)\Delta d$; arbitrary smooth surface patches are allowed before harmonicity is imposed.

3. **Complete harmonic classification.** Suppose $u$ is harmonic and nonconstant on $\Omega$. The following four conditions are equivalent: $V_u$ is a gradient on some nonempty open subset of $\Omega$; its curl vanishes on some nonempty open subset; $u$ has throughout $\Omega$ one of the forms
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{plane:}&u=b+c\,e\cdot x,\quad |e|=1,\\[1mm]
\text{cylinder:}&u=b+c\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,\ell)}{R_*}\right),\quad \ell\text{ an affine line},\\[1mm]
\text{sphere:}&u=b+c/|x-x_c|,
\end{array}
\qquad c\ne0;
\tag{I.13c.6.4}
$$
and $V_u$ is a gradient on all of $\Omega$. Here $R_*>0$ is an arbitrary reference length, whose choice is absorbed in $b$. The singular line or point in (I.13c.6.4) is disjoint from $\Omega$. Every nonconstant case has no critical points. A constant $u$ gives $V_u=0$; its spatial clock has no finite regular-point value.

4. **Vacuum-clock slopes.** In the three nonconstant cases, the clock $\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=(a_\chi/|\nabla u|)^n$ is respectively
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{geometry}&|\nabla u|&\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}\\ \hline
\text{plane}&|c|&(a_\chi/|c|)^n\\
\text{cylinder}&|c|/R&(R/L)^n,\quad L=|c|/a_\chi\\
\text{sphere}&|c|/R^2&(R/L)^{2n},\quad L=\sqrt{|c|/a_\chi}
\end{array}
\tag{I.13c.6.5}
$$
Here $R$ is distance to the axis or center. The cylindrical and spherical logarithmic slopes are $n$ and $2n$; the planar clock is constant. At $n=3/2$ the two nonconstant radial exponents are $3/2$ and $3$. The response is $A_G(1-e^{-\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}})$, and the constant planar clock has no Equation-I.4 representation with $m>0$ on an open distance interval.

5. **Compact isolated sources.** Let $\rho_b$ be a nonzero finite nonnegative compactly supported Borel mass measure, let $M_b:=\int d\rho_b>0$, and let $E$ be the unbounded connected component of $\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{supp}\rho_b$. For
$$
u(x)=-G\int\frac{d\rho_b(y)}{|x-y|},\qquad G>0,
$$
the field $V_u$ is a gradient on some nonempty open subset of $E$ exactly when it is a gradient on all of $E$, and exactly when
$$
u(x)=-\frac{GM_b}{|x-x_c|}\quad(x\in E),
\qquad
x_c=\frac1{M_b}\int y\,d\rho_b(y)\notin E.
\tag{I.13c.6.6}
$$
The center is unique. Equivalently, all exterior multipoles of degree at least two, computed about this barycenter, vanish. Any nonzero centered higher multipole obstructs exact scalar enhancement on every nonempty exterior open set. A translated monopole can have a nonzero dipole about another origin. The conclusion fixes the exterior potential: smooth nonradial nonnegative densities can have this same monopole exterior, and $x_c$ can lie in a bounded vacuum cavity.

6. **Identification with the fixed action.** Suppose additionally $A_G\le A_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)$, and extend the response of Theorem I.13c.5 by $\mu(0)=1/(1+A_G)$. Whenever $V_u=\nabla\Phi$, one has
$$
\mu\!\left(\frac{|\nabla\Phi|}{a_\chi}\right)\nabla\Phi=\nabla u,
\qquad
\nabla\cdot\left[\mu\!\left(\frac{|\nabla\Phi|}{a_\chi}\right)\nabla\Phi\right]=\Delta u.
\tag{I.13c.6.7}
$$
Thus on every bounded Lipschitz $D\Subset\Omega$, $\Phi$ is the unique action solution with source $\rho_b=\Delta u/(4\pi G)$ and its own Dirichlet trace. Its equality with a specified action solution for that source is equivalent to equality of their Dirichlet traces. For (I.13c.6.6), the normalized exterior primitive is
$$
\Phi_M(R)=-\int_R^\infty\frac{GM_b}{t^2}\,
\nu_\chi\!\left(\frac{GM_b}{a_\chi t^2}\right)dt,
\qquad R=|x-x_c|.
\tag{I.13c.6.8}
$$
It tends to zero at infinity and solves the action's vacuum equation on $E$. Identifying it with the exterior field generated by a particular interior action problem requires matching that problem's actual boundary data; the Newtonian monopole exterior alone does not supply those data.

For $A_G=0$, $V_u=\nabla u$ for every $u$ and every domain, so exactness places no restriction on source geometry. The clock remains the registered function of $|\nabla u|$, while its response vanishes identically. The action statement in item 6 reduces to the Poisson equation with $\mu=1$.

*Proof.* Item 1. Define
$$
T(p)=(1+A_G)p-A_Ge^{-(a_\chi/|p|)^n}p\quad(p\ne0),\qquad T(0)=0.
$$
Every derivative of the exponential correction near $p=0$ is bounded by a finite sum of powers of $|p|^{-1}$ times $e^{-(a_\chi/|p|)^n}$, which tends to zero faster than any positive power of $|p|$. Extension by zero therefore gives a smooth function flat at zero. Hence $T\in C^\infty$, $DT(0)=(1+A_G)I$, and $V_u=T(\nabla u)\in C^1$. At regular points,
$$
\nu_\chi'(y)=-A_Gn\,y^{-n-1}e^{-y^{-n}}<0,
\qquad
\nabla\times V_u=
\frac{\nu_\chi'(|\nabla u|/a_\chi)}{a_\chi}
\nabla|\nabla u|\times\nabla u.
\tag{I.13c.6.9}
$$
At a critical point, $DV_u=(1+A_G)D^2u$ is symmetric. This proves the closedness assertion even when the critical set has interior. A gradient has zero periods. Conversely, integrate $V_u\cdot dx$ from a fixed base point along a piecewise $C^1$ path. Connected open subsets of Euclidean space are polygonally connected, and zero periods make the integral independent of the chosen path. Integration along short segments gives $\nabla\Phi=V_u$, hence $\Phi\in C^2$. The difference of two primitives has zero gradient and is constant. For a closed one-form, Stokes' theorem makes the integral invariant under path homotopy and dependent only on real homology, giving the stated reductions. The regular-point condition alone need not make $|\nabla u|$ a single-valued function of $u$ across disconnected level sets; the period condition retains the global information.

Item 2. At a regular point, take submersion coordinates $(t,z_1,z_2)$ with $t=u$ and connected product slices in $z$. The differential condition says that the $z$ derivatives of $|\nabla u|$ vanish, so $|\nabla u|=q(u)$ locally for a positive $C^2$ function $q$. Set
$$
d(x)=\int_{u(x_0)}^{u(x)}\frac{dt}{q(t)}.
$$
Then $|\nabla d|=1$ and $D^2d\nabla d=0$. The integral curves of $\nabla d$ are straight unit-speed lines normal to the level surface $d=0$. After shrinking the surface patch and neighborhood, the normal map $(z,r)\mapsto X(z)+rN(z)$ is a diffeomorphism and $d=r$ is signed distance. Inverting the scalar integral gives $u=f(d)$ with $f'=q(f)>0$. Conversely, $u=f(d)$ gives $\nabla u=f'(d)\nabla d$ and $|\nabla u|=|f'(d)|$, whose gradients are parallel. Taking the Laplacian gives the density formula. A local enhanced primitive is $W(d)$ with $W'(r)=\nu_\chi(|f'(r)|/a_\chi)f'(r)$.

Item 3. First work near a regular point where the curl vanishes. Harmonicity gives smoothness, and item 2 gives $u=f(d)$. On the level patch $d=0$, use the shape operator $S=DN$ with $N=\nabla d$; an outward-oriented sphere has positive principal curvatures $\kappa_1,\kappa_2$. The normal map multiplies a principal tangent direction by $1+r\kappa_i$, while its normal derivative is multiplied by $\kappa_i$, so
$$
\Delta d(z,r)=\frac{\kappa_1(z)}{1+r\kappa_1(z)}+
\frac{\kappa_2(z)}{1+r\kappa_2(z)}.
\tag{I.13c.6.10}
$$
Since $0=\Delta u=f''(r)+f'(r)\Delta d(z,r)$ and $f'\ne0$, this rational function is independent of $z$ for all sufficiently small $r$. Its value and derivative at $r=0$ make $\kappa_1+\kappa_2$ and $\kappa_1^2+\kappa_2^2$ constant. Hence $\kappa_1\kappa_2$ and the unordered pair of principal curvatures are constant on the patch.

If both curvatures equal $\kappa$, then $\kappa=0$ gives a constant normal and a plane; for $\kappa\ne0$, the tangent derivatives of $X-N/\kappa$ vanish, giving a sphere about a fixed center. If they are distinct, choose local orthonormal principal fields $e_1,e_2$. The two tangent components of the Codazzi identity
$$
(\nabla^\Sigma_{e_1}S)e_2=(\nabla^\Sigma_{e_2}S)e_1
$$
are $(\kappa_2-\kappa_1)\langle\nabla^\Sigma_{e_1}e_2,e_1\rangle e_1$ and $(\kappa_1-\kappa_2)\langle\nabla^\Sigma_{e_2}e_1,e_2\rangle e_2$. Thus both connection coefficients vanish. The frame is parallel, its intrinsic curvature is zero, and the Gauss equation gives $\kappa_1\kappa_2=0$. Write $\kappa_1=\kappa\ne0$, $\kappa_2=0$. All ambient derivatives of $e_2$ along the surface vanish, since both their tangent components and the second-fundamental-form entries involving $e_2$ vanish. Consequently $e_2$ is a fixed direction. The map $X-N/\kappa$ has derivative zero along $e_1$ and $e_2$ along $e_2$; its image lies on a fixed affine line parallel to $e_2$. Every surface point has distance $1/|\kappa|$ from that line, giving a circular cylinder. Parallel patches share the same plane normal, axis or center. The harmonic equation in their natural coordinate becomes respectively $f''=0$, $f''+R^{-1}f'=0$ or $f''+2R^{-1}f'=0$, whose nonconstant solutions are (I.13c.6.4).

Now suppose the curl vanishes on a nonempty open subset of the connected harmonic domain. That subset contains a regular point: otherwise harmonic analyticity would make $u$ constant throughout $\Omega$. The local model just obtained is harmonic everywhere except for its line or point singularity. Removing an affine line or a point from a connected open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ leaves it connected. To see this, cover a polygonal path by a finite chain of balls lying in the domain with nonempty open successive overlaps; each ball with that line or point removed is path connected, and each overlap retains a point. Connect through those retained overlaps. Harmonic uniqueness of continuation now identifies $u$ with its model on all of $\Omega$ away from the singular set. If any point of that set belonged to $\Omega$, the model would diverge on approach to it while $u$ stayed bounded on a compact neighborhood. Thus the singular set is disjoint from $\Omega$, and (I.13c.6.4) holds throughout.

Each model has nonzero gradient and a global scalar coordinate $s=e\cdot x$, $s=\operatorname{dist}(x,\ell)$ or $s=|x-x_c|$. Writing $u=f(s)$, integration of $W'(s)=\nu_\chi(|f'(s)|/a_\chi)f'(s)$ on its scalar interval supplies a global primitive $W(s)$. This also proves zero periods on domains with nontrivial topology. The implications from a global primitive to a local primitive and then to zero curl complete the equivalences. Constant $u$ is immediate.

Item 4 follows by differentiating the three profiles in (I.13c.6.4) and substituting into $\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=(a_\chi/|\nabla u|)^n$.

Item 5. The Newtonian integral is smooth and harmonic on $E$. Compact support gives, uniformly as $r=|x|\to\infty$,
$$
u(x)=-\frac{GM_b}{r}-G\frac{x\cdot p_b}{r^3}+O(r^{-3}),
\qquad p_b=\int y\,d\rho_b(y).
$$
It is nonconstant. Item 3 therefore applies. An affine function cannot tend uniformly to zero at infinity with this nonzero $1/r$ term; the logarithmic model also cannot do so, and its unbounded singular line would meet $E$, which contains the complement of a sufficiently large ball. The spherical model has additive constant zero and coefficient $-GM_b$. Its center lies outside $E$. Expansion of the shifted monopole gives dipole $M_bx_c$, so $x_c=p_b/M_b$ and the center is unique. The converse is the spherical case of item 3. The convergent exterior spherical-harmonic expansion outside a ball containing the source and barycenter identifies absence of all centered higher multipoles with the monopole there; harmonic continuation extends that identity to $E$.

To verify the interior-density scope, take a radial $\rho_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ that is nonnegative and strictly positive on $B_1(0)$. Choose a nonzero smooth compactly supported function $\psi(x)=\eta(|x|^2)(x_1^2-x_2^2)$ supported in $B_{1/2}(0)$. Its nonzero Laplacian has spherical-harmonic degree two. For sufficiently small nonzero $\varepsilon$,
$$
\rho_\varepsilon=\rho_0+\frac{\varepsilon}{4\pi G}\Delta\psi
$$
is nonnegative, smooth and nonradial. Integration by parts gives $\int\Delta\psi=0$ and $\int x_i\Delta\psi=0$. Its Newtonian potential is $u_0+\varepsilon\psi$: both solve the same Poisson equation and vanish at infinity, so their difference is an entire harmonic function vanishing at infinity. On their common unbounded exterior they therefore have the same monopole potential. A hollow spherical shell separately shows that the barycenter can lie in a bounded vacuum cavity.

Item 6. For $\nabla u\ne0$, put $y=|\nabla u|/a_\chi$. Then $|V_u|/a_\chi=h_\chi(y)$ and Theorem I.13c.5 gives $\mu(h_\chi(y))=1/\nu_\chi(y)$, proving (I.13c.6.7). At a critical point both vector sides vanish. Taking the divergence proves the source equation. On $D\Subset\Omega$, the primitive is $C^2$ on a neighborhood of $\overline D$, hence has a $W^{1,2}$ lifting of its trace; its continuous source belongs to $W^{-1,2}(D)$. Theorem I.6 supplies uniqueness for this actual trace, proving the boundary equivalence. In the monopole case, $1\le\nu_\chi\le1+A_G$ makes (I.13c.6.8) convergent and bounded in magnitude by $(1+A_G)GM_b/R$. Differentiation gives $\nabla\Phi_M=V_u$, and (I.13c.6.7) supplies the vacuum equation. The same uniqueness argument applies to every bounded Lipschitz $D\Subset E$ with matched traces. Finally, $A_G=0$ gives $\nu_\chi=\mu=1$ directly. ∎

The curl and local potential-level criterion used here is the algebraic-field criterion of Brada and Milgrom [1995, equations (5)--(7)], in the nonlinear scalar-action framework of Bekenstein and Milgrom [1984]. The vacuum proof uses the classical Euclidean constant-principal-curvature classification and includes its local derivation and global continuation. Theorem I.13c.6 applies these criteria to the fixed spatial-clock response, with its critical points, global periods, compact-source exterior and action boundary data stated explicitly.

<a id="theorem-i13c7-complete-nonspherical-action-response-and-flux-certificate"></a>**Theorem I.13c.7 (Complete Nonspherical Action Response and Flux Certificate).** Fix the action of Theorem I.13c.5 with $a=a_\chi>0$, $n>0$ and $0\le A_G\le A_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)$, and write $L=1+A_G$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, $f=4\pi G\rho_b\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$, and $g\in H^1(\Omega)$ a lifting of the prescribed Dirichlet trace. Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Psi(j)&=a^2\int_0^{|j|/a}h_\chi(t)\,dt,
& H(j)&=\nu_\chi(|j|/a)j,\quad H(0)=0,\\
\mathscr J_f&=\left\{j\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):
 \int_\Omega j\cdot\nabla v=-\langle f,v\rangle\ \text{for all }v\in H_0^1(\Omega)\right\},
& Z&=\{s\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}s=0\},\\
\mathcal P(w)&=\int_\Omega\mathcal F(\nabla g+\nabla w)+\langle f,w\rangle,
&\mathcal D(j)&=\int_\Omega\Psi(j)-\int_\Omega j\cdot\nabla g.
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13c.7.1}
$$
The divergence in $Z$ is distributional, with no imposed normal-flux boundary condition. The primal energy is the source energy multiplied by $4\pi G$ and expressed relative to the lifting; the pairing is therefore defined for every stated $H^{-1}$ source.

1. The dual density is exactly $\Psi=\mathcal F^*$, with $\nabla\Psi=H$. Both extrema are attained uniquely, and
$$
\Phi_*=g+w_*,\qquad j_* =\nabla\mathcal F(\nabla\Phi_*),\qquad
H(j_*)=\nabla\Phi_*,\qquad
\mathcal P(w_*)+\mathcal D(j_*)=0.
\tag{I.13c.7.2}
$$
Thus $\Phi_*$ is the action solution for every admitted source and boundary datum. For any Newtonian reference $u$ with $\Delta u=f$ and $\nabla u\in L^2$, the exact response is
$$
j_*=\nabla u+S_*,\qquad \operatorname{div}S_*=0,\qquad
\nabla\Phi_*=
\nu_\chi\!\left(\frac{|\nabla u+S_*|}{a}\right)(\nabla u+S_*),
\tag{I.13c.7.3}
$$
where $S_*$ is the unique minimizer of $\mathcal D(\nabla u+S)$ over the entire space $Z$, including its harmonic flux components.

2. Let $P_Z$ be the $L^2$ orthogonal projection onto $Z$. Starting from any $j_0\in\mathscr J_f$, the sequence
$$
j_{r+1}=j_r-\frac1L P_Z[H(j_r)-\nabla g],\qquad
q_r=\nabla g+(I-P_Z)[H(j_r)-\nabla g]
\tag{I.13c.7.4}
$$
remains feasible in flux and produces conservative fields $q_r$ with the required Dirichlet trace. Every step uses the registered pointwise response and a linear Dirichlet Poisson solve. Put
$$
N=\|j_0\|_2,\qquad B=\|\nabla g\|_2,\qquad
D=(1+\sqrt L)N+2B.
$$
For every $r\ge1$,
$$
\mathcal D(j_r)-\mathcal D(j_*)\le\frac{LD^2}{2r},\qquad
\max\{\|H(j_r)-\nabla\Phi_*\|_2,\|q_r-\nabla\Phi_*\|_2\}
\le\frac{LD}{\sqrt r}.
\tag{I.13c.7.5}
$$
The fluxes converge weakly to $j_*$, and both displayed fields converge strongly. These conclusions include the critical amplitude $A_G=A_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)$ when it is finite.

3. For $v-g\in H_0^1$ and $j\in\mathscr J_f$, the computable primal–dual gap is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Gap}(v,j)
&=\mathcal P(v-g)+\mathcal D(j)\\
&=\int_\Omega[\mathcal F(\nabla v)+\Psi(j)-j\cdot\nabla v]\ge0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13c.7.6}
$$
and it certifies
$$
\|\nabla v-\nabla\Phi_*\|_2^2+
\|H(j)-\nabla\Phi_*\|_2^2
\le2L\operatorname{Gap}(v,j).
\tag{I.13c.7.7}
$$
The one-dimensional inverse defining $\mathcal F$ is the same monotone inverse as in Theorem I.13c.5.

4. For a feasible Newtonian reference $j_N=\nabla u$, define
$$
R_N=P_Z[H(j_N)-\nabla g],\qquad r_N=\|R_N\|_2.
\tag{I.13c.7.8}
$$
Then $R_N=0$ if and only if $S_*=0$. This tests the complete boundary and topology conditions, as well as local curl. For every admitted amplitude,
$$
\|H(j_N)-\nabla\Phi_*\|_2\ge r_N,\qquad
\|S_*\|_2\ge\frac{r_N}{L},\qquad
\mathcal D(j_N)-\mathcal D(j_*)\ge\frac{r_N^2}{2L}.
\tag{I.13c.7.9}
$$
For $0<n\le1$, or for $n>1$ with $A_G<A_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)$, set
$$
m_\chi=
\begin{cases}
1,&0<n\le1,\\
1-A_G\bigl[ne^{-(n-1)/n}-1\bigr],&n>1.
\end{cases}
\tag{I.13c.7.10}
$$
Then $m_\chi>0$ and
$$
\begin{gathered}
\|S_*\|_2\le\frac{r_N}{m_\chi},\qquad
\mathcal D(j_N)-\mathcal D(j_*)\le\frac{r_N^2}{2m_\chi},\\
r_N\le\|H(\nabla u)-\nabla\Phi_*\|_2
\le\sqrt{\frac{L}{m_\chi}}\,r_N.
\end{gathered}
\tag{I.13c.7.11}
$$
At the critical endpoint the exact test, lower bounds and convergent construction remain valid. For $A_G=0$ with compatible Newtonian Dirichlet data, the residual and correction vanish and the action response is Newtonian.

*Proof.* Write $k_\chi=h_\chi^{-1}$. Alignment of the vectors in a radial Legendre supremum reduces conjugacy to the one-dimensional inverse-derivative identity: the derivative of $\mathcal F$ in the radial variable is $a k_\chi(|q|/a)$, while that of $\Psi$ is $a h_\chi(|j|/a)$. Thus $\Psi=\mathcal F^*$, $\nabla\Psi=H$, and $H$ and $\nabla\mathcal F$ are inverse maps, including zero. The radial and tangential eigenvalues of $D^2\Psi$ are $h_\chi'(y)$ and $\nu_\chi(y)$. The derivative calculation in Theorem I.13c.5 gives
$$
0\le h_\chi'(y)\le L,\qquad
1\le\nu_\chi(y)\le L,\qquad
\frac{|j|^2}{2}\le\Psi(j)\le\frac{L|j|^2}{2}.
\tag{I.13c.7.12}
$$
The exponential correction is flat at zero, where $D^2\Psi(0)=LI$. Consequently $H$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz and $\Psi$ is strictly convex, even when $h_\chi'$ vanishes at its one critical radius. The strict radial increase of $h_\chi$ proves strict convexity there.

The conjugate $\mathcal F$ is $1/L$-strongly convex. To see this directly, put $j_1=\nabla\mathcal F(q_1)$ and use the trial vector $j_1+(q_2-q_1)/L$ in the conjugate formula for $\mathcal F(q_2)$. The $L$-smooth upper bound for $\Psi$ gives
$$
\mathcal F(q_2)\ge\mathcal F(q_1)+j_1\cdot(q_2-q_1)
+\frac{|q_2-q_1|^2}{2L}.
\tag{I.13c.7.13}
$$
This argument uses no bounded derivative of the inverse map at the critical radius.

Theorem I.13c.5 supplies the primal minimizer; alternatively its quadratic coercivity, the $H^{-1}$ source bound and the direct method give existence, and (I.13c.7.13) gives uniqueness. The zero-boundary Poisson solution of $\Delta u_0=f$ gives a feasible flux $j_0=\nabla u_0$, so $\mathscr J_f$ is nonempty. It is a closed affine subspace with translation space $Z$. The quadratic bounds in (I.13c.7.12) give coercivity and weak lower semicontinuity of $\mathcal D$, hence a minimizer; strict convexity gives uniqueness.

The gradient range $\nabla H_0^1$ is closed in $L^2$ by Poincaré's inequality. Its orthogonal complement is exactly $Z$, by the distributional definition of divergence. The dual Euler equation is

$$
H(j_*)-\nabla g\perp Z,
$$

so $H(j_*)=\nabla g+\nabla w$ for a unique $w\in H_0^1$. Inversion and the feasible divergence identity give the primal weak equation. Its unique solution is $g+w=\Phi_*$. Pointwise Fenchel equality and the weak source pairing prove (I.13c.7.2). Every feasible flux is $\nabla u+S$ for exactly one $S\in Z$, proving (I.13c.7.3). No normal-flux restriction was inserted.

For $v\in L^2$, the projection is $P_Zv=v-\nabla p$, where $p\in H_0^1$ is the unique solution of
$$
\int_\Omega\nabla p\cdot\nabla w=\int_\Omega v\cdot\nabla w
\quad(w\in H_0^1).
\tag{I.13c.7.14}
$$
Thus (I.13c.7.4) has the asserted form. On the feasible affine space the gradient of $\mathcal D$ is

$$
G_r=P_Z[H(j_r)-\nabla g],
$$

with Lipschitz constant $L$. Convexity and the smooth descent inequality give
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D(j_r)-\mathcal D(j_*)&\le\langle G_r,j_r-j_*\rangle,\\
\mathcal D(j_{r+1})&\le\mathcal D(j_r)-\frac{\|G_r\|_2^2}{2L},\\
\mathcal D(j_{r+1})-\mathcal D(j_*)&\le
\frac L2\bigl(\|j_r-j_*\|_2^2-\|j_{r+1}-j_*\|_2^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13c.7.15}
$$
The last line follows by expanding the squared norm in the update. It proves Fejér monotonicity. Summing it and using the nonincreasing objective values gives

$$
\mathcal D(j_r)-\mathcal D(j_*)\le L\|j_0-j_*\|_2^2/(2r).
$$

Moreover $\mathcal D(j_*)\le\mathcal D(j_0)$ and (I.13c.7.12) imply
$$
\|j_*\|_2\le B+\sqrt{B^2+LN^2+2BN}
\le2B+\sqrt L N,
$$
so $\|j_0-j_*\|_2\le D$.

For any convex $L$-smooth density, its Bregman divergence satisfies
$$
D_\Psi(x,y)\ge\frac{|H(x)-H(y)|^2}{2L}.
\tag{I.13c.7.16}
$$
Indeed apply the smooth descent inequality to
$\Psi(z)-\Psi(y)-H(y)\cdot(z-y)$, whose minimum is zero, at $z=x$ with the step $-[H(x)-H(y)]/L$. On feasible fluxes, the dual stationarity removes the linear term at $j_*$; integrate (I.13c.7.16) to obtain the first field bound in (I.13c.7.5). Orthogonal projection onto $\nabla g+\nabla H_0^1$ is contractive and fixes $\nabla\Phi_*$, proving the bound for $q_r$. Boundedness of $j_r$, objective convergence and weak lower semicontinuity make every weak cluster point a dual minimizer. Uniqueness therefore gives weak convergence of the full flux sequence. The quantitative bounds already give strong field convergence.

For item 3, feasibility yields

$$
\langle f,v-g\rangle=-\int j\cdot\nabla(v-g),
$$

proving (I.13c.7.6). Subtract the two optimal values. The primal difference is the integrated Bregman divergence of $\mathcal F$ at $\nabla\Phi_*$, while the dual difference is that of $\Psi$ at $j_*$. Equations (I.13c.7.13) and (I.13c.7.16) bound their sum from below by the left side of (I.13c.7.7) divided by $2L$.

Finally $R_N$ is the restricted dual gradient at $j_N$. Its vanishing is equivalent to the unique minimizer, hence to $S_*=0$. Projection of $H(j_N)-H(j_*)$ onto $Z$ equals $R_N$, proving the first bound in (I.13c.7.9); Lipschitz continuity proves the second. One feasible descent step from $j_N$ proves the energy lower bound. In the subcritical case the same derivative computation gives $D^2\Psi\ge m_\chi I$. Strong monotonicity and the strong-convexity support inequality give the flux and energy upper bounds in (I.13c.7.11). Adding (I.13c.7.16) in the two directions gives
$$
|H(x)-H(y)|^2\le L\langle H(x)-H(y),x-y\rangle.
$$
Integrate this with $x=j_N$, $y=j_*$. Since $j_N-j_*\in Z$, the right side is

$$
L\langle R_N,j_N-j_*\rangle\le Lr_N^2/m_\chi.
$$

This proves the final field bound. At $A_G=0$ the constitutive maps are the identity; compatible Newtonian data have zero residual. ∎

<a id="theorem-i13c8-all-mode-response-and-quantified-nonspherical-perturbations"></a>**Theorem I.13c.8 (All-Mode Response and Quantified Nonspherical Perturbations).** Use the fixed action and notation of Theorem I.13c.7, and put $\mathcal A(q)=\nabla\mathcal F(q)$. Let $0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, and let $\Phi_0\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ solve $\operatorname{div}\mathcal A(\nabla\Phi_0)=f_0$. Assume that $\mathcal A$ is smooth on a compact neighborhood of the background gradient range and that $h_\chi'\ge c_0>0$ on the corresponding flux radii. These conditions hold on every bounded field range for $0<n\le1$, and for $n>1$ when $A_G<A_{\mathrm{crit}}(n)$. At the finite critical amplitude they hold for backgrounds avoiding the degenerate constitutive radius. Ordinary zero-gradient points satisfy the conditions because $D\mathcal A(0)=I/(1+A_G)$.

1. For $f_1\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ and a boundary perturbation $g_1$ that is the trace of a $C^{2,\alpha}$ lifting, the exact first variation is the unique solution
$$
\mathcal L_0v:=\operatorname{div}[B(x)\nabla v]=f_1,
\qquad v|_{\partial\Omega}=g_1,
\qquad B(x)=D\mathcal A(\nabla\Phi_0(x)).
\tag{I.13c.8.1}
$$
Writing $y=|\mathcal A(\nabla\Phi_0)|/a$, the radial and transverse eigenvalues of $B$ are
$$
b_r=\frac1{h_\chi'(y)},\qquad b_t=\frac1{\nu_\chi(y)},
\qquad \frac1L I\le B\le\frac1{c_0}I,
\tag{I.13c.8.2}
$$
where $c_0$ is decreased to at most $1$ if necessary. At zero the same formula is interpreted by continuity.

There is an explicit nonlinear error bound. Let $K$ be the norm of the homogeneous Dirichlet inverse of $\mathcal L_0$ from $C^{0,\alpha}$ to $C^{2,\alpha}$. Choose a radius $r_0>0$ on which the constitutive hypotheses hold and a constant $M>0$ bounding the second Fréchet derivative of $\Phi\mapsto\operatorname{div}\mathcal A(\nabla\Phi)$ from $C^{2,\alpha}\times C^{2,\alpha}$ to $C^{0,\alpha}$. Put $V=\|v\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}$. If $V>0$ and
$$
|\varepsilon|\le\min\left\{\frac{r_0}{2V},\frac1{4KMV}\right\},
\tag{I.13c.8.3}
$$
then the exact action solution for source $f_0+\varepsilon f_1$ and trace $\Phi_0|_{\partial\Omega}+\varepsilon g_1$ obeys
$$
\|\Phi_\varepsilon-\Phi_0-\varepsilon v\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}
\le2KMV^2\varepsilon^2.
\tag{I.13c.8.4}
$$
If $V=0$, the data and solution are unchanged.

2. On an annulus $r_-<|x|<r_+$ with $0<r_-<r_+<\infty$, take the monopole background
$$
y(r)=\frac{GM_b}{ar^2},\qquad
\nabla\Phi_0=a h_\chi(y)e_r,\qquad M_b>0,
\tag{I.13c.8.5}
$$
and require $h_\chi'(y(r))\ge c_0>0$ on the closed annulus. Expand the perturbation and source in spherical harmonics $Y_{\ell m}$. For every $\ell\ge0$ and $-\ell\le m\le\ell$, the complete response is
$$
[p(r)v_{\ell m}'(r)]'-q_\ell(r)v_{\ell m}(r)=r^2f_{\ell m}(r),
\qquad
p(r)=\frac{r^2}{h_\chi'(y(r))},\quad
q_\ell(r)=\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{\nu_\chi(y(r))}.
\tag{I.13c.8.6}
$$
Its Green operator is fixed as follows. Let $U_\ell,V_\ell$ solve the homogeneous equation with
$$
U_\ell(r_-)=0,\quad p(r_-)U_\ell'(r_-)=1,
\qquad
V_\ell(r_+)=0,\quad p(r_+)V_\ell'(r_+)=-1.
$$
Then
$$
W_\ell=p(U_\ell'V_\ell-U_\ell V_\ell')>0,
\qquad
G_\ell(r,s)=\frac{U_\ell(\min\{r,s\})V_\ell(\max\{r,s\})}{W_\ell},
\tag{I.13c.8.7}
$$
where $W_\ell$ is independent of $r$. For boundary coefficients $a_{\ell m}$ at $r_-$ and $b_{\ell m}$ at $r_+$,
$$
v_{\ell m}(r)=
a_{\ell m}\frac{V_\ell(r)}{V_\ell(r_-)}+
b_{\ell m}\frac{U_\ell(r)}{U_\ell(r_+)}-
\int_{r_-}^{r_+}G_\ell(r,s)s^2f_{\ell m}(s)\,ds.
\tag{I.13c.8.8}
$$
For an $H^{-1}$ source, the last term is the corresponding one-dimensional dual pairing, equivalently the energy limit of smooth sources. With boundary data admitting an $H^1$ lifting, the full modal sum converges in $H^1$ to the unique weak solution of (I.13c.8.1). In the Hölder class of item 1 it is the derivative in (I.13c.8.4). When the annulus is part of a larger source problem, its two boundary traces are those of that same action problem.

3. The first intrinsic angular failure of direct scalar enhancement is the quadrupole. More precisely, perturb the Newtonian monopole $u_0=-GM_b/r$ by
$$
v_N(r,\omega)=b_\ell(r)Y_{\ell m}(\omega),
\qquad b_\ell(r)=Cr^{-\ell-1},\quad C\ne0.
$$
For $A_G>0$ and $\ell\ge1$, the first variation of $H(\nabla u_0+\varepsilon\nabla v_N)$ is a gradient exactly when $\ell=1$. Its radial and tangential components are
$$
h_\chi'(y)b_\ell'(r)Y_{\ell m},
\qquad
\nu_\chi(y)\frac{b_\ell(r)}r\nabla_{S^2}Y_{\ell m},
\tag{I.13c.8.9}
$$
and the radial mismatch forced by its tangential part is
$$
[\nu_\chi(y)b_\ell]' - h_\chi'(y)b_\ell'
=\nu_\chi'(y)[y'b_\ell-yb_\ell']
=(\ell-1)\nu_\chi'(y)\frac{yb_\ell}{r}.
\tag{I.13c.8.10}
$$
Thus every $\ell\ge2$ requires a nonzero solenoidal correction, with the actual first-order action response given by item 2. The $\ell=0$ perturbation stays radial. The $\ell=1$ field is the infinitesimal translation of the spherical solution; identifying it with a specified full source perturbation requires the corresponding translated boundary traces. For $A_G=0$, every mode is Newtonian.

*Proof.* The inverse relation $H\circ\mathcal A=I$ makes $D\mathcal A(q)$ the inverse of $DH(\mathcal A(q))$ on the regular constitutive range. The radial and transverse eigenvalues of the latter are $h_\chi'$ and $\nu_\chi$. This gives (I.13c.8.2), including its continuous limit at zero. The coefficients of $\mathcal L_0$ are $C^{1,\alpha}$, uniformly elliptic and bounded. The Dirichlet maximum principle gives uniqueness, and uniform elliptic Schauder theory gives existence and the bounded inverse used in item 1.

For the error bound, write $\Phi_\varepsilon=\Phi_0+\varepsilon v+w$ with zero trace for $w$. Taylor's formula for the nonlinear source operator gives
$$
\mathcal L_0w=-N(\varepsilon v+w),\qquad
\|N(z)\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le\frac M2\|z\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}^2,
$$
and, on a ball of radius $R\le r_0$,
$\|N(z_1)-N(z_2)\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le MR\|z_1-z_2\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}$.
Smoothness of $\mathcal A$ on the compact constitutive neighborhood supplies this bound; its second derivative is
$$
D^2\bigl[\operatorname{div}\mathcal A(\nabla\Phi)\bigr][v,w]
=\operatorname{div}\bigl(D^2\mathcal A(\nabla\Phi)[\nabla v,\nabla w]\bigr).
$$
On the closed ball $\|w\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le2KMV^2\varepsilon^2$, condition (I.13c.8.3) gives $\|\varepsilon v+w\|\le2|\varepsilon|V\le r_0$. The map
$w\mapsto-\mathcal L_0^{-1}N(\varepsilon v+w)$ sends this ball into itself and has Lipschitz constant at most $2KM|\varepsilon|V\le1/2$. Its unique fixed point gives (I.13c.8.4). The weak action problem is globally unique by Theorem I.13c.7, so this classical solution is the same action solution. When $V=0$, (I.13c.8.1) gives $f_1=0$ and $g_1=0$.

For item 2, spherical symmetry gives $B=b_re_r\otimes e_r+b_t(I-e_r\otimes e_r)$. The spherical divergence formula and $\Delta_{S^2}Y_{\ell m}=-\ell(\ell+1)Y_{\ell m}$ yield (I.13c.8.6). The fundamental solutions are uniquely specified by their initial data. They can be constructed by the Volterra integral equations for the first-order system $(v,pv')'=(p^{-1}(pv'),q_\ell v)$; successive approximation converges on the finite interval because the coefficient matrix is continuous and bounded.

The solution $U_\ell$ is initially increasing and positive. As long as it is nonnegative, $(pU_\ell')'=q_\ell U_\ell\ge0$, hence $pU_\ell'\ge1$; it cannot return to zero. Applying the same argument backward gives $V_\ell>0$ in the annulus. Direct differentiation gives $W_\ell'=0$, and evaluation at $r_-$ gives $W_\ell=V_\ell(r_-)>0$. The derivative jump of $G_\ell$ at $r=s$ is $-1/p(s)$. It vanishes at both endpoints, so its negative is the inverse kernel for the plus-divergence operator in (I.13c.8.6). This proves (I.13c.8.8), its sign and its boundary normalization.

Finite harmonic sums are dense in the relevant Sobolev spaces and their projections commute with this radial operator. Orthogonality and $B\ge I/L$ make the zero-boundary energy form coercive. Subtract an $H^1$ lifting of the boundary trace and apply the energy estimate to the difference between successive projected problems. The projected sources converge in $H^{-1}$ and the liftings in $H^1$, so the solutions converge in $H^1$. This proves the assertion for all admitted Sobolev data and identifies the smooth-data sum with the unique solution of item 1.

Finally, differentiating the radial map $H$ gives (I.13c.8.9). For $\ell\ge1$, its tangential component forces a scalar potential of the form $\nu_\chi(y)b_\ell Y_{\ell m}$, up to a radial function. The radial function cannot cancel a nonconstant spherical harmonic. Matching its radial coefficient therefore requires (I.13c.8.10) to vanish. Here $y'=-2y/r$, $b_\ell'=-(\ell+1)b_\ell/r$ and $h_\chi'=\nu_\chi+y\nu_\chi'$. For $A_G>0$, $\nu_\chi'(y)<0$ at every finite $y>0$, so the mismatch vanishes exactly at $\ell=1$. Differentiating the background solution with respect to its center yields the potential proportional to $\Phi_0'(r)Y_{1m}=ah_\chi(y)Y_{1m}$ and verifies the translated homogeneous mode. The radial and $A_G=0$ cases follow directly. ∎

Theorem I.13c.8 supplies the classical derivative on its stated regular backgrounds. Theorem I.13c.7 supplies the full nonlinear response and certified field approximation at the critical amplitude as well. The amplitude menu $\{1,3,7\}$ at $n=3/2$ is strictly subcritical. The angular construction uses the nonlinear scalar-action perturbation method of Milgrom [1986], evaluated here for the registered constitutive function with an explicit nonlinear remainder and complete boundary data.

<a id="remark-i13c8a-size-of-the-solenoidal-correction-on-a-flattened-source"></a>**Remark I.13c.8a (Size of the Solenoidal Correction on a Flattened Source).** In units $G=a_\chi=1$, take $n=3/2$, $A_G=7$ and the smooth positive axisymmetric source with Newtonian potential
$$
u(R,z)=-\frac{M}{\sqrt{R^2+\bigl(a+\sqrt{z^2+b^2}\bigr)^2}},\qquad
\rho_b=\frac{\Delta u}{4\pi},\qquad
M=10,\quad a=1,\quad b=\tfrac12 .
\tag{I.13c.8a.1}
$$
On the level surface $R^2+\bigl(a+\sqrt{z^2+b^2}\bigr)^2=9$ of $u$ the field magnitude $|\nabla u|$ equals $10\sqrt{6.75}/27=0.962\ldots$ on the midplane and $10\sqrt{3.75}/18=1.075\ldots$ on the axis. The differential condition of (I.13c.6.2) therefore fails at a point of that surface, the algebraic field $\nu_\chi(|\nabla u|)\nabla u$ is not a gradient on any domain containing it, and on every such bounded domain the action solution of Theorem I.13c.7 carries a nonzero solenoidal correction $S_*$ of the flux in (I.13c.7.3), so its field differs from the algebraic field.

The following diagnostic computation evaluates that difference on the midplane. The Euler–Lagrange equation of (I.13c.5.4) is solved on $0\le R\le L$, $|z|\le L$ with reflection symmetry in $z$ and Dirichlet trace $(1+A_G)u=8u$ on $R=L$ and $|z|=L$, by continuous piecewise-linear finite elements with the cylindrical weight $R$ on a uniform triangulation of mesh size $h$ of the quarter-square $0\le R,z\le L$, and by Newton iteration to relative residual below $10^{-11}$. The midplane force $\partial_R\Phi_*(R,0)$ is read as the centred difference of nodal potentials. With $g_N(R)=MR/(R^2+(a+b)^2)^{3/2}$ the Newtonian midplane force, the algebraic value $\nu_\chi(g_N)g_N$ of (I.13c.5.5) and the action force at $L=8$, $h=1/32$ are

| $R$ | $1/2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| $\nu_\chi(g_N)g_N$ | $5.735$ | $6.025$ | $5.748$ | $3.868$ |
| $\partial_R\Phi_*(R,0)$ | $3.81$ | $5.29$ | $5.47$ | $3.78$ |
| $\partial_R\Phi_*(R,0)/(\nu_\chi(g_N)g_N)-1$ | $-34\%$ | $-12\%$ | $-4.9\%$ | $-2.4\%$ |

Refining the mesh from $h=1/16$ to $h=1/32$ changes these forces by at most $0.5\%$ and from $h=1/32$ to $h=1/64$ by at most $0.1\%$, reversing the diagonal of every triangle at $h=1/32$ changes them by at most $0.11\%$, and moving the boundary from $L=8$ to $L=24$ at $h=1/16$ changes them by less than $0.03\%$. The same discretization reproduces the Newtonian midplane force for $A_G=0$ within $3.2\times10^{-4}$, and for $A_G=7$ the exact action force of the spherical source $\rho_b=30/[4\pi(r^2+1)^{5/2}]$ with its exact trace within $10^{-4}$, both relative, at $h=1/32$. The trace $8u$ is a declared far-field approximation, the leading low-field form of the exterior field; the domain test measures the sensitivity of the four forces to its placement. The four values are discretization estimates; a numerical certificate for them requires the gap bound (I.13c.7.7) with its Poisson-solve and quadrature errors.

For $\beta_\chi=1$, $a_\chi=g_\Lambda=1.17674\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (the central value used in (H.6d)) and length unit $1\,\mathrm{kpc}$, the mass unit $a_\chi\,\mathrm{kpc}^2/G$ is $8.44\times10^{8}M_\odot$, so (I.13c.8a.1) has the baryonic mass and scale lengths of a late-type disk galaxy. On such a source the action force lies about one third below the spherical law (I.13c.5.5), applied to the Newtonian midplane force, at half the radial scale length and about one eighth below it at one scale length. The forward map of a rotation-curve comparison on this branch is the action solution of Theorem I.13c.7 for a declared three-dimensional baryonic source and boundary trace.

<a id="remark-i13c8b-retrospective-rotation-curve-comparison-of-the-spatial-clock-benchmark"></a>**Remark I.13c.8b (Retrospective Rotation-Curve Comparison of the Spatial-Clock Benchmark).** The spatial-clock benchmark is the Definition I.13c.1 branch with $(A_G,n,\beta_\chi)=(7,3/2,1)$. Its amplitude $A_G=d_0-1$ is the backbone-motivated benchmark of Definition I.13a, the endpoint of the Proposition I.13c.3 menu; its exponent is the power clock of Remark K.9.5i adopted in Definition I.13c.1; and $\beta_\chi=1$ is a convention that sets $a_\chi=g_\Lambda$ and, through Corollary H.1a.3, places the sheet transition at $\Sigma_\dagger$. Theorem I.13c.10 selects $A_G=1$ on the source of Construction I.13c.9.

On the sample and inputs of Remark I.5j, the spherical law (I.13c.5.5) of the benchmark, applied to each $g_{\mathrm{bar}}$, gives median ratio $g_{\mathrm{pred}}/g_{\mathrm{obs}}=2.20$ and root-mean-square residual $0.403$ dex, against $0.133$ dex for the empirical radial acceleration relation, and has the larger per-galaxy residual in 135 of the 149 galaxies; over the nine mass-to-light pairs of Remark I.5j that count lies between 115 and 142. The member $A_G=1$, $\beta_\chi=1$ gives median ratio $0.706$, $0.292$ dex and 122 galaxies. Remark I.13c.8a shows that on a flattened source the action force lies below the spherical law, so the full-field comparison uses the action solution of Theorem I.13c.7. For the reconstructed sources of Remark I.5j, axisymmetric finite-element solutions give root-mean-square rotation-speed residuals of $48.5$, $8.56$ and $86.7\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for NGC 2403, DDO 154 and NGC 3198 ($60.8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for NGC 2403 with catalog-normalized totals), against $15.2$, $5.11$ and $10.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ ($8.5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$) for (I.5j.1) on the Newtonian fields of the same sources, and they overpredict 66 (71) of 73, 12 of 12 and 43 of 43 measured speeds. With $A_G=1$ and $\beta_\chi=1$ the NGC 2403 residual is $40.5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ ($33.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$). The benchmark has the larger residual in every pooled-sample comparison made, against the empirical relation, and in every full-field comparison, against (I.5j.1).

The bounded response does not have the shape of these data. Its spherical enhancement satisfies $\nu_\chi\le1+A_G=8$, while 117 of the 2700 radii, in 23 galaxies, have $g_{\mathrm{obs}}/g_{\mathrm{bar}}>8$, and the empirical relation exceeds that cap for $g_{\mathrm{bar}}<g_\dagger\ln^2(8/7)=2.14\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The rate modulus at which the $A_G=7$ law equals the empirical relation rises from $0.038$ at $g_{\mathrm{bar}}=10^{-11.5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ to $0.18$ at $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $0.35$ at $10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so no single $\beta_\chi$ reproduces the relation. Fitted to the sample after the fact, $\beta_\chi=0.075$ gives $0.177$ dex with 113 galaxies worse than the relation, and a joint fit of $A_G\le A_{\mathrm{crit}}(3/2)$ and $\beta_\chi$ gives $(A_G,\beta_\chi)=(3.94,0.178)$, $0.156$ dex and 100 galaxies worse.

These comparisons are retrospective: the SPARC data and the empirical relation were public and had been inspected before the comparisons were specified, and the three galaxies belong to the SPARC sample. The falsification condition of Proposition I.13b requires an exclusion within a stated model and uncertainty ledger; these comparisons propagate no joint uncertainty for distances, inclinations, mass-to-light ratios or gas and do not trigger it. Per-galaxy values, all variations and the full-field details are given in [the retrospective SPARC tables](../related/calculation_companions/appendix_i/gal-sparc-retrospective-tables.md).

Theorems I.13c.6–I.13c.8 give the fixed-action nonspherical response and zero-correction classification: global periods and critical points, complete vacuum geometries, compact-source exterior monopole equivalence, a convergent all-source construction through the critical amplitude, explicit field certificates and all angular modes with a nonlinear remainder. The higher-multipole scalar-field obstruction in Theorem I.13c.8 is a first-order statement; the full nonlinear response is supplied by Theorem I.13c.7. Its error bounds concern exact continuum operations. A numerical certificate additionally records the Poisson-solve, discretization and quadrature errors. Construction I.13c.9 and Theorem I.13c.10 derive the spatial-clock premises, rate, direction selector and calibration on a declared source. The static action and these conditional consequences do not fix the common covariant and lensing projections.

<a id="construction-i13c9-occupancy-capacitor-clock-source"></a>**Construction I.13c.9 (Occupancy–Capacitor Clock Source).** Work in units $c=\hbar=1$ with a time unit $t_*>0$ fixed in item 7. Fix a length $\ell_0>0$, an intensity $\lambda_0>0$, a capacitor coefficient $K_{\mathrm{cap}}>0$ (a field magnitude times an area), a temperature $\theta>0$, a number $N\ge1$ of streams and a refinement $s\ge1$, and put
$$
\ell_s=\frac{\ell_0}{s},\qquad \Delta_s=\lambda_0\ell_s^3,\qquad p_s=1-e^{-\Delta_s},\qquad b=\frac{4\pi\lambda_0}{3},\qquad a_\chi=K_{\mathrm{cap}}\,b^{2/3}.
\tag{I.13c.9.1}
$$

1. *Occupancy.* In each stream $i\in\{1,\dots,N\}$ the cubes of side $\ell_s$ centred at the points of $\ell_s\mathbb Z^3$ are occupied independently, each with probability $p_s$, so that a cube is empty with probability $e^{-\lambda_0\ell_s^3}$. The $N$ streams are independent.

2. *Scan and exposure.* A probe at $x\in\mathbb R^3$ lists the cube centres $c_1(x),c_2(x),\dots$ in nondecreasing distance from $x$, ties broken by a fixed rule that does not depend on the occupancies. After $k$ centres its exposure is $t_k=k\Delta_s$. Write $\omega_{i,k}\in\{0,1\}$ for the occupancy in stream $i$ of the cube centred at $c_k(x)$.

3. *Capacitor threshold.* Let $\rho_i(x)$ be the distance from $x$ to the nearest occupied centre of stream $i$. The threshold of stream $i$ at $x$ is the Coulomb field $T_i(x)=K_{\mathrm{cap}}/\rho_i(x)^2$ of a point source with Gauss coefficient $K_{\mathrm{cap}}$ at that centre, with $T_i(x)=0$ when no centre is occupied. A probe in a Newtonian field of magnitude $g>0$ fires in stream $i$ when $T_i(x)\ge g$, that is, when an occupied centre lies within the capacitor radius $r(g)=(K_{\mathrm{cap}}/g)^{1/2}$. Its response cut is $k(x,g)=\#\{k:|c_k(x)-x|\le r(g)\}$.

4. *Live signs and refresh stocks.* Stream $i$ carries a sign $\varsigma_{i,0}\in\{\pm1\}$ with $\Pr(\varsigma_{i,0}=1)=(1+N^{-1/2})/2$. At rank $k\ge1$, if $\omega_{i,k}=1$ the sign is replaced by a fresh sign of mean $\beta_{i,k}\in[-1,1]$ taken from a refresh stock; otherwise $\varsigma_{i,k}=\varsigma_{i,k-1}$. A causal policy $\pi$ chooses each $\beta_{i,k}$ as a function of the initial signs, of the occupancies and signs at ranks below $k$, and of a private randomization independent of all occupancies. The fair policy $\pi_0$ has $\beta_{i,k}=0$. The mean response of $\pi$ at rank $k$ is
$$
u_k=1-m_k,\qquad m_k=N^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E\,\varsigma_{i,k},
\tag{I.13c.9.2}
$$
and $\pi$ is admissible when $u_k\ge0$ for every $k$. With $\alpha_k=N^{-1/2}\sum_i\mathbb E\,\beta_{i,k+1}$, the interpolated response is $u^\pi=1-m^\pi$, where $m^\pi(t)=e^{-(t-t_k)}m_k+\bigl(1-e^{-(t-t_k)}\bigr)\alpha_k$ on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.

5. *Price.* A stock of bias $\beta$ is a two-level register in the state $\mathrm{Ber}((1+\beta)/2)$ with degenerate Hamiltonian. Its free energy at temperature $\theta$ exceeds that of the fair Gibbs state by $\theta\,d(\beta)$, where
$$
d(\beta)=D\Bigl(\mathrm{Ber}\bigl(\tfrac{1+\beta}2\bigr)\,\Big\|\,\mathrm{Ber}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)\Bigr)=\frac{1+\beta}2\ln(1+\beta)+\frac{1-\beta}2\ln(1-\beta)=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{\beta^{2j}}{2j(2j-1)},
\tag{I.13c.9.3}
$$
and an energy-conserving exchange with a fair target register transfers that state to the target. The normalized price of $\pi$ counts the initial signs and every consumed refresh stock:
$$
\Pi_{s,N}[\pi]=N\,d(N^{-1/2})+\sum_{k\ge1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E\bigl[\omega_{i,k}\,d(\beta_{i,k})\bigr].
\tag{I.13c.9.4}
$$

6. *Direction challenge.* Three interface directions are available. A configuration is a nonempty $J\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$ with $j=|J|$ participating directions and amplitude $A(J)=2^j-1$, the number of its banks, one for each nonempty subset of $J$. Its preparation activates the $j$ port registers and the $2^j-1$ banks of $J$, one per tick and one activation quantum each, and then tests and locks, one tick each. It therefore locks at tick $j+2^j+1$ and consumes $q(J)=j+2^j-1$ quanta. A challenge $(Y,Z,W)$ has $Y$ fair and $Z,W$ independent of $Y$ and of each other, with $\Pr(Z=1)=\Pr(W=1)=1/4$. A prediction register holds the hint $Y\oplus W$; at the end of tick $5$ a sampling gate replaces its content by $Y$ if the configuration is locked; at tick $6$ the prediction is scored against $Y\oplus Z$. The score $S(J)$ is the probability of a correct prediction. A configuration $J$ and a policy $\pi$ give the static coupling $G/G_0=1+A(J)\,u_{k(x,g)}$ at a probe $x$ in a field of magnitude $g$.

7. *Body, coupling and units.* The body is a ball of uniform density, mass $M$ and radius $a$ centred at the origin. Its Newton coupling is $G_0=\delta_c^2/(8\ln2)$ for a link pitch $\delta_c>0$, the value that (E.9) assigns to one boundary link of capacity $2\ln2$ per area $\delta_c^2$ with $\chi=1$. A source time, length, mass, acceleration and Newton coupling have the physical values $t_*t$, $ct_*x$, $\hbar M/(c^2t_*)$, $(c/t_*)g$ and $(c^5t_*^2/\hbar)G_0$. The calibration that identifies $G_0$ with the measured Newton constant $G$ fixes
$$
t_*=\Bigl(\frac{\hbar G}{c^5G_0}\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\tag{I.13c.9.5}
$$

*Declared instance.* $\ell_0=5\times10^5$, $\lambda_0\ell_0^3=\ln(4/3)$ (each volume $\ell_0^3$ is empty with probability $3/4$), $K_{\mathrm{cap}}=17/16$, $\delta_c=4\times10^8$, $M=10^{-14}$ and $a=\delta_c/100$.

<a id="theorem-i13c10-source-derivation-of-the-spatial-clock-premises-rate-direction-selector-and-calibration"></a>**Theorem I.13c.10 (Source Derivation of the Spatial-Clock Premises, Rate, Direction Selector and Calibration).** On the source of Construction I.13c.9 put $\sigma(g)=(a_\chi/g)^{3/2}$ for $g>0$ and
$$
I[u]=\frac12\int_0^\infty\bigl(u'(t)+u(t)-1\bigr)^2\,dt .
$$

1. *Spatial clock and rate.* Under the fair policy, at every probe $x$ and field magnitude $g>0$, the response at the cut is $u_{k(x,g)}=1-e^{-t_{k(x,g)}}=\Pr\bigl(T_i(x)\ge g\bigr)$, and
$$
\Bigl|u_{k(x,g)}-\bigl(1-e^{-\sigma(g)}\bigr)\Bigr|\le L_bh_s,
\qquad h_s=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ell_s,
\qquad L_b=3b^{1/3}\Bigl(\frac23\Bigr)^{2/3}e^{-2/3}.
\tag{I.13c.10.1}
$$
At the baryonic field $g=|\nabla\Phi_b(x)|$ the limit $s\to\infty$ is therefore $1-e^{-\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}}$ with $\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=s_{\mathrm{loc}}^{3/2}$ and $s_{\mathrm{loc}}=a_\chi/|\nabla\Phi_b|=\beta_\chi g_\Lambda/|\nabla\Phi_b|$, where
$$
\beta_\chi=\frac{a_\chi}{g_\Lambda},\qquad a_\chi=K_{\mathrm{cap}}\Bigl(\frac{4\pi\lambda_0}3\Bigr)^{2/3}.
\tag{I.13c.10.2}
$$
Registrations (1) and (2) of Definition I.13c.1 hold on this source with $n=3/2$, and $\beta_\chi$ is fixed by $\lambda_0$, $K_{\mathrm{cap}}$ and $g_\Lambda$; no body mass, field datum or response curve enters it. For the declared instance $a_\chi=\tfrac{17}{16}\bigl(\tfrac{4\pi}3\ln\tfrac43\bigr)^{2/3}\ell_0^{-2}$ and $L_bh_s<6/(5s)$.

2. *Response cost.* (a) For every causal policy and every $k\ge0$,
$$
m_{k+1}=(1-p_s)m_k+p_s\alpha_k,
\qquad
\Pi_{s,N}[\pi]\ge N\,d(N^{-1/2})+\frac{p_s}2\sum_{k\ge0}\alpha_k^2= N\,d(N^{-1/2})+\frac{p_s}{\Delta_s}\,I[u^\pi].
\tag{I.13c.10.3}
$$
(b) Let $s_n\to\infty$ and $N_n\to\infty$, write $\Pi_n=\Pi_{s_n,N_n}$, and let $\pi_n$ be admissible policies. If $\sup_n\Pi_n[\pi_n]<\infty$, then $(u^{\pi_n})$ is precompact for locally uniform convergence on $[0,\infty)$. If $u^{\pi_n}\to u$ locally uniformly, then $\liminf_n\Pi_n[\pi_n]\ge\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]$, with $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}=+\infty$ off $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ as in (K.9.5b.2). For every $u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ there are admissible deterministic policies $\pi_n$ with $u^{\pi_n}\to u$ locally uniformly and $\Pi_n[\pi_n]\to\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]$.

(c) For every $(s,N)$ the fair policy minimizes $\Pi_{s,N}$, with minimum $N\,d(N^{-1/2})$. A policy is a minimizer exactly when every bias vanishes almost surely, and every minimizer has $u_k=1-e^{-t_k}$ for all $k$.

Hence the limiting price of the source is the registered response action (K.9.5b.2) on its full class $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$, the selected profile at every resolution is $u_*(t)=1-e^{-t}$ of Theorem K.9.5c on the exposure grid, the coefficient ratio of Remark K.9.5d is one, and with item 1 the static response is $A\,(1-e^{-\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}})$: registration (3) of Definition I.13c.1 holds on this source.

3. *Direction selector.* The scores and consumptions are
$$
S(J)=\tfrac34,\ q(J)=2\ \ (j=1);\qquad S(J)=\tfrac58,\ q(J)=5\ \ (j=2);\qquad S(J)=\tfrac58,\ q(J)=10\ \ (j=3).
\tag{I.13c.10.4}
$$
The single-direction configurations have the largest score and the smallest consumption, with gaps $1/8$ and at least $3$, and they are the only configurations at least as good as every other in both. Every selection rule that is nondecreasing in the score and strictly decreasing in the consumption, in particular every linear trade-off with nonnegative weight on the score and positive weight on the consumption, selects $j=1$, and the same holds for every sampling tick in place of $5$. The selected amplitude is $A_G=2^1-1=1$, the serialized member of Proposition I.13c.3, and the endpoint amplitude $7$ of Definition I.13a is strictly dominated.

4. *Mass, geometry and observable calibration.* The body's Newtonian field is $g_N(R)=G_0MR/a^3$ for $R\le a$ and $g_N(R)=G_0M/R^2$ for $R\ge a$. With $n=3/2$, $A_G=1$ and $a_\chi$ of (I.13c.10.2), item 3 of Theorem I.13c.5 gives the static field $|\nabla\Phi|=\nu_\chi(g_N/a_\chi)\,g_N$, whose coefficient $\nu_\chi(g_N/a_\chi)=1+\bigl(1-e^{-\sigma(g_N)}\bigr)$ is, at every radius, one plus the limiting response of items 1–3. For $R\ge a$,
$$
G(R):=\frac{R^2|\nabla\Phi(R)|}{M}=G_0\Bigl[1+\Bigl(1-e^{-(R/L_0)^3}\Bigr)\Bigr],
\qquad
L_0=\Bigl(\frac{G_0M}{a_\chi}\Bigr)^{1/2},
\qquad
v_c(R)^2=R\,|\nabla\Phi(R)|,
\tag{I.13c.10.5}
$$
which is Equation I.4 with $m=3$, $A_G=1$ and the Proposition I.13c.2 map with mass datum $M_b=M$ and exterior-Keplerian geometry datum $R\ge a$; $v_c$ is the circular speed of slow test bodies. For the declared instance
$$
\frac{400}{119}<\frac{L_0^2}{a^2}<\frac{75}{17},
\tag{I.13c.10.6}
$$
so the transition lies outside the body.

5. *Units.* With $t_*$ of (I.13c.9.5) the physical acceleration scale is $a_\chi c/t_*$, so $\beta_\chi=a_\chi c/(t_*g_\Lambda)$ for $g_\Lambda=c^2\sqrt\Lambda/8$; the physical transition length is $ct_*L_0$ and the physical mass is $\hbar M/(c^2t_*)$, while $m$, $A_G$, $L_0/a$ and $v_c/c$ are unit-free.

*Proof.* Item 1. Under $\pi_0$ the sign of stream $i$ has mean $N^{-1/2}$ until its first occupied cube and mean zero afterwards, since a fair refresh has mean zero and every later refresh is fair. Hence $\mathbb E\varsigma_{i,k}=N^{-1/2}(1-p_s)^k$ and $m_k=(1-p_s)^k=e^{-t_k}$, and $1-m_k$ is the probability that one of the first $k$ cubes of a stream is occupied. At $k=k(x,g)$ this is $\Pr(\rho_i(x)\le r(g))=\Pr(T_i(x)\ge g)$. Let $U$ be the union of the cubes whose centres lie within $r=r(g)$ of $x$. Every point lies within the half-diagonal $h_s$ of the centre of a cube containing it, so $B(x,r-h_s)\subseteq U\subseteq\bar B(x,r+h_s)$; since $t_{k(x,g)}=\lambda_0|U|$, one has $b(r-h_s)_+^3\le t_{k(x,g)}\le b(r+h_s)^3$. The function $\varrho\mapsto e^{-b\varrho^3}$ has derivative of absolute value $3b\varrho^2e^{-b\varrho^3}\le L_b$, the maximum being at $b\varrho^3=2/3$, so $|e^{-t_{k(x,g)}}-e^{-br^3}|\le L_bh_s$. Finally $br(g)^3=b(K_{\mathrm{cap}}/g)^{3/2}=(K_{\mathrm{cap}}b^{2/3}/g)^{3/2}=\sigma(g)$, which proves (I.13c.10.1). With $g=|\nabla\Phi_b|$, $s_{\mathrm{loc}}=a_\chi/|\nabla\Phi_b|=\beta_\chi/\chi_b$ is the sparsity variable of Definition I.13c.1 with $\beta_\chi$ of (I.13c.10.2), and $\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=s_{\mathrm{loc}}^{3/2}$ is its power clock. For the instance, $3<\pi<22/7$ and $1/4<\ln(4/3)<1/3$ give $1<b\ell_0^3=\tfrac{4\pi}3\ln\tfrac43<88/63$, and $L_bh_s=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2\bigl(\tfrac23\bigr)^{2/3}e^{-2/3}(b\ell_0^3)^{1/3}s^{-1}<1.02\cdot1.12\,s^{-1}<6/(5s)$.

Item 2(a). The occupancy $\omega_{i,k+1}$ is independent of the past and of $\beta_{i,k+1}$, and a fresh sign has conditional mean $\beta_{i,k+1}$; hence $\mathbb E\varsigma_{i,k+1}=(1-p_s)\mathbb E\varsigma_{i,k}+p_s\mathbb E\beta_{i,k+1}$, and summing over $i$ gives the first identity. The series in (I.13c.9.3) gives $d(\beta)\ge\beta^2/2$, and independence, Jensen's inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bound the price of rank $k+1$:
$$
p_s\sum_i\mathbb E\,d(\beta_{i,k+1})\ge\frac{p_s}2\sum_i\bigl(\mathbb E\beta_{i,k+1}\bigr)^2\ge\frac{p_s}{2N}\Bigl(\sum_i\mathbb E\beta_{i,k+1}\Bigr)^2=\frac{p_s}2\alpha_k^2 .
$$
The interpolant has $m^\pi(t_{k+1})=m_{k+1}$ because $1-e^{-\Delta_s}=p_s$, and $(m^\pi)'=-m^\pi+\bar\alpha$ with $\bar\alpha=\alpha_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1})$. Thus $\bar\alpha=1-u^\pi-(u^\pi)'$ and $I[u^\pi]=\tfrac{\Delta_s}2\sum_k\alpha_k^2$, which gives the equality in (I.13c.10.3). On each interval $m^\pi$ moves monotonically from $m_k$ to $m_{k+1}$, so $u^\pi\ge0$ for admissible $\pi$, and $u^\pi(0)=0$.

Item 2(b). Since $p_s/\Delta_s\ge1-\Delta_s/2$, a bound $\Pi_n[\pi_n]\le C$ gives $\|\bar\alpha_n\|_{L^2(0,\infty)}^2\le4C$ once $\Delta_{s_n}\le1$. The formula $m_n(t)=e^{-t}+\int_0^te^{-(t-\tau)}\bar\alpha_n(\tau)\,d\tau$ gives $|m_n|\le1+\|\bar\alpha_n\|_2$ and $|m_n(t)-m_n(t')|\le|t-t'|\sup|m_n|+|t-t'|^{1/2}\|\bar\alpha_n\|_2$, and the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem with a diagonal argument gives the precompactness. Let $u^{\pi_n}\to u$ locally uniformly with $\liminf_n\Pi_n[\pi_n]<\infty$, and pass to a subsequence realizing the lower limit. On $[0,T]$ a further subsequence has $\bar\alpha_n\rightharpoonup\bar\alpha$ weakly in $L^2(0,T)$. The integral formula passes to the limit pointwise, so $m=1-u$ satisfies $m'=-m+\bar\alpha$, that is $\bar\alpha=1-u-u'$ on $(0,T)$, and weak lower semicontinuity gives $\tfrac12\int_0^T(u'+u-1)^2\,dt\le\liminf_nI[u^{\pi_n}]$. Letting $T\to\infty$ and using $p_s/\Delta_s\to1$ and $N\,d(N^{-1/2})\to\tfrac12$ gives $\liminf_n\Pi_n[\pi_n]\ge\tfrac12+I[u]$. Then $\alpha=1-u-u'\in L^2(0,\infty)$, Young's inequality gives $\|1-u\|_2\le2^{-1/2}+\|\alpha\|_2$, and $u'=(1-u)-\alpha\in L^2$; with $u(0)=0$ and $u\ge0$ this is $u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$, and (K.9.5c.1) gives $\tfrac12+I[u]=\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]$.

For the recovery let $u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$, $m=1-u$ and $\alpha=m+m'\in L^2(0,\infty)$, so that $m'=-m+\alpha$, $m(0)=1$ and $m\le1$. For $Q\ge1$ let $\alpha_Q=\max(-Q,\min(Q,\alpha))$, and let $m_Q\le1$ solve $m_Q'=-m_Q+\alpha_Q-\eta_Q$, $m_Q(0)=1$, with $\eta_Q\ge0$ vanishing where $m_Q<1$. This solution exists and is unique: it is the fixed point of $y\mapsto\Gamma\bigl(1+\int_0^\cdot(\alpha_Q-y)\,d\tau\bigr)$, where the Skorokhod map $\Gamma(z)(t)=z(t)-\max_{\tau\le t}(z(\tau)-1)_+$ is $2$-Lipschitz for the supremum norm, so Picard iteration converges on successive intervals of length below $1/2$. Where $m_Q=1$ one has $m_Q'=0$ almost everywhere, so the effective control $\hat\alpha_Q=\alpha_Q-\eta_Q$ equals $1\le\alpha_Q$ there and $\alpha_Q$ elsewhere; hence $\hat\alpha_Q^2\le\alpha^2$. For $w=m_Q-m$,
$$
\tfrac12(w^2)'=-w^2+w(\alpha_Q-\alpha)-w\eta_Q\le-w^2+|w|\,|\alpha_Q-\alpha|,
$$
because $\eta_Q>0$ only where $m_Q=1\ge m$. Therefore $|w(t)|\le\int_0^te^{-(t-\tau)}|\alpha_Q-\alpha|\,d\tau\le2^{-1/2}\|\alpha_Q-\alpha\|_2$, which tends to $0$ as $Q\to\infty$. For $T>0$ replace $\hat\alpha_Q$ by $0$ after $T$; the trajectory then relaxes as $m_Q(T)e^{-(t-T)}\le1$ and the action stays at most $I[u]$. On the exposure grid put $\alpha_k=p_s^{-1}\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}e^{-(t_{k+1}-\tau)}\hat\alpha_Q(\tau)\,d\tau$. Variation of constants shows that $m_{k+1}=(1-p_s)m_k+p_s\alpha_k$ reproduces the continuous trajectory at every grid point, so the policy is admissible; both trajectories take values in $[-Q,1]$ and have slope at most $2Q$, so the interpolant differs from the continuous trajectory by at most $4Q\Delta_s$; and weighted Jensen gives $\tfrac{p_s}2\sum_k\alpha_k^2\le\tfrac12\int_0^\infty\hat\alpha_Q^2\,dt\le I[u]$. Realize $\alpha_k$ by the deterministic biases $\beta_{i,k+1}=\alpha_kN^{-1/2}$, which lie in $[-2^{-1/2},2^{-1/2}]$ when $Q^2\le N/2$. The bound $0\le d(\beta)-\beta^2/2\le\beta^4/(12(1-\beta^2))$, which follows from the series in (I.13c.9.3), and $p_s\le\Delta_s$ give
$$
\Pi_{s,N}[\pi]\le N\,d(N^{-1/2})+I[u]+\frac{(T+\Delta_s)Q^4}{6N}.
$$
Choosing $Q_n,T_n\to\infty$ with $Q_n^2\le N_n/2$, $Q_n^4(T_n+1)/N_n\to0$ and $Q_n\Delta_{s_n}\to0$ gives $u^{\pi_n}\to u$ locally uniformly and $\limsup_n\Pi_n[\pi_n]\le\tfrac12+I[u]=\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]$, which with the lower bound proves $\Pi_n[\pi_n]\to\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]$.

Item 2(c). By (I.13c.9.4) and the independence of $\omega_{i,k}$ from $\beta_{i,k}$, $\Pi_{s,N}[\pi]-N\,d(N^{-1/2})=p_s\sum_{i,k}\mathbb E\,d(\beta_{i,k})\ge0$, with equality exactly when $d(\beta_{i,k})=0$, that is $\beta_{i,k}=0$, almost surely for all $i,k$. Every such policy has the fair means computed in item 1. For the concluding statement: on a response-cost branch the profile enters the objective (K.9.5b.3) only through $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}$ (Theorem K.9.5c, item 3); (b) identifies $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}$ with the limiting price; (c) selects $u_*$ on the exposure grid at every resolution; the refresh hazard per unit exposure equals the occupancy hazard, so $c_0=c_1$ in Remark K.9.5d; and the exposure is the clock of item 1.

Item 3. A configuration with $j=1$ locks at tick $4$, so at the end of tick $5$ its prediction is $Y$, which is correct exactly when $Z=0$, with probability $3/4$. A configuration with $j\ge2$ locks at tick $j+2^j+1\ge7$, keeps the hint $Y\oplus W$, and is correct exactly when $W=Z$, with probability $(3/4)^2+(1/4)^2=5/8$. The consumptions are $j+2^j-1$. For a sampling tick $\tau$ the score is $3/4$ when $j+2^j+1\le\tau$ and $5/8$ otherwise, which is nonincreasing in $j$, while the consumption increases strictly with $j$. Both statements about selection rules follow.

Item 4. The enclosed mass of the uniform ball is $M\min(R^3/a^3,1)$, and Gauss's law gives $g_N$. Since $A_G=1<A_{\mathrm{crit}}(3/2)$, item 3 of Theorem I.13c.5 applies and gives the radial field (I.13c.5.5); its coefficient at radius $R$ is $\nu_\chi(g_N/a_\chi)=1+(1-e^{-(a_\chi/g_N)^{3/2}})$, which is one plus the limiting response of item 1 at $g=g_N(R)$, with the profile of item 2 and the amplitude of item 3. For $R\ge a$, $(a_\chi/g_N)^{3/2}=(a_\chi R^2/(G_0M))^{3/2}=(R/L_0)^3$, which gives (I.13c.10.5); a slow test body in circular orbit has $v_c^2/R=|\nabla\Phi|$. For the instance, $1<\tfrac{4\pi}3\ln\tfrac43<88/63$ and $(88/63)^2<(5/4)^3$ give $\tfrac{17}{16}\ell_0^{-2}<a_\chi<\tfrac{85}{64}\ell_0^{-2}$, and $2/3<\ln2<7/10$ gives $\tfrac5{28}\delta_c^2<G_0<\tfrac3{16}\delta_c^2$. With $L_0^2/a^2=10^4G_0M/(a_\chi\delta_c^2)$, $M=10^{-14}$ and $\ell_0^2=2.5\times10^{11}$ this gives $\tfrac5{28}\cdot\tfrac{64}{85}\cdot25=\tfrac{400}{119}<L_0^2/a^2<\tfrac3{16}\cdot\tfrac{16}{17}\cdot25=\tfrac{75}{17}$.

Item 5. Each quantity is converted by the dictionary of item 7 of Construction I.13c.9: accelerations carry the factor $c/t_*$, lengths the factor $ct_*$ and masses the factor $\hbar/(c^2t_*)$, and $m$, $A_G$, $L_0/a$ and $v_c/c$ are ratios of like quantities. ∎

**Definition I.13d (Covariant Dark-Susceptibility and Effective-Action Certificate).** A covariant dark-susceptibility certificate is a finite record
$$
\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{DS}}
=
\left(
\mathfrak H_g,
\Gamma_{\mathrm{DS}},
\mathcal K_{\mathrm{DS}},
T_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{DS}},
\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}},
\Pi_{\mathrm{wf}},
\Pi_{\mathrm{lens}},
\Pi_{\mathrm{cl}},
\Pi_{\mathrm{loc}},
\Pi_{\mathrm{CMB}},
\Pi_{\mathrm{hom}},
\mathfrak B_D,
\mathcal J_{\mathrm{DS}},
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{DS}},
\chi_{\mathrm{DS}}
\right)
\tag{I.13d.1}
$$
with the following entries and their structural dependencies recorded under Definition 2.4.1d.

1. $\mathfrak H_g$ is the accepted Appendix H acceleration bridge record fixing $g_\Lambda=c^2\sqrt\Lambda/8$ on the same vacuum branch used by the metric sector.

2. $\Gamma_{\mathrm{DS}}[g,T_b;\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}}]$ is either a generally covariant finite effective action or a causal nonlocal susceptibility functional with a finite Ward identity. In the action case,
$$
T_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{DS}}
=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta\Gamma_{\mathrm{DS}}}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}.
\tag{I.13d.2}
$$
In the susceptibility case, $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{DS}}$ must supply the retarded kernel and the finite conservation proof replacing (I.13d.2).

3. $T_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{DS}}$ is the conserved response tensor, including anisotropic stress. The accepted record must prove
$$
\nabla_\mu\left(T_b^{\mu\nu}+T_{\mathrm{DS}}^{\mu\nu}\right)=0.
\tag{I.13d.3}
$$

4. $\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}}=(L_0,A_G,m,K,q,A_{\mathrm{PM}},\Theta_{\mathrm{hom}})$ is the finite ansatz coordinate vector. $\Theta_{\mathrm{hom}}$ is either strict $\Lambda$ behavior, a finite-parameter law for $w(z)$, a density-dependent relaxation law, or a homogeneous-sparsity law.

5. $\Pi_{\mathrm{wf}}$ proves that the quasistatic galaxy projection of $T_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{DS}}$ is equivalent to Equation I.4 with the displayed $(L_0,A_G,m)$.

6. $\Pi_{\mathrm{lens}}$ proves the lensing projection, including the relation between potential response, anisotropic stress, and light deflection.

7. $\Pi_{\mathrm{cl}}$ proves the cluster and merger projections, including Equation I.7 or its accepted replacement with the displayed $(K,q,A_{\mathrm{PM}})$ and the stated merger/offset limits.

8. $\Pi_{\mathrm{loc}}$ proves the local-gravity limit and supplies the solar-system residual interval.

9. $\Pi_{\mathrm{CMB}}$ proves the CMB-era safety condition for the same kernel.

10. $\Pi_{\mathrm{hom}}$ proves the homogeneous late-time law, including conserved stress-energy, the density evolution equation, and the residual interval for $w(z)$ or strict $w=-1$ behavior.

11. $\mathfrak B_D$ is the RCD-Buchert-Cheeger and elliptic scale-bridge ledger. It contains the domain datum of Definition I.3e, the first Neumann spectral gap, predictive-stress variance, source-energy rate density, and finite defect budgets.

12. $\mathcal J_{\mathrm{DS}}$ is the finite PCE susceptibility functional on the retained ansatz family, with a unique minimizer $\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}}^*$ and strict gap $g_{\mathrm{DS}}>0$ modulo response equivalence.

13. $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{DS}}$ is a finite residual interval for weak-field, lensing, cluster, merger, local-gravity, CMB-era, homogeneous, and backreaction projections.

14. $\chi_{\mathrm{DS}}$ verifies acyclic dependencies under Definition 2.4.1d for $\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}}^*$, the parameter-fixed constitutive kernel $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{DS}}$, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{DS}}$, the projection maps, and $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{DS}}$. For $(L_0,A_G,m)$ and the other coordinates of $\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}}$, the record gives the derivation from the backbone and bridge, the explicit branch assumption, or the declared empirical input and its uncertainty. A dataset used to choose any coordinate or bound is calibration data for that branch. The unique-minimizer claim requires the independently specified $\mathcal J_{\mathrm{DS}}$ and its gap proof.

The certificate is accepted only when (I.13d.3) holds, the local high-acceleration projection satisfies $G(R)\to G_0$ with the solar-system residual bounded by $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{DS}}$, the CMB projection is inside its certified residual interval, and the homogeneous projection is either strict $\Lambda$ or the recorded finite-parameter conserved law.

**Theorem I.13e (Dark-Kernel Determinacy from Covariant Susceptibility).** If $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{DS}}$ is accepted, then the galaxy response kernel, cluster/lensing response, conserved stress-energy tensor, anisotropic-stress projection, merger and cluster limits, local-gravity limit, CMB-era behavior, homogeneous late-time law, RCD-Buchert-Cheeger backreaction bound, elliptic scale bridge, predictive-stress variance, source-energy rate density, and finite defect budgets are deterministic outputs of the accepted susceptibility/effective-action branch, up to $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{DS}}$.

If $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{DS}}$ is absent, the acceleration-scale identity $g_\Lambda=c^2\sqrt\Lambda/8$ remains available only on an independently accepted Definition H.0 bridge-law branch; it is not thereby identified with a realized observable. The remaining galaxy, cluster, lensing, homogeneous, and backreaction data remain phenomenological or branch-classification data.

*Proof.* Items 2 and 3 supply a generally covariant action or retarded susceptibility with a conserved stress tensor. Items 5--10 are the finite projection maps to galaxy dynamics, lensing, clusters, local tests, CMB-era behavior, and homogeneous late-time evolution. Item 11 supplies the RCD-Buchert-Cheeger and elliptic scale bridge, while item 12 supplies the assumed unique minimizing response class $\Theta_{\mathrm{DS}}^*$ and strict PCE gap. Evaluating the registered projection maps on that selected response class gives the stated kernels and stress-energy components with residuals $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{DS}}$. Without an accepted $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{DS}}$, this conditional theorem supplies no dark-sector determinacy conclusion. Theorem P.14.1f proves non-identifiability when two admissible completions satisfying all prior constraints give inequivalent outputs. ∎

**Theorem I.13f (Harmonic Recoverability Realization of the Dark-Susceptibility Kernel).** Let $\mathcal D_B$ be a finite causal-diamond complex on a regular emergent metric branch, and choose a reference orientation set $E_+$ containing exactly one orientation of each retained unoriented inclusion edge. For $e:D_-\to D_+$ in $E_+$, let
$$
\Phi_{e,*}:\mathcal A(D_+)_{*}\to\mathcal A(B_e)_{*}
$$
be a linear Schrödinger-picture completely positive trace-preserving map on the finite-dimensional predual spaces, restricting to a channel between their convex state spaces. Equivalently, its Heisenberg adjoint $\Phi_e:\mathcal A(B_e)\to\mathcal A(D_+)$ is unital and completely positive. Let $\rho_{D_+}$ and $\omega_{D_+}$ be the retained state and a faithful local PCE/KMS reference state. Define
$$
J_{\mathrm{rec}}(e)
:=
D(\rho_{D_+}\Vert\omega_{D_+})
-
D(\Phi_{e,*}\rho_{D_+}\Vert\Phi_{e,*}\omega_{D_+})
\ge0
\qquad(e\in E_+),
\tag{I.13f.1}
$$
project the result to the retained response quotient, and define the reverse orientation by
$$
J_{\mathrm{rec}}(\bar e):=-J_{\mathrm{rec}}(e).
$$
Then $J_{\mathrm{rec}}\in C^1(\mathcal D_B)$ is an antisymmetric retained edge current. No global vertex potential is assumed.

Equip the finite cochain complex of $\mathcal D_B$ with the BKM/QFI inner products of the accepted local states and write the predictive Hodge decomposition of Theorem X.8l.2 as
$$
J_{\mathrm{rec}}
=d_0\phi+\delta_1\psi+h,
\qquad
h\in\ker\Delta_1.
\tag{I.13f.2}
$$
Assume that the accepted dark-susceptibility certificate $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{DS}}$ supplies all of the following harmonic realization data:

1. the stationary conditions
$$
d_1J_{\mathrm{rec}}=0,
\qquad
\delta_0J_{\mathrm{rec}}=0;
\tag{I.13f.6}
$$

2. invertibility of the compressed Schur operator
$$
\Lambda_h
:=
\left.\Pi_{\mathrm{harm}}\Lambda_\partial\Pi_{\mathrm{harm}}
\right|_{\ker\Delta_1},
\qquad
\mathcal K_{\mathrm{DS}}
=
\Pi_{\mathrm{harm}}\Lambda_h^{-1}\Pi_{\mathrm{harm}};
$$

3. a finite null-tomography record for the linear map
$$
\mathcal L_x:
\operatorname{Sym}^2(T_x^*M)\big/\operatorname{span}\{g\}
\longrightarrow\mathbb R^9,
\qquad
\mathcal L_x([S])_i=S_{\mu\nu}k_i^\mu k_i^\nu,
\tag{I.13f.3a}
$$
where $k_1,\ldots,k_9$ are null and $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal L_x=9$. The map is well defined because $g_{\mu\nu}k_i^\mu k_i^\nu=0$. Pointwise in an orthonormal Lorentz frame, one exact witness is
$$
\begin{aligned}
k_1&=(1,1,0,0),&k_2&=(1,-1,0,0),\\
k_3&=(1,0,1,0),&k_4&=(1,0,-1,0),\\
k_5&=(1,0,0,1),&k_6&=(1,0,0,-1),\\
k_7&=(1,\tfrac35,\tfrac45,0),&
k_8&=(1,\tfrac35,0,\tfrac45),&
k_9&=(1,0,\tfrac35,\tfrac45).
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13f.3b}
$$
In the quotient gauge $S_{00}=0$ and ordered coordinates
$$
(S_{01},S_{02},S_{03},S_{11},S_{22},S_{33},S_{12},S_{13},S_{23}),
$$
the exact determinant of the resulting $9\times9$ evaluation matrix is
$$
\det\mathcal L_x=-\frac{884736}{15625}\ne0.
\tag{I.13f.3c}
$$
The record also contains a specified linear harmonic-to-null-response map
$$
\mathscr Q_x:
\ker\Delta_1
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Quad}(\mathcal N_x),
\qquad
h\longmapsto\mathcal Q_h,
$$
where $\operatorname{Quad}(\mathcal N_x)$ denotes the real homogeneous quadratic functions on the retained null cone, with values of dimension $L^{-2}$. Its nine recorded responses satisfy
$$
8\pi G\,T^{\mathrm{DS}}_{\mu\nu}k_i^\mu k_i^\nu
=
\mathcal Q_h(k_i),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,9.
\tag{I.13f.3}
$$

4. a tenth scalar datum $\tau_{\mathrm{DS}}=g^{\mu\nu}T^{\mathrm{DS}}_{\mu\nu}$ compatible with the conservation law (I.13d.3) and the cosmological boundary ledger.

Then the rank-nine null-tomography map and the trace datum determine a unique symmetric tensor $T^{\mathrm{DS}}_{\mu\nu}$. The metric equation on this branch is
$$
G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}
=
8\pi G\bigl(T^{\mathrm{MPU}}_{\mu\nu}+T^{\mathrm{DS}}_{\mu\nu}\bigr),
\tag{I.13f.4}
$$
with $8\pi G$ replaced by $8\pi G/c^4$ in SI units. If $h=0$ and the ordinary-branch trace datum is $\tau_{\mathrm{DS}}=0$, then $T^{\mathrm{DS}}_{\mu\nu}=0$. The weak-field acceleration scale remains
$$
g_\Lambda=\frac{c^2\sqrt\Lambda}{8}.
\tag{I.13f.5}
$$

*Proof.* Data processing for the CPTP maps in (I.13f.1) gives the nonnegative reference-orientation slacks. Finiteness of $\mathcal D_B$ and positive definiteness of the supplied BKM/QFI quotient inner products give the orthogonal Hodge decomposition (I.13f.2) by Theorem X.8l.2.

The stationary conditions imply
$$
\langle\Delta_1J_{\mathrm{rec}},J_{\mathrm{rec}}\rangle
=
\|d_1J_{\mathrm{rec}}\|^2
+
\|\delta_0J_{\mathrm{rec}}\|^2
=0.
$$
Hence $J_{\mathrm{rec}}\in\ker\Delta_1$. Uniqueness of the orthogonal decomposition then gives $d_0\phi=0$, $\delta_1\psi=0$, and $J_{\mathrm{rec}}=h$. An exact current arising from one global vertex potential has zero harmonic projection, so it cannot yield a nonzero $h$.

Invertibility of $\Lambda_h$ makes $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{DS}}$ a well-defined finite operator on the harmonic subspace. Nullity of the nine vectors in (I.13f.3b) makes $\mathcal L_x$ well defined on the covariant quotient by $\operatorname{span}\{g\}$. Equation (I.13f.3c) proves that this map has rank $9$, equal to the quotient dimension, so the nine values in (I.13f.3) determine the trace-free covariant tensor class uniquely. The trace datum fixes the remaining multiple of $g_{\mu\nu}$, and (I.13d.3) verifies conservation compatibility. This proves uniqueness and the source equation (I.13f.4). If $h=0$, then every recorded $\mathcal Q_h(k_i)$ vanishes; together with $\tau_{\mathrm{DS}}=0$, injectivity gives $T^{\mathrm{DS}}_{\mu\nu}=0$. Equation (I.13f.5) is Corollary I.3a. ∎

**Corollary I.13g (Chern-Simons Inflow as a Dark-Susceptibility Subcertificate).** Let
$$
\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{CS}}
=
(\partial M,A,k,J_\partial,\mathcal G_{\mathrm{ret}},\chi_{\mathrm{CS}})
$$
be preregistered before cluster or lensing comparison. Suppose its variation supplies a conserved retained boundary current $J_\partial$, its anomaly variation cancels a retained boundary/interface anomaly without converting a gauge redundancy into a physical anomaly, and its retarded boundary-to-bulk map $\mathcal G_{\mathrm{ret}}$ supplies the susceptibility-kernel entry $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{DS}}$ of Definition I.13d. Then $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{CS}}$ is an admissible subcertificate for those entries only. Theorem I.13e applies if and only if the same branch also supplies every remaining entry and every acceptance condition in Definition I.13d, including bulk conservation (I.13d.3), the local, CMB, homogeneous, and backreaction projections, the residual ledger, the strict PCE minimizer, and the validation lock. A Chern-Simons term alone determines neither the cluster kernel $K$ nor the exponent $q$ in Equation I.7.

*Proof.* The stated variation and anomaly hypotheses provide a boundary current and a retarded boundary-to-bulk map. They do not provide the remaining entries enumerated in Definition I.13d.
