The positive slice energy consists of the time and spatial derivative squares and $(1+v)|Y_v|^2$. The derivative of the mass term cancels the leading $vY_v$ term from the equation. The variations of slice volume, lapse, spatial metric and the fixed positive fiber norm are bounded multiples of the same energy, including its mass term. The lower-order terms are controlled by the $v$-independent parts of the energy. Thus the derivative of the energy square root is at most a fixed constant times itself plus a fixed multiple of $\|J\|_{L^2(\Sigma_t)}$. The zero initial energy and Grönwall's inequality prove (I.13m.a.5). This is an estimate for the auxiliary wave equations using a positive analytical norm. It does not give positivity of the action's energy.

Let $\mathcal B_v(g)[k]$ denote the metric variation of $\int\mathcal L_v\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$ at a smooth compactly supported metric test $k$, holding $X_v,\phi_v$ fixed during variation and then evaluating the solutions. Integrate the rough wave term by parts before taking this local variation. The variations of curvature are linear in $k,\nabla k,\nabla^2k$, multiplied by $Y_v$. The remaining terms are contractions of $\nabla Y_v\,\nabla Y_v$, $Y_v\nabla Y_v$, $Y_v^2$, and $vY_v^2$, multiplied by bounded coefficient tensors using $k$ and its first derivatives. For the tensor field this includes the variation of the connection in $\nabla X_v$. The fixed slab estimates and Cauchy–Schwarz thus give
$$
|\mathcal B_v(g)[k]|\le C_{g,T}\|k\|_{C^2},
\tag{I.13m.a.6}
$$
uniformly in $v$. The constant may include the fixed curvature-source norms. No differentiation of the retarded solution with respect to the test metric is used in this Euler pairing.

On every bounded mass interval $[0,M]$, $\mathcal B_v(g)[k]$ is Lipschitz in $v$ with constant $C_{g,T,M}\|k\|_{C^2}$. In fact $Y_v-Y_u$ has zero data and solves
$$
(\Box_g-v)(Y_v-Y_u)=(v-u)Y_u .
$$
Apply (I.13m.a.5) and the uniform bound for $Y_u$, then use the bilinear difference identity for each quadratic term of the metric variation. For the mass term use $vY_v^2-uY_u^2=(v-u)Y_u^2+v(Y_v^2-Y_u^2)$, with $v\le M$. This also proves the asserted continuity of the pairing at $v=0$.

Partition $[0,M]$ into finitely many Borel cells of diameter at most $\eta$ and assign each cell's $\rho_A$ mass to one of its points. Place the tail mass at $0$ for a mass-preserving approximation. The quadrature error in the Euler pairing is bounded by
$$
\left|\int \mathcal B_v(g)[k]\rho_A(dv)-\int\mathcal B_v(g)[k]\rho_n(dv)\right|
\le\|k\|_{C^2}
\left[q_A C_{g,T,M}\eta+2C_{g,T}\rho_A((M,\infty))\right].
\tag{I.13m.a.7}
$$
Choose $M\uparrow\infty$ and refine each mesh sufficiently at that stage. The resulting finite-bank responses converge distributionally on the slab, with no assumed first moment of $\rho_A$. The integral defines the same response independently of the approximants. Equivalently first take the limit of the tails on a fixed test and then take weak approximations on each bounded mass interval. Conservation passes to the limit by (I.13m.a.4). Causal locality and covariance also pass to the integral, since both hold for every mass. This proves the nonlinear conserved response claim on prescribed metric histories.

*Minkowski symbol and retarded normalization.* At flat space all background auxiliary fields are zero. In the metric Euler tensor linearization their only surviving contributions come from varying the curvature terms of (I.13m.a.1) against their linear retarded solutions. For the bilinear calculation the same normalization can be read from the formally eliminated quadratic curvature combination
$$
\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}F_n(\Box)\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}
-\tfrac12 R^{(1)}F_n(\Box)R^{(1)},\qquad
F_n(s)=\sum_j\frac{w_j}{s-v_j}-\frac{q_A}{s}.
\tag{I.13m.a.8}
$$
This formula computes the symbol and does not prescribe a single-history retarded Hessian. In the equation each denominator means the corresponding zero-past Green operator, because it comes from (I.13m.a.3). On a transverse representative $\partial^\mu h_{\mu\nu}=0$, with $h=\eta^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu}$, one has
$$
R^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}=-\tfrac12(\Box h_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h),
\qquad R^{(1)}=-\Box h .
$$
The cross terms between $\Box h_{\mu\nu}$ and $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h$ integrate to zero by transversality. Two integrations by parts give the scalar contraction of the latter with itself as $(\Box h)F_n(\Box)(\Box h)$. Thus (I.13m.a.8) on transverse fields is
$$
\tfrac14(\Box h_{\mu\nu})F_n(\Box)(\Box h^{\mu\nu})
-\tfrac14(\Box h)F_n(\Box)(\Box h).
$$
The quadratic part of $2\int R\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$ on that representative is $+\tfrac12\int h_{\mu\nu}\Box h^{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12\int h\Box h$ in the usual Ricci convention above. To see the sign, varying the Einstein–Hilbert action with respect to covariant metric components gives $-2G^{\mu\nu}$, and its linearization on a transverse field gives $+\Box h^{\mu\nu}-\eta^{\mu\nu}\Box h+\partial^\mu\partial^\nu h$. Equation (I.13j.1) normalizes its gravitational quadratic form with the opposite sign. The Einstein term $-2\int R\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$ in (I.13m.a.2) therefore contributes the $a=c=1$ kinetic form of (I.13j.1) with the source convention there. In (I.13m.a.2) the curvature bilinear is multiplied by $-2$. Therefore the resulting form factors are
$$
a_n(s)=c_n(s)=1+sF_n(s)
=\frac1{1+A}+s\sum_j\frac{w_j}{s-v_j}.
\tag{I.13m.a.9}
$$
Equivalently the spin-zero eigenvalue is $a_n-3c_n=-2a_n$. Gauge invariance supplies the full operator on arbitrary perturbations. In the zero-past equation this identity also follows by commuting the flat retarded wave resolvents with the derivatives in the linear Ricci variations, so the identification uses the common causal prescription at singular frequencies. The finite weights sum to $q_A$, explaining the constant $1-q_A=1/(1+A)$ and the sign of the massless compensator. The finite-slab flat resolvent estimates of Theorem I.13l and the same bounded-mass quadrature imply convergence to
$$
a(s)=c(s)=\frac1{1+A}+s\int\frac{\rho_A(dv)}{s-v}=\frac1{\mu(s)}
$$
as the retarded equation on its zero-past source class. In this flat linear limit, its inverse and the weak-field potentials are those already derived in Theorems I.13l.a and I.13j. This proves matching of both linear spin eigenvalues on the nonlinear covariant parent branch. It supplies no positivity representation of the combined tensor action, no coupled nonlinear evolution for the metric, and no nonlinear projection onto the common galaxy, cluster, lensing, CMB and homogeneous observables of Definition I.13d. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mb"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mb-finite-time-passivity-obstruction-and-sharp-two-port-spectral-cost"></a>**Theorem I.13m.b (Finite-Time Passivity Obstruction and Sharp Two-Port Spectral Cost).** Use the flat no-slip Weibull response of Theorem I.13l.a with $0<m\le1$ and $A>0$. Fix a real normalized transverse-traceless spatial Fourier mode of wave number $k>0$, with light speed one and the source-to-response normalization of that theorem. The signed propagator cannot be realized as the linear response of a passive single port whose drive and readout are conjugate in the work ledger. A real compact-time force and an explicit negative margin certify the obstruction. Any positive oscillator realization with independent real source and detector ports has a sharp, nonzero lower bound on the sum of its diagonal spectral residues. Its uncoupled ground-state realization attains the corresponding minimum noise in that oscillator class.

*Work convention and the actual signed response.* Write $\Omega_v=\sqrt{k^2+v}$ and $K_v(t)=\mathbf1_{t\ge0}\sin(\Omega_v t)/\Omega_v$. The retarded operator (I.13l.1) on this spatial mode is $G_v=-K_v*$, where $*$ is time convolution. Define the drive force by the convention in which the massless Einstein component has positive work, namely $f$ couples as $H_{\rm int}=-f(t)X$ at a reciprocal port. With the common overall source sign and coupling absorbed in $f$ and its conjugate readout, the transferred response is
$$
X_f(t)=\int (K_v*f)(t)\,dW(v),\qquad
W=(1+A)\delta_0-A\sigma_m .
\tag{I.13m.b.1}
$$
Here $\sigma_m$ is the probability in (I.13l.a.3), supported on $(0,\infty)$. In particular the signs in (I.13m.b.1) follow from (I.13l.a.4) with the same overall sign on the massless and massive terms, and the massive weight has the opposite sign to the calibrated positive massless pole. A real normalized spatial mode can be taken on a periodic flat box because the prescribed translation-invariant wave resolvents act on each Fourier mode separately. Equivalently one can compare this individual real mode of the source and detector of Theorem I.13l.d. The comparison fixes the spatial mode, clock and readout normalization throughout.

For a cyclic force supported inside $[0,T]$, write $\widehat f(\omega)=\int e^{i\omega t}f(t)\,dt$. The work done on the driven system is $-\int f'(t)X_f(t)\,dt=\int f(t)\dot X_f(t)\,dt$. For a positive unit oscillator with response $K_v*f$, the latter is the final oscillator energy. Directly, its position and velocity at the end of the pulse are the sine and cosine integrals, with the position multiplied by $\Omega_v$ in the energy. Thus its energy is $|\widehat f(\Omega_v)|^2/2$. By linearity in the signed measure,
$$
\mathcal W(f)=
\frac12(1+A)|\widehat f(k)|^2
-\frac A2\int_{(0,\infty)}|\widehat f(\Omega_v)|^2\,\sigma_m(dv).
\tag{I.13m.b.2}
$$
The integral is justified by $|\widehat f|\le\|f\|_1$ and finite total variation. No absolute value is taken on the negative massive contribution. The force normalization can equally be expressed with the fixed positive Einstein coupling retained as one common positive prefactor multiplying this work formula.

*Finite pulse with a certified margin.* Choose a compact interval $[v_1,v_2]\subset(0,\infty)$ with positive $\sigma_m$ mass. For $m=1$ it can be chosen inside $(L^{-2},\infty)$, and for $m<1$ every such nonempty interval has positive mass by Theorem I.13l.a. Set $T>0$ so that $T\sqrt{k^2+v_2}\le\pi/3$. Choose a nonzero nonnegative real $g\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and put
$$
f=g''+k^2g .
\tag{I.13m.b.3}
$$
Integration by parts gives $\widehat f(\omega)=(k^2-\omega^2)\widehat g(\omega)$, so the positive massless contribution to (I.13m.b.2) is exactly zero. On the chosen mass interval the real part of $\widehat g(\Omega_v)$ is at least $\tfrac12\int g$. Consequently
$$
\mathcal W(f)\le
-\frac{A v_1^2}{8}\,\sigma_m([v_1,v_2])
 \left(\int g\right)^2
=:-\mathcal M<0 .
\tag{I.13m.b.4}
$$
This is a finite pulse on the declared mode. It uses no asymptotic static extrapolation.

For a finite spectral bank approximating $\sigma_m$, partition its part in $(0,V]$ into cells of mass-squared diameter at most $\eta$ and send the remaining mass to one representative. Put the positive massless residue at zero exactly as in (I.13m.b.1). The bound $|\partial_v K_v(t)|\le t^3/6$ for $t\ge0$ follows by differentiating the cosine integral for $K_v$, including the continuous derivative at zero. Also $|K_v(t)|\le t$. Hence on $[0,T]$ the finite and exact readouts satisfy
$$
\sup_t|X_{f,n}(t)-X_f(t)|
\le A\|f\|_1\left(\frac{T^3\eta}{6}
                    +2T\,\sigma_m((V,\infty))\right).
\tag{I.13m.b.5}
$$
Their work discrepancy is at most this bound times $\|f'\|_1$. Taking the latter product smaller than $\mathcal M/2$ preserves strict negative work on the same finite window. Other uniform readout errors on this window enter with the same factor $\|f'\|_1$.

For a passive port, every cyclic work input has nonnegative work. In particular if a passive response is defined as the first variation under $H_{\rm int}=-\epsilon fX$, its work at small amplitude is $\epsilon^2\mathcal W(f)+o(\epsilon^2)$. The linear term from the stationary unperturbed readout integrates to zero because the force returns to zero. A negative value (I.13m.b.4) contradicts passivity for all sufficiently small positive amplitudes. This implication uses a regular linear response and applies in particular to a ground-state unitary source, where a cyclic drive leaves the same undriven Hamiltonian and its expectation cannot fall below the initial ground energy. Uniform finite-window limits of such passive linear responses also have nonnegative work by the continuity estimate above. Thus they cannot equal the transfer in (I.13m.b.1). The conclusion concerns a work-conjugate drive and readout at the same port.

*Sharp spectral cost of two distinct ports.* In a positive oscillator bank let $Q_v,P_v$ be canonical unit-mass coordinates for frequency $\Omega_v$, with positive free energy $(P_v^2+\Omega_v^2Q_v^2)/2$. A set of independent copies at the same frequency is allowed. For real coefficients $b_v,c_v$ let the source port use $X_s=\sum b_v Q_v$ and the detector port use $X_d=\sum c_v Q_v$, with sums replaced by the named finite-measure realization if a continuum is used. The drives enter the Hamiltonian with $-f_sX_s-f_dX_d$. Then the spectral residues of the ordered responses $(X_s,X_d)$ to $(f_s,f_d)$ are the positive semidefinite measure of rank-one contributions
$$
d\mathsf M=
\begin{pmatrix}dM_{ss}&dM_{sd}\\dM_{ds}&dM_{dd}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(b_v,c_v)^{\mathsf T}
(b_v,c_v)
\quad\text{per copy}.
\tag{I.13m.b.6}
$$
In particular the source-to-detector residue is the real product $c_vb_v$, and the reverse response has its adjoint product $b_vc_v$. A negative cross residue can be made by opposite coefficient signs without a negative free energy. The two diagonal residues are $b_v^2,c_v^2$ and are positive. If an oscillator completion realizes (I.13m.b.1), its cross spectral measure is $W$. Indeed the retarded time kernel uniquely determines its finite mass measure at fixed $k$: differentiating for positive times yields the cosine transform of its pushforward under the injective map $v\mapsto\Omega_v$. Uniqueness of the Fourier transform of its even finite extension gives the measure.

More generally for any positive two-port residue measure with off-diagonal measure $W$, take densities with respect to the dominating trace measure $M_{ss}+M_{dd}$. Positivity makes the two diagonal densities nonnegative and their product at least the squared magnitude of the off-diagonal density almost everywhere. The pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality therefore gives
$$
dM_{ss}+dM_{dd}\ \ge\ 2\,|dW|.
\tag{I.13m.b.7}
$$
The statement is an inequality of measures on every Borel mass band. It holds also with complex coefficients and the adjoint off-diagonal entries. For the real measure (I.13m.b.1), one oscillator coordinate per mass with coefficient vector $(1,\operatorname{sgn}dW)$ and reference measure $|W|$ realizes equality, using positive free energy. At a discrete atom $w$ these coefficients in unit counting measure are $\sqrt{|w|}$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)\sqrt{|w|}$. The finite approximants can therefore attain (I.13m.b.7) at every stage. In particular the sum of total diagonal residues is at least $2(1+2A)$, with a massive contribution at least $2A$. Equality in the measure bound requires equal diagonal densities and rank one on the cross support, and no extra diagonal support. The distinct-port completion has a positive full matrix even though its selected scalar cross entry fails the single-port work test.

For the quantum canonical oscillator class in an uncoupled stationary ground state, the centered symmetrized equal-time variance of a unit coordinate is $\hbar/(2\Omega_v)$. In a stationary number-state mixture it is $\hbar(2n_v+1)/(2\Omega_v)$ with $n_v\ge0$. For independent modes or uncorrelated number-state mixtures this gives, on every mass band $B$, the sum of the two diagonal symmetrized variances bounded below by
$$
\hbar\int_B\frac{|dW(v)|}{\sqrt{k^2+v}} .
\tag{I.13m.b.8}
$$
The balanced rank-one ground-state completion above attains it. This noise statement specifies the state and oscillator class used. The residue inequality itself needs only the positive matrix measure and makes no assumption about noise in a more general device.

The passive work test and the additional positive residues apply to a fixed signed transfer on a declared flat source mode. Coupled covariant metric evolution, a nonlinear realization of the two-port bank and the common-source cosmological projections in Definition I.13d require their own source dynamics. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mc"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mc-positive-two-port-clock-bank-coupled-to-einstein-evolution"></a>**Theorem I.13m.c (Positive Two-Port Clock Bank Coupled to Einstein Evolution).** Retain the signed mass measure $W=(1+A)\delta_0-A\sigma_m$ of Theorem I.13m.b. Its finite approximations can be realized by a generally covariant local matter system with a dynamical scalar clock, dynamical source field and positive oscillator energies on a uniform open field domain. Each finite system admits causal local Einstein–matter evolution from smooth constraint-satisfying Cauchy data, with conserved total matter stress. For every fixed finite mass cutoff there is also a coupled local continuum bank obtained as the strong limit of finite banks on a common time interval. With zero initial oscillator data, the independent material detector on each bank has the exact signed conditional transfer from the actual clock and source fields on the evolving metric. The full unbounded spectral transfer is obtained on prescribed smooth histories. These statements concern distinct material source and detector ports.

*Covariant local action and positivity.* Let the signed finite bank have nonzero atoms $w_j$ at squared masses $v_j\ge0$. Put $b_j=\sqrt{|w_j|}$ and $c_j=\operatorname{sgn}(w_j)b_j$. Use real scalar fields $C$ (clock), $\chi$ (source), and $\Phi_j$ (bank), with target metric and potential
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf G
 &=dC^2+d\chi^2+\sum_j d\Phi_j^2
          +2\chi\,dC\sum_j b_j\,d\Phi_j,\\
V&=\tfrac12 m_\chi^2\chi^2+\tfrac12\sum_j v_j\Phi_j^2,\qquad
m_\chi^2\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.c.1}
$$
Here the mixed term is the symmetric tensor product with components $\mathsf G_{Cj}=\mathsf G_{jC}=\chi b_j$. The gravitational action is $\int R\,d\mathrm{vol}_g/(16\pi G)$ in the ordinary positive-energy Einstein convention. The matter action has density $-\tfrac12\mathsf G_{AB}(Y)g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu Y^A\partial_\nu Y^B-V(Y)$ for $Y=(C,\chi,\Phi)$. No spacetime frame is supplied. The clock is a scalar field varied in the action. Units for the target fields and couplings are fixed so that $\chi b_j$ is dimensionless and $v_j$ has inverse-length-squared units.

The target eigenvalues are $1\pm|\chi|\|b\|_2$ on the two-dimensional clock and coupled bank subspace, and $1$ on the remaining directions. On the domain $|\chi|\|b\|_2\le1-\epsilon$ with $\epsilon>0$, its quadratic form is at least $\epsilon$ times the canonical norm. The matter energy in a unit-normal frame is the sum of half the positive target norms of normal and spatial gradients and $V$, and is nonnegative. The massless atom is allowed because the signed cross coefficient is carried by the readout, while the local source coupling is derivative mixing in the positive kinetic metric. In particular there is no negative mass potential to compensate that atom.

*Local causal evolution and a nontrivial branch.* The scalar equations have the normally hyperbolic principal part $\Box_g Y^A$ after multiplying by the inverse target metric. Their remaining terms are the target Christoffel contractions of first derivatives and the raised potential gradient. The stress in the Einstein equation is algebraic in $g,Y,\partial Y$. In wave coordinates the coupled equations are quasilinear wave equations with the same Lorentzian principal symbol. The local energy iteration for this system gives a unique local development in wave gauge from smooth constraint-satisfying data in a strict subdomain of the positive target metric. The development is unique up to the induced coordinate changes and has the metric domain of dependence. Matter conservation follows directly from its covariant action and the scalar equations. It implies the homogeneous wave equation for the wave-gauge constraint from the contracted Bianchi identity. The Einstein constraints and the initial gauge conditions set both initial gauge data to zero, so the reduced development solves the full equations. The positive field domain and a timelike initial clock gradient persist for a short time by continuity. See Choquet-Bruhat (2008).

For example choose a flat spatial three-torus initially, spatially constant data $C=\chi=\Phi=0$, normal derivatives $nC=c_0\ne0$, $n\chi=d_0\ne0$, $n\Phi=0$, and extrinsic curvature $K_{ij}=H\gamma_{ij}$ where $\gamma$ is the flat induced metric. The momentum constraints vanish because the spatial field gradients and the spatial derivatives of $K$ vanish. The matter energy is $(c_0^2+d_0^2)/2$, so the Hamiltonian constraint is satisfied by $6H^2=8\pi G(c_0^2+d_0^2)$. These data are independent of the masses and bank size. They give a dynamical metric and clock, and a nonzero initial drive in the detector calculation below.

*Exact on-shell conditional transfer.* In the signature $(-,+,+,+)$, variation in each $\Phi_j$ gives
$$
(\Box_g-v_j)\Phi_j=-b_j f,\qquad
f=\nabla_\mu(\chi\nabla^\mu C).
\tag{I.13m.c.2}
$$
On the actual solution use zero field and normal derivative for $\Phi$ on the past Cauchy slice. Then $\Phi_j=-b_jG^g_{v_j}f$ with the retarded scalar Green operator of $\Box_g-v_j$ and this past condition. The detector $D=\sum_j c_j\Phi_j$ has the exact readout
$$
D=-\sum_j w_jG^g_{v_j}f.
\tag{I.13m.c.3}
$$
The drive $f$ is the same covariant source functional for every mass. For the homogeneous initial data above it is initially $-c_0d_0$, since $\chi=0$ there. On a flat comparison history with $C=t$, $f=-\partial_t\chi$, and $-G_v$ has the sign of the oscillator kernel in Theorem I.13m.b. Thus (I.13m.c.3) gives its signed transfer from $f$ to the independent material detector, including the massless residue. On a coupled solution $f$ is generated by the actual clock and source fields, including their response to the bank. The response (I.13m.c.3) uses the resulting dynamical source functional and a material detector. Driving the detector as its own conjugate force uses its positive diagonal residue.

*Coupled continuum with finite mass cutoff.* Fix $M>0$ and let $W^{[M]}$ be the restriction of $W$ to $[0,M]$, including its massless atom. Let $\nu=|W^{[M]}|$ and $\mathcal H=L^2([0,M],\nu;\mathbb R)$. Replace the finite bank coordinates by $\Phi\in\mathcal H$, the coupling $\sum b_jd\Phi_j$ by $\langle\mathbf1,d\Phi\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, and the detector by $\langle\operatorname{sgn} W^{[M]},\Phi\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. The bank potential is $\langle\Phi,V_M\Phi\rangle_{\mathcal H}/2$, where $V_M$ is multiplication by $v$. The target metric and its inverse are bounded positive operators on the same strict branch, since $\|\mathbf1\|^2=\nu([0,M])\le1+2A$. The derivatives of the inverse are bounded on a smaller positive domain, and the potential gradient uses a bounded operator of norm at most $M$.

Take finite partitions of the mass interval with mesh at most $\eta$, separating the massless atom. Replace $V_M$ by multiplication by a chosen constant in each cell. Its operator-norm error is at most $\eta$. On zero bank initial data the cell-constant subspace is invariant: the bank equation (I.13m.c.2) has cell-constant coefficients and a common source, so the orthogonal complement solves the homogeneous zero-data equations. The induced finite action is (I.13m.c.1) with canonical coordinates $\Phi_j=\sqrt{\nu_j}$ times the cell value, and $b_j=\sqrt{\nu_j}$. Choose each cell inside one sign sector, so the detector has exactly the corresponding signed atom.

Here is the uniform local estimate underlying the limit. On a compact initial slice choose integer Sobolev order $s\ge5$, smooth common constraint data, and zero initial bank field and normal derivative. On a bounded $H^s\times H^{s-1}$ neighborhood with a strict positive target bound and uniformly spacelike slices, the linear energy for the reduced wave system controls $H^s$ fields and $H^{s-1}$ time derivatives. The constants in the Sobolev product and differentiated energy estimates are independent of the dimension of the bank subspace: pointwise target contractions are bounded by the product of Hilbert norms, the product estimates follow by Leibniz and spatial Sobolev embedding, and the target inverse and its derivatives use bounded rank-one operators with norms controlled by $\|\mathbf1\|$. The linear mass term is bounded in the same Sobolev spaces by $M$. The reduced Einstein source uses only the same Hilbert inner products. Applying the usual wave iteration with these bounds gives a common existence interval for all the cell-constant systems. The initial Einstein constraints are identical for these systems because the zero bank data contribute neither kinetic nor potential stress there.

Subtract the reduced wave equations of two such systems in their common coordinate gauge. The wave energy one derivative below the existence order bounds their solution difference by its initial difference, its own time integral with a common bounded coefficient, and the time integral of the operator-norm difference of their mass multipliers times a common bounded field norm. This follows by subtracting the principal coefficients as well: the resulting forcing is the metric difference times a second derivative of one solution, controlled at the lower order by the common higher-order bound. Grönwall's inequality gives a bound $C_{M,T}(\eta+\eta')$ for the differences in $C_tH^{s-1}$ and for the time derivatives in $C_tH^{s-2}$. Thus the systems converge strongly on a common interval, including the metric, clock, source, detector and stress. The limit satisfies the reduced equations with $V_M$ by this strong convergence and the operator-norm limit. The gauge constraints and covariant stress conservation pass to it by the same convergence. The energy argument also gives uniqueness in the common class. In this cutoff continuum, (I.13m.c.3) is the mass integral against $W^{[M]}$ on the actual local development.

*Full measure on a specified history.* On a fixed smooth compact-Cauchy metric slab with fixed smooth $C,\chi$, the uniform auxiliary wave estimate (I.13m.a.5) bounds $\|G^g_v f\|_{C_tL^2}$ independently of $v$. The difference equation for two masses gives a Lipschitz bound on every compact mass interval. Thus replacing each cell by one representative incurs $C_{g,T,M}\eta\,|W|([0,M])\|f\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}$ in the detector norm, and omitting the tail incurs $C_{g,T}|W|((M,\infty))\|f\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}$. These errors tend to zero by truncation and refinement and give the full conditional transfer $-\int G^g_v f\,W(dv)$. No positive first moment of the mass measure is required for this response limit. The coupled existence interval and stability estimates above are for fixed $M$. A common coupled limit as $M$ tends to infinity requires mass-uniform estimates. A metric self-response with the Weibull factors, tensor source maps and the nonlinear cosmological projections of Definition I.13d remain separate conditions. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13md"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13md-unbounded-mass-coupled-homogeneous-clock-bank"></a>**Theorem I.13m.d (Unbounded-Mass Coupled Homogeneous Clock Bank).** Use the positive clock and two material ports of Theorem I.13m.c. Take the full signed mass measure $W=(1+A)\delta_0-A\sigma_m$ and put $\nu=|W|$, $\mathcal H=L^2([0,\infty),\nu;\mathbb R)$, $e=\mathbf1$ and $d=\operatorname{sgn}W$. Let $V$ be the nonnegative self-adjoint multiplication by $v$ in $\mathcal H$. No first moment of $\nu$ is assumed. In the spatially flat homogeneous sector on a compact three-torus, there is a nontrivial zero-past branch of the coupled Einstein, clock, source and bank system on a common time interval. Finite positive banks with mass cutoff $M$ and compact mass mesh at most $\eta$ converge to it. On a sufficiently short fixed interval the metric, source and clock converge with their first derivatives, and the bank converges in displacement, velocity and positive mass-energy norms, with error bounded by
$$
C_T\left(\eta+\sqrt{\nu((M,\infty))}\right).
\tag{I.13m.d.1}
$$
The branch has conserved total stress and the exact full-measure signed detector on its own evolving metric. The coupled construction applies to homogeneous data and gives the distinct material detector response.

*Homogeneous equations and initial constraints.* Write the metric as $-dt^2+a(t)^2d\mathbf x^2$ on the flat torus, with $a>0$ and $H=\dot a/a$. Use $C(t)$, $\chi(t)$, $\Phi(t)\in\mathcal H$. The homogeneous kinetic expression from (I.13m.c.1) is
$$
\frac12\left(\dot C^2+\dot\chi^2+\|\dot\Phi\|^2
        +2\chi\dot C\,\langle e,\dot\Phi\rangle\right)
$$
and the potential is $(m_\chi^2\chi^2+\|V^{1/2}\Phi\|^2)/2$. Denote these by $\mathcal K$ and $\mathcal U$, and put $\mathcal R=\mathcal K+\mathcal U$, $\mathcal P=\mathcal K-\mathcal U$. The pressure here is $\mathcal P$, distinct from the conserved scalar clock momentum $P$. The Einstein equations are
$$
\dot a=aH,\qquad
\dot H=-8\pi G\,\mathcal K,\qquad
3H^2=8\pi G\,\mathcal R .
\tag{I.13m.d.2}
$$
The homogeneous fields have action with common factor $a^3$. Since $C$ is cyclic,
$$
P=a^3(\dot C+\chi\langle e,\dot\Phi\rangle)
$$
is constant. Write $B(\chi)=I-\chi^2|e\rangle\langle e|$. Substituting $\dot C=P/a^3-\chi\langle e,\dot\Phi\rangle$ into the other equations gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
B\ddot\Phi+(3HB+\dot B)\dot\Phi+V\Phi
 &=-P a^{-3}\dot\chi\, e,\\
\ddot\chi+3H\dot\chi+m_\chi^2\chi
 &=\dot C\,\langle e,\dot\Phi\rangle .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.d.3}
$$
For the first line, the momentum per physical volume before eliminating $C$ is $\dot\Phi+\chi\dot C e=B\dot\Phi+Pa^{-3}\chi e$. Its equation is the time derivative plus $3H$ times itself, plus $V\Phi=0$. This also checks the sign of the bank forcing.

Take $a(0)=a_0>0$, $\chi(0)=C(0)=0$, $\dot C(0)=c_0\ne0$, $\dot\chi(0)=d_0\ne0$, and $\Phi(0)=\dot\Phi(0)=0$. Set $P=a_0^3c_0$ and choose the expanding $H(0)>0$ with $6H(0)^2=8\pi G(c_0^2+d_0^2)$. These are the homogeneous constraint data of Theorem I.13m.c. The momentum constraint vanishes, and the displayed relation imposes the Hamiltonian constraint. The same data work for every bank. The actual initial detector drive is nonzero, because $f=-a^{-3}\partial_t(a^3\chi\dot C)$ starts at $-c_0d_0$.

*Finite banks on one carrier and first energy bound.* For a cutoff $M$ let $e_M=\mathbf1_{[0,M]}e$. Partition $[0,M]$ into cells of diameter at most $\eta$, separating the massless atom. Let $V_{M,\eta}$ multiply by one mass representative in each cell below the cutoff and by the actual $v$ above it. Define the finite-bank detector direction as $d_M=\mathbf1_{[0,M]}d$. On the cell-constant subspace supported below the cutoff, these data give precisely the finite actions of Theorem I.13m.c after rescaling the cell values by the square roots of their masses. This subspace is invariant under the kinetic rank-one operator and the potential operator, and the zero-data tail is identically zero. Thus every finite-bank solution can be viewed in the same $\mathcal H$. Its positive target bound is uniform for $|\chi|\|e\|\le1-\epsilon$.

For a finite bank the scalar equations give the exact matter energy identity
$$
\dot{\mathcal R}=-6H\mathcal K=-3H(\mathcal R+\mathcal P).
\tag{I.13m.d.4}
$$
It follows by pairing each field equation with its velocity, including the derivative of the target metric in the kinetic energy. Differentiating the Einstein constraint in (I.13m.d.2) and using (I.13m.d.4) shows its preservation under the first two equations in (I.13m.d.2). With $H(0)>0$ there is a common short time on which $H$ stays positive and $a$ stays bounded away from zero: during positivity, $\mathcal R$ is nonincreasing and $|\dot H|\le 8\pi G\mathcal R(0)$. The positive target norm then bounds all velocities and the bank mass energy uniformly. Choose the interval shorter if necessary so that $|\chi|\|e\|\le1-\epsilon$ persists by integrating the velocity bound, using $\chi(0)=0$. These estimates and the finite-dimensional continuation theorem give a common existence interval, independent of the cutoff and the number of cells. They also bound $\ddot\chi$ and $\dot H$ by (I.13m.d.2)–(I.13m.d.3), without requiring $Ve\in\mathcal H$.

*One differentiated wave energy.* For a finite bank write $Z=\dot\Phi$ and $F=-Pa^{-3}\dot\chi\,e_M$. Differentiate its first line in (I.13m.d.3). With $B=I-\chi^2|e_M\rangle\langle e_M|$ one obtains
$$
B\ddot Z+(3HB+2\dot B)\dot Z+V_{M,\eta}Z
=\dot F-(3\dot H B+3H\dot B+\ddot B)Z .
\tag{I.13m.d.5}
$$
The coefficients $B,\dot B,\ddot B,H,\dot H$ and the norm of $\dot F$ are bounded uniformly by the first energy bound and the $\chi$ equation. At time zero $Z=0$ and $\dot Z=-Pa_0^{-3}d_0 e_M$, since $B(0)=I$. Pair (I.13m.d.5) with $\dot Z$ in $\mathcal H$. The derivative of the positive energy
$$
\tfrac12\langle\dot Z,B\dot Z\rangle
+\tfrac12\|V_{M,\eta}^{1/2}Z\|^2+\tfrac12\|Z\|^2
$$
is bounded by a constant times this energy plus a fixed constant from $\dot F$. The mass term differentiates exactly, and $\dot B$ is a bounded operator. Grönwall's inequality bounds $\ddot\Phi$ and $V_{M,\eta}^{1/2}\dot\Phi$ uniformly. The undifferentiated bank equation then bounds $V_{M,\eta}\Phi$ in $\mathcal H$. All these bounds also hold with $V$ in place of $V_{M,\eta}$ up to constants for $\eta\le1$, because their difference is bounded by $\eta$ on the entire common carrier. In particular the argument never applies $V^{1/2}$ or $V$ to the direction $e$.

*Strong convergence in the coupled equations.* Consider two finite approximants on the common carrier, with indices $i,j$, masses $V_i,V_j$ and directions $e_i,e_j$. Write the first bank equation as
$$
B_i\ddot\Phi_i+(3H_iB_i+\dot B_i)\dot\Phi_i+V\Phi_i
=F_i+(V-V_i)\Phi_i .
$$
Subtract the two equations using $B_i$ and $V$ on the left. All forcing terms are bounded in $\mathcal H$ by a fixed constant times the differences of $a,H,\chi,\dot\chi$, the bank energy difference, and
$$
\eta_i+\eta_j+\|e_i-e_j\|.
$$
For the leading kinetic coefficient difference this follows because $(B_i-B_j)\ddot\Phi_j$ has bounded $\ddot\Phi_j$ by the preceding estimate. The differences of $\dot B$ are bounded by the differences of $\chi,\dot\chi$ and the source directions. The potential perturbations are bounded directly by $\|V-V_i\|\le\eta_i$. The scalar clock velocities satisfy the same Lipschitz estimate by the formula for $P$. The two Einstein equations for $a,H$ and the source equation for $\chi$ are Lipschitz in these scalar differences and the bank displacement and velocity differences on the uniform bounded set. Their right sides use the kinetic energy and clock velocity. If the constraint is used instead, the mass norm is also controlled by the bank energy difference.

Pair the difference bank equation with its velocity difference, using the positive $B_i$ energy with common mass term $\|V^{1/2}(\Phi_i-\Phi_j)\|^2$ and added displacement term $\|\Phi_i-\Phi_j\|^2$. The derivative estimate for its square root, combined with the scalar difference equations and the common initial data, gives by Grönwall
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(&|a_i-a_j|+|H_i-H_j|
 +|\chi_i-\chi_j|+|\dot\chi_i-\dot\chi_j|
 +|C_i-C_j|+|\dot C_i-\dot C_j|\\
 &+\|\Phi_i-\Phi_j\|+\|\dot\Phi_i-\dot\Phi_j\|
 +\|V^{1/2}(\Phi_i-\Phi_j)\|\big)
 \le C_T(\eta_i+\eta_j+\|e_i-e_j\|).
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.d.6}
$$
The common carrier allows this pairing without a projection error. In fact the two solutions vanish outside their respective finite cutoff sets and their difference belongs to the domain of $V$ at every finite comparison. Also $\|e_i-e_j\|\le\sqrt{\nu((M_i,\infty))}+\sqrt{\nu((M_j,\infty))}$. This proves strong convergence and (I.13m.d.1) for each finite approximation to the limit. The actual finite-bank mass energy differs from the common $V$ energy by a bounded form of norm at most $\eta_i$.

To identify the equations of the limit, use the uniform bounds on $\ddot\Phi_i$ and $V\Phi_i$ to take weak limits in time and the strong displacement and velocity convergence to identify them as $\ddot\Phi$ and $V\Phi$. Multiplication by the strongly convergent scalar and bounded operator coefficients then passes (I.13m.d.3) to the limit in distributions. The resulting solution lies in the strong energy class with $V\Phi,\ddot\Phi,V^{1/2}\dot\Phi$ essentially bounded. In this class the same difference energy estimate gives uniqueness on the common local interval. The scalar evolution, Einstein constraint, energy and stress identity pass by strong energy convergence. Thus the homogeneous Einstein equations and conserved matter stress hold on the limit with the actual unbounded bank.

*Exact full detector.* The detected variable is $D=\langle d,\Phi\rangle$. Its finite-bank approximants converge uniformly by the strong displacement bound and $\|d-d_M\|=\sqrt{\nu((M,\infty))}$. Recover $C$ from the conserved momentum and use (I.13m.d.3) to reverse the elimination. The original bank equation then reads, for almost every mass,
$$
\ddot\Phi_v+3H\dot\Phi_v+v\Phi_v
=f,\qquad f=-a^{-3}\partial_t(a^3\chi\dot C)
$$
with zero initial values. The forcing is locally bounded by the differentiated energy and clock relation. The scalar zero-data oscillator problem has a unique solution for each mass, so the full conditional detector is
$$
D(t)=-\int G_v^{g}f(t)\,W(dv)
\tag{I.13m.d.7}
$$
on the coupled homogeneous history. For instance the scalar oscillator energy with a harmless added position term and bounded $H$ bounds its zero-data response uniformly in $v$ on this interval, justifying the mass integral. This is the full unbounded Weibull transfer with dynamical gravitational backreaction through the positive matter stress. The source and detector remain distinct material observables. The argument differentiates the homogeneous equations in their single time variable after eliminating a cyclic momentum; the inhomogeneous problem requires mass-uniform spatial estimates. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13me"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13me-exact-tensor-metric-response-of-the-homogeneous-scalar-bank"></a>**Theorem I.13m.e (Exact Tensor Metric Response of the Homogeneous Scalar Bank).** On the coupled homogeneous Einstein branch of Theorem I.13m.d, the scalar clock, source and auxiliary bank have zero linear transverse-traceless spatial stress. Consequently the zero-past transverse-traceless metric response to an independent conserved transverse-traceless stress is exactly the ordinary massless Einstein response on the actual evolving scale factor. This holds on every finite bank and on the unbounded-mass branch. The signed material detector transfer is a different response. In particular, on the same evolving metric the signed scalar-wave resolvent continuation of the flat Weibull transfer differs strictly from the metric response on a finite positive pulse, with the bound below.

*Tensor response on the actual source.* Use cosmic time and write $g=-dt^2+a(t)^2d\mathbf x^2$. For either a finite bank or the Hilbert-valued bank of Theorem I.13m.d, the stress in mixed indices is
$$
T^\mu{}_\nu
=\mathsf G_Y(\partial^\mu Y,\partial_\nu Y)
-\delta^\mu{}_\nu
 \left(\tfrac12\mathsf G_Y(\partial^\alpha Y,\partial_\alpha Y)+V(Y)\right),
\tag{I.13m.e.1}
$$
where $Y=(C,\chi,\Phi)$ and the positive target metric and potential are those of Theorem I.13m.c. For the unbounded bank the potential pairing is its quadratic form. On the homogeneous branch $\partial_i Y=0$, so the first term in the mixed spatial stress is quadratic in first spatial variations and the second is proportional to the identity. Therefore its linear transverse-traceless projection is zero. This argument uses arbitrary retained scalar variations of finite energy and does not require identifying their linear evolution. In particular, changing the background scalar stress changes $a$ and $H$, while the mixed spatial stress has no tensor response coefficient on that background.

There is also an exact tensor-only linearized solution of the scalar equations with $\delta Y=0$. Indeed for $g_{ij}=a^2(\delta_{ij}+h_{ij})$ with $h_{ii}=0$ and $\partial_i h_{ij}=0$, and no variation of lapse or shift, the first variation of $\sqrt{-g}$ is zero and $\delta g^{0\mu}=0$. Thus $\delta\Box_g Y(t)=0$ in divergence form. The contractions of background first derivatives in the target Christoffel terms depend only on $g^{00}$, so they also have zero first variation. The potential and mass operator are fixed at $\delta Y=0$. This conclusion holds distributionally on the actual homogeneous unbounded-mass branch. Its regularity from Theorem I.13m.d suffices for the scalar equations in divergence form.

For a nonzero comoving wave number $k$, let $h(t)$ denote the amplitude of one transverse-traceless polarization and $\Pi(t)$ the amplitude of an independent first-order mixed spatial stress in that polarization. A stress with only these transverse-traceless spatial components is conserved in the background: its spatial divergence vanishes by transversality, and the temporal connection contribution is proportional to its spatial trace. In the tensor sector no scalar or vector constraints enter. Varying the mixed spatial Einstein tensor, or equivalently using the trace-free variation of the spatial extrinsic curvature and spatial Ricci tensor, gives
$$
\delta G^i{}_j{}_{\rm TT}
=\tfrac12\bigl(\ddot h^i{}_j+3H\dot h^i{}_j-a^{-2}\Delta h^i{}_j\bigr).
$$
For example the trace-free extrinsic-curvature variation in the convention $K^i{}_j=\tfrac12g^{i\ell}\dot g_{\ell j}$ is $\tfrac12\dot h^i{}_j$, and the trace-free mixed spatial Ricci variation is $-\Delta h^i{}_j/(2a^2)$. The mixed-index background pressure is proportional to the identity, so there is no separate linear term proportional to $h^i{}_j$ from the pressure. The resulting zero-past mode equation is
$$
\ddot h+3H\dot h+(k^2/a^2)h=16\pi G\,\Pi .
\tag{I.13m.e.2}
$$
This is the standard tensor perturbation identity (Caprini and Figueroa 2018) specialized to the actual source, with no assumed response from the scalar detector.

*Matched curved transfer and finite separation.* Let $\mathscr R_v^a$ be the positive-sign zero-past scalar mode Green operator for $\partial_t^2+3H\partial_t+k^2/a^2+v$ on this same scale factor. Define the signed comparison with the fixed flat spectral weights of Theorem I.13m.b by
$$
\mathscr R_W^a=(1+A)\mathscr R_0^a
              -A\int_{(0,\infty)}\mathscr R_v^a\,\sigma_m(dv).
\tag{I.13m.e.3}
$$
This is the scalar-wave resolvent continuation being compared. It reduces to the declared signed transfer at constant unit scale factor and is the same massive resolvent family used for the material detector. The actual metric response in (I.13m.e.2), after absorbing its common positive source factor, is $\mathscr R_0^a$.

On a compact subinterval of the actual homogeneous development use the Liouville variable $z=a^{3/2}h$. The corresponding kernel before restoring the scale factors is the solution $y_v(t,s)$ of
$$
\partial_t^2 y_v+(q(t)+v)y_v=0,\quad
y_v(s,s)=0,\quad \partial_t y_v(s,s)=1,\qquad
q(t)=k^2/a(t)^2-\tfrac32\dot H(t)-\tfrac94H(t)^2 .
\tag{I.13m.e.4}
$$
The retarded kernel of $\mathscr R_v^a$ is $(a(s)/a(t))^{3/2}y_v(t,s)$ for $t\ge s$. The coefficient $q$ is continuous and bounded on the stated compact interval. Choose a mass band $[v_1,v_2]\subset(0,\infty)$ of positive $\sigma_m$ mass and a time length $T>0$ with $T^2(\|q\|_\infty+v_2)\le1/4$. On every ordered subinterval of length at most $T$ and for $0\le v\le v_2$ the Volterra equation from (I.13m.e.4) implies
$$
\tfrac12\le\partial_t y_v(t,s),\qquad
\tfrac12(t-s)\le y_v(t,s)\le2(t-s).
\tag{I.13m.e.5}
$$
In fact, writing $B=\|q\|_\infty+v_2$ and $U=\sup|\partial_t y_v|$ on such a subinterval gives $|\partial_t y_v-1|\le B T^2U/2$. Hence $U\le(1-BT^2/2)^{-1}<2$, and the lower derivative bound follows. In particular $y_0$ is positive and increasing off the diagonal.

There is a comparison for every $v\ge0$, with no upper mass cutoff. For $t>s$ set $u=y_v/y_0$. Then
$$
u''+2\frac{\partial_t y_0}{y_0}u'+v u=0,\qquad
u(s+)=1,\quad u'(s+)=0 .
$$
The limiting initial derivative follows by the Volterra expansion $y_v(t,s)=(t-s)+O_v((t-s)^3)$ and the corresponding differentiated expansion. For $v>0$ the derivative of $u'^2+v u^2$ is $-4(\partial_t y_0/y_0)u'^2\le0$. Starting at any $s+\epsilon$ and taking $\epsilon\downarrow0$ gives $|u|\le1$. For $v=0$ the ratio is one. Thus $y_0-y_v\ge0$ for every mass throughout the short interval. This also bounds all those kernels by the same integrable finite-time envelope for the finite measure $\sigma_m$.

On the finite band the Volterra resolvent identity gives
$$
y_0(t,s)-y_v(t,s)=
 v\int_s^t y_0(t,\tau)y_v(\tau,s)\,d\tau
 \ge\frac{v(t-s)^3}{24}
\tag{I.13m.e.6}
$$
by (I.13m.e.5). Let $a_-,a_+$ bound the positive scale factor below and above on the comparison interval. For a nonzero nonnegative smooth force $F=16\pi G\,\Pi$ supported strictly inside the interval, and a readout time $t$ after the pulse with every $t-s\le T$, (I.13m.e.3)–(I.13m.e.6) now yield
$$
\bigl[(\mathscr R_W^a-\mathscr R_0^a)F\bigr](t)
\ge
\frac{A v_1\,\sigma_m([v_1,v_2])}{24}
 \left(\frac{a_-}{a_+}\right)^{3/2}
 \int (t-s)^3 F(s)\,ds >0 .
\tag{I.13m.e.7}
$$
Every mass outside the selected band contributes with the same weak sign. The bound uses only the band mass. The test uses one common history and a real finite-time tensor stress and readout. Thus the scalar clock bank's positive covariant backreaction does not give the Weibull tensor metric response on this branch. The argument leaves tensor-valued material couplings with nonzero anisotropic stress, scalar-sector metric responses, and the nonlinear common-source projections open. General inhomogeneous unbounded-mass evolution requires its own initial-value theorem. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mf"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mf-full-mass-linear-scalar-response-on-the-homogeneous-clock-source"></a>**Theorem I.13m.f (Full-Mass Linear Scalar Response on the Homogeneous Clock Source).** Use the actual homogeneous Einstein development of Theorem I.13m.d and any fixed nonzero comoving Fourier mode of the spatial three-torus. The linear Einstein and matter equations with a prescribed conserved scalar probe have a causal Cauchy evolution for smooth finite-energy mode data satisfying the linearized constraints, with the full unbounded mass bank retained. The bank has zero linear scalar anisotropic stress. If the independent probe also has zero anisotropic stress, the two scalar metric potentials coincide and their exact Poisson source is the total comoving density, including the evolved bank stress. The resulting bare-source susceptibility is not determined by the material detector transfer. In particular there is a prepared Cauchy-slice comparison with unit bare-source susceptibility, which excludes an instantaneous promotion of the Weibull static multiplier on this source. A late-time or static bare-source multiplier requires a separate comparison.

*The linear mode and a mass-uniform evolution.* Work first in synchronous coordinates, fixing the residual coordinate freedom by the initial coordinate data. Write the metric perturbation as $a^2\gamma_{ij}$ with unperturbed lapse and shift, and let $\tau=\operatorname{tr}\gamma$. Use the background target field $Y=(C,\chi,\Phi)$ and $q=\delta Y$. On the common real target Hilbert space $\mathcal X=\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathcal H$, let $\mathsf M$ denote the nonnegative potential operator $0\oplus m_\chi^2\oplus V$, so the target potential is $\langle Y,\mathsf MY\rangle/2$. Let $G(t)=\mathsf G_{Y(t)}$ denote the bounded positive target metric operator of Theorem I.13m.c. Its time derivative is bounded, and its lower positive bound is uniform on the selected compact time slab. Write $p_0=G\dot Y$. The background regularity established in Theorem I.13m.d gives bounded $\dot Y,\ddot Y,\mathsf MY$ on this slab in $\mathcal X$, with the latter two interpreted almost everywhere.

In the scalar target equations, variation of the volume factor gives $\delta\sqrt{-g}=a^3\tau/2$. The perturbed target momentum in the time direction is
$$
\delta(a^3G\dot Y)
=a^3\left(G\dot q+DG[q]\dot Y+\tfrac12\tau p_0\right).
\tag{I.13m.f.1}
$$
Here $DG[q]$ means the field derivative of the target metric evaluated at $q$. In the Euler equation the terms with undifferentiated $\tau$ cancel by the background equation. The resulting metric force is $-\dot\tau p_0/2$. Thus the linear scalar field equations have the form
$$
G\ddot q+\mathsf Mq
=B_1(t)\dot q+B_0(t,k)q-\tfrac12\dot\tau p_0 ,
\tag{I.13m.f.2}
$$
with bounded operators $B_1,B_0$ on $\mathcal X$. To see the unbounded part explicitly, use the lower-index target equation before raising with $G^{-1}$:
$$
a^{-3}\partial_t(a^3\mathsf G_Y\dot Y)
-\tfrac12D\mathsf G_Y[\cdot](\dot Y,\dot Y)
+\mathsf MY=0
$$
on the background. Linearizing its time derivative gives (I.13m.f.1). Apart from $G\ddot q$ the resulting terms contain only $q,\dot q$, bounded target derivatives, $\dot Y$ and $\ddot Y$. The spatial derivative contributes the bounded term $-(k^2/a^2)Gq$ on this fixed mode. The potential variation is exactly $\mathsf Mq$, with no coefficient times an unbounded derivative of the background mass energy. This verifies the asserted structure of (I.13m.f.2).

The spatial mixed trace-reversed matter stress is $V(Y)\delta^i_j+\mathsf G_Y(\partial^iY,\partial_jY)$ in four dimensions. Its linear variation on the homogeneous branch is therefore $\langle\mathsf MY,q\rangle\delta^i_j$. In synchronous coordinates the mixed spatial Ricci variation is
$$
\delta R^i{}_j
=\delta{}^{(3)}R^i{}_j
 +\tfrac12\ddot\gamma^i{}_j
 +\tfrac32 H\dot\gamma^i{}_j+\tfrac12H\dot\tau\,\delta^i_j ,
\tag{I.13m.f.3}
$$
where $\delta{}^{(3)}R$ is the linear spatial Ricci operator of the perturbed slice. Indeed the mixed extrinsic curvature with positive time-derivative convention is $H\delta^i_j+\dot\gamma^i{}_j/2$, and the spatial Ricci evolution term is its time derivative plus its product with its trace. At fixed $k$ the spatial term is a bounded finite-dimensional matrix. Thus (I.13m.f.3) and the spatial trace-reversed Einstein equation give a finite metric system driven by $q$ through the bounded functional $\langle\mathsf MY,q\rangle$, and by the external probe. The scalar sector is invariant under these equations because the background is spatially homogeneous and isotropic.

For completeness, the principal equation $G\ddot q+(1+\mathsf M)q=F$ has a well-defined propagator in the energy norm $\|q\|+\|\mathsf M^{1/2}q\|+\|\dot q\|$. One construction uses the common carrier and finite mass meshes of Theorem I.13m.d, but keeps the actual background coefficients fixed. Project the coupling vector in $G$ to the finite cutoff and keep $\chi(t)$ of the full background. Approximate the mass multiplier on its compact cells, leaving it unchanged above the cutoff. Smooth-in-time forcing with values in a finite span of bounded-mass simple functions is dense in $L^1_t\mathcal X$, and bounded-mass simple initial data are dense in the energy data. Start with those dense data and choose refinements including their supports and cells. The finite principal equation preserves the cell subspace. Its positive kinetic and mass energies give a uniform propagator bound with $L^1_t\mathcal X$ forcing. To prove strong convergence for the dense data, differentiate this principal equation once. With $z=\dot q$ its equation is $G\ddot z+(1+\mathsf M)z=\dot F-\dot G\dot z$ at the corresponding finite stage, with uniformly bounded initial acceleration because the dense initial displacement has bounded mass support. This gives a uniform bound for $\ddot q$ by the same energy estimate. The difference of two principal equations has leading coefficient error $(G_i-G_j)\ddot q_j$, which tends to zero in $L^1_t\mathcal X$ since the kinetic rank-one directions converge in Hilbert norm. The compact mass-mesh multiplier error tends to zero in operator norm on the common carrier. A difference energy estimate now gives strong convergence. Density and the uniform principal bound extend the propagator to the full energy data and $L^1$ forcing.

Add the bounded lower terms of (I.13m.f.2) and the finite metric system (I.13m.f.3) by their Volterra integral equations on the product energy space. The uniform principal bound and bounded coupling coefficients make this a contraction on sufficiently short subintervals, followed by concatenation on the common slab. The result has uniqueness and continuous dependence in the mode energy norm, including the finite metric coordinates and their first derivatives. In particular it has the time-retarded response to a probe vanishing before the initial slice. The principal estimate differentiates only the time-dependent kinetic operator on the fixed background. The lower coefficients enter through bounded perturbations in the energy evolution.

The constraints propagate for this linear evolution. To see it, let $E_{\mu\nu}$ be the residual of the linear Einstein equation after moving the conserved probe and bank stress to its right side. The linearized contracted Bianchi identity gives its homogeneous divergence equation, using the background Einstein equation and the scalar equations just solved. Conservation of the linear bank stress follows by variation of its local stress identity, equivalently by pairing the energy solution with compact smooth variations in the mass form domain and using density. The spatial trace-reversed equations give $E_{ij}=\frac12 g_{ij} E^\alpha{}_\alpha$. Taking the trace yields $E_{ij}=g_{ij}E_{00}$ in the unperturbed cosmic-time coordinates. Thus the divergence equation is a closed homogeneous first-order system for $E_{00},E_{0i}$, with bounded coefficients at fixed Fourier wave number. Vanishing initial constraints force it to vanish. The synchronous representation supplies the evolution. The scalar potential comparison uses its gauge-invariant Newtonian representative.

*Exact metric-source split.* For a nonzero scalar Fourier mode, take the Newtonian potentials $U,\Psi$ defined by $g_{00}=-(1+2U)$ and $g_{ij}=a^2(1-2\Psi)\delta_{ij}$ in zero shift and zero scalar shear. Write $\delta T^0{}_i=\partial_i\delta q_{\rm mom}$ and $\delta T^0{}_0=-\delta\rho$. The subscript on the scalar momentum avoids confusion with the target variation $q$. Since each background target field is homogeneous, the product of its two spatial gradients has zero linear variation. Its mixed spatial stress is therefore isotropic. If the independent scalar probe is also isotropic, the trace-free spatial Einstein equation gives $U=\Psi$ for $k\ne0$. The time and longitudinal momentum constraints in these conventions are
$$
-\frac{k^2}{a^2}\Psi-3H(\dot\Psi+HU)=4\pi G\,\delta\rho,
\qquad
\dot\Psi+HU=-4\pi G\,\delta q_{\rm mom}.
\tag{I.13m.f.4}
$$
They follow by substituting the Newtonian lapse and spatial metric into the normal Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. In particular the linear spatial scalar curvature is $4a^{-2}\Delta\Psi$, and the variation of the local expansion rate is $-\dot\Psi-HU$. These are the standard scalar constraints (Bardeen 1980) with the stated mixed-index convention.

With $\Delta=\delta\rho-3H\delta q_{\rm mom}$, elimination gives the exact observable identity
$$
-\frac{k^2}{a^2}U=4\pi G(\Delta_{\rm probe}+\Delta_{\rm bank}).
\tag{I.13m.f.5}
$$
Under a first-order change of time slice the density and momentum changes cancel in $\Delta$ by the background continuity equation. For the independently conserved probe of zero background, its first-order stress is itself unchanged under that gauge transformation. Thus the split in (I.13m.f.5) has the stated gauge-invariant meaning. The bank part is explicitly the stress pairing of its evolved perturbation. In the Newtonian representative, set $\delta P_Y=\dot q-U\dot Y$, the perturbed normal target velocity. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta\rho_{\rm bank}
 &=\langle G\dot Y,\delta P_Y\rangle
   +\tfrac12 DG[q](\dot Y,\dot Y)
   +\langle\mathsf MY,q\rangle,\\
\delta q_{{\rm mom},{\rm bank}}&=-\langle G\dot Y,q\rangle .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.f.6}
$$
The scalar Fourier transformation from synchronous to Newtonian coordinates uses the finite metric mode and its derivatives. These stress pairings extend to the mode energy class since $\dot Y$ and $\mathsf MY$ are bounded Hilbert vectors. The formulas involve the bank energy and its source fields. The independent material detector of Theorem I.13m.d is a separate linear functional of the bank displacement. For example, one may prescribe a compactly started smooth scalar $\Delta_{\rm probe}$ on a fixed mode. An explicit isotropic conserved probe is obtained by taking
$$
\delta q_{{\rm mom},{\rm probe}}=
\frac{\dot\Delta_{\rm probe}+3H\Delta_{\rm probe}}
     {k^2/a^2-3\dot H},\quad
\delta\rho_{\rm probe}=\Delta_{\rm probe}
                        +3H\delta q_{{\rm mom},{\rm probe}},\quad
\delta p_{\rm probe}=-\partial_t\delta q_{{\rm mom},{\rm probe}}
                        -3H\delta q_{{\rm mom},{\rm probe}} .
\tag{I.13m.f.7}
$$
The denominator is strictly positive by (I.13m.d.2). The momentum conservation equation is the last displayed equality. The density equation is $\partial_t\delta\rho_{\rm probe}+3H(\delta\rho_{\rm probe}+\delta p_{\rm probe})-(k^2/a^2)\delta q_{{\rm mom},{\rm probe}}=0$, which follows from the first two equalities. This defines a causal prepared source without attributing an unregistered equation of state to it. Together with (I.13m.f.2)–(I.13m.f.6) it gives an evolved bare-source metric response on the actual background.

*Initial susceptibility and its scope.* As a separate prepared slice comparison, take $\Delta_{\rm probe}=\delta\rho_{\rm probe}\ne0$ and zero probe momentum on the initial slice. Specify $q=0$ and $\delta P_Y=0$ for the bank there. Equation (I.13m.f.6) gives both bank density and momentum perturbations zero. In Newtonian coordinates the constraints then fix $U=\Psi=-4\pi Ga^2\Delta_{\rm probe}/k^2$ and $\dot\Psi=-HU$ on that slice. These are compatible linear scalar Cauchy data: the spatial scalar curvature fixes the Hamiltonian constraint, and the zero variation of local expansion fixes the momentum constraint, while the physical normal field velocities are the stated free data. The equivalent synchronous initial data are obtained by the linear gauge change. The exact ratio $-k^2U/(4\pi Ga^2\Delta_{\rm probe})$ is one. The fixed-scale Weibull factor at the same physical wave number is $1+A\int v/(v+k^2/a^2)\,\sigma_m(dv)>1$. Thus the instantaneous bare-density promotion of that factor fails this prepared test. An evolved bare-source response, including any static limit, requires the bank stress from (I.13m.f.6). The nonlinear metric and cosmological source conditions retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mg"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mg-mass-uniform-inhomogeneous-linear-evolution-on-the-homogeneous-clock-source"></a>**Theorem I.13m.g (Mass-Uniform Inhomogeneous Linear Evolution on the Homogeneous Clock Source).** Fix a compact subinterval of the actual unbounded-mass homogeneous Einstein development of Theorem I.13m.d, with the positive target metric bounded uniformly away from zero and the scale factor positive. The full spatially inhomogeneous linearized Einstein–bank equations in relative wave gauge have a unique Sobolev energy evolution for all spatial Fourier modes at once. The estimate is uniform in the retained spectral masses and in the Fourier cutoff. It gives the metric domain of dependence. For initial data satisfying the linearized Einstein and gauge constraints and a prescribed conserved probe, the solution satisfies the full linearized Einstein equations, and has conserved linearized total stress. This is an inhomogeneous linear theorem on the actual homogeneous background.

*Wave gauge and the principal system.* Use the FLRW background metric $g$ and target history $Y=(C,\chi,\Phi)$ from Theorem I.13m.d. Let $h=\delta g$ be a covariant symmetric metric variation and $q=\delta Y$. Put $\mathcal X=\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathcal H$, use the background target metric $G(t)=\mathsf G_{Y(t)}$, and retain the nonnegative potential operator $\mathsf M=0\oplus m_\chi^2\oplus V$ on $\mathcal X$. On the fixed interval $G,\dot G$ are bounded and $G$ is uniformly positive. The background vectors $\dot Y,\ddot Y,\mathsf MY$ are bounded in $\mathcal X$, with the last two understood almost everywhere, by Theorem I.13m.d.

Define the linear relative wave-gauge covector by
$$
Z_\mu=\nabla^\alpha h_{\alpha\mu}
-\tfrac12\nabla_\mu(\operatorname{tr}_g h).
\tag{I.13m.g.1}
$$
In the linearized trace-reversed Einstein equation subtract $\nabla_{(\mu}Z_{\nu)}$ from the linearized Ricci tensor, where parentheses denote averaging over the two orders. The principal part of the resulting metric equation is $-\Box_g h_{\mu\nu}/2$. This follows by varying the connection,
$$
\delta\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu}
=\tfrac12 g^{\alpha\beta}
  (\nabla_\mu h_{\nu\beta}+\nabla_\nu h_{\mu\beta}
                         -\nabla_\beta h_{\mu\nu}),
$$
and commuting covariant derivatives, whose commutators contribute only curvature times $h$. This is the ordinary relative wave reduction (Lindblad and Rodnianski 2010) applied at the fixed background.

In components with the fixed cosmic-time and periodic spatial coordinates the reduced system takes the form
$$
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t^2h-a^{-2}\Delta h
 &=\mathcal L_h(t)(h,\partial_t h,\nabla_{\mathbf x}h,
                       q,\partial_t q,\nabla_{\mathbf x}q)+J_h,\\
G(\partial_t^2q-a^{-2}\Delta q)+\mathsf Mq
 &=\mathcal L_q(t)(h,\partial_t h,\nabla_{\mathbf x}h,
                       q,\partial_t q,\nabla_{\mathbf x}q)+J_q .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.g.2}
$$
Here each displayed lower term is a bounded linear map of its listed entries with time-dependent coefficients only. $J_h$ includes the fixed trace-reversed probe. The optional $J_q$ denotes an additional target forcing in the reduced energy statement. For the Einstein constraint claim below take $J_q=0$, or include the covariantly conserved stress exchange of an explicitly coupled probe.

To verify the bounded structure, use the lower-index target equation as in Theorem I.13m.f, before raising it with $G^{-1}$. The variation of the potential is exactly $\mathsf Mq$. Varying the spacetime wave operator on $Y(t)$ contributes metric variations times $\dot Y,\ddot Y$ and first metric derivatives times $\dot Y$. Differentiating the bounded target coefficients contributes only $q,\partial_t q$ and background first and second derivatives. The trace-reversed bank stress is $\mathsf G_Y(\partial_\mu Y,\partial_\nu Y)+V(Y)g_{\mu\nu}$, so its linear variation is bounded by $q,\partial q,h$ through $\dot Y$ and the functional $\langle\mathsf MY,q\rangle$. The mass operator never acts on the fixed coupling vector or on a metric variation. The FLRW tensor-wave connection and curvature coefficients are bounded on the compact interval. This proves (I.13m.g.2) without requiring a first moment of the spectral measure.

*Uniform spatial energy.* Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and use the coordinate Sobolev norms on the spatial torus. For each spatial multi-index $\alpha$ of order at most $s-1$ apply $\partial_{\mathbf x}^{\alpha}$ to (I.13m.g.2). It commutes with all its coefficients and with $\mathsf M$. For each differentiated pair of fields use the positive energy density equal to one half of
$$
\begin{aligned}
&|\partial_t h|^2+a^{-2}|\nabla_{\mathbf x}h|^2+|h|^2\\
&+\langle\partial_t q,G\partial_t q\rangle
 +a^{-2}\sum_i\langle\partial_i q,G\partial_i q\rangle
 +\|\mathsf M^{1/2}q\|^2+\|q\|^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.g.3}
$$
The metric component norm here is a positive Euclidean norm on the ten coordinate entries. Sum its spatial integral over $\alpha$ to obtain $\mathcal E_s$. It is equivalent, uniformly on the chosen slab, to the square of
$$
\mathcal N_s(h,q)=
 \|h\|_{H^s}+\|\partial_t h\|_{H^{s-1}}
 +\|q\|_{H^s(\mathcal X)}+\|\partial_t q\|_{H^{s-1}(\mathcal X)}
 +\|\mathsf M^{1/2}q\|_{H^{s-1}(\mathcal X)} .
\tag{I.13m.g.4}
$$
Pair (I.13m.g.2) with the corresponding time derivatives, after the same spatial differentiations. Integration by parts cancels the spatial wave terms against the gradient-energy derivatives. The potential pairing differentiates the positive mass term exactly. The derivatives of $a^{-2}$ and $G$ multiply terms already in the energy. The bounded lower terms are estimated by Cauchy–Schwarz in the coordinate and target norms. Consequently
$$
\mathcal E_s(t)^{1/2}
\le C_T\left[\mathcal E_s(0)^{1/2}
 +\int_0^t\!\left(\|J_h(u)\|_{H^{s-1}}
                 +\|J_q(u)\|_{H^{s-1}(\mathcal X)}\right)\,du\right].
\tag{I.13m.g.5}
$$
This follows from the differential inequality for the square root and Grönwall's inequality. It first holds for finite systems and then by energy convergence. The constant depends on the displayed bounded background coefficients and positivity margin. It is independent of the highest Fourier mode, the number of bank coordinates and the largest mass. No spatial commutator with an unbounded mass term is present because the background is homogeneous.

*Construction and stability of the limiting response.* The principal target operator at each fixed Fourier mode is the time-dependent positive kinetic wave operator of Theorem I.13m.f, now with the additional bounded gradient multiplier $Gk^2/a^2$. It has the principal energy propagator constructed there by common-carrier mass meshes, first on bounded-mass smooth data and then by energy density. The finite metric wave equation and the bounded first-order couplings are added by the same Volterra construction on that mode. Equivalently use spectral-cutoff step spaces, compress the bounded lower operators to those spaces, and approximate the kinetic coupling vector by its cutoff. The mass multiplier is unchanged above the cutoff and differs from the true multiplier by at most the cell mesh in operator norm. All bounded coefficients of the reduced system use the fixed actual background. The finite approximants use the same fixed background at every mass cutoff.

For any fixed finite set of Fourier modes, the principal strong convergence proof in Theorem I.13m.f and the Volterra estimate give strong convergence of these reduced finite-mass systems. In applying that proof to a compressed bounded coefficient, use that the projections converge strongly and are uniformly bounded. For each fixed vector-valued history its projected lower term therefore converges in $L^1_t\mathcal X$ by domination, including when the background coefficients are merely essentially bounded in time. The same argument works for the finite metric variables coupled to the target. Spatial Fourier truncation commutes with every time coefficient. Applying (I.13m.g.5) to the high-mode tails bounds them by the tails of the common initial Sobolev energy and forcing. Those tails tend to zero by the square-summability of the Sobolev data and dominated convergence for the time-integrated forcing. Thus the fixed-mode limits sum to a strong energy solution on the spatial torus. This also shows strong convergence in (I.13m.g.4) for independent refinements of Fourier and mass cutoffs, with energy-convergent initial approximants and forcing. The energy estimate gives uniqueness and continuous dependence. The argument uses spatially homogeneous coefficients of the fixed background to obtain its uniform Sobolev estimate.

For the domain of dependence, use the reduced finite-mass systems with spatially localized smooth initial data and forcing, and retain all spatial modes during this comparison. Their lower terms are spatially local, including the fixed Hilbert projections in the target. Apply the undifferentiated energy identity on a backward metric cone. In the spatial boundary flux, the velocity-gradient term is bounded by the corresponding normal energy flux using $2ab\le a^2+b^2$, once for each metric component and in the positive $G$ norm for the target. The potential and undifferentiated terms are nonnegative in the outgoing energy and do not produce spatial flux. Thus zero initial and forcing data in the cone give zero solution there by the localized version of (I.13m.g.5). Finite-mass approximation preserves the spatial support of the initial and forcing data, and strong energy convergence passes this property to the full system. Localization and energy density extend the result to the stated Sobolev data. The cone is that of the actual FLRW metric.

*Full constraints and observables.* Use an independent first-order probe whose background is zero and whose stress variation is covariantly conserved in the background. The matter equations give the on-shell linearized stress identity, including the connection variation against the nonzero background stress. For the unbounded bank this identity follows from the local target action by using the potential as the closed quadratic form of $\mathsf M^{1/2}$. For example, in the perturbation stress the potential variation is $\langle\mathsf MY,q\rangle$. Its time derivative uses $\langle\mathsf MY,\partial_t q\rangle$ and $\langle\mathsf M^{1/2}\dot Y,\mathsf M^{1/2}q\rangle$, which are defined by the background bounds of Theorem I.13m.d and the energy space. This justifies the distributional identity by time regularization and mass-form-domain density. The spatial derivatives are justified by the Sobolev energy. No Ward identity is assumed for the intermediate reduced fixed-background approximants.

In the limiting reduced equations the full Einstein residual is the trace reversal of $\nabla_{(\mu}Z_{\nu)}$. The linearized contracted Bianchi identity and the total stress identity imply its covariant divergence is zero. Commuting derivatives gives the homogeneous vector wave equation
$$
\Box_g Z_\nu+R_\nu{}^\alpha Z_\alpha=0
\tag{I.13m.g.6}
$$
with the background curvature convention of the wave reduction. Initially impose $Z=0$ and the normal components of the full Einstein constraint. Since the tangential derivatives of $Z$ then vanish, those normal components of the trace-reversed gauge residual impose the zero normal derivative of each component of $Z$. Wave uniqueness yields $Z=0$ throughout the interval. This proves the full linearized Einstein equations for the limiting response. For instance one can take $s\ge3$ in this constraint statement to read the initial data and residuals in Sobolev trace spaces, with the energy construction applying already at $s=1$.

In each nonzero scalar Fourier sector the exact gauge-invariant split of Theorem I.13m.f applies to the resulting metric and bank stress. In the tensor sectors the exact massless response of Theorem I.13m.e likewise applies. The present theorem supplies one spatially inhomogeneous causal linear response containing all those modes, with a uniform high-frequency estimate. It leaves nonlinear inhomogeneous unbounded-mass evolution, a late-time bare-source susceptibility and the common cosmological observable maps open. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mh"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mh-sharp-initial-mass-energy-regularity-of-the-full-clock-bank"></a>**Theorem I.13m.h (Sharp Initial Mass-Energy Regularity of the Full Clock Bank).** Use the nontrivial zero-past homogeneous coupled solution of Theorem I.13m.d, with the Weibull exponent $0<m\le1$ and initial force $f_0=-c_0d_0\ne0$. Its full mass distribution has infinite first moment. With $e=\mathbf1$, the bank's short-time positive energy has the exact asymptotics
$$
\begin{aligned}
\|V^{1/2}\dot\Phi(t)\|^2
 &\sim A c_m f_0^2\, t^m
   \int_0^\infty \sin^2\sqrt u\,u^{-1-m/2}\,du,\\
\|\ddot\Phi(t)-f_0e\|^2
 &\sim A c_m f_0^2\, t^m
   \int_0^\infty (1-\cos\sqrt u)^2\,u^{-1-m/2}\,du ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.h.1}
$$
where $c_m=m/(2L^m\Gamma(2-m))$. The integrals are finite and positive. The second line uses the strong representative constructed below. Thus the exponent $m/2$ is sharp for these two increments at the initial time. In particular the bank does not have a strong third time derivative in its unweighted Hilbert space at the initial time. A nonlinear inhomogeneous construction can use a weaker energy class.

*Mass tail.* For $0<m<1$, write $I(y)=\int_{(0,y]}x\,\nu_m(dx)$ for the Bernstein measure of (I.13l.a.3). Its Laplace–Stieltjes transform is
$$
\int_{(0,\infty)} e^{-rx}\,dI(x)
=m L^{-m}r^{m-1}e^{-(r/L)^m}.
$$
To obtain $I(y)\sim m L^{-m}y^{1-m}/\Gamma(2-m)$ directly, rescale the positive measures by $y^{m-1}dI(yu)$ to get Laplace transforms tending to $m L^{-m}r^{m-1}$, the transform of $mL^{-m}u^{-m}du/\Gamma(1-m)$. To justify convergence at the interval $[0,1]$ directly, weight those measures by $e^{-u}$, then use convergence of their total masses and Laplace transforms, with tightness at infinity from the same transforms at $r=1/2$. The uniqueness of Laplace transforms gives their weak limit, which has no atom at either endpoint. Undoing the weight on $[0,1]$ gives the stated constant. When $m=1$, $\nu_1=\delta_{1/L}$ and $I(y)=1/L$ for $y\ge1/L$. The same constant formula therefore holds. By (I.13l.a.3),
$$
\frac{d\sigma_m}{dv}(v)\sim c_m v^{-1-m/2}.
\tag{I.13m.h.2}
$$
It is bounded above by $C v^{-1-m/2}$ at large $v$ and its first moment diverges. The atom of $|W|$ at zero changes neither assertion.

*Uniform oscillatory bound.* The large-frequency density entering $\int\sqrt v\sin(t\sqrt v)\,|W|(dv)$ after writing $x=\sqrt v$ is $A g(x)$ with $g(x)=I(x)/x$. For $X$ sufficiently large, $g(X)\le C X^{-m}$ and the variation of $g$ on $[X,\infty)$ is at most $C X^{-m}$. In fact the product rule for the Stieltjes measure gives the two bounds
$$
\int_{(X,\infty)} x^{-1}\,dI(x)=\nu_m((X,\infty)),
\qquad
\int_X^\infty I(x)x^{-2}\,dx\le C X^{-m}.
$$
The first is at most $C X^{-m}$ by

$$
(1-e^{-1})\nu_m((X,\infty))\le1-e^{-(LX)^{-m}}.
$$

For $0<x\le X$ use $|\sin(tx)|\le tx$. For the remaining interval use Stieltjes integration by parts and the variation estimate. Splitting at $X=1/t$ gives for all sufficiently small $t>0$, uniformly in the cutoff $M$,
$$
\left|\int_{[0,M]}\sqrt v\,\sin(t\sqrt v)\,|W|(dv)\right|
\le C t^{m-1}.
\tag{I.13m.h.3}
$$
For example the first part is bounded by $C t(1+X^{2-m})$ and the second by $C X^{-m}/t$. The finite part near zero is harmless since $I(x)\le x$. This estimate also treats the jump of $I$ for $m=1$.

*Comparison on the actual expanding branch.* First take exact cutoff multiplication $V$ on the continuum $v\le M$, with $e_M=\mathbf1_{[0,M]}e$. These cutoff coupled solutions are obtained by the bounded-mass mesh limits of Theorems I.13m.c and I.13m.d. At each fixed $M$ the differentiated equations pass to the cutoff solution, since multiplication is bounded on that subspace. Their estimates in Theorem I.13m.d are uniform in $M$. Write $Z_M=\dot\Phi_M$, $B_M=I-\chi_M^2|e_M\rangle\langle e_M|$. Equation (I.13m.d.5) shows
$$
B_M\ddot Z_M+VZ_M=F_M^{\rm bd},
\qquad \|F_M^{\rm bd}(t)\|\le C
\tag{I.13m.h.4}
$$
on the common interval. Indeed all coefficients in (I.13m.d.5) and the norms of $Z_M,\dot Z_M$ are bounded there, uniformly in $M$. In particular $B_M$ has a uniform positive bound, $\dot B_M$ is bounded, and $\chi_M(t)=O(t)$. The initial conditions are $Z_M(0)=0$, $\dot Z_M(0)=f_0 e_M$, with the same $f_0$ at every cutoff.

Compare to $Z_M^0=f_0\sin(t\sqrt V)V^{-1/2}e_M$, with the quotient read as $t$ at zero mass. It solves $\ddot Z_M^0+VZ_M^0=0$ with the same data. The difference of its equation from (I.13m.h.4), using $B_M$ on the left, adds only the forcing $(I-B_M)\ddot Z_M^0$ to $F_M^{\rm bd}$. Although $\ddot Z_M^0$ need not be bounded in Hilbert norm uniformly in $M$, the rank-one factor involves only $\langle e_M,\ddot Z_M^0\rangle$. By (I.13m.h.3) this has magnitude at most $C t^{m-1}$, so $(I-B_M)\ddot Z_M^0$ is bounded by $C t^{m+1}$. Pair the difference equation with its velocity. The energy uses $B_M$, the positive mass potential and an added squared displacement term. Its square root has derivative bounded by a constant times itself plus a bounded forcing, and its initial value is zero. Hence
$$
\|\dot Z_M(t)-\dot Z_M^0(t)\|
+\|V^{1/2}(Z_M(t)-Z_M^0(t))\|\le Ct
\tag{I.13m.h.5}
$$
uniformly for small $t$, with the bound on the actual scale factor and scalar fields from the nonlinear coupled solution. There is no replacement of that solution by a fixed flat history.

For the limiting bank Theorem I.13m.d gives strong convergence of $\Phi_M,\dot\Phi_M$ and weak limits of the differentiated energy variables. The free terms converge strongly in the relevant Hilbert norms by dominated convergence. Weak lower semicontinuity transfers (I.13m.h.5) to $\ddot\Phi$ and $V^{1/2}\dot\Phi$ almost everywhere. To obtain a strong representative, view the full differentiated equation as the linear wave with kinetic operator $B(t)$ and fixed positive mass $V$, with bounded Hilbert forcing as in (I.13m.h.4). The standard energy propagator for this equation can be constructed by the principal cutoff argument of Theorem I.13m.f: approximate the rank-one direction in $B$ by $e_M$, approximate bounded-mass data and smooth forcing, differentiate once for those dense data to obtain a mass-uniform acceleration estimate, and apply the difference energy on the common carrier. Extend by the uniform energy bound to all energy data and $L^1$ forcing. Uniqueness in the weak energy class follows from the usual time-regularized energy identity for the positive kinetic form with bounded $\dot B$, or by duality against the same backward energy propagator on dense data. The distributional differentiated solution with the stated initial traces is this energy solution. Therefore $\ddot\Phi$ and $V^{1/2}\dot\Phi$ have strong continuous representatives. The almost-everywhere bound (I.13m.h.5) then holds throughout the interval.

*Leading norms.* The two free squared norms are
$$
f_0^2 A\int \sin^2(t\sqrt v)\,\sigma_m(dv),\qquad
f_0^2 A\int (1-\cos(t\sqrt v))^2\,\sigma_m(dv).
$$
Their bounded-mass contributions are $O(t^2)$ and $O(t^4)$ respectively. On the large-mass part set $u=t^2v$ and use (I.13m.h.2). After division by $t^m$, dominated convergence applies: the sine-square multiplier is bounded by $\min(u,1)$ and the cosine-square difference by a constant times $\min(u^2,1)$. Their products with $u^{-1-m/2}$ are integrable at both ends. This gives the constants in (I.13m.h.1). Finally the difference (I.13m.h.5) is $O(t)=o(t^{m/2})$ in norm, so it does not change either leading squared norm. This proves the stated sharp initial exponent on the actual source. A nonlinear formulation for these prepared zero-past data must accommodate this initial regularity. Other preparations have their own mass-energy tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mi"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mi-exact-positive-scalar-tensor-force-slip-and-lensing-range"></a>**Theorem I.13m.i (Exact Positive Scalar–Tensor Force, Slip and Lensing Range).** Consider the generally covariant two-derivative class with one metric universally and minimally coupled to material matter in the Jordan frame, with gravitational coefficient $F(Y)>0$ multiplying $R$, and with positive physical scalar kinetic metric after transformation to the Einstein frame. Work first at a constant scalar Minkowski vacuum, with zero vacuum potential and gradient, fixed tensor coupling, and a nonnegative scalar mass operator.
