This includes a finite positive scalar bank, or a positive Hilbert-valued linear bank with a nonnegative self-adjoint mass operator and a finite-norm conformal charge vector. The exact scalar force correction is positive and nondecreasing with wave number. The two Jordan metric potentials have equal and opposite scalar corrections and their lensing average is the tensor value. This class cannot realize the registered fixed-scale Weibull bare-matter force with positive enhancement, even if the slip requirement is dropped. The exclusion has a quantitative finite-band form. Finite positive mass banks realize every finite positive spectral correction of the displayed type and have local causal Einstein–matter evolution on the positive branch.

*Conventions and physical ports.* Use signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and $M_{\rm Pl}^{-2}=8\pi G_*$. Rescale the constant background Jordan units so that $F(Y_0)=1$, where $Y_0$ is the constant scalar vacuum. Write $g^E=F g^J$, and put $A_c(Y)=F(Y)^{-1/2}$, so material matter couples to $g^J=A_c^2g^E$. For a finite scalar class one may start with the local gravitational action
$$
\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^2}{2}\int\sqrt{-g^J}
  \left[F R(g^J)-K_{ab}\partial_\mu Y^a\partial^\mu Y^b-2U_J\right].
\tag{I.13m.i.1}
$$
The conformal curvature identity, followed by integration by parts for compact variations, gives the Einstein kinetic metric $G^E=F^{-1}K+\tfrac32\,d\log F\otimes d\log F$ and potential $U_E=F^{-2}U_J$. Equivalently one may specify directly the positive Einstein target and its universal material metric $A_c^2g^E$. Physical scalar positivity in this theorem refers to the Einstein kinetic metric and its nonnegative linear mass operator. The positivity test uses the transformed scalar kinetic form. Normalize the vacuum target kinetic metric to the identity in its real Hilbert space $\mathcal X$ and let $\mathsf M\ge0$ be the vacuum Hessian of $U_E$ in this normalization. Let $\alpha\in\mathcal X$ be the gradient of $\log A_c$ at $Y_0$. Finite norm of $\alpha$ makes the single physical material port bounded on the target. The static formulas below follow from this universally conformal port, rather than from separate source and detector scalar charges. See Damour and Esposito-Farèse (1996).

*Static response and positive spectral characterization.* Use a first-order conserved material dust mode of real density $\rho$ at nonzero spatial wave number $k$, with no independent background matter. Write $q=\delta Y$. The variation of the material action in the scalar direction is $\langle\alpha,q\rangle T$ in background volume units, with $T=-\rho$. The scalar field equation is $(\Box-\mathsf M)q=-\alpha T/M_{\rm Pl}^2$. The scalar stress has zero linear variation because the vacuum is constant and the potential and its first derivative vanish there. The linear Einstein metric therefore has equal scalar potentials $\Phi_E=\Psi_E=\Phi_*=-\rho/(2M_{\rm Pl}^2 k^2)$ for this mode. The zero homogeneous scalar static boundary convention gives
$$
q=-\frac{\rho}{M_{\rm Pl}^2}(k^2+\mathsf M)^{-1}\alpha,\qquad
\delta\log A_c=\langle\alpha,q\rangle .
\tag{I.13m.i.2}
$$
For a Hilbert bank the resolvent is bounded for every $k>0$, and its value lies in the operator domain of $\mathsf M$. The Jordan clock and spatial rulers give $U_J=\Phi_E+\delta\log A_c$, $\Psi_J=\Psi_E-\delta\log A_c$, using the metric conventions of Theorem I.13j. Consequently, in the fixed tensor units,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\rm dyn}(k)&=U_J/\Phi_*=1+E(k),\\
\nu_{\rm sl}(k)&=\Psi_J/\Phi_*=1-E(k),\\
\Sigma_{\rm lens}(k)&=(U_J+\Psi_J)/(2\Phi_*)=1,\\
E(k)&=2k^2\langle\alpha,(k^2+\mathsf M)^{-1}\alpha\rangle
      =2\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{k^2}{k^2+v}\,\zeta(dv),
\qquad
\zeta(B)=\|\mathsf E_{\mathsf M}(B)\alpha\|^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.i.3}
$$
Here $\mathsf E_{\mathsf M}$ is the spectral resolution. The sign follows from the same $\alpha$ in the driving source and the physical conformal readout. Spectral positivity implies $E\ge0$ and monotonicity in $k$. The massless term, if any, is constant. Since the integrand is strictly positive at every finite mass and every $k>0$, zero slip on any such mode requires $\alpha=0$ in the active target. Universal conformal matter can therefore enhance the attractive potential or leave it unchanged. It cannot add a no-slip enhancement, and its scalar contribution to the lensing average vanishes identically.

Conversely any finite positive measure $\zeta$ is realized in the linear scalar class by $\mathcal X=L^2(\zeta)$, multiplication by $v$ and $\alpha=1$. A finite atomic measure uses one canonical scalar for each atom, with $\alpha_j=\sqrt{\zeta_j}$. On this finite branch choose $U_E=\tfrac12\sum_jv_j(Y_j-Y_{0j})^2$ and $A_c=\exp(\sum_j\alpha_j(Y_j-Y_{0j}))$, with canonical positive scalar kinetic metric. These are local smooth covariant couplings. Its vacuum has zero matter and its small perturbations have nonnegative quadratic scalar energy; the scalar matter stress on the pure bank is positive in a unit-normal frame. For a prescribed independent first-order source the linear equations have retarded evolution, using the positive Klein–Gordon modes of the actual source. With dynamical matter of a specified well-posed minimally coupled class, the conformally coupled equations have the standard local Einstein–scalar–matter development on constraint-satisfying data where that matter's evolution remains hyperbolic. In particular in vacuum outside the probe, the finite local Einstein–scalar branch itself has the usual constraint propagation and causal Cauchy evolution; the metric and scalar equations in wave gauge have the common Einstein metric wave principal part, and their total stress is conserved by the covariant action on shell. This existence assertion requires no infinite-mass nonlinear continuation. Finite positive truncations approximate every Hilbert-bank static response uniformly on a compact positive $k$ interval by the spectral resolvent bound and mass quadrature.

*Finite-band separation from the Weibull force.* Write the fixed-scale multiplier of (I.13l.a.4) as
$$
\mu_W(k)=1+A\int_{(0,\infty)}\frac{v}{v+k^2}\,\sigma_m(dv).
$$
For $A>0$ and $0<k_1<k_2$ it strictly decreases between those two wave numbers. Every force multiplier from (I.13m.i.3) is nondecreasing. Any single positive rescaling of its fixed gravitational normalization preserves that ordering. For any such normalized comparator $\widetilde\mu$,
$$
\sup_{k\in[k_1,k_2]}|\widetilde\mu(k)-\mu_W(k)|
\ge \frac{\mu_W(k_1)-\mu_W(k_2)}2
=\frac{A(k_2^2-k_1^2)}2
 \int_{(0,\infty)}
 \frac{v\,\sigma_m(dv)}{(v+k_1^2)(v+k_2^2)} >0 .
\tag{I.13m.i.4}
$$
Indeed the difference between the two target endpoint values is at most the sum of the two endpoint errors, since the comparator's endpoint difference has the opposite weak sign. The integral is finite and positive with no first moment assumption. At fixed tensor normalization, matching the force at even one wave number with positive enhancement forces a nonzero scalar slip and leaves the lensing multiplier equal to one. Thus it cannot match both the force and the equal-potential lensing response of the registered no-slip pair. The use of the same physical Jordan metric for the material source, the force and the lensing observable is part of this result. Assigning unrelated scalar charges to the two ports changes the response experiment.

*Tensor response on a homogeneous nonminimal branch.* On any smooth homogeneous FLRW solution of the same finite scalar class with positive $F(t)$, the Jordan-frame transverse-traceless strain is equal to its Einstein-frame counterpart because the conformal factor is a scalar. The scalar target has zero linear transverse-traceless mixed stress on such a background. Let $t,a,H$ now be the Jordan proper time, scale factor and Hubble rate. Let $\Pi^J$ be a transverse-traceless mixed spatial external stress in this frame. The exact Jordan tensor equation for a comoving mode is
$$
\ddot h+\left(3H+\frac{\dot F}{F}\right)\dot h
 +\frac{k^2}{a^2}h
=\frac{2}{M_{\rm Pl}^2F}\Pi^J .
\tag{I.13m.i.5}
$$
Indeed in Einstein variables $dt_E=\sqrt F\,dt$, $a_E=\sqrt F\,a$, and the mixed tensor stress scales as $\Pi^E=F^{-2}\Pi^J$ by variation of the minimally coupled material action at fixed scalars. Substitution into the ordinary Einstein tensor mode equation of Theorem I.13m.e gives (I.13m.i.5): the second derivative contributes $-\dot F\,\dot h/(2F)$ after multiplying by $F$, while $3H_E$ contributes $3H+3\dot F/(2F)$. The spatial term is unchanged after the same multiplication. This shows the actual additional tensor effect of the scalar branch is a local coefficient in the homogeneous metric evolution. The homogeneous tensor operator is local and second order. General couplings producing independent tensor anisotropic stress, nonuniversal or derivative matter couplings, and the nonlinear common-source projections of Definition I.13d remain outside the displayed class. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mj"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mj-positive-material-frame-bank-with-actual-tensor-metric-memory"></a>**Theorem I.13m.j (Positive Material-Frame Bank with Actual Tensor Metric Memory).** There is a generally covariant local positive matter system with a dynamical material frame and an independent massive shear bank. Every finite bank has nonlinear local Einstein evolution on an open positive-energy branch and admits the same explicit expanding homogeneous background. The linear transverse-traceless metric equation on this actual background has a nonzero retarded memory from the physical anisotropic stress of the bank. A full unbounded positive massive spectral measure is admitted in this tensor response, with a strong finite-bank limit and a coercive coupled tensor energy under the stated bound. The response is a metric self-response to a conserved tensor probe. Its local elastic term and positive memory weights are fixed by its own action.

*Covariant matter and a common background.* Take spacetime spatial slices to be a flat three-torus, with coordinates of period $L_*$, and use three angular material scalars $X^I$ of target period $sL_*$, with $s>0$. Write $\mathcal S_0$ for the five-dimensional real symmetric trace-free matrices with their Frobenius inner product. At a finite bank use independent fields $Q_j\in\mathcal S_0$, squared masses $v_j\ge v_*>0$ and coefficients $b_j\in\mathbb R$. Put $B=\sum_jb_jQ_j$. The action uses the ordinary Einstein term $R/(16\pi G)$ and the matter Lagrangian
$$
\mathcal L_{\rm mat}
=-\tfrac12(\delta_{IJ}+2B_{IJ})\,g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu X^I\partial_\nu X^J
-\tfrac12\sum_j\left(g^{\mu\nu}\langle\partial_\mu Q_j,\partial_\nu Q_j\rangle_F
                         +v_j\|Q_j\|_F^2\right).
\tag{I.13m.j.1}
$$
The matrix indices label the internal material coordinates. The contraction uses spacetime scalars and $g$, and the angular derivatives are globally defined. This construction couples the material coordinates to an independent dynamical shear bank. See Endlich et al. (2013).

On the open domain $I+2B\succ0$ the full finite matter target kinetic metric is positive and the mass potential is nonnegative. Thus the matter energy in the unit-normal frame is nonnegative. The finite nonlinear equations in wave coordinates have the Einstein wave principal part and a positive target-metric multiple of the scalar wave principal part. The remaining couplings contain only first derivatives of the fields and a smooth potential. For each finite bank the ordinary local Einstein–matter Cauchy argument, with constraint-satisfying data in the positive target domain, gives causal local solutions and propagation of the gauge constraints by total stress conservation.

For every bank take $X^I=sx^I$ as a winding map, $Q_j=0$, and $g=-dt^2+a(t)^2d\mathbf x^2$. The material equation is the divergence of a constant spatial gradient with time-dependent scalar coefficient and vanishes. The $Q_j$ equation is sourced by the trace-free part of $g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu X^I\partial_\nu X^J=s^2a^{-2}\delta^{IJ}$ and also vanishes. The common density and pressure are $3s^2/(2a^2)$ and $-s^2/(2a^2)$. Thus the flat expanding Einstein solution with $a(0)=a_0>0$ is
$$
a(t)=a_0+\sqrt{4\pi G}\,s\,t .
\tag{I.13m.j.2}
$$
Indeed $H^2=4\pi Gs^2/a^2$ and the matter continuity equation holds. This is an actual solution with the same state, clock and scale factor for every finite bank. The bank fields have exactly zero energy on it.

*Tensor closure and the actual stress.* On a Fourier mode with comoving wave number $k$, choose a real transverse-traceless polarization of unit Frobenius norm. Let $h$ be the amplitude of $g_{ij}/a^2-\delta_{ij}$ and let $Q_j$ in the following equations denote the amplitude of the corresponding material matrix polarization, using the winding identification of spatial and material axes. Set the material perturbations $\delta X^I$ to zero. Their linear equations are satisfied: the change of their spatial flux contains only the divergences of the transverse $h$ and $Q_j$, and the volume trace variation vanishes. The trace-free variation of the strain is $-s^2a^{-2}h$ in that polarization. The independent scalar matrix equation from (I.13m.j.1) is $(\Box_g-v_j)Q_j=b_j(g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu X\partial_\nu X)_{\rm STF}$. Therefore with $L_v=\partial_t^2+3H\partial_t+k^2/a^2+v$ it becomes
$$
L_{v_j}Q_j=s^2a^{-2}b_jh .
\tag{I.13m.j.3}
$$
No other component of the material matrix is forced in this closed tensor sector.

The mixed spatial material stress is
$$
T^i{}_j=(\delta_{IJ}+2B_{IJ})\partial^iX^I\partial_jX^J
+\sum_\ell\langle\partial^iQ_\ell,\partial_jQ_\ell\rangle_F
+\delta^i_j\mathcal L_{\rm mat}.
$$
At first order the second term vanishes and the last has no transverse-traceless component. In the first term, the inverse spatial metric variation supplies $-h$ and the material target metric variation supplies $2\sum b_jQ_j$. Thus its exact first-order tensor stress amplitude is
$$
\Pi_{\rm mat}=s^2a^{-2}\left(2\sum_j b_jQ_j-h\right).
\tag{I.13m.j.4}
$$
The term $-s^2a^{-2}h$ comes from the positive material gradient energy on the same background. A first-order mixed spatial transverse-traceless probe $\Pi_{\rm ext}$ with zero temporal components is covariantly conserved on this background. The ordinary Einstein tensor equation of Theorem I.13m.e then gives
$$
L_0 h+16\pi Gs^2a^{-2}h-32\pi Gs^2a^{-2}\sum_jb_jQ_j
 =16\pi G\,\Pi_{\rm ext}.
\tag{I.13m.j.5}
$$
These equations are also verified by the quadratic tensor action below. Tensor closure follows from the displayed material equations and the Einstein tensor decomposition. It is a linear calculation on the common actual nonlinear solution.

*Positive coupled tensor energy and continuum response.* Set $\gamma=h/\sqrt{32\pi G}$ and $C(t)=\sqrt{32\pi G}\,s^2a^{-2}$. The tensor equations have common damping $3H$ and symmetric potential
$$
\mathcal V_{\rm TT}
=\tfrac12(k^2+16\pi Gs^2)a^{-2}\gamma^2
+\tfrac12\sum_j(k^2/a^2+v_j)Q_j^2
-C(t)\gamma\sum_j b_jQ_j .
\tag{I.13m.j.6}
$$
Their kinetic energy is $(\dot\gamma^2+\sum_j\dot Q_j^2)/2$. The force on $\gamma$ is $16\pi G\,\Pi_{\rm ext}/\sqrt{32\pi G}$. Differentiation of (I.13m.j.6) gives both signs and the reciprocal off-diagonal product in (I.13m.j.3) and (I.13m.j.5). If $a_-$ is the minimum scale factor on the chosen compact interval, assume
$$
4s^2a_-^{-2}\sum_j b_j^2/v_j\le1 .
\tag{I.13m.j.7}
$$
Writing $m_h^2=(k^2+16\pi Gs^2)/a^2$ and $E_Q=\sum_j(k^2/a^2+v_j)Q_j^2$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives the cross term at most $m_h|\gamma|\sqrt{E_Q}/\sqrt2$, because
$$
C(t)^2\sum_j\frac{b_j^2}{k^2/a^2+v_j}
 \le 32\pi Gs^4a^{-4}\sum_j b_j^2/v_j
 \le m_h^2/2 .
$$
Consequently $\mathcal V_{\rm TT}\ge(1-1/\sqrt2)(m_h^2\gamma^2+E_Q)/2$. This verifies positivity for the actual coupled tensor oscillator energy, in addition to positivity of the local matter target. The expanding background does not make this quadratic energy time-independent.

For a continuum let $\nu$ be any finite positive measure on $[v_*,\infty)$, take the bank carrier $L^2(\nu)$ per polarization, $V$ multiplication by $v$, and $b=\mathbf1$. In (I.13m.j.7) use $\int v^{-1}\nu(dv)$. A finite bank uses atoms with $b_j=\sqrt{\nu_j}$. For example one may take a sufficiently small positive multiple of the massive Weibull measure restricted to $v\ge v_*$, which is nonrational and unbounded in mass. The linear equations on the actual common background have positive mass energy, with forcing and coupling through the bounded vector $b$. Existence can be obtained directly on the common carrier: truncate $b$ at mass $M$, partition the retained interval into mass cells, and approximate $V$ by a cell-constant multiplier there, leaving it unchanged in the unused tail. Choose each representative at least as large as its cell masses to preserve (I.13m.j.7). The operator error is bounded by the mesh size $\eta$, and the direction error is $\|b-b_M\|=\sqrt{\nu((M,\infty))}$. Zero oscillator data keep the finite cell subspace invariant. This yields exactly the finite systems on the same background. Pair the difference equations with the velocity differences in the common positive energy, adding a squared displacement norm if needed. The time derivatives of $a^{-2}$ and $C(t)$ are bounded on the interval. Their terms are controlled by the coercive energy, and the cutoff and mesh errors are bounded forces with norms controlled by $\|b-b_M\|+\eta$. Grönwall's estimate gives strong uniform-in-time convergence in the displacement, velocity and positive mass-energy norms on every fixed compact interval for a fixed $k$ and zero-past data. The same estimate gives uniqueness for the linear energy solution. The metric and bank fields in this limiting calculation are linear variations, not independent infinite-bank nonlinear backgrounds.

*Exact retarded metric memory.* Let $\mathscr R_v^a$ be the zero-past inverse of $L_v$ on this actual scale factor, as in Theorem I.13m.e. Eliminating only the bank fields from (I.13m.j.3) gives the exact metric equation
$$
L_0h+16\pi Gs^2a^{-2}h
-32\pi Gs^4a^{-2}\int \mathscr R_v^a(a^{-2}h)\,\nu(dv)
=16\pi G\,\Pi_{\rm ext}.
\tag{I.13m.j.8}
$$
The memory uses the positive square of the same physical shear coupling on the two legs. The scalar wave energy on a compact interval gives the mass-uniform bound needed for this integral. For nonzero $\nu$ it is an actual nonzero retarded term. For example take a positive mass band of nonzero measure and sufficiently short times. The causal Green kernel on that band is positive immediately after its diagonal, while the full integrated kernel has leading value proportional to $\nu([v_*,\infty))(t-u)$ as $t\downarrow u$. For the last statement, divide the kernel by $t-u$, use its unit initial slope at each fixed mass, and dominate by the uniform short-time bound $|\mathscr R_v^a(t,u)|\le C(t-u)$. That bound follows from the positive scalar oscillator energy with initial unit velocity and the estimate on its derivative from the bounded time variation of $k^2/a^2$ and damping, with an added position term. The limit of the ratio is therefore the positive total measure by dominated convergence. Thus (I.13m.j.8) changes the actual tensor metric equation through anisotropic stress on a positive covariant branch.

The physical response in (I.13m.j.8) retains both the local elasticity and the positive mass measure fixed by the action. The registered signed Weibull self-response, nonlinear unbounded-mass inhomogeneous evolution, the scalar weak-field coefficient map and the common cosmological projections of Definition I.13d require further arguments. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mk"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mk-nonlinear-spatial-evolution-of-an-unbounded-material-shear-bank"></a>**Theorem I.13m.k (Nonlinear Spatial Evolution of an Unbounded Material Shear Bank).** Use the generally covariant winding material source of Theorem I.13m.j, including its Einstein metric, with bank carrier $\mathcal H=L^2(\nu;\mathcal S_0)$ on $v\ge v_*>0$ and mass multiplication $VQ(v)=vQ(v)$. For an integer $s\ge5$ assume $\int (1+v)^s\nu(dv)<\infty$. There is a nonlinear local Cauchy evolution for inhomogeneous constraint data near the winding solution in the mixed energy below. The actual stress is conserved and the Einstein and gauge constraints propagate. On an explicit nonconstant family of such cuts, finite positive atomic banks with their own exact constraints converge on a common time slab in spatial and mass energy. The causal limit keeps the full unbounded bank and the common evolving geometry.

*System and mixed energy.* Use the action (I.13m.j.1) with the sum replaced by its $\nu$ integral and $B=\int Q\,d\nu$. Denote $A=(1+V)^{1/2}$ and let $b$ be the constant scalar vector in $L^2(\nu)$. The metric of the material $X$ fields is $I+2B$. Work in an open neighborhood where this matrix, the spatial metric $h_{ij}$ and the lapse $N$ have fixed positive lower bounds, with slices spacelike and compact. Use a wave gauge relative to the smooth winding solution so that the Einstein equation has a scalar wave principal part in every metric component. In the $X$ equation divide by the positive target block. Its right side uses only $\partial B$ and $\partial X$. The $Q$ equation is $(\Box_g-V)Q=b(g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu X\partial_\nu X)_{\mathrm{STF}}$. The trace-reversed Einstein equation uses first derivatives of the material fields, the rank-five integral $B$, and the mass potential $\|V^{1/2}Q\|^2$. The maps giving these sources are pointwise bounded multilinear maps in the corresponding Hilbert norms, with smooth finite-dimensional metric coefficients.

For each scalar wave use its normal derivative $P=N^{-1}(\partial_t-\beta^i\partial_i)Q$ and spatial derivative $W_i=\partial_iQ$, where $\beta^i$ is the shift. For the bank include $R=V^{1/2}Q$. Write $U_Q=(P,W,R)$ and use the squared norm
$$
\mathcal N_s(U_Q)^2
=\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\int_{\mathbb T^3}
       \left\|A^{s-|\alpha|}\partial_x^\alpha U_Q\right\|^2\,dx .
\tag{I.13m.k.1}
$$
The norms for the metric and $X$ variables are the corresponding unweighted $H^s$ norms of first derivatives and fields. In winding coordinates use $X^I-s_*x^I$ as the periodic perturbation for fixed winding $s_*>0$. The positive mass lower bound bounds every $Q$ norm here by the corresponding $R$ norm.

In the first-order wave reduction the top spatial terms for $P,W_i$ are $Nh^{ij}\partial_iW_j$ and $N\partial_iP$, in addition to the shift transport. Commuting the shift past the spatial derivative of $Q$ contributes only $(\partial_i\beta^j)W_j$. The equation for $R$ has shift transport and the term $NV^{1/2}P$. The corresponding mass term in the $P$ equation is $-NV^{1/2}R$. With the positive multiplier $|P|^2+h^{ij}\langle W_i,W_j\rangle+|R|^2$, the spatial terms cancel after integration by parts up to derivatives of the finite-dimensional coefficients, and the two principal mass terms cancel exactly. Use this multiplier on every term of (I.13m.k.1). The standard first-order wave reduction gives the same spatial cancellation for the metric and $X$ equations (Fischer and Marsden 1973).

For clarity, the mass commutator after $\alpha$ spatial derivatives has terms with $0<\gamma\le\alpha$ of the form
$$
(\partial^\gamma N) A^{s-|\alpha|}V^{1/2}
                 \partial^{\alpha-\gamma}U_Q .
\tag{I.13m.k.2}
$$
It costs one mass derivative and releases at least one spatial derivative. At fixed $k=|\alpha|$ the field $A^{s-k+1}U_Q$ has $H^{k-1}$ norm bounded by (I.13m.k.1), since $A\ge I$. Thus $A^{s-k+1}\partial^{\alpha-\gamma}U_Q$ has the remaining $H^{|\gamma|-1}$ derivatives. The coefficient $\partial^\gamma N$ has $H^{s+1-|\gamma|}$ regularity from the metric norm. Their indices sum to $s>3/2$, and both are nonnegative, so the three-dimensional Sobolev product bound into $L^2$ controls (I.13m.k.2). The same count for the spatial commutator uses $A^{s-k}\partial^{\alpha-\gamma}\partial_iU_Q$ with remaining $H^{|\gamma|-1}$ regularity. Coefficients containing one metric derivative in lower-order terms belong to $H^s$. Multiplying by such a coefficient on the bank term of spatial order $k$ is bounded in $H^k$, $k\le s$, using the spatial $H^k$ algebra estimate when $k>3/2$ and the $H^s$ multiplier bound when $k\le3/2$. The forcing through $b$ has the required weighted norm because $\|A^s b\|^2=\int(1+v)^s\nu(dv)$. The same product estimates bound the Einstein and $X$ sources in $H^s$, using the unweighted $H^s$ portion of (I.13m.k.1) for the full Hilbert-valued bank. In particular the mass potential uses $R$, which is already a first-order energy variable.

These estimates give $\dot E_s\le C(E_s)$ on bounded subsets of the positive domain, with $E_s$ the sum of the symmetrized energies and the field norms. The constant depends on the lower metric bounds and $\|A^sb\|$, uniformly in the largest retained mass. The finite-bank solutions therefore share a positive time slab for convergent initial data in the interior of that domain. The corresponding difference estimate at order $s-1$ is a Grönwall inequality. In a difference of principal operators the change in the finite-dimensional coefficient multiplies one spatial or mass derivative of a solution bounded at order $s$. For the mass term this uses $\|A^{s-1-k}V^{1/2}U_Q\|_{H^k}\le\|A^{s-k}U_Q\|_{H^k}$. This controls the extra derivative without imposing an operator-norm bound on $V$.

*Finite-bank approximation and constraints.* Retain $v\le M$ and partition that mass interval into finitely many cells with mesh $\eta$, assigning one representative in each cell. On the common carrier use the cell averages of the initial data and replace $V$ by its representative multiplier on the retained interval, leaving it unchanged on the unused tail. Truncate $b$ on the same interval. With zero tail data, the cell-constant subspace is invariant and is exactly a finite atomic bank with weights equal to cell masses. Use $R=V_n^{1/2}Q$ in each approximation, where $V_n$ is its multiplier. The mixed norms using $A_n$ and $A$ are equivalent with factors tending to one as $\eta\to0$. The difference of the square-root multipliers on the common carrier is bounded by $\eta/(2\sqrt{v_*})$. Compare any two approximants on this common carrier, bounding the coefficient-independent mass error by the sum of their mesh sizes and the difference of the force vectors by their two weighted tails. The lower energy difference is bounded on the common slab by a uniform constant times these errors and the initial difference. For initial vectors the required cell-average approximation follows first on continuous functions of $v$ with compact support and then by density in the finite weighted $L^2$ norms of (I.13m.k.1). The strong order-$(s-1)$ limit and the uniform order-$s$ bound pass all products and the weak wave equations. This constructs the reduced evolution for general initial data, with the constraints imposed on the limiting cut. The difference estimate gives uniqueness and continuous dependence in the lower energy. The principal energy flux is that of the common metric wave cone, and the mass terms cancel also on localized cones. The same difference estimate on such domains gives metric causal dependence.

To exhibit constraint data, set the background spatial scale on the initial cut to one, write $h=\psi^4\delta$ and take the extrinsic curvature $K_{ij}=\tau h_{ij}/3$ with the constant expanding background trace $\tau$, where $\tfrac23\tau^2=24\pi Gs_*^2$. Set both matter normal velocities to zero, keep $X^I=s_*x^I$, and choose a small spatially nonconstant bank displacement, for example $Q_0(x,v)=\epsilon q_*(v)S\cos(2\pi x_1/L_*)$ with nonzero trace-free constant $S$ and a nonzero bounded mass-profile $q_*$ of compact mass support. The momentum constraint holds. Put $D_X=(\delta_{IJ}+2B_{IJ})\delta^{ij}\partial_iX^I\partial_jX^J$, $D_Q=\delta^{ij}\langle\partial_iQ,\partial_jQ\rangle$ and $M_Q=\|V^{1/2}Q\|^2$. The Hamiltonian constraint is
$$
-8\Delta\psi+\bigl(\tfrac23\tau^2-8\pi G M_Q\bigr)\psi^5
                 -8\pi G(D_X+D_Q)\psi=0 .
\tag{I.13m.k.3}
$$
Here $D_X=3s_*^2$ because $B$ is trace free. At $Q=0$, $\psi=1$ solves the equation and the derivative in $\psi$ is $-8\Delta+96\pi Gs_*^2$, invertible on periodic Sobolev spaces. The implicit function theorem gives a positive $\psi$ for all sufficiently small choices in this family and gives convergent constraint data for the atomic approximants using their own $V_n$. Choose the initial lapse and shift, and their first derivatives, to impose the wave gauge on the cut. In the limit the stress is the Hilbert variation of the displayed integral action. The material wave equations imply its distributional divergence vanishes, by the chain rule and the $V^{1/2}$ energy identity. Equivalently this follows from strong convergence of all stress terms and the metric connection in the finite-bank divergence identities. The initial Einstein constraints and wave gauge propagate, either by the homogeneous gauge wave equation or by the corresponding finite-bank identities and convergence. This proves the full conserved nonlinear development on the indicated data.

For example a sufficiently small multiple of $e^{-v}dv$ on $[v_*,\infty)$ has unbounded support, satisfies the mixed moment requirement and obeys the linear tensor coercivity bound of Theorem I.13m.j. The moment premise controls spatially commuted mass terms. The registered Weibull mass tail, its signed metric response and the joint observable projections require further estimates and identification. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13ml"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13ml-full-signed-weibull-detector-on-a-nonlinear-inhomogeneous-einstein-source"></a>**Theorem I.13m.l (Full Signed Weibull Detector on a Nonlinear Inhomogeneous Einstein Source).** Fix the complete signed measure $W=(1+A)\delta_0-A\sigma_m$ of Theorem I.13m.b, with $0<m\le1$ and $A>0$. The winding material action of Theorem I.13m.j has a positive continuum realization with all these masses and a source-conditioned material detector with the exact full signed kernel $W$. The physical bank and Einstein geometry solve the nonlinear inhomogeneous equations on a common slab. Finite positive atomic banks converge there in the energy of Theorem I.13m.k and in the energy of the detector. The detector uses a signed weighting of the actual oscillator histories. The conserved metric stress uses the positive weighting fixed by the action.

*Physical bank and actual constraint cuts.* Let $s\ge5$ be an integer and write $\mathscr S=\mathcal S_0$ for the internal trace-free tensor space. Use the action (I.13m.j.1) with the physical positive measure
$$
d\nu(v)=\xi(1+v/v_c)^{-s}\,d|W|(v),\qquad \xi,v_c>0,
\tag{I.13m.l.1}
$$
where $v_c$ is a fixed reference squared mass in the declared units. The material coefficient is $B=\int Q,d\nu$. The reference $1+v$ in the norm of Theorem I.13m.k is interpreted in fixed mass units, so $\int(1+v)^s\,d\nu<\infty$. This choice changes the physical stress weight while preserving the full support of the mass measure, including the atom at zero. Each mass obeys
$$
(\Box_g-v)Q(v)=F(g,X),\qquad
F(g,X)=\bigl(g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu X\partial_\nu X\bigr)_{\mathrm{STF}} .
\tag{I.13m.l.2}
$$
All masses see the same actual metric and strain. The winding background $Q=0$ still solves the system, since its strain is proportional to the identity.

The mixed-energy proof of Theorem I.13m.k extends to $v\ge0$. Add the unweighted-in-spatial-order mass-scaled displacement terms $\|(1+V)^{(s-|\alpha|)/2}\partial_x^\alpha Q\|^2$ at every order in (I.13m.k.1). The displacement equation uses shift transport and the normal velocity, with no mass multiplier. The added commutators and sources satisfy the same mixed estimates. The skew cancellation between $P$ and $V^{1/2}Q$ remains exact. The added displacement norm controls the undifferentiated field and the coefficient $B$, also at $v=0$. In the finite-bank comparison keep the atom at zero fixed and use $|\sqrt{v}-\sqrt{w}|\le\sqrt{|v-w|}$, so the bounded square-root multiplier error is at most $\sqrt\eta$ for mesh $\eta$. These changes give the same common-time and convergence arguments. In particular the construction applies with $Q$ and its normal velocity zero on the initial cut.

For explicit inhomogeneous cuts use the conformal metric and constant mean curvature of (I.13m.k.3), with zero normal velocities for $X,Q$ and $Q=0$. Perturb the first winding field by $\epsilon\sin(2\pi x_1/L_*)$, leaving the other two winding fields fixed. The momentum density vanishes. In (I.13m.k.3) use the resulting $D_X$ and set $D_Q=M_Q=0$. The derivative in $\psi$ at the winding background is unchanged. The implicit function theorem gives an exact positive conformal factor for small $\epsilon$, with the same initial data in every bank. For nonzero $\epsilon$, $D_X$ is nonconstant, so the Hamiltonian equation excludes a constant conformal factor. The strain is trace-free nonzero at points where the squared first winding gradient differs from the squared other gradients. Thus the actual bank is driven on these cuts. The subsequent evolution, constraint propagation and stress conservation follow from the extended mixed energy. The physical measure $\nu$ and the geometry enter the Hilbert stress and its conservation identity.

*Detector on the actual sourced histories.* Write $\mathscr R_v^g$ for the zero-initial-data inverse of $-(\Box_g-v)$ on the slab. With the cut data above, the actual bank coordinate is $Q(v)=-\mathscr R_v^g F$. Define its signed detector by
$$
\mathcal D=-\int Q(v)\,dW(v)
=\int \mathscr R_v^g F\,dW(v).
\tag{I.13m.l.3}
$$
This is a causal functional of the actual bank trajectory. In particular it uses neither an independently prescribed metric nor a separate re-solved background. The two signs of $W$ enter the detector; (I.13m.l.1) assigns nonnegative mass-energy weights to every field.

The usual uncommuted wave energy on the actual slab, with a positive displacement term included, gives
$$
\sup_{t\le T}\left(\|Q(t,v)\|_{H^1_x}+\|\partial_tQ(t,v)\|_{L^2_x}
+\sqrt v\|Q(t,v)\|_{L^2_x}\right)
\le C_T\int_0^T\|F(t)\|_{L^2_x}\,dt .
\tag{I.13m.l.4}
$$
The constant uses the lapse, shift and spatial metric bounds and their first derivatives. It is independent of $v$: the two mass terms in the normal velocity and mass-displacement equations cancel in the energy, and shift transport only differentiates metric coefficients. For example this is the zeroth spatial-order estimate in the proof of Theorem I.13m.k, using the added displacement term. Hence (I.13m.l.3) exists in $C_tH^1_x\cap C_t^1L^2_x$. Its tail beyond $M$ is bounded in those norms by the right side of (I.13m.l.4) times $|W|((M,\infty))$. This bounds the full infinite detector on the sourced histories even though $dW/d\nu$ grows at high mass.

For the finite comparison keep the zero atom and choose one representative per cell up to the cutoff. Assign the physical atom the cell mass of $\nu$, and the detector coefficient in (I.13m.l.3) the cell mass of $W$. The finite matter equations are (I.13m.l.2) on their own finite-bank metric $g_n$ and strain $F_n$. On any fixed compact mass interval, the difference wave equation bounds the order-zero energy error uniformly in the mass in terms of the metric difference, strain difference and cell mesh. To see this, use the inverse metric difference times the second derivatives of the limiting compact-mass solution, together with the connection difference times first derivatives and the mass representative difference times the displacement. The limiting compact-mass solutions have uniformly bounded second derivatives from the spatially commuted linear energy with bounded masses and from (I.13m.l.2). The required coefficient and strain convergence follows from the order-$(s-1)$ common-source convergence. Use (I.13m.l.4) on each actual finite geometry for the complement of that compact interval. Its constants are uniform along the nonlinear approximants. The resulting compact-mass error and two detector tails tend to zero by taking a large fixed compact interval and then fine finite banks. The physical cutoff and mesh convergence of the stress follows independently from the physical mixed-energy estimate. This proves joint convergence, including the time derivative of the detector, on a common inhomogeneous slab.

The detector's domain is specified by the source and initial conditions. For example the unrestricted instantaneous velocity functional $U\mapsto\int U,dW$ cannot be bounded by the physical $L^2(\nu)$ velocity norm on the full bank. Its squared norm would be $\int |dW/d\nu|^2d\nu=\xi^{-1}\int(1+v/v_c)^s,d|W|$, which diverges by the Weibull tail of Theorem I.13m.h. Testing its truncated densities gives the divergence of the norm directly. This is compatible with the uniform causal bound on the driven trajectory. The resulting signed transfer concerns the material strain and detector in (I.13m.l.2)–(I.13m.l.3). The metric remains the response of the conserved stress of the positive action; the signed reciprocal metric law and common cosmological projection ledger retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mm"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mm-finite-time-weibull-separation-for-the-actual-shear-metric"></a>**Theorem I.13m.m (Finite-Time Weibull Separation for the Actual Shear Metric).** Use the material-frame shear action of Theorem I.13m.j on its expanding winding background. Retain any finite positive shear mass measure $\nu$ on $[0,\infty)$, including the measure (I.13m.l.1) of the nonlinear source. On a sufficiently short explicitly bounded time interval, its physical transverse-traceless metric response to a nonnegative pulse amplitude in a fixed conserved tensor polarization is strictly below the massless Einstein response on that same background. The signed Weibull continuation (I.13m.e.3) is strictly above the massless response for the same pulse. The two metric responses therefore differ by an explicit finite-time margin. The result uses the local elastic term of the physical action and the full positive shear bank, including arbitrarily large masses.

*Common clock and positive Green kernels on a short interval.* Fix one real normalized tensor polarization and a nonzero comoving wave number. In (I.13m.j.8) write $F=16\pi G\Pi_{\rm ext}$, and put
$$
p(t)=16\pi Gs^2 a(t)^{-2},\qquad
b(t)=\sqrt{32\pi G}\,s^2 a(t)^{-2},\qquad
q(t)=k^2/a(t)^2-\tfrac32\dot H(t)-\tfrac94H(t)^2.
$$
Use $z=a^{3/2}h$ for the metric and the same multiplication for every shear mode. Then the kernel equation for the metric follows from
$$
\begin{aligned}
\ddot z+(q+p)z-b(t)\int z_v\,\nu(dv)&=a^{3/2}F,\\
\ddot z_v+(q+v)z_v&=b(t)z,
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.m.1}
$$
with zero incoming variations. Here the coefficient product on the two legs is the square of the original coupling when the two times agree. The finite systems satisfy (I.13m.m.1) exactly. Their linear response converges for every finite positive $\nu$ on the compact slab: the kinetic, mass and displacement energies, with an added positive displacement term for each block, give a Grönwall bound because $b$ couples through a bounded vector and $q,p$ are bounded. This estimate also holds for the possible atom at zero. Approximating the bounded coupling and the mass multiplier by the cutoffs and meshes of Theorem I.13m.j gives the energy solution of (I.13m.m.1). For the nonlinear source of Theorem I.13m.l this is the tensor linearization on its common winding background. The coefficients are the derivatives of its actual stress and of the material equations, with the mass integral taken in their energy domain.

Let $y_v(t,u)$ be the normalized bare kernel of (I.13m.e.4), including its massless member $y_0$. On a compact background interval put $p_-=\inf p>0$, $p_+=\sup p$, $b_+=\sup|b|$, and $N_\nu=\nu([0,\infty))$. Choose any compact positive mass band $[v_1,v_2]$ with $\sigma_m([v_1,v_2])>0$. Restrict all time differences to at most $T$ with $T^2(\|q\|_\infty+v_2)\le1/4$. The proof of Theorem I.13m.e gives
$$
\tfrac12(t-u)\le y_0(t,u)\le2(t-u),\qquad
|y_v(t,u)|\le y_0(t,u)\quad(v\ge0).
\tag{I.13m.m.2}
$$
Thus the full shear-memory kernel is bounded in absolute value by $2b_+^2N_\nu(t-u)$ after including its two coupling factors.

*Ordering the physical response.* Denote the normalized metric Green kernel of (I.13m.m.1) by $y(t,u)$, with unit initial slope at $u$. At fixed $u$ its scalar Volterra equation is
$$
\begin{split}
y(t,u)=y_0(t,u)+\int_u^t y_0(t,r)\Bigl[ -p(r)y(r,u)
+b(r)\int_u^r\int y_v(r,w)\,\nu(dv)\,b(w)y(w,u)\,dw\Bigr]dr .
\end{split}
\tag{I.13m.m.3}
$$
On the norm $\sup_{t>u}|y(t,u)|/(t-u)$ the Volterra correction has operator norm bounded by
$$
\varepsilon_T=\frac{p_+T^2}{3}+\frac{b_+^2N_\nu T^4}{30}.
\tag{I.13m.m.4}
$$
Indeed the two convolution integrals use $\int_u^t(t-r)(r-u)dr=(t-u)^3/6$ and $\int_u^t(t-r)\int_u^r(r-w)(w-u)dw\,dr=(t-u)^5/120$, with factors $2$ and $4$, respectively, from (I.13m.m.2). Require $\varepsilon_T\le1/16$ and $(4/3)b_+^2N_\nu T^2\le p_-/8$. Such a positive $T$ always exists, with the second inequality automatic for a zero bank. Equation (I.13m.m.3) gives $\|y\|\le2/(1-\varepsilon_T)\le4$ and $\|y-y_0\|\le4\varepsilon_T$. In particular $y(t,u)\ge(t-u)/4$. For any $r\in[u,t]$, the magnitude of the positive-bank term in square brackets is at most $(4/3)b_+^2N_\nu(r-u)^3$, by (I.13m.m.2) and the upper bound on $y$. The elastic contribution has $p(r)y(r,u)\ge p_-(r-u)/4$. It follows that the square bracket in (I.13m.m.3) is at most $-p_-(r-u)/8$, irrespective of the signs of the individual massive Green values. The lower bound on $y_0$ then proves
$$
y_0(t,u)-y(t,u)\ge \frac{p_-}{96}(t-u)^3 .
\tag{I.13m.m.5}
$$

Restore the common factor $(a(u)/a(t))^{3/2}$ in the physical kernels. For $F\ge0$ smooth with nonempty compact support strictly before the readout time $t$ in the chosen interval, write $h_{\rm mat}(t)$ for the metric response of the material action and $h_W(t)=(\mathscr R_W^a F)(t)$. Equations (I.13m.e.7) and (I.13m.m.5) give
$$
h_W(t)-h_{\rm mat}(t)\ge
\left(\frac{p_-}{96}+\frac{A v_1\sigma_m([v_1,v_2])}{24}\right)
\left(\frac{a_-}{a_+}\right)^{3/2}
\int (t-u)^3F(u)\,du>0 .
\tag{I.13m.m.6}
$$
The same stress probe and physical tensor readout are used in the entire comparison. On the material source of Theorem I.13m.l the signed detector remains well defined, while the conserved metric stress leads to (I.13m.m.6). The bound concerns the registered tensor continuation on this action. Other metric couplings and the common-source cosmological projections retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13mn"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13mn-weibull-short-time-tensor-signature-and-bounded-coupling-exclusion"></a>**Theorem I.13m.n (Weibull Short-Time Tensor Signature and Bounded-Coupling Exclusion).** Use the signed retarded tensor continuation (I.13m.e.3) on a smooth positive scale factor, in the original clock, comoving mode and force unit. Remove the common factor $(a(u)/a(t))^{3/2}$ from its Green kernel. If $\tau=t-u>0$, the normalized signed kernel $y_W$ satisfies
$$
y_W(u+\tau,u)-y_0(u+\tau,u)
=A c_m\,\mathcal I_m\,\tau^{1+m}+o(\tau^{1+m}),
\qquad
\mathcal I_m=\int_0^\infty
 \left(1-\frac{\sin\sqrt x}{\sqrt x}\right)x^{-1-m/2}\,dx>0,
\tag{I.13m.n.1}
$$
uniformly on compact intervals in the interior of the background, where $c_m$ is the mass-tail coefficient of Theorem I.13m.h. A canonical unit-inertia metric mode with the same bare clock and wave symbol, bounded local stiffness, and any finite collection or Hilbert bank coupled through bounded displacement coefficients has a correction $O(\tau^3)$ to $y_0$. This excludes the signed kernel for the whole stated class, independent of the sign of a bounded local stiffness or of the memory correction. It also gives a finite short-pulse test.

*The mass-tail signature.* Write $K_v(\tau)=\sin(\sqrt v\tau)/\sqrt v$, with $K_0(\tau)=\tau$. In the variables of (I.13m.e.4), the exact normalized kernel obeys
$$
y_v(t,u)=K_v(t-u)-\int_u^t K_v(t-r)q(r)y_v(r,u)\,dr .
\tag{I.13m.n.2}
$$
On the small intervals of (I.13m.m.2), $|K_v(s)|\le s$ and $|y_v(t,u)|\le2(t-u)$ for every $v\ge0$. Hence $|y_v(u+\tau,u)-K_v(\tau)|\le \|q\|_\infty\tau^3/3$ uniformly in the mass. In particular
$$
y_W-y_0=A\tau\int_{(0,\infty)}
 \left(1-\frac{\sin(\tau\sqrt v)}{\tau\sqrt v}\right)\sigma_m(dv)
 +O(\tau^3).
\tag{I.13m.n.3}
$$
Here $\sigma_m$ has total mass one. On any bounded mass interval the integral in (I.13m.n.3) is $O(\tau^2)$ by $0\le 1-\sin y/y\le y^2/6$ for real $y$. For sufficiently large $v$, Theorem I.13m.h gives a density $f_m(v)\sim c_m v^{-1-m/2}$ bounded by a fixed multiple of that power. In the remaining integral put $x=\tau^2v$. After division by $\tau^m$, dominated convergence uses the envelope $C\min(x,1)x^{-1-m/2}$ and gives $c_m\mathcal I_m$. This envelope is integrable at both ends because $0<m\le1$. The integrand is positive on an interval, which proves positivity of the coefficient. All background errors are uniform in the initial time $u$. Thus the result holds for the full measure and includes $m=1$.

*The bounded-coupling comparison class.* Fix a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, a nonnegative self-adjoint $V$ on it and bounded measurable coefficient families $p(t)\in\mathbb R$, $B(t)\in\mathcal H$, and $C(t)\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ with $C(t)=C(t)^*$. The reciprocal normalized mode equations are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\ddot z+(q+p)z-\langle B(t),Q\rangle&=a^{3/2}F,\\
\ddot Q+(V+C(t))Q&=B(t)z .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13m.n.4}
$$
The same estimate holds if the two $B$ coefficients are different bounded drive and readout coefficients. This statement is for the metric Green kernel with zero incoming variation and direct forcing only in the metric equation. For the impulse at $u$, the initial data are $(z,\dot z,Q,\dot Q)=(0,1,0,0)$. The bare bank kernel $\sin(s\sqrt V)/\sqrt V$ is defined by spectral calculus and has operator norm at most $s$. Its mild equation gives $\|Q(u+\tau)\|\le O(\tau^3)$ uniformly for bounded normalized metric kernels $|z(u+\tau)|/\tau$. In detail the normalized map $Q\mapsto-\int_u^t \sin((t-r)\sqrt V)V^{-1/2} C(r)Q(r)dr$ has norm at most $\|C\|_\infty T^2/6$ in $\sup_{t>u}\|Q(t)\|/(t-u)$. The driving map from $z$ has norm at most $\|B\|_\infty T^2/6$ on the same norm, or the pointwise bound $\|B\|_\infty\|z\|_{\rm norm}\tau^3/6$ before dividing by $\tau$. Applying the inverse on each subinterval of length $\tau$ gives the claimed cubic bound with a uniform constant. The metric equation with $y_0$ as its free kernel then bounds the correction from $p$ by $O(\tau^3)$ and the correction from $Q$ by $O(\tau^5)$. Joint small-time existence and bounded normalized kernels follow by contraction of these two integral equations for sufficiently small $T$. The wave energy with an added displacement term extends the solution on each finite interval of bounded coefficients. The estimates are uniform under spectral truncation of $V$ and require no bound on any positive moment of the bank masses. This proves the asserted $O(\tau^3)$ bound, in particular for the winding shear bank of Theorem I.13m.j with its actual time-varying stiffness and mass coupling.

Since $1+m<3$, (I.13m.n.1) gives a positive separation for every sufficiently short positive time difference against the full class (I.13m.n.4). Fix such an interval and a smooth nonzero nonnegative pulse $F$ supported strictly before its readout time inside that interval. Integrating the kernel gap against $F$ and restoring the common positive scale-factor factor gives a strictly positive difference on the same source/readout comparison. Quantitative versions follow by choosing a mass-tail interval on which the density bounds in Theorem I.13m.h hold, and integrating over a fixed rescaled band, for example $1\le\tau^2v\le2$. That part alone bounds the signed correction from below by a positive multiple of $\tau^{1+m}$ after subtracting the uniform $O(\tau^3)$ term. The result applies to displacement-coupled second-order metric modes. Unbounded derivative couplings, different principal kinetic structure and the joint cosmological projections require their own comparisons. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13n-abelian-inflow-and-the-harmonic-only-causality-obstruction"></a>**Theorem I.13n (Abelian Inflow and the Harmonic-Only Causality Obstruction).** Fix the following bulk and boundary conventions. $M$ is an oriented smooth five-manifold with oriented boundary $N=\partial M$, the boundary orientation being outward-normal first. Variations have compact support away from corners; if temporal ends are present they vanish there. On a trivialized $U(1)$ bundle write the real connection as $A$, its curvature as $F=dA$, and a gauge transformation as $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$. Set $c_k=k/(4\pi^2)$.

1. The local bulk functional and its exact variation are
$$
S_{\mathrm{bulk}}=c_k\int_M A\wedge F\wedge F,
\qquad
\delta S_{\mathrm{bulk}}=3c_k\int_M\delta A\wedge F\wedge F
-2c_k\int_N A\wedge\delta A\wedge F.
\tag{I.13n.1}
$$
In particular $\delta_\lambda S_{\mathrm{bulk}}=c_k\int_N\lambda F\wedge F$. On the boundary introduce a real scalar $\varphi$ with $\delta_\lambda\varphi=\lambda|_N$, a fixed Lorentzian boundary metric and $f_*^2>0$. Put $B=d\varphi-A|_N$ and
$$
\Gamma_N=-\frac{f_*^2}{2}\int_N B\wedge *_NB
-c_k\int_N\varphi F\wedge F.
\tag{I.13n.2}
$$
Then $S_{\mathrm{bulk}}+\Gamma_N$ is invariant under every globally defined real gauge parameter of this trivialized branch. Defining the boundary consistent current by $\delta_A\Gamma_N=\int_N\delta A\wedge J_{\mathrm{con}}$, one obtains
$$
J_{\mathrm{con}}=f_*^2*_NB-2c_k\,d\varphi\wedge F,
\qquad
f_*^2d(*_NB)=c_kF\wedge F
\tag{I.13n.3}
$$
where the second equation is the $\varphi$ equation. Thus $dJ_{\mathrm{con}}=c_kF\wedge F$ on shell. Including the boundary term in (I.13n.1) gives
$$
J_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{con}}+2c_kA\wedge F,
\qquad dJ_{\mathrm{cov}}=3c_kF\wedge F.
\tag{I.13n.4}
$$
The latter divergence cancels the normal bulk inflow from the bulk Euler current $3c_kF\wedge F$. The separate boundary current has the displayed anomaly; the total variational Ward identity is conserved.

2. The normalization in item 1 has an integral bulk definition. For an oriented closed five-manifold with a line-bundle connection extending over an oriented six-manifold $W$, define its phase by
$$
\exp(iS)=\exp\left(2\pi i k\int_W\left(\frac{F}{2\pi}\right)^3\right).
\tag{I.13n.5}
$$
It is independent of the chosen extension for all such data exactly when $k\in\mathbb Z$. For a manifold with boundary the same difference-of-extensions statement applies after fixing the boundary trivialization and extension data. Item 1 proves the local boundary cancellation on its trivialized real-scalar branch. Theorem I.13n.a supplies all-winding large-gauge sewing on the trivial-bulk branch and proves the integral obstruction to a charge-one phase on a nontrivial boundary bundle. Theorem I.13n.c gives an extension-independent relative phase for every bulk bundle with a supplied boundary section.

3. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected positive-dimensional Riemannian manifold, and let $P(x,y)$ be the smooth integral kernel of a nonzero finite-rank operator on a smooth vector bundle. In particular, $P$ can be the Hodge-harmonic kernel with a positive-definite matrix $\Lambda_h^{-1}$ on the harmonic space. On the ultrastatic spacetime $\mathbb R\times\Sigma$, consider the harmonic-only response kernel
$$
K(t,x;s,y)=r(t-s)P(x,y),
\tag{I.13n.6}
$$
where $r$ is a nonzero distribution supported in $[0,\infty)$ and $\inf\operatorname{supp}r=0$. This kernel violates local metric-cone causality. More exactly, a separated kernel of this form can be causal only if
$$
\inf\operatorname{supp}r\ \ge
\sup\{d_\Sigma(x,y):(x,y)\in\operatorname{supp}P\}.
\tag{I.13n.7}
$$
This condition is also sufficient for its support to lie in the ultrastatic causal cone. Hence a nonzero smooth harmonic-only response with immediate onset cannot itself be a local causal bulk response. This assertion concerns interpreting its output pointwise; a globally smeared retained observable may legitimately have a nonlocal projection.

There are causal kernels with exactly the same harmonic compression. On $\Sigma=\mathbb T^3$ with its unit flat metric, for every $m>0$ the zero-past operator $(\partial_t^2+\Delta_H+m^2)^{-1}_{\mathrm{ret}}$ on one-forms is causal, where $\Delta_H\ge0$ is the Hodge Laplacian. If $P_h$ is its harmonic projector, then
$$
P_h(\partial_t^2+\Delta_H+m^2)^{-1}_{\mathrm{ret}}P_h
=\mathbf1_{t\ge0}\frac{\sin(mt)}m P_h,
\qquad
P_h(\Delta_H+m^2)^{-1}P_h=m^{-2}P_h.
\tag{I.13n.8}
$$
The full spatial-mode response supplies the causal support; its harmonic projection alone has the obstruction above. For any supplied positive-definite $\Lambda_h$ on the three-dimensional constant-one-form space, the same construction with the constant positive matrix $\Lambda_h$ in place of $m^2I$ has static harmonic compression $\Lambda_h^{-1}$. Orthogonal diagonalization gives its causal modes and positive energy. This is an ultrastatic one-form comparison, with its chosen frame and bundle; identifying it with the Lorentz-covariant conserved metric operator of Theorem I.13l requires a source-to-tensor intertwiner and every retained projection.

*Proof.* Since $\delta F=d\delta A$ and $dF=0$,
$$
\delta(A\wedge F\wedge F)
=\delta A\wedge F\wedge F+2A\wedge d\delta A\wedge F
=3\delta A\wedge F\wedge F-2d(A\wedge\delta A\wedge F).
$$
Stokes' theorem proves (I.13n.1). Under a gauge variation $\delta F=0$, the original integrand changes by $d\lambda\wedge F^2=d(\lambda F^2)$, proving its stated gauge variation with the fixed boundary sign. In (I.13n.2), $B$ and $F$ are invariant and the scalar term changes by $-c_k\int_N\lambda F^2$, so the cancellation is exact.

For the scalar variation, integration of $-f_*^2d(\delta\varphi)\wedge *_NB$ gives $f_*^2\delta\varphi\,d(*_NB)$, while the second term gives $-c_k\delta\varphi F^2$. This proves the second equation in (I.13n.3). For the connection variation, the kinetic term gives $f_*^2\delta A\wedge *_NB$. The other term gives $-2c_k\varphi\,d\delta A\wedge F$; integration by parts changes it to $-2c_k\delta A\wedge d\varphi\wedge F$. These are the claimed current terms. Since $d(d\varphi\wedge F)=0$ and $d(A\wedge F)=F^2$, taking derivatives proves (I.13n.3)–(I.13n.4). Under $\delta A=d\lambda$, the bulk Euler contribution integrates to $3c_k\int_N\lambda F^2$ and the total boundary-current contribution to $-\int_N\lambda dJ_{\mathrm{cov}}$; they cancel. This gives the explicit total Ward identity, rather than incorrectly declaring the anomalous boundary current conserved by itself.

For item 2, gluing two extensions with opposite orientations gives a closed oriented six-manifold $Z$. The difference of exponents is $2\pi k\langle c_1(L)^3,[Z]\rangle$. The pairing is an integer by the integral first Chern class, proving sufficiency. Necessity follows by adding a disjoint closed component $\mathbb{CP}^3$ carrying its degree-one hyperplane line bundle: its integral cohomology ring is $\mathbb Z[h]/(h^4)$ with $\int h^3=1$, so this permitted change of extension changes the phase by $e^{2\pi ik}$. The ring and normalization follow from the standard one-cell-in-each-even-dimension decomposition and the transverse intersection of three generic hyperplanes at one positively oriented point. Thus independence for every extension forces $k\in\mathbb Z$. Locally $d(AF^2)=F^3$, so (I.13n.5) has exactly the coefficient in (I.13n.1).

For item 3, the distributional support of $r\otimes P$ is the product of the two supports. To verify this directly near any support point, select component test functions with nonzero pairings against $r$ and against a nonzero component of $P$; their product has nonzero pairing. A smooth nonzero $P$ cannot be supported on the spatial diagonal, which has empty interior: continuity would make it zero there as well. Hence some support pair has $d_\Sigma(x,y)>0$. Since temporal support accumulates at zero, their product gives a support point with $0\le t-s<d_\Sigma(x,y)$, outside the causal cone. Taking the supremum over spatial support pairs proves necessity of (I.13n.7); if it holds, every product support point has $t-s\ge d_\Sigma(x,y)$, proving sufficiency.

On the flat torus, Fourier expansion of one-forms gives mode frequencies $\sqrt{4\pi^2|k|^2+m^2}$ and the same sine solution as (I.13l.1), with the sign changed because the wave operator is $-\Box+m^2$. The wave energy identity in Theorem I.13l applies on torus charts and on their lifts, proving finite propagation with the geodesic distance. Only $k=0$ survives harmonic projection, giving both equations in (I.13n.8). For a positive matrix $\Lambda_h$, choose a fixed orthonormal eigenbasis; each component is a positive-mass scalar wave. The sum of their energies $\frac12\int(|u_t|^2+|\nabla u|^2+u^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_hu)$ is positive and obeys the same cone flux estimate. Static inversion on constant modes gives $\Lambda_h^{-1}$. ∎

<a id="theorem-i13na-global-phase-sewing-boundary-stress-and-the-zero-background-tensor-obstruction"></a>**Theorem I.13n.a (Global Phase Sewing, Boundary Stress and the Zero-Background Tensor Obstruction).** Retain the charge-one boundary field, coefficient $c_k=k/(4\pi^2)$ and positive kinetic coefficient $f_*^2$ of Theorem I.13n. A circle-valued phase means a smooth unit section; defects and zeros are excluded. The following statements give its global sewing and its actual metric variation.

1. For a Hermitian line bundle $L\to M$, the charge-one boundary phase exists exactly when $L|_N$ is trivial, equivalently $c_1(L|_N)=0$ in integral cohomology. This condition includes torsion. It is independent of $k$.

2. On a compact oriented smooth five-manifold $M$ with closed boundary $N$, trivial bulk bundle and global connection one-form $A$, put
   $$
   u:N\longrightarrow U(1),\qquad
   \alpha=-iu^{-1}du,\qquad B=\alpha-A|_N,\qquad F=dA.
   \tag{I.13n.a.1}
   $$
   The form $\alpha$ is real and closed, with periods in $2\pi\mathbb Z$. For any fixed Lorentzian metric on $N$ for which the boundary kinetic term is defined, the globally defined functional
   $$
   S[A,u;g_N]
   =c_k\int_M A\wedge F\wedge F
   +c_k\int_N\alpha\wedge A\wedge F
   -\frac{f_*^2}{2}\int_N B\wedge *_NB
   \tag{I.13n.a.2}
   $$
   is exactly invariant under every smooth bulk gauge map $v:M\to U(1)$, acting by
   $$
   A\longmapsto A+\beta,\qquad
   u\longmapsto(v|_N)u,\qquad \beta=-iv^{-1}dv.
   \tag{I.13n.a.3}
   $$
   Neither $u$ nor $v$ needs a global real logarithm. When $u=e^{i\varphi}$ has one, (I.13n.a.2) equals the functional in (I.13n.1)–(I.13n.2). The boundary equations and consistent/covariant currents are
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   f_*^2d(*_NB)&=c_kF\wedge F,\\
   J_{\mathrm{con}}&=f_*^2*_NB-2c_k\alpha\wedge F,\\
   J_{\mathrm{cov}}&=J_{\mathrm{con}}+2c_kA\wedge F
                   =f_*^2*_NB-2c_kB\wedge F,\\
   dJ_{\mathrm{con}}&=c_kF\wedge F,\qquad
   dJ_{\mathrm{cov}}=3c_kF\wedge F.
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{I.13n.a.4}
   $$
   The last line holds on the phase equation. $J_{\mathrm{cov}}$ is gauge invariant and its anomaly cancels the bulk inflow as in Theorem I.13n. This trivial-bulk functional is gauge invariant for every real $k$; compatibility with the nontrivial-bundle extension class of (I.13n.5) retains that theorem's integer-level condition.

3. The local equations of (I.13n.a.2) have an exact causal phase response on a fixed smooth globally hyperbolic Lorentzian four-manifold $N$ without boundary. Fix a global $A$, a reference phase $u_0:N\to U(1)$ and its form $\alpha_0=-iu_0^{-1}du_0$. Write $u=u_0e^{i\theta}$, with real $\theta$, $B_0=\alpha_0-A$, and
   $$
   F\wedge F=\mathcal P\,dV_{g_N},\qquad
   q=\frac{c_k}{f_*^2}\mathcal P-\nabla^a(B_0)_a.
   \tag{I.13n.a.5}
   $$
   If $q\in C_c^\infty(N)$, the unique solution with $\theta$ supported in $J^+(\operatorname{supp}q)$ is
   $$
   \theta=(\Box_{g_N})^{-1}_{\mathrm{ret}}q,\qquad
   B=B_0+d\theta.
   \tag{I.13n.a.6}
   $$
   It preserves every integer period of $\alpha_0$. These are fixed-connection phase equations; a dynamical connection requires its own field equation and source data.

4. The boundary Hilbert stress, with $A,u$ held fixed in the metric variation, is
   $$
   T^N_{ab}=f_*^2\left(B_aB_b-\frac12(g_N)_{ab}B_cB^c\right),\qquad
   T^N_{ab}\ell^a\ell^b=f_*^2(B_a\ell^a)^2
   \tag{I.13n.a.7}
   $$
   for every null vector $\ell$. Its exact exchange identity is
   $$
   \nabla^aT^N_{ab}
   =f_*^2(\nabla^aB_a)B_b-f_*^2B^aF_{ab}
   =c_k\mathcal P B_b-f_*^2B^aF_{ab}
   \tag{I.13n.a.8}
   $$
   on the phase equation. In particular its first metric-source response at $B=0$ vanishes: for every differentiable finite-dimensional source family $B(h)$ with $B(0)=0$, $D_hT^N(0)=0$. Consequently this kinetic stress cannot realize a nonzero linear harmonic-to-null map $\mathscr Q_x$ of Theorem I.13f on a neighborhood of the zero source through the identification
   $$
   8\pi G\,T^N_{ab}(h)\ell^a\ell^b=\mathscr Q_x(h)(\ell).
   \tag{I.13n.a.9}
   $$
   A nonzero background or a different response coupling changes this source class and carries its own field and projection record.

*Proof. Sewing obstruction.* On a good cover of $N$, choose local potentials $A_j=A_i+d\lambda_{ij}$ and transition functions $g_{ij}=e^{i\lambda_{ij}}$. The phase must obey $u_j=g_{ij}u_i$ so that $-iu_j^{-1}du_j-A_j=-iu_i^{-1}du_i-A_i$. The unit values $u_i$ are therefore a nowhere-zero section of the restricted line bundle. Such a section gives a trivialization by $(x,z)\mapsto z u(x)$; a trivialization conversely gives a unit section. Smooth complex line bundles are classified by their integral first Chern class (Hatcher 2017, Proposition 3.10), so the vanishing criterion follows. The existence of the section precedes and is independent of any choice of action coefficient.

The torsion qualification has a concrete flat witness. Over $\mathbb{RP}^3=S^3/(z\sim-z)$ take
$$
L_-=(S^3\times\mathbb C)/((z,w)\sim(-z,-w)).
\tag{I.13n.a.10}
$$
Its constant transition functions define a flat connection, and $L_-^{\otimes2}$ is trivial. A unit section would lift to a smooth $f:S^3\to U(1)$ satisfying $f(-z)=-f(z)$. Since $S^3$ is simply connected, write $f=e^{i\vartheta}$ with continuous real $\vartheta$. Connectedness makes $\vartheta(-z)-\vartheta(z)$ one constant odd multiple of $\pi$. Applying the antipodal map twice would make twice that nonzero odd multiple equal to zero, a contradiction. Thus $L_-$ is nontrivial with nonzero order-two $c_1$. Pull it back to $N_0=S^1\times\mathbb{RP}^3$ and to the bulk cylinder $[0,1]\times N_0$. Its boundary bundles admit no charge-one phase although $F=0$ and all real Chern forms vanish. The trivial and nontrivial bundles have the same underlying rational cochain data and zero curvature; the integral transition record distinguishes their sewing outcomes.

*Global action and currents.* Locally $u=e^{i\varphi}$, so $\alpha=d\varphi$; changing the local logarithm by $2\pi n$ leaves $\alpha$ unchanged. Its periods count the winding number of $u$ along closed curves. The same assertions hold for $\beta$. If a global logarithm exists, Stokes' theorem on closed $N$ gives
$$
\int_Nd\varphi\wedge A\wedge F=-\int_N\varphi F\wedge F,
$$
recovering the owner's Wess–Zumino term with its sign. Under (I.13n.a.3), $B$ and $F$ are unchanged. The bulk change is $c_k\int_M\beta\wedge F^2$, while the boundary topological change is
$$
c_k\int_N(\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge F+\beta\wedge A\wedge F).
$$
Because
$$
d(\beta\wedge A\wedge F)=-\beta\wedge F^2,
\qquad d(\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge A)=\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge F,
\tag{I.13n.a.11}
$$
Stokes cancels the first change against the second term, and the remaining integral is zero. This proves exact invariance without a global logarithm of $u$ or $v$. No divisibility condition on $k$ was used on this trivial-bulk domain.

Every infinitesimal variation within a winding sector has $\delta\alpha=d(\delta\theta)$. Its action variation is
$$
\int_N\delta\theta\,[f_*^2d(*_NB)-c_kF^2].
$$
For a connection variation, closedness of $\alpha$ gives
$$
\delta_A\int_N\alpha\wedge A\wedge F
=-2\int_N\delta A\wedge\alpha\wedge F.
$$
Together with the kinetic variation and the bulk boundary term from (I.13n.1), these yield both currents in (I.13n.a.4). Their derivatives use $d\alpha=0$, $dB=-F$, and $dF=0$, giving precisely the coefficients $1$ and $3$ in their anomalies.

*Causal phase and stress.* On the globally hyperbolic domain of item 3, $d(*_NB)=(\nabla^aB_a)dV_{g_N}$ converts the phase equation to $\Box_{g_N}\theta=q$. The unique retarded Green operator for the normally hyperbolic scalar wave equation, the same existence theorem used in Theorem I.12b.2c, proves (I.13n.a.6) and its causal support. The zero-past support fixes the homogeneous solution. Since $d\theta$ is exact, it changes no period. This dynamics follows from the retained positive kinetic term. Compactly supported variations define the local action here without assuming that its integral over infinite time converges.

The two topological integrals are metric independent. Varying the kinetic integral with respect to $(g_N)^{ab}$ gives (I.13n.a.7). Its contraction with a unit timelike observer is $f_*^2[(B\cdot v)^2+|B_\perp|^2]/2$, so it is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when $B=0$. Direct differentiation gives
$$
\nabla^aT^N_{ab}
=f_*^2\{(\nabla^aB_a)B_b+B^a(\nabla_aB_b-\nabla_bB_a)\},
$$
which proves (I.13n.a.8). The quadratic formula makes its derivative at $B=0$ zero. Differentiating (I.13n.a.9) at $h=0$ would therefore force the linear map $\mathscr Q_x$ to vanish, proving the claimed obstruction.

A nonzero phase-on-shell family at fixed connection exhibits the distinction exactly. On $N=\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^3$ with the flat ultrastatic metric, take a nonzero constant spatial one-form $b$, $u=1$ and $A_s=-s b$. Then $F_s=0$, $B_s=s b$, $d(*_NB_s)=0$ and
$$
J_{\mathrm{cov},s}=f_*^2s\,*_Nb,\qquad
T^N_{ab}(s)=f_*^2s^2\left(b_ab_b-\frac12(g_N)_{ab}b_cb^c\right).
\tag{I.13n.a.12}
$$
The dual one-form current is a nonzero harmonic current linear in $s$, while its stress is quadratic and unchanged by $s\mapsto-s$. The obstruction is therefore realized by a family with nonzero current and nonzero null stress. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nb-affine-phase-stress-rank-classification"></a>

**Theorem I.13n.b (Affine Phase-Stress Rank Classification).** Fix a point of the boundary metric of Theorem I.13n.a, its real four-dimensional cotangent space, a nondegenerate Lorentz metric $g$, and $f_*^2>0$. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, connected and open, and let $B:U\to T_x^*N$ be $C^2$. The parameter $h\in U$ labels a supplied source family. The metric and null probes are fixed as $h$ varies. Write
$$
T_{ab}(h)=f_*^2\left(B_a(h)B_b(h)-\frac12g_{ab}B_c(h)B^c(h)\right),
\qquad
\mathcal N(h)=[T(h)]\in\operatorname{Sym}^2(T_x^*N)/\operatorname{span}\{g\}.
\tag{I.13n.b.1}
$$
Equality in this quotient is equivalent to equality of all null contractions. The rank-nine null-tomography map of Theorem I.13f also tests this equality.

1. The null response $\mathcal N$ is affine on $U$ if and only if either $B\equiv0$, or there are one fixed nonzero covector $b$ and one real affine function $L$ with $L(h)>0$ on $U$ such that
   $$
   B(h)=\sqrt{L(h)}\,b,
   \qquad
   \mathcal N(h)=f_*^2L(h)[b\otimes b].
   \tag{I.13n.b.2}
   $$
   A constant sign is absorbed into $b$. In the nonzero case the complete stress is affine as well, and the linear part of either the full or null response has rank at most one. This covers background-subtracted affine responses about a nonzero $B(h_0)$.

2. If the supplied source relation is itself affine, $B(h)=b_0+Ch$ for a linear map $C$, then an affine null response on $U$ forces $C=0$. Thus a nonconstant affine relation between $h$ and $B$ cannot give an exact affine null-stress law on an open source set. When every family member also has $F=0$, the fixed Hodge dual gives $J_{\mathrm{cov}}=f_*^2*B$; the same conclusion applies to affine boundary-current coordinates on that $F=0$ class.

3. At one nonzero background $B_0=B(h_0)$ the infinitesimal null response instead has
   $$
   D\mathcal N(h_0)[v]
   =f_*^2[B_0\otimes DB(h_0)[v]+DB(h_0)[v]\otimes B_0],
   \qquad
   \operatorname{rank}D\mathcal N(h_0)=\operatorname{rank}DB(h_0)\le4.
   \tag{I.13n.b.3}
   $$
   At $B_0=0$ this derivative is zero. The rank-four tangent bound is sharp; it is distinct from the rank-one bound for an exact affine response on a neighborhood.

4. The rank-one alternative has a phase-on-shell representative with a prescribed nondynamical connection for each family member; that connection varies with $h$. On flat $N=\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^3$, choose one nonzero constant spatial one-form $b$, set $u_h=1$ and $A_h=-\sqrt{L(h)}b$, and keep $h$ constant over spacetime within each family member. Then
   $$
   F_h=0,\quad B_h=\sqrt{L(h)}b,\quad
   J_{\mathrm{cov},h}=f_*^2\sqrt{L(h)}\,*b,\quad
   T_{ab}(h)=f_*^2L(h)\left(b_ab_b-\tfrac12g_{ab}b_cb^c\right).
   \tag{I.13n.b.4}
   $$
   The phase equation holds and the displayed stress is conserved. The parameter $h$ in this witness is a source coordinate: the harmonic boundary current carries $\sqrt{L(h)}$ and the stress carries $L(h)$.

*Proof.* If a symmetric tensor vanishes on every null vector, it is a multiple of $g$. In an orthonormal Lorentz frame write a null vector as $(1,\mathbf n)$ with $|\mathbf n|=1$. Vanishing of
$S_{00}+2S_{0i}n_i+S_{ij}n_in_j$ for $\mathbf n$ and $-\mathbf n$ gives $S_{0i}=0$. Taking $\mathbf n$ along each coordinate axis gives $S_{ii}=-S_{00}$, and taking $(\mathbf e_i+\mathbf e_j)/\sqrt2$ gives $S_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$. Hence $S=-S_{00}g$. Theorem I.13f's rank-nine retained probes are an equivalent finite test. Since the metric term in (I.13n.b.1) vanishes in the quotient, affineness of $\mathcal N$ is affineness of $[B\otimes B]$.

Suppose that quotient-valued map is affine. Fix $h\in U$ and a parameter direction $v$. Since $U$ is open, its second directional derivative vanishes. Put $a=DB(h)[v]$ and $c=D^2B(h)[v,v]$. For some real $\lambda$,
$$
2a\otimes a+B\otimes c+c\otimes B=\lambda g.
\tag{I.13n.b.5}
$$
The left side has matrix rank at most three: its image is contained in the span of the three covectors $a,B,c$. The metric has rank four, so $\lambda=0$. If $B\ne0$, evaluation on $(z,z)$ for $z\in\ker B$ gives $2a(z)^2=0$. Thus $a$ annihilates $\ker B$, and $a$ is proportional to $B$. This holds for every $v$.

If $B$ vanishes at any $h_0$, the first derivative of $[B\otimes B]$ vanishes there. An affine map has constant derivative, so this map is identically zero. Then $B(h)\otimes B(h)$ is a multiple of $g$ for every $h$. Its rank is at most one, which forces that multiple and $B(h)$ to vanish. This is the first alternative.

Otherwise choose $h_0\in U$ and put $b=B(h_0)\ne0$. The preceding proportionality shows that every first derivative of $[B\otimes B]$ at $h_0$ is a multiple of $[b\otimes b]$. Its value at $h_0$ is that same nonzero class. Because the map is affine, there is a real affine $L$ with $L(h_0)=1$ and
$$
[B(h)\otimes B(h)]=L(h)[b\otimes b]\qquad(h\in U).
$$
The difference of these two rank-one tensors has rank at most two. It can therefore be a multiple of the rank-four metric only when that multiple is zero. Hence
$$
B(h)\otimes B(h)=L(h)b\otimes b.
\tag{I.13n.b.6}
$$
Choose a tangent vector $z$ with $b(z)\ne0$ and evaluate on $(z,z)$ to obtain $L(h)\ge0$. A real affine function that is nonnegative on an open set and vanishes at an interior point has zero linear part there, hence is identically zero. That contradicts $L(h_0)=1$, so $L>0$ throughout $U$. Equation (I.13n.b.6) gives $B(h)=\epsilon(h)\sqrt{L(h)}b$ with $\epsilon(h)\in\{-1,1\}$. Continuity and connectedness make the sign constant; its value at $h_0$ is positive. This proves (I.13n.b.2). Conversely that formula makes both the full stress and its null class affine, with linear part in one tensor line, proving item 1.

If $B=b_0+Ch$, equation (I.13n.b.5) has $c=0$. For each $v$ it becomes $2(Cv)\otimes(Cv)=\lambda g$. Rank at most one again forces $\lambda=0$ and $Cv=0$. Thus $C=0$, proving item 2.

Differentiation proves the formula in (I.13n.b.3). For $B_0\ne0$, the linear map
$$
a\longmapsto[B_0\otimes a+a\otimes B_0]
\tag{I.13n.b.7}
$$
is injective. Indeed a tensor in its kernel would be a multiple of $g$; its rank is at most two, so it is zero. Choose $z$ with $B_0(z)\ne0$. Evaluation on $(z,z)$ gives $a(z)=0$, and evaluation on $(z,w)$ then gives $a(w)=0$ for every $w$. Composition with the injective map (I.13n.b.7) gives the rank equality in item 3. A local family $B(h)=B_0+\sum_{i=1}^4h_i e^i$, where the $e^i$ form a covector basis, has rank-four derivative and proves sharpness. Its exact response contains quadratic terms, in agreement with item 2.

For item 4, $L(h)$ is a spacetime constant within each member, so $F_h=dA_h=0$, $dB_h=0$ and $d(*B_h)=0$. Theorem I.13n.a's phase equation, current and stress formulas give (I.13n.b.4). Its exchange identity has both terms zero, establishing conservation. The nonlinear current coefficient in (I.13n.b.4) follows from that same variation; it is retained when comparing this witness with a proposed harmonic-current coordinate. The connection is prescribed separately for each member, and the construction imposes the phase equation rather than a dynamical connection equation. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nc"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nc-relative-differential-character-sewing-for-nontrivial-bulk-bundles"></a>**Theorem I.13n.c (Relative Differential-Character Sewing for Nontrivial Bulk Bundles).** Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth five-manifold with closed boundary $N$, with the conventions of Theorem I.13n. Let $L\to M$ be a Hermitian line bundle with connection $A$ and curvature $F$. Let $u$ be the actual charge-one unit section of $L|_N$, whenever it exists. The relative bulk and boundary phase exists for every such pair $(L,u)$ at every integer level $k$. It is invariant under every simultaneous bulk gauge transformation and retains all boundary winding choices. Its first variation gives the phase equation and covariant current in (I.13n.a.4) and the same bulk Euler current as (I.13n.1). The kinetic Hilbert stress and its exchange identity are (I.13n.a.7)–(I.13n.a.8). For the extension of the cubic level convention (I.13n.5) to all admitted bundles, integrality of $k$ is necessary. For a specified $M$ the topological pair classes are exactly $H^2(M,N;\mathbb Z)$, including torsion and the boundary winding quotient. This is a sewing and classification result for supplied classes.

*Proof.* The section $u$ exists precisely when $c_1(L)|_N=0$ by Theorem I.13n.a. In the boundary frame $u$ let $a=A|_N-\alpha=-B$ be the real connection one-form. Here the local phase has $\alpha=-iu^{-1}du$ in any local frame, and $a$ is global. Thus $da=F|_N$. Normalize the curvature by $f=F/(2\pi)$ and put $b=a/(2\pi)$. Let $\widehat c\in\widehat H^2(M;\mathbb Z)$ be the differential character of $(L,A)$, with holonomy convention $\exp(i\int A)$ in a trivialization. In the relative mapping cone for $i:N\hookrightarrow M$, use the chain differential $(s,t)\mapsto(\partial s+i_*t,-\partial t)$ and the form differential $(\omega,\eta)\mapsto(d\omega,i^*\omega-d\eta)$. The unit section gives the relative character $\widehat c_u$ with curvature pair $(f,b)$ and underlying class $c_1(L,u)$. Indeed its evaluation on a degree-one relative cycle uses parallel transport on the one-chain with endpoints read in the prescribed frames. On the boundary of a relative two-chain its value is $\exp(2\pi i(\int_s f+\int_t b))$. This also fixes the sign convention for the relative character. The relative and absolute character product used below is the mapping-cone module product of Becker (2014, §4.2).

Use the relative fundamental cycle $([M],-[N])$ and define
$$
\mathcal Z_k(A,u;g_N)
=
\big(\widehat c_u\cdot\widehat c\cdot\widehat c\big)([M],-[N])^{\,k}
\exp\left(-\frac{i f_*^2}{2}\int_N B\wedge *_NB\right).
\tag{I.13n.c.1}
$$
The product has curvature pair $(f^3,b\,i^*f^2)$ and characteristic class $c_1(L,u)c_1(L)^2$. The evaluation is independent of subdivisions and representatives of the relative fundamental cycle with the prescribed smooth orientations. Indeed an added cone boundary is evaluated by the curvature pair and both form degrees exceed the corresponding manifold dimensions on $M$ and $N$. The product is natural under bundle isomorphisms carrying $u$ to its transformed section. This gives gauge invariance of the phase including all windings. The action is defined modulo $2\pi$ by (I.13n.c.1) even on data without a bounding extension. When a compatible six-dimensional filling is given, the defining character relation gives the relative curvature integral over that filling. For closed five-dimensional data it gives exactly (I.13n.5).

To vary (I.13n.c.1), put the family of fields on $[0,1]\times M$, with connection in temporal gauge along the variation and the interpolating boundary frame. Apply the relative character relation to $([0,1]\times M,[0,1]\times N)$ with product orientations. The two side chains cancel in its cone boundary, leaving the difference of the endpoint relative cycles. With $A_\tau=A+\tau\,\delta A$ and $u_\tau=e^{i\tau\varphi}u$ at first order, the curvature on the cylinder is $F+d\tau\wedge\delta A+O(\tau)$ and the boundary connection has $d\tau$ coefficient $-\varphi$. The first variation of the phase angle of the topological factor is therefore
$$
\delta S_{\rm top}
=3c_k\int_M\delta A\,F^2
+c_k\int_N\big(-2\delta A\,B F-\varphi F^2\big).
\tag{I.13n.c.2}
$$
For the side term this follows by taking the $d\tau$ component of $(a_\tau-\varphi\,d\tau)(F+d\tau\wedge\delta A)^2$, with $a_0=-B$. The kinetic variation adds $\int_N f_*^2\delta A\wedge *_NB+\int_N f_*^2\varphi\,d(*_NB)$. Thus the global boundary coefficient of $\delta A$ is $f_*^2*_NB-2c_k B\wedge F$, and varying $\varphi$ gives $f_*^2d(*_NB)=c_k F^2$. This proves the covariant boundary and bulk Ward identity. Since the character term is metric independent, the kinetic variation also gives the announced Hilbert stress and exchange law. The scalar retarded phase construction of Theorem I.13n.a extends on any fixed globally hyperbolic boundary with the stated support hypotheses by using the globally defined $B_0$ from a chosen section and varying it by $d\theta$.

For a trivial bulk bundle hold $u$ fixed and set $A_\tau=\tau A$. At $\tau=0$ the absolute character is trivial, so the topological factor in (I.13n.c.1) is one for every boundary winding. Along this path use (I.13n.c.2) with $\delta A=A$, $F_\tau=\tau F$ and $B_\tau=\alpha-\tau A|_N$. The bulk coefficient integrates as $\int_0^1 3\tau^2\,d\tau=1$. The boundary term uses $A\wedge A=0$ and $-A\wedge\alpha=\alpha\wedge A$, with $\int_0^1 2\tau\,d\tau=1$. Hence the topological angle is
$$
c_k\left(\int_M A F^2+\int_N \alpha A F\right)
\quad \bmod 2\pi .
\tag{I.13n.c.3}
$$
This recovers (I.13n.a.2) at integer $k$. Its trivial-bulk functional is also defined at real levels. Necessity of an integer for a single filling-independent level on all bundle data follows by adjoining the closed $\mathbb{CP}^3$ filling difference with the hyperplane line, whose cubed first Chern number is one.

Finally, line bundles with a specified trivialization on $N$ are classified by maps of pairs to $(BU(1),*)$ up to homotopy, hence by $H^2(M,N;\mathbb Z)$. The long exact sequence gives the full accounting
$$
0\longrightarrow
H^1(N;\mathbb Z)/i^*H^1(M;\mathbb Z)
