\longrightarrow H^2(M,N;\mathbb Z)
\longrightarrow \ker\big(H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(N;\mathbb Z)\big)
\longrightarrow0 .
\tag{I.13n.c.4}
$$
Smooth gauge maps to $U(1)$ realize the indicated integral winding images. For example take $M$ to be $S^2\times S^3$ with an open five-ball removed. A line with Chern number one on $S^2$ is nontrivial in the bulk and trivial on $S^4=\partial M$. Its relative Chern class is nonzero, and every connection on it with any chosen boundary unit section enters (I.13n.c.1). On a given bundle the phase responds to winding by the actual relative class, while the current depends on the actual connection and boundary form. Selection of a bundle, winding, or level from a dynamical physical source is a separate predicate. ∎

<a id="theorem-i13nd"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nd-selection-of-relative-bundle-and-winding-by-a-biased-curvature-preparation"></a>**Theorem I.13n.d (Selection of Relative Bundle and Winding by a Biased Curvature Preparation).** Let
$$
M=(D^2\times S^1\times S^2)\mathbin{\#}(S^2\times S^3)
$$
be the interior connected sum with the indicated closed five-manifold, and orient $N=\partial M=T^2\times S^2$ as in Theorem I.13n.c. The sewn relative classes form a two-dimensional integral period lattice. One lattice coordinate measures the boundary meridian winding relative to a fixed frame on a spanning disk, and the other measures the interior bulk Chern period that restricts to zero on $N$.

Equip the compact preparation with a fixed Riemannian metric. Use the relative preparation boundary condition $A|_N-\alpha=0$, where $u$ is the boundary unit frame and $\alpha=-iu^{-1}du$ in a local trivialization. Let $\beta$ be a prescribed smooth closed relative two-form, $i^*\beta=0$, in the normalized curvature units $f=F/(2\pi)$. On every sewn relative class, compare the attainable bulk energy
$$
\mathcal E_\beta(A,u)=\frac{c_B}{2}\|f-\beta\|_{L^2(M)}^2,\qquad c_B>0,
\tag{I.13n.d.1}
$$
with the bulk coefficient and curvature bias fixed before class selection. The minimizing class is the nearest lattice point to the actual bias period vector in the positive definite relative Hodge norm of the preparation. Its least energy is attained by a smooth connection and unit frame. The selection is unique away from the lattice Voronoi boundaries. There are nonempty open regions of independent interior and meridian bias periods for which the selected class has nonzero bulk and meridian coordinates simultaneously. This preparation theorem applies at any supplied integer level of Theorem I.13n.c.

*Proof.* Removing a five-ball from either summand and gluing on $S^4$ leaves the cohomology in degrees one and two equal to the corresponding direct sum. Thus $H^1(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ from the old $S^1$, and $H^2(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$ from the two sphere classes. On $N$ the old circle maps to its own circle, and the meridian circle bounds the original disk. The first sphere class restricts to the displayed $S^2$ generator of $H^2(N;\mathbb Z)$, and the second sphere class restricts to zero. Equation (I.13n.c.4) is therefore an extension of $\mathbb Z$ by $\mathbb Z$ and splits over the integers. Choose a meridian disk away from the connected-sum site and a sphere in the closed summand away from its removed ball. Their relative periods give integral coordinates. The disk detects the boundary meridian generator with sign fixed by orientation, and the sphere detects the generator of the restriction kernel. The splitting uses these marked cycles. The classification includes all sewn relative classes on this preparation.

Any smooth relative bundle/frame pair admits a connection that is trivial in the actual frame on a collar of $N$. To construct it, extend the frame through the collar, choose any smooth global connection, subtract its connection form in the collar frame multiplied by a smooth cutoff equal to one near the boundary, and extend the subtracted form by zero. Hence the boundary preparation constraint is feasible on every relative class. It constrains the connection in the supplied frame, leaving the frame's relative winding free. A smooth pair satisfying that constraint has $i^*f=0$. Its relative de Rham class is represented by $f$, by (I.13n.c.4) and the curvature convention of Theorem I.13n.c. The difference between any two smooth curvature representatives of this class is $dv$ with $i^*v=0$. Conversely adding $2\pi v$ to the connection realizes each such change without changing its boundary preparation.

Use the relative Hodge–Morrey–Friedrichs theorem on the compact Riemannian preparation (Schwarz 1995). For each $c\in H^2(M,N;\mathbb R)$ let $h_c$ be its unique smooth relative harmonic representative. For any smooth closed relative two-form $f$ of class $c$, there is a smooth relative one-form $v$ with $f=h_c+dv$. The harmonic part is $L^2$-orthogonal to every such $dv$: integration by parts gives zero from $\delta h_c=0$ in the interior and zero boundary term from $i^*v=0$. Apply this to $f-\beta$. For class $c$ its least possible energy is
$$
\mathcal E_\beta^*(c)=\frac{c_B}{2}\|h_{c-[\beta]}\|_{L^2(M)}^2.
\tag{I.13n.d.2}
$$
Indeed the minimizer has curvature $\beta+h_{c-[\beta]}$, a smooth closed relative representative of $c$. Starting with any prepared connection in class $c$, its difference from that curvature is a relative exact form, so the corresponding smooth relative one-form changes the connection to the minimizer. Residual flat connections within a selected class may persist.

Let $c=(c_1,c_2)$ and $\zeta=(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$ be the periods on the marked disk and sphere. For their integral dual class basis $e_1,e_2$ the matrix $G_{ij}=c_B\langle h_{e_i},h_{e_j}\rangle_{L^2(M)}$ is positive definite because the harmonic representatives are linearly independent. Then
$$
\mathcal E_\beta^*(c)=\frac12(c-\zeta)^{\mathsf T}G(c-\zeta).
\tag{I.13n.d.3}
$$
Every bounded energy sublevel contains finitely many lattice points, so the discrete minimum exists. Equality of the energy for two distinct classes is their affine bisector. The nearest-point cell of any lattice point contains an open neighborhood of that point. Smooth relative bias representatives with arbitrary real periods can be constructed from the two relative harmonic forms. Therefore independent bulk and meridian bias controls give the claimed open regions. All comparisons use the actual curvature response of the declared compact preparation, with a common positive bulk norm. The selected pair belongs to the globally sewn action of Theorem I.13n.c. This Euclidean preparation does not identify the Lorentzian retarded metric response or supply the relation between its observation sectors. ∎

<a id="theorem-i13ne"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13ne-level-identification-by-an-independent-bulk-current-port"></a>**Theorem I.13n.e (Level Identification by an Independent Bulk Current Port).** Keep the relative preparation and sewn compact manifold of Theorems I.13n.c–I.13n.d, with a fixed metric and a bias in an open cell selecting nonzero interior and meridian periods. The curvature bias functional alone has the same minimizers and values at every integer level. On every such selected class there is a smooth attained preparation and an independently specified compactly supported connection port whose real variational response determines the integer level uniquely. The calibration uses the prepared curvature and the oriented normalized charge unit. A charged source with an independently specified matching current therefore selects at most one integer on this family. The current test can be implemented away from the boundary and leaves the relative class, boundary frame and winding unchanged.

*An interior preparation and probe with nonzero level sensitivity.* Use normalized curvature $f=F/(2\pi)$. Start with a smooth relative bias $\beta$ in the open cell for the selected class $c$. The prepared minimum has curvature $f_*=\beta+h_{c-[\beta]}$ by (I.13n.d.2). Choose a small interior coordinate ball disjoint from the marked cycles used to read the two periods and write its orientation as $dx^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^5$. Choose a smooth compactly supported one-form $v$ on the ball that equals $s(x^1dx^2+x^3dx^4)$ on a smaller ball. Replacing $\beta$ by $\beta+dv$ preserves both periods and every class's least energy. Its attained curvature is $f_*+dv$ in the same relative class. At the center of the small ball the coefficient of $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4$ in $(f_*+dv)^2$ is a quadratic polynomial in $s$ with leading term $2s^2$. Thus it is nonzero for some rational $s$ and has one sign on a neighborhood of that center. Fix such a bias and write its attained curvature as $f_c$. Take the probe $a=\chi\,dx^5$, where $\chi$ is a nonnegative smooth bump supported in that neighborhood and not identically zero. Then
$$
Q_a=3\int_M a\wedge f_c\wedge f_c\ne0 .
\tag{I.13n.e.1}
$$
Reversing the sign of the probe fixes either desired orientation convention. The bias perturbation, its curvature, and the support and normalization of the probe are specified independently of the unknown level.

*Current readout and class selection.* Vary the connection by $A_\varepsilon=A+\varepsilon a$ while retaining the actual frame on the boundary and the metric. This is a global smooth variation of connections on the same line bundle. The tangent of the curvature preparation energy at its minimum vanishes for this direction by relative Hodge orthogonality, since the curvature tangent is $da/(2\pi)$. By (I.13n.1) and Theorem I.13n.c, the logarithmic derivative of the sewn phase along the variation is
$$
\left.\frac{1}{i}\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}
\log\left(\frac{\exp(iS_k[A_\varepsilon,u])}{\exp(iS_k[A,u])}\right)
\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
=\frac{3k}{4\pi^2}\int_M a\wedge F\wedge F
= kQ_a .
\tag{I.13n.e.2}
$$
The logarithm is any continuous local lift at $\varepsilon=0$, so its derivative has no integer ambiguity. The probe has no boundary term. Pure gauge directions of compact support give zero by closure of $f_c^2$ and Stokes' theorem. Thus the current comparison is on the gauge quotient and includes the full inflow normalization of the sewn source. See Bardeen and Zumino (1984).

If an independent retained current source prescribes real response $J_a$ in this port, exact matching selects $k=J_a/Q_a$ if this ratio is integral, and rules out every level otherwise. If a certified current interval is supplied, the allowed set is precisely $\{k\in\mathbb Z:kQ_a\text{ lies in that interval}\}$ for this port, and it contains at most one integer when the interval has width less than $|Q_a|$. The same sewing and curvature preparation coexist with this calibrated test. Without the independent current datum the test is an identification of the distinct candidate levels. Indeed the functional (I.13n.d.1), its Euler equation and its selected relative class contain no level, so repeating the curvature minimization alone leaves all integers. Constructing an internally selected charged-current datum and the Lorentzian boundary-to-metric response with its projection ledger remains part of the full certificate. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nf"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nf-a-rank-nine-boundary-stress-map-from-a-maxwell-triad"></a>**Theorem I.13n.f (A Rank-Nine Boundary Stress Map from a Maxwell Triad).** On a Lorentzian four-dimensional boundary let three Abelian connections carry the generally covariant action
$$
S_{\rm triad}=-\frac{\zeta}{4}\sum_{I=1}^3\int\sqrt{-g}\,
\mathcal{F}^I_{ab}\mathcal{F}_I^{ab}\,d^4x,\qquad \zeta>0.
\tag{I.13n.f.1}
$$
On the homogeneous electric triad specified below, the fixed-metric differential from first field-strength data to trace-free Hilbert stress is onto, with an explicit right inverse. At every nonzero spatial Fourier mode, imposing one electric and one magnetic Gauss constraint per connection reduces its rank to eight. The single linear relation fixes the longitudinal normal stress in terms of the energy density. The sector admits a causal retarded linear response on the same homogeneous Einstein–Maxwell branch.

*Source and homogeneous solution.* In conformal time $\eta$ put $g=a(\eta)^2(-d\eta^2+d\mathbf x^2)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^3$ on an interval with $a>0$. In an orthonormal frame use $E_i^I=\mathcal{F}_{0i}^I$ and $B_i^I=\epsilon_{ijk}\mathcal{F}_{jk}^I/2$. Take all magnetic fields zero and set $E_i^I=e\,\delta_{iI}$ with $e=E_*a^{-2}$ and $E_*\ne0$. These strengths are the exact curvatures of the global connection potentials $E_*\eta\,dx^I$ on the trivial bundles. Four-dimensional Maxwell theory is conformally invariant, so the constant comoving fields solve the source-free equations. Their stress has $\rho=3\zeta e^2/2$ and $p=\rho/3$. With Einstein coefficient $M^2>0$ and a declared cosmological constant $\Lambda\ge0$, the flat Friedmann equation is $(a'/a^2)^2=(\Lambda+\rho/M^2)/3$. Its positive expanding solution exists on an open time interval by the regular first-order ordinary differential equation for $a>0$. The second Friedmann equation follows by differentiating and using $\rho'+4(a'/a)\rho=0$. Thus the background has nonzero flux, its stress is conserved, and the metric is solved on the same source. The stress calculation uses the electric triad and a common orthonormal frame. See Yamamoto et al. (2012).

*Local map and its calibration.* Let $X_{iI}=\delta E_i^I$ and $Y_{iI}=\delta B_i^I$ denote strengths at a point in the fixed background orthonormal frame. Write $S=(X+X^{\mathsf T})/2$ after identifying the internal labels by the prepared triad. The Hilbert stress of (I.13n.f.1) gives
$$
\delta T_{00}=\zeta e\,\operatorname{tr}X,\qquad
\delta T_{0i}=\zeta e\sum_{I,k}\epsilon_{\mathrm{iIk}}Y_{kI},\qquad
\delta T_{ij}=\zeta e\bigl(\operatorname{tr}X\,\delta_{ij}-2S_{ij}\bigr).
\tag{I.13n.f.2}
$$
The spatial trace equals $\delta T_{00}$. For any trace-free symmetric tensor $t$, take $X_{ij}=(t_{00}\delta_{ij}-t_{ij})/(2\zeta e)$ and $Y_{kI}=\sum_j\epsilon_{\mathrm{jIk}}t_{0j}/(2\zeta e)$. The $\epsilon$ contraction shows that (I.13n.f.2) returns precisely $t$. The pointwise kernel is the antisymmetric part of $X$ and the symmetric part of $Y$. The trace-free target identifies canonically with the quotient of symmetric tensors by the metric. In particular the resulting rank-nine map has the null-contraction normalization of Theorem I.13f, determined by the independently prepared flux and action coefficient.

On the fixed trivial magnetic bundles, every tangent magnetic curvature is exact on the spatial torus and its harmonic spatial component vanishes. All nine homogeneous electric strength entries are free Maxwell initial data at fixed metric. Their symmetric part gives the six independent stress entries allowed by trace freedom and zero momentum density. Thus the strictly harmonic fixed-magnetic-class map has rank six. A background flat holonomy changes none of these stresses. The unrestricted pointwise inverse uses local strength data.

*Gauss-constrained rank.* For a spatial Fourier mode of wave vector $\mathbf k\ne0$ on a slice, first freeze the metric and use transverse Maxwell initial perturbations. In the background frame their constraints are $k_i X_{iI}=k_iY_{iI}=0$ for each $I$. Rotate the two index frames together so that $\mathbf k$ points along axis three. Thus the third row of $X,Y$ vanishes, and (I.13n.f.2) implies $\delta T_{33}=\delta T_{00}$. The allowed $X$ produces every remaining trace-compatible spatial entry: $X_{11},X_{22}$ fix the two transverse diagonal entries, $X_{12}+X_{21}$ fixes entry $12$, and $X_{13},X_{23}$ fix entries $13,23$. These are five independent outputs including the energy fixed by the transverse diagonal entries. The entries $Y_{23},Y_{13},Y_{21}-Y_{12}$ independently give all three momentum entries. Thus the image is exactly the trace-free tensors with $k_ik_jt_{ij}=|\mathbf k|^2 t_{00}$, of dimension eight. Each such datum is allowable Maxwell initial data at this mode. Magnetic rows arise as curls of periodic vector potentials because the mode is nonzero and transverse. In the coupled perturbation, changes of the metric also enter the Gauss law and Hilbert tensor, so this rank statement is specifically the fixed-metric input map.

*Retarded metric coupling.* Vary the full Einstein–Maxwell action with (I.13n.f.1). The identity $\nabla^a T_{ab}=\zeta\sum_I\mathcal{F}^I_{bc}\nabla_a\mathcal{F}_I^{ac}$, with the index convention in (I.13n.f.2), follows by applying the Bianchi identity to the quadratic stress. Thus its linear variation includes the metric terms required by the variation of covariant conservation. In wave gauge for the metric and Lorenz gauge for the three potentials, the linearized system has a diagonal wave principal part on the smooth background, with couplings of first or zeroth differential order. Its retarded solution on compact time slabs exists uniquely in these gauges for smooth compact-time compatible sources. For this fact the energy estimate for a linear normally hyperbolic system on a globally hyperbolic slab applies to the direct sum bundle and absorbs the bounded lower-order matrix couplings. Equivalently, one can use the time-slice energy and finite propagation on the torus cover, followed by periodic identification. The linearized Maxwell divergence and contracted Bianchi identities give homogeneous constraint propagation for compatible sources and zero-past data. Hence the retarded map has metric-cone support and determines a gauge class of metric perturbations with the conserved total stress of that variation. See Loizelet (2006).

The local triad map supplies an explicit tensor coupling beyond fixed-modulus phase stress. Its calibrated harmonic electric and fixed-metric transverse responses belong to the same Einstein–Maxwell source. Its identification with the relative bundle and inflow preparation and with the joint observational projections of Definition I.13d remains required. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13ng"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13ng-relative-flux-and-boundary-charge-fix-the-inflow-level"></a>**Theorem I.13n.g (Relative Flux and Boundary Charge Fix the Inflow Level).** On a time slab over a compact connected oriented spatial four-manifold $X$ with boundary $Y$, use the sewn Abelian Chern–Simons action of Theorem I.13n.c at integer level $k$, a positive bulk Maxwell term, and the positive boundary phase kinetic term of Theorem I.13n.a. Variations are supported away from the temporal ends. On a spatial cut on which the magnetic curvature is relative, the integrated Gauss constraint ties the boundary phase charge to the bulk charge and the relative square of the magnetic class. The square vanishes on all framed classes of $S^2\times D^2$. On the punctured projective plane it equals $n^2$ in class $n$, so for $n\ne0$ independently specified charges select at most one integer level. The Gauss equation and its flux boundary condition have smooth electric data on that cut whenever the integrated constraint holds.

*Relative spatial form.* The bundle must admit the boundary unit frame on the chosen cut. For $X=S^2\times D^2$ the restriction of $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ to $Y$ is injective. Consequently a charge-one boundary unit frame forces the bulk bundle to be trivial on this product. The integral relative lattice is $\mathbb Z$, generated by the disk class, and its relative square is zero because that class is pulled back from $(D^2,S^1)$. This simple product cannot distinguish levels by the integrated Gauss law below.

Use instead $X=\mathbb {CP}^2\setminus\operatorname{int}(B^4)$ with its complex orientation, so $Y=S^3$. The absolute generator restricts trivially to the boundary and has a unique relative lift $h\in H^2(X,Y;\mathbb Z)$ because $H^1(Y)=H^2(Y)=0$. Its relative pairing satisfies $\langle h\smile h,[X,Y]\rangle=1$: cap the cut with the removed ball and extend the trivially framed line over it to recover the hyperplane intersection on $\mathbb {CP}^2$. A connection flat in the prescribed frame near $Y$ exists by the collar construction in Theorem I.13n.d. In class $nh$, its normalized magnetic curvature $f$ gives
$$
\int_X f\wedge f=n^2 .
\tag{I.13n.g.1}
$$
This is unchanged by smooth relative exact curvature variations by Stokes' theorem. More generally, when the magnetic curvature pulls back to zero but the connection in the boundary frame is flat with nonzero periods, the relative class represented by the curvature can differ from the framed class by a connecting class from $H^1(Y;\mathbb R)$. This difference lies in the radical of the relative intersection pairing: its image in absolute cohomology vanishes, and the relative product can be computed using the relative–absolute product. Thus the relative square still has the stated value. On the fixed positive Riemannian metric of the spatial preparation, the curvature bias energy of Theorem I.13n.d applies with the one-dimensional lattice. A smooth closed relative bias with period in $(n-1/2,n+1/2)$ selects the class $nh$ uniquely. The metric and the magnetic bias are source inputs independent of $k$.

*Gauss law and normalization.* Use the Lorentzian product orientation $dt\wedge\operatorname{vol}_X$ and the Maxwell convention $-\frac{Z}{2}\int F\wedge *F$, $Z>0$. For the topological variation one may extend the cut data into a time chart of $S^1\times X$, with the frame on $S^1\times Y$, and use variations supported in that chart. The sewn formula then has only the lateral boundary term. The Euler equations on the time slab depend only on this local variation. Let a bulk matter force be the four-form $J_{\rm b}$ in the convention $\delta S_{\rm b}=\int_M\delta A\wedge J_{\rm b}$, and let $J_{\rm ph}=f_*^2*_N B$ with $B=\alpha-A|_N$. The first variation in a bulk direction is the equation
$$
-Z\,d(*F)+3k f\wedge f+J_{\rm b}=0 .
$$
The boundary coefficient in the same variation includes $-Z*F|_N$ and the total inflow boundary current of Theorem I.13n.c. With the boundary orientation induced from $M$ it sets $Z*F|_N=J_{\rm ph}$ on the cut when the pulled back magnetic curvature is zero there. Indeed the additional sewn contribution contains the pulled back $F$ as a factor in the boundary frame, so its spatial pullback vanishes on this cut. The displayed equality of spatial pullbacks is all that the integrated law needs. Integrate the bulk equation on $X$, with $Y$ oriented as $\partial X$, and use the boundary equation in the induced orientation. In the charge convention $Q_{\rm b}=\int_X J_{\rm b}$ and $Q_{\rm ph}=\int_Y J_{\rm ph}$ this gives
$$
Q_{\rm ph}-Q_{\rm b}=3k\int_X f\wedge f .
\tag{I.13n.g.2}
$$
Both charges are dimensionless in the primitive gauge unit of Theorem I.13n.c. Gauge transformations preserve the framed curvature and the charge integrals. The factor three comes from varying the cubic bulk phase, including all three curvature factors. It is independent of the Maxwell and boundary kinetic coefficients.

For $X=\mathbb {CP}^2\setminus\operatorname{int}(B^4)$ and a magnetic sector $n\ne0$, a specified charge difference $Q_{\rm ph}-Q_{\rm b}$ requires $k=(Q_{\rm ph}-Q_{\rm b})/(3n^2)$. A nonintegral ratio rules out all levels in this convention. For an outward charge interval of width smaller than $3n^2$, at most one integer is compatible.

To see sufficiency for the Gauss data on a connected cut, fix smooth prescribed charge densities $J_{\rm b}|_X$ and $J_{\rm ph}|_Y$ with these integrals. Choose a smooth Riemannian cut metric and write the electric flux as $\mathcal E=*_X d\phi$. The Neumann problem
$$
d(*_X d\phi)=Z^{-1}(3k f\wedge f+J_{\rm b}|_X),
\qquad (*_X d\phi)|_Y=Z^{-1}J_{\rm ph}|_Y
$$
has a smooth solution modulo constants exactly under (I.13n.g.2). Indeed on mean-zero $H^1(X)$ its weak form has the coercive Dirichlet bilinear form by the Poincaré inequality, with bounded bulk and boundary linear terms by the trace inequality. Compatibility makes the weak form valid also against constant functions. Elliptic Neumann regularity gives smoothness. Take the initial electric field whose Lorentzian dual pulls back to $\mathcal E$ and the temporal phase velocity whose boundary dual gives the prescribed charge density. A relative magnetic representative flat near $Y$ gives zero spatial phase difference in the prescribed frame. This realizes the bulk Gauss equation and the spatial flux boundary condition on the cut. The nonlinear charged evolution, the common Lorentzian metric realization and the projection ledger of Definition I.13d retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nh"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nh-common-bundle-winding-and-level-selection-on-a-sewn-cut"></a>**Theorem I.13n.h (Common Bundle, Winding and Level Selection on a Sewn Cut).** Let
$$
X=(S^2\times D^2)\mathbin{\#}\mathbb {CP}^2
$$
be the interior oriented connected sum, with $Y=S^2\times S^1$. Use the actual boundary frame in the Abelian sewing of Theorem I.13n.c and the time-slab action of Theorem I.13n.g. There is a relative integral basis in which the magnetic class is $(m,n)$, the first coordinate records meridian winding relative to a marked disk frame, the second records the bulk hyperplane flux, and the relative intersection form is $\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$. Independently supplied curvature bias and total charges select a single triple $(m,n,k)$ whenever the bias has a unique minimizing class with $n\ne0$ and the charge difference belongs to $3n^2\mathbb Z$. A nonintegral level ratio rules out the declared charges for the selected magnetic class. The unique admissible triple has a smooth sewn configuration with the bulk Gauss and boundary electric-flux constraints on the same cut.

*Integral relative data.* In degrees one and two, the connected sum away from the boundary gives $H^1(X;\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$, by Mayer–Vietoris along $S^3$. The class of the $S^2$ factor restricts to the generator on $Y$, and the hyperplane class restricts to zero. The exact sequence for the pair then gives
$$
0\longrightarrow H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(X,Y;\mathbb Z)
\longrightarrow \mathbb Z h\longrightarrow0,
$$
where $h$ is the hyperplane generator in absolute cohomology. Choose the oriented spanning disk of the old $S^1$ and a hyperplane sphere in the projective summand disjoint from the neck. Evaluation on those two cycles gives coordinates on the relative classes. The connecting class from the meridian generator evaluates to one on the marked disk and to zero on the sphere. The relative lift of the hyperplane class can be represented away from the disk by a curvature supported in the punctured projective summand. The latter lift has unit square by (I.13n.g.1). The meridian connecting class has zero absolute image and is in the radical of the relative pairing, since the relative product can be evaluated as a relative–absolute product. Thus the normalized relative curvature of class $(m,n)$ satisfies $\int_X f\wedge f=n^2$. The two periods record the actual relative bundle and boundary frame up to the simultaneous gauge action.

*Joint preparation.* Choose a fixed smooth Riemannian cut metric and the class-comparison energy of Theorem I.13n.d on relative two-forms. It is the positive squared Hodge distance of the candidate lattice point to the prescribed bias periods, with the exact Gram matrix of the two relative harmonic representatives. It selects a unique class on each open Voronoi cell, including nonempty open cells with both $m$ and $n$ nonzero. In its own boundary frame each class has a smooth curvature representative that is flat near $Y$, by the collar construction. The exact Hodge minimizer also has relative curvature and zero tangential boundary connection in that frame, because its connection differs from such a collar representative by a relative one-form. The gauge-invariant spatial phase difference vanishes at the cut. The winding remains in the marked relative data.

For a concrete choice of charge controls use no bulk matter charge and prepare the phase charge with spatial density $Q\,d\operatorname{vol}_Y/\operatorname{vol}(Y)$ for a fixed real $Q$ in the primitive charge convention. The curvature energy does not contain the level. By (I.13n.g.2) the compatibility test is exactly $Q=3kn^2$. For example, a bias in the open cell of $(1,1)$ and a prescribed phase charge $Q=3$ give $k=1$. This example demonstrates compatibility for the supplied controls. The level depends on the chosen phase charge, and the construction gives no preferred charge among the admissible preparations.

The Neumann construction of Theorem I.13n.g applies to the same magnetic minimizer with the prescribed boundary charge density. Its electric flux and the corresponding phase velocity are smooth and solve both cut constraints. This gives a time-cut field configuration with the actual relative class, framed winding and selected level on one sewn action. The marked disk period distinguishes the winding classes. The field histories, the boundary-to-metric intertwiner, and the retarded metric and observational projections of Definition I.13d retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13ni"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13ni-rank-nine-stress-on-the-common-sewn-constraint-cut"></a>**Theorem I.13n.i (Rank-Nine Stress on the Common Sewn Constraint Cut).** Take the branch of Theorem I.13n.h with a strict magnetic-class selector, $n\ne0$, and prescribed charge $Q=3kn^2$. On its actual boundary cut $Y=S^2_R\times S^1_L$, with $0<L<R$, add the three independent boundary Maxwell fields of (I.13n.f.1) and use the boundary Einstein constraints with Einstein coefficient $M^2>0$ and cosmological constant $\Lambda\ge0$. For sufficiently large finite prepared electric strength $e>0$ there are smooth common data satisfying the sewn Gauss and boundary electric-flux constraints, the three auxiliary Maxwell Gauss constraints, and the boundary Einstein Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. At every marked point the differential of the null-stress map of the total boundary phase and triad stress has rank nine on an actual smooth family of such data. The relative bundle, framed winding, integer level, phase charge and auxiliary magnetic bundle classes remain fixed throughout that family.

*Common background.* Write $\bar h$ for the round product metric, $\eta=L\,d\theta$ for the unit circle one-form, and $\nu^I$, $I=1,2,3$, for the Euclidean coordinates of the unit sphere. Using the oriented sphere Hodge star, set
$$
\omega^I=R*_2d\nu^I+\nu^I\eta .
$$
The sphere metric is $R^2\sum_I d\nu^I\otimes d\nu^I$ and $\sum_I\nu^I d\nu^I=0$, so $\sum_I\omega^I\otimes\omega^I=\bar h$. The three $\omega^I$ form an orthonormal coframe. They are co-closed because the sphere divergence of $*_2d\nu^I$ vanishes and the coefficient of $\eta$ is circle independent. Let $\bar E_0^I=e(\omega^I)^\sharp$, with zero magnetic fields. These are smooth Gauss data on trivial auxiliary bundles. Their energy density is $\rho_{\rm M,0}=3\zeta e^2/2$, their spatial stress is $\rho_{\rm M,0}\bar h/3$, and their momentum vanishes.

Choose a bulk preparation metric inducing $\bar h$ on $Y$. In Theorem I.13n.h use the constant boundary charge density $q_0=Q/\operatorname{vol}_{\bar h}(Y)$ and the zero spatial phase difference. The sewn phase has $\rho_{\rm ph,0}=q_0^2/(2f_*^2)$, the same isotropic pressure, and zero momentum. The auxiliary fields carry no charge for the sewn connection. With $\bar R=2/R^2$, choose constant $\tau$ by
$$
\bar R+\frac{2}{3}\tau^2-2\Lambda
=2M^{-2}(\rho_{\rm M,0}+\rho_{\rm ph,0}).
$$
For large enough $e$ the equation has a real nonzero $\tau$. The second fundamental form $K=\tau\bar h/3$ then satisfies both boundary Einstein constraints. The sewn Maxwell electric data are those of the Neumann construction in Theorem I.13n.g with this same phase charge.

*Magnetic data and the momentum constraint.* Work in circle-invariant conformal data $\bar E^I$ with $\operatorname{div}_{\bar h}\bar E^I=0$ and $\bar B^I=(*_{\bar h}dA^I)^\sharp$ for global one-forms $A^I$. The only conformal Killing fields of $\bar h$ are the three rotations and the circle translation. Indeed the conformal factor of a conformal Killing field on this constant-scalar-curvature three-manifold satisfies $-\bar\Delta\sigma=(\bar R/2)\sigma$, from the infinitesimal scalar-curvature change under $\delta h=2\sigma h$. The product eigenvalues $\ell(\ell+1)/R^2+j^2/L^2$ exclude $\bar R/2=1/R^2$ for $L<R$. Thus every conformal Killing field is Killing. The distinct Ricci eigenspaces separate the sphere and circle factors, and the connected Killing algebra is the direct sum of the two factor algebras.

Let $\bar J$ be the signed Maxwell momentum density in the Einstein momentum constraint, with the convention for the normal to the cut fixed once. For a Killing field $\xi$, the integral of $\bar J(\xi)$ is, up to the common sign of the normal convention,
$$
\zeta\sum_I\int_Y(\iota_\xi dA^I)(\bar E^I)\,dV_{\bar h}
=-\zeta\sum_I\int_Y A^I([\xi,\bar E^I])\,dV_{\bar h}.
$$
Cartan's identity gives the first integration by parts using electric Gauss, and Killing invariance of the volume gives the second. For the circle generator this integral vanishes by invariance. Fix a marked point $p$ and choose a nonnegative sphere bump $\chi$ with open positive set away from its sphere coordinate. For a basis $\xi_\alpha$ of rotations put $A^{I,\alpha}=\chi[\xi_\alpha,\bar E^I_0]^\flat$. Their three moments at $\bar E_0$ give a signed positive-definite Gram matrix. A zero linear combination of the commutators on the positive set would force $\xi\nu^I=0$ for all $I$ there, by the circle component of $[\xi,\bar E^I_0]$, hence $\xi=0$. The moment matrix stays invertible for nearby electric data. Add a unique linear combination of the three triples $A^{I,\alpha}$ to any small chosen magnetic potentials to set all rotational moments to zero. The correction is smooth in the data and supported away from $p$. All magnetic curvatures remain exact.

Write $\bar{\mathcal L}$ for the trace-free symmetrized gradient. The elliptic equation $\operatorname{div}_{\bar h}\bar{\mathcal L}W=M^{-2}\bar J^\sharp$ has a smooth solution orthogonal to the Killing fields, since integration by parts identifies the kernel with the conformal Killing fields and the prescribed right-hand side is orthogonal to it. Use $h=\phi^4\bar h$ with $\phi>0$, the contravariant fields $E^I=\phi^{-6}\bar E^I$, $B^I=\phi^{-6}\bar B^I$, and
$$
K^{ij}=\frac{\tau}{3}h^{ij}+\phi^{-10}(\bar{\mathcal L}W)^{ij}.
$$
The divergence of the trace-free term and the contravariant Maxwell momentum both scale by $\phi^{-10}$, so this solves the physical momentum constraint. Electric Gauss is preserved by volume scaling, and the physical magnetic two-form remains $dA^I$. Keep the phase charge form fixed as $q_0dV_{\bar h}$, so $q=\phi^{-6}q_0$ and the physical phase momentum remains zero.

*Hamiltonian equation and sewn data.* With $\bar\rho_{\rm M}=(\zeta/2)\sum_I(|\bar E^I|_{\bar h}^2+|\bar B^I|_{\bar h}^2)$, the scalar curvature identity for $h$ reduces the Hamiltonian constraint to
$$
-8\bar\Delta\phi+\bar R\phi
+\left(\frac{2}{3}\tau^2-2\Lambda\right)\phi^5
-|\bar{\mathcal L}W|_{\bar h}^2\phi^{-7}
-2M^{-2}\bigl(\bar\rho_{\rm M}\phi^{-3}+\rho_{\rm ph,0}\phi^{-7}\bigr)=0.
$$
Its derivative in $\phi$ at $\phi=1$, $W=0$, and the background Maxwell data is
$$
\mathcal A=-8\bar\Delta-4\bar R+2M^{-2}(8\rho_{\rm M,0}+12\rho_{\rm ph,0}).
$$
Increase the finite $e$ so the zero-order coefficient is strictly positive. The operator is invertible on the usual Hölder domains by elliptic regularity and the positive quadratic form. The implicit function theorem yields a positive $\phi$ smoothly depending on small smooth perturbations, with smooth spatial regularity from the equation. This uses the constant-mean-curvature conformal constraint construction (Isenberg and Maxwell 2021) with the stated weights.

Extend $h$ smoothly into a collar of $X$ by perturbing the fixed bulk preparation metric there. The strict Hodge lattice minimum persists, since the Hodge Gram matrix is continuous in these smooth metrics and uniformly positive near the reference metric. In detail, the least eigenvalue gives a common quadratic lower bound on the distance to the bias periods, leaving only finitely many competitors near the reference cost. Their strict cost gaps persist by continuity. Reapply the Neumann problem of Theorem I.13n.g to the resulting relative Hodge curvature and the fixed charge form $q_0dV_{\bar h}$. Its compatibility equation remains $Q=3kn^2$, and the phase temporal velocity realizes $q$ with zero spatial phase difference. This supplies the actual bulk and boundary fluxes for each perturbed cut.

*Rank and normalization.* Identify physical orthonormal frames at $p$ by conformal rescaling of a fixed background frame and keep the unit normal convention fixed. Use the trace-free representative of $\operatorname{Sym}^2(T_p^*N)/\operatorname{span}\{g_N(p)\}$. For each basis vector $t$ of this nine-dimensional target, use the explicit inverse in (I.13n.f.2) to choose the required variations $X,Y$ of electric and magnetic field entries at $p$ in the background frame. These values can be realized by coexact local changes of the electric one-forms and by local magnetic potentials. In local oriented orthonormal sphere coordinates and the circle coordinate, take potentials linear in the two sphere coordinates and multiply by a sphere cutoff equal to one at $p$. The independent first derivatives of the circle component give the two sphere components of the curl; the sphere components give its circle component. Thus every desired vector value is realized by a circle-invariant potential. For a sphere support of radius $r$, the potentials have size $O(r)$, and the curls have size $O(1)$ uniformly as $r\downarrow0$. The remote moment correction leaves $Y$ at $p$ unchanged.

In the Hamiltonian linearization both the magnetic energy and the squared trace-free extrinsic curvature have zero derivative at the reference cut. Thus the conformal derivative $\psi$ satisfies
$$
\mathcal A\psi=2M^{-2}\delta\bar\rho_{\rm M},
\qquad
\delta\bar\rho_{\rm M}=\zeta\sum_I\bar h(\bar E_0^I,\delta\bar E^I).
$$
The right-hand side is bounded on a cylinder whose sphere area is $O(r^2)$. For $p_*>3/2$ the elliptic $W^{2,p_*}$ estimate and embedding into continuous functions give $|\psi(p)|=O(r^{2/p_*})$ for each of the nine chosen directions. In physical frames the Maxwell fields scale by $\phi^{-4}$ and the phase energy by $\phi^{-12}$. The exact normalized differential on these nine input coordinates is consequently
$$
t\longmapsto t+\ell(t)v,\qquad
\ell(t)=\psi_t(p),\qquad
v=-8T_{\rm M,0}-12(T_{\rm ph,0})^{\rm tf}.
$$
Here $\mathrm{tf}$ takes the trace-free representative in the boundary Lorentz metric and the tensors in $v$ are evaluated at $p$. For sufficiently small $r$ one has $|\ell(v)|<1$. The calibrated inverse is $t\mapsto t-\ell(t)v/(1+\ell(v))$. This proves rank nine on the joint constraint manifold and uses action coefficients, prepared electric strengths, and a solved elliptic equation for its normalization. All field strengths and stresses in the map are invariant under the corresponding connection and phase gauge actions.

The construction joins the sewn class selection and the tensor intertwiner on the boundary Einstein constraint cut. The bulk metric in the constraint preparation is extended from the cut for the Maxwell Neumann problem. A coupled Lorentzian evolution with conserved boundary stress must also control the tangential momentum flux from the bulk Maxwell field. The evolution and the joint projections and ledgers of Definition I.13d remain to be supplied. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nj"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nj-conserved-lorentzian-development-with-a-sewn-product-collar"></a>**Theorem I.13n.j (Conserved Lorentzian Development with a Sewn Product Collar).** Take the cut of Theorem I.13n.i with a bias centered at a smooth relative curvature representative that is flat in a collar of $Y$. Retain a sufficiently small part of its constraint family. On a common open time slab there is a smooth development that solves the sewn Maxwell–Chern–Simons and phase equations, the three auxiliary Maxwell equations, and the boundary Einstein equations. The bulk metric is a background argument of the matter action, with product collar inducing the evolving boundary metric in this solution family. The boundary equations use the Hilbert variation of the boundary terms at fixed bulk background before restricting to the matched solutions. The phase and triad give a conserved boundary stress, and the rank-nine normalized cut intertwiner is realized by these histories. The linearized boundary equations on the product-collar branch have a retarded metric response to compatible smooth sources with zero-past data.

*A centered preparation.* Supply a smooth closed relative curvature bias \(\beta\) supported away from the boundary with integral periods and nonzero hyperplane period \(n\). The collar-flat representatives of Theorem I.13n.h give such inputs. Use the same \(\beta\) throughout the family. The class \([\beta]\) has zero preparation cost for every positive preparation metric, attained by the normalized curvature \(F_X/(2\pi)=\beta\), and all other classes have positive cost. The marked relative class \((m,n)\) and flat collar curvature are fixed under the metric changes of Theorem I.13n.i. Realize this curvature by a prepared connection which is zero on the collar in the initial boundary unit frame, using the chosen relative representative. Supply the fixed phase charge form with integral \(Q\) in the primitive charge convention. The charge compatibility equation selects \(k=Q/(3n^2)\) when this is integral. The auxiliary Maxwell and Einstein initial data are those of Theorem I.13n.i.

*Boundary evolution.* On the boundary time slab $N$ take the Einstein equations with the three Maxwell fields and the stress of $B=d\vartheta$ for a real massless phase $\vartheta$. Use the phase initial value $\vartheta|_{t=0}=0$ in the initial boundary frame and the signed normal derivative prescribed by $J_{\rm ph}=f_*^2 *_N d\vartheta$, with $J_{\rm ph}|_Y$ equal to the fixed charge form. This stress is exactly the phase Hilbert stress of (I.13n.a.7). The Gauss and Einstein constraints hold by Theorem I.13n.i. In harmonic coordinates and Lorenz gauges the reduced Einstein, scalar and Maxwell equations form a quasilinear wave system. Each metric, scalar and potential component has principal operator $g_N^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. The scalar stress adds products of first derivatives and its equation adds first-derivative metric terms in $\Box_{g_N}\vartheta$. The smooth local Cauchy theorem for quasilinear wave systems on compact slices gives a common interval for a sufficiently small finite-parameter family. The Maxwell and diffeomorphism identities propagate the gauges and constraints by homogeneous hyperbolic equations, since $\Box_{g_N}\vartheta=0$ and the Maxwell fields are source free. In particular $\nabla^a(T^{\rm ph}_{ab}+T^{\rm triad}_{ab})=0$. See Choquet-Bruhat (2014).

*Exact collar solution.* Write the signed collar coordinate as $r\le0$, increasing outward, with $r=0$ on $N$. Use the product bulk metric $dr^2+g_N$ on this collar and the orientation $\operatorname{vol}_M=dr\wedge\operatorname{vol}_N$. In the fixed trivialization continuing the initial boundary frame set
$$
u=\exp(i\vartheta),\qquad
A_{\rm col}=\frac{f_*^2}{Z}\,r\,d_N\vartheta,\qquad
F_{\rm col}=\frac{f_*^2}{Z}\,dr\wedge d_N\vartheta .
$$
Then $B=d_N\vartheta$ and $F_{\rm col}|_N=0$. The product Hodge rule is $*_5(dr\wedge b)=*_N b$ for any tangential one-form $b$: wedging with $dr\wedge b$ gives the defining inner product against $dr\wedge\operatorname{vol}_N$. Thus $Z*_5 F_{\rm col}|_N=f_*^2 *_N d_N\vartheta=J_{\rm ph}$ with the boundary orientation of Theorem I.13n.g. Also $F_{\rm col}^2=0$, $dF_{\rm col}=0$, and $d*_5F_{\rm col}=0$ by the scalar equation. The Chern–Simons boundary variation has the factor $F|_N$ in both the connection and phase terms of (I.13n.c.2), so it vanishes here. This realizes both sewn boundary equations with their actual signs. The charge is constant by Stokes' theorem applied to $dJ_{\rm ph}=0$ on $N$. The bulk Maxwell traction along $N$ is zero because $F_{\rm col}$ has one normal factor and no tangential two-form part. Equivalently the phase exchange identity (I.13n.a.8) vanishes directly.

*Global cut and doubling.* Extend $dr^2+g_N$ away from the collar to a smooth background Lorentzian metric on a slab over $X$, using a common time function. This can be done after shortening the slab, by using lapse and spatial metrics, smoothly interpolating the positive lapse and positive spatial forms and extending the shift. On the initial cut, the collar magnetic form is zero because $d_Y\vartheta|_{t=0}=0$. The collar electric flux $\mathcal E_{\rm col}=(*_5F_{\rm col})|_{X}$ is a closed tangential three-form, independent of $r$ in the collar, with boundary value $Z^{-1}J_{\rm ph}|_Y$. Extend it as a smooth three-form $\mathcal E_0$ on $X$ using a collar cutoff equal to one near $Y$. Define
$$
\mathcal S=Z^{-1}\,3k(F_X/2\pi)^2-d_X\mathcal E_0 .
$$
The four-form $\mathcal S$ has compact support in $X^\circ$, and its integral is $Z^{-1}(3kn^2-Q)=0$ by the selected charge and Stokes' theorem. On a connected oriented four-manifold without boundary, integration identifies compactly supported top de Rham cohomology with $\mathbb R$. Hence there is a smooth compactly supported three-form $\mathcal C$ in $X^\circ$ with $d_X\mathcal C=\mathcal S$. The flux $\mathcal E=\mathcal E_0+\mathcal C$ agrees with the product collar and solves the full cut Gauss law. For the family of Theorem I.13n.i, $F_X$ and the phase charge form are fixed. The tangential $\mathcal E_{\rm col}$ on the initial collar equals the same charge form divided by $Z$, so a common cutoff and the same $\mathcal C$ suffice.

Double the spatial cut, giving the reflected copy opposite orientation and using the dual sewn line bundle on that copy. Glue the bundle along the chosen unit frame. Glue the initial magnetic curvature by odd reflection and the flux by even reflection. These are smooth across the seam because the magnetic curvature is identically zero and the electric flux is a tangential form independent of $r$ there. A spatial connection realizing the reflected curvature is obtained by gluing the initial connection to its reflected dual, since both are zero in the collar frame. The product metric extends smoothly and evenly. Orientation reversal changes the sign of the Hodge star under pullback. Consequently odd reflection of the physical curvature corresponds to even reflection of the electric flux, as required. In particular the square of the magnetic curvature and $d_X\mathcal E$ both pull back evenly, so the same signed Gauss equation holds across the double. The collar ansatz extends smoothly across the seam and satisfies the same local equations there.

On the double solve the Maxwell–Chern–Simons Cauchy problem on that bundle and metric. Relative to a smooth reference connection, a Lorenz-gauge equation for the difference one-form is normally hyperbolic, with smooth lower-order terms and a nonlinearity quadratic in the first derivatives through $F\wedge F$. The Maxwell–Chern–Simons source is closed by $dF=0$. Taking the divergence of the reduced equation therefore gives the homogeneous wave equation for the gauge constraint. The gauge choice sets its initial trace to zero, so its initial tangential derivatives vanish, and the cut Gauss equation then sets its normal derivative to zero. Local smooth existence and finite propagation follow from the Cauchy energy estimate for this wave system on the compact double. The curvature agrees with $F_{\rm col}$ on the domain of dependence of the open collar in the initial cut. To see uniqueness directly, the difference of two curvatures satisfies the first-order Maxwell evolution with a smooth algebraic coefficient, since \(F_1^2-F_2^2=(F_1+F_2)\wedge(F_1-F_2)\). The local domain-of-dependence energy estimate gives zero difference from zero initial data there. On a shorter time slab that domain contains the entire sewn boundary. The boundary potential can be set to the collar ansatz in its frame by a gauge change: the potential difference is closed on that neighborhood and its class vanishes on the initial cut, where the initial collar connection is fixed. Extend the gauge change from a smaller collar by a cutoff of its real gauge function. The restricted double solution thus realizes the original sewn bulk and boundary equations. The relative data stay in the same class because the connections and prescribed phase frame vary smoothly on a fixed bundle.

*Retarded boundary response.* On each such background, vary the coupled boundary Einstein, Maxwell and massless phase system, with compatible smooth sources supported to the future of a chosen cut and zero-past data. For example a smooth conserved stress probe may enter the linearized Einstein equation with the scalar and Maxwell equations homogeneous in their full coupled variations. In the indicated gauges the principal operator is the wave operator of the same boundary metric on a finite direct sum of tensor bundles, and the lower-order terms are smooth. The linear wave energy estimate gives the unique zero-past retarded solution in these gauges, with metric-cone support. The gauge constraints propagate by the linearized diffeomorphism and Maxwell identities, with the source condition given by their homogeneous divergence identities. The construction thus determines the metric response modulo gauge. On the family of product-collar bulk backgrounds its phase and metric variations induce the variation of the exact collar solution, still with zero tangential bulk traction. In this response class the bulk metric is supplied as an external geometry extending $dr^2+g_N$. The argument concerns boundary causal response and does not include a bulk gravitational evolution equation or an arbitrary fixed-bulk-metric timelike-boundary problem.

These histories realize the selected relative classes, the cut intertwiner, and the conserved retarded boundary response on one smooth source family. The projection maps, scale bridge, PCE selector, residual intervals and dependency ledger of Definition I.13d retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nk"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nk-finite-local-optical-readout-on-the-sewn-lorentzian-branch"></a>**Theorem I.13n.k (Finite Local Optical Readout on the Sewn Lorentzian Branch).** Use the matched product-collar histories of Theorem I.13n.j, the rank-nine family of Theorem I.13n.i at a marked cut point \(p\), and the same Einstein coefficient \(M^2\). A finite set of nine short, affinely normalized boundary light bundles measures the metric-quotient stress at \(p\). Their area-distance coefficients recover the full nine-dimensional null-stress tensor, with an explicit finite-length error. For all sufficiently short common lengths the map from the nine source controls to the nine finite-length area-distance readings itself has rank nine. This supplies a local lensing response on the same conserved sewn source.

*Optical transfer.* For each history, use the marked future unit observer \(u\) normal to the cut and the orthonormal frame continued from Theorem I.13n.i. For a unit spatial direction \(n\), launch the boundary null ray with \(k(0)=u+n\), so \(-g_N(u,k(0))=1\), and use its affine parameter \(s\). Work on a common small interval in the boundary slab. In a parallel orthonormal screen let \(\mathcal R_n(s)\) be its optical tidal matrix, with curvature convention fixed by the Jacobi equation \(D_n''=-\mathcal R_nD_n\). The vertex Jacobi map satisfies \(D_n(0)=0\), \(D_n'(0)=I_2\), and \(\operatorname{tr}\mathcal R_n=\operatorname{Ric}(k,k)\). These statements follow by projecting geodesic deviation on the screen. The missing two directions in the curvature trace are the two null frame directions; their trace contributions vanish by curvature antisymmetry. The infinitesimal area distance is \(d_n(s)=\sqrt{\det D_n(s)}\) on a short interval free of conjugate points. The affine length and the angular vertex normalization are part of the light-bundle protocol. See Kristian and Sachs (1966).

Choose \(K,L\ge0\) with \(\|\mathcal R_n(s)\|\le K\) and \(\|\mathcal R_n(s)-\mathcal R_n(0)\|\le Ls\) on the chosen interval, for all nine rays. For \(K s^2\le1\), the Volterra equation
$$
D_n(s)=sI_2-\int_0^s(s-v)\mathcal R_n(v)D_n(v)\,dv
\tag{I.13n.k.1}
$$
gives \(\sup_{0<v\le s}\|D_n(v)/v\|\le(1-Ks^2/6)^{-1}\le6/5\), using \(\int_0^s(s-v)v\,dv=s^3/6\). It also gives \(\|D_n(v)-vI_2\|\le Kv^3/5\). Substitute this last inequality in (I.13n.k.1) and compare \(\mathcal R_n(v)\) with its vertex value to obtain
$$
\left\|\frac{D_n(s)}s-I_2+\frac{s^2}{6}\mathcal R_n(0)\right\|
\le \frac{Ls^3}{12}+\frac{K^2s^4}{100}.
\tag{I.13n.k.2}
$$
Indeed the integrals with \(v^2\) and \(v^3\) are \(s^4/12\) and \(s^5/20\). The matrix \(D_n(s)/s=I_2+E\) has \(\|E\|\le Ks^2/5\). Then \(\det(I_2+E)=1+\operatorname{tr}E+\det E\) and \(|\operatorname{tr}E+\det E|\le(11/5)\|E\|\le11/25\). The scalar square-root identity bounds \(|\sqrt{\det(I_2+E)}-1-\operatorname{tr}(E)/2|\le 2\|E\|^2\). Therefore the direct affine-length estimator and its finite-length error are
$$
\mathcal{O}_n(s)=\frac{12}{s^2}\left(1-\frac{d_n(s)}s\right),\qquad
\big|\mathcal{O}_n(s)-\operatorname{Ric}_p(k(0),k(0))\big|
\le Ls+\frac{27}{25}K^2s^2 .
\tag{I.13n.k.3}
$$
The local curvature bounds use the actual branch metric, including its Weyl tidal part. The trace isolates Ricci curvature at leading order while retaining the finite-length Weyl contribution in the error bound.

*Nine directions and normalization.* Einstein's equation implies \(M^2\operatorname{Ric}(k,k)=T(k,k)\) because both the trace term and cosmological term vanish on \(k\). Here \(T\) is the phase plus triad Hilbert stress on the sewn solution. Write \(t\) for its Lorentz-trace-free representative. Use the six directions \(\pm e_i\), \(1\le i\le3\), and the three directions \((e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2\), \(i<j\). Let \(q_i^\pm=t(u\pm e_i,u\pm e_i)\) and \(q_{ij}=t(u+(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2,u+(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2)\). In the observer frame define \(b_i=(q_i^++q_i^-)/2\). Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{00}&=\tfrac14\sum_i b_i,&
t_{0i}&=(q_i^+-q_i^-)/4,&
t_{ii}&=b_i-t_{00},\\
t_{ij}&=q_{ij}-t_{00}-\sqrt2(t_{0i}+t_{0j})-\tfrac12(t_{ii}+t_{jj}) \quad(i<j).
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13n.k.4}
$$
The first line uses \(t_{00}=\sum_i t_{ii}\), and the second evaluates the corresponding null quadratic form. This map is an inverse on the entire quotient. Substituting \(M^2\mathcal{O}_n(s)\) for the exact contractions in (I.13n.k.4) gives an entrywise error bounded by \(5M^2[Ls+(27/25)K^2s^2]\). For this bound the intermediate error factors for \(t_{00},t_{0i},t_{ii}\) are \(3/4,1/2,7/4\), and the factor for \(t_{ij}\) is at most \(7/2+\sqrt2<5\).

*Rank for actual finite bundles.* In the smooth nine-parameter family, the rays and transported screens depend smoothly on the prepared data by the geodesic and transport equations. On a compact small parameter neighborhood, \(\mathcal R_n\) is jointly smooth in the affine parameter and the controls. Rescale \(v=sw\) in (I.13n.k.1); the solution \(D_n(s)/s\) extends smoothly in \(s\) and the controls with initial value \(I_2\). Its first nonconstant coefficient is \(-s^2\mathcal R_n(0)/6\) by that same equation, also after differentiating with respect to the controls. Thus the finite-length map \((M^2\mathcal{O}_n(s))_n\) converges in \(C^1\) to the nine null contractions as \(s\downarrow0\). By (I.13n.k.4) and Theorem I.13n.i the limiting differential on the nine controls is invertible. Its nonzero smallest singular value persists for sufficiently short \(s>0\). The nine finite-length readings then give local coordinates on the prepared source family by the inverse function theorem. This is a light-deflection and focusing calculation on actual sewn histories, using the observer frame, the source metric and its equations. The galaxy-scale lensing projection, the other observation sectors, and the scale and residual ledgers of Definition I.13d require their own constructions. \(\square\)

<a id="theorem-i13nl"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nl-homogeneous-evolution-and-directional-optical-distances-of-the-sewn-source"></a>**Theorem I.13n.l (Homogeneous Evolution and Directional Optical Distances of the Sewn Source).** Take Theorem I.13n.j on the homogeneous datum of Theorem I.13n.i, with a centered relative curvature bias, $n\ne0$, $Q=3kn^2\ne0$, $\Lambda>0$ and the expanding sign of the extrinsic curvature. Use proper time, the round unit sphere metric $\gamma$, and the angle $\theta$ of period $2\pi$. The boundary solution has metric $g_N=-dt^2+a^2\gamma+b^2d\theta^2$. Its matter has a finite system of homogeneous evolution equations, with exact energy density, two principal pressures and a positive-pressure mean equation of state. Both symmetry directions give explicit redshift and angular-diameter distances. These formulas apply to the common sewn slab. Under the small-curvature and small-density conditions below, the boundary solution also expands for all future proper times with a quantitative approach to the cosmological-constant equation of state for the combined matter and vacuum.

*Invariant fields and stresses.* Write $H_a=\dot a/a$, $H_b=\dot b/b$, $a(0)=a_0$, $b(0)=b_0<a_0$. Let $\beta^I=*_2d\nu^I$ on the unit sphere, with $\nu^I$ the three unit Cartesian coordinate functions. The phase is homogeneous and the three auxiliary connections have potentials
$$
A^I=U(t)\beta^I+V(t)\nu^I\,d\theta,\qquad
U(0)=V(0)=0,\quad \dot U(0)=ea_0,\quad \dot V(0)=eb_0.
$$
The potentials and their initial electric data agree with the coframe of Theorem I.13n.i. They are in Lorenz gauge because $\delta_2\beta^I=0$ and $V\nu^I$ is independent of the circle angle. The unit-sphere Hodge Laplacian has eigenvalue two on both $\nu^I$ and $\beta^I$, and $d\beta^I=-2\nu^I\,d\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$. The spatial Maxwell operator on this product preserves the two indicated components. Since $dA^I=dt\wedge(\dot U\beta^I+\dot V\nu^I d\theta)+U\,d\beta^I+V\,d\nu^I\wedge d\theta$, its full Maxwell equations are
$$
(b\dot U)^{\boldsymbol\cdot}+\frac{2b}{a^2}U=0,\qquad
\left(\frac{a^2}{b}\dot V\right)^{\boldsymbol\cdot}+\frac{2}{b}V=0 .
\tag{I.13n.l.1}
$$
For example the kinetic and magnetic terms summed over $I$ in the action, with the common constant spatial volume factor suppressed, have Lagrangian $\zeta[b\dot U^2+(a^2/2b)\dot V^2-(2b/a^2)U^2-V^2/b]$. Orthogonality of the sphere eigenspaces and of sphere and circle components gives the same equations by direct substitution before variation. Define the nonnegative squared strength sums per physical spatial direction
$$
s_a=\frac{\dot U^2}{a^2}+\frac{V^2}{a^2b^2},\qquad
s_b=\frac{\dot V^2}{b^2}+\frac{4U^2}{a^4}.
$$
The sphere identities $\sum_I d\nu^I\otimes d\nu^I=\gamma$, $\sum_I\nu^I d\nu^I=0$, and $\sum_I(\nu^I)^2=1$ make the momentum zero and the stresses diagonal. In particular the sphere components of both the electric one-form and the dual magnetic one-form are proportional to $\beta^I$; the mixed sphere–circle contributions sum to zero. The Maxwell density and directional pressures are
$$
\rho_{\rm M}=\frac{\zeta}{2}(2s_a+s_b),\qquad
p_a^{\rm M}=\frac{\zeta}{2}s_b,\qquad
p_b^{\rm M}=\zeta s_a-\frac{\zeta}{2}s_b .
\tag{I.13n.l.2}
$$
The volume is $8\pi^2a^2b$. The conserved phase charge fixes its density and pressure by
$$
\rho_{\rm ph}=p_{\rm ph}
=\frac{Q^2}{2 f_*^2(8\pi^2 a^2 b)^2}.
\tag{I.13n.l.3}
$$
Set $\rho=\rho_{\rm M}+\rho_{\rm ph}$ and $p_i=p_i^{\rm M}+p_{\rm ph}$ for $i=a,b$. In particular $|p_i|\le\rho$, $\rho+p_a\ge\rho$, and
$$
\bar p=\frac{2p_a+p_b}{3}=\frac{\rho_{\rm M}}3+\rho_{\rm ph},\qquad
\dot\rho=-2H_a(\rho+p_a)-H_b(\rho+p_b).
\tag{I.13n.l.4}
$$
The conservation law follows either from (I.13n.l.1)–(I.13n.l.3) or from the Ward identities in Theorem I.13n.j. If $Q\ne0$ and $e>0$, then $1/3<\bar p/\rho<1$ at every finite regular time. The Maxwell density cannot vanish at such a time because all four oscillator Cauchy entries would vanish and then vanish identically by uniqueness.

*Einstein equations and future estimate.* With $\rho_\Lambda=M^2\Lambda$, the diagonal Einstein equations are
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_a^2+2H_aH_b+a^{-2}&=\Lambda+\rho/M^2,\\
2\dot H_a+3H_a^2+a^{-2}&=\Lambda-p_b/M^2,\\
\dot H_a+\dot H_b+H_a^2+H_b^2+H_aH_b&=\Lambda-p_a/M^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{I.13n.l.5}
$$
The spatial Ricci curvatures of the time-dependent metric give $R_{\hat a\hat a}=\dot H_a+(2H_a+H_b)H_a+a^{-2}$ and $R_{\hat b\hat b}=\dot H_b+(2H_a+H_b)H_b$. These and $R_{00}=-2(\dot H_a+H_a^2)-(\dot H_b+H_b^2)$ yield (I.13n.l.5). The initial expansion rates coincide and obey the first equation by Theorem I.13n.i. The derivative of the constraint error from the two evolution equations and (I.13n.l.4) is minus $(2H_a+H_b)$ times that error. Thus the finite ODE solves the full Einstein equations and by local Cauchy uniqueness agrees with Theorem I.13n.j on the common slab. See Constantin et al. (2023).

Let $h_\Lambda=\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$, $\mathcal H=(2H_a+H_b)/3$, and $D=H_b-H_a$. The constraint and the difference of the spatial Ricci equations give
$$
3\mathcal H^2=\Lambda+\rho/M^2-a^{-2}+\frac{D^2}{3},\qquad
\dot D+3\mathcal H D=a^{-2}+(p_b-p_a)/M^2 .
\tag{I.13n.l.6}
$$
Take $a_0^{-2}\le h_\Lambda^2/100$ and $\rho(0)/M^2\le h_\Lambda^2/100$. These conditions are compatible with the rank theorem. For example fix $b_0=a_0/2$ and all positive couplings, take $a_0$ sufficiently large and set $\rho_{\rm M}(0)/M^2=h_\Lambda^2/200$. Then the phase contribution to $\rho(0)$ is $O(a_0^{-6})$, the positive zero-order condition of Theorem I.13n.i holds, and the expanding initial constraint is real. On a bootstrap interval $H_a,H_b\ge h_\Lambda/2$, equation (I.13n.l.4) gives $\rho(t)\le \rho(0)e^{-h_\Lambda t}$, and $a^{-2}\le a_0^{-2}e^{-h_\Lambda t}$. Since $\mathcal H$ is initially positive, (I.13n.l.6) then gives $\mathcal H\ge\sqrt{299/300}\,h_\Lambda>3h_\Lambda/4$. Set $C=a_0^{-2}+2\rho(0)/M^2$. By the integrating factor for $D$ and $D(0)=0$,
$$
|D(t)|\le\frac{4C}{5h_\Lambda}e^{-h_\Lambda t}.
\tag{I.13n.l.7}
$$
Indeed the forcing has size at most $Ce^{-h_\Lambda t}$ and the damping is at least $9h_\Lambda/4$. Since $C\le3h_\Lambda^2/100$, (I.13n.l.7) strictly improves both bootstrap inequalities through $H_a=\mathcal H-D/3$ and $H_b=\mathcal H+2D/3$. The constraint gives finite upper bounds on both rates. On finite intervals the radii therefore stay in positive compact ranges, and the oscillator and phase variables stay bounded there by their equations. The continuation criterion for the ODE gives the claimed complete future proper-time interval of the boundary solution.

The constraint also gives $|\mathcal H-h_\Lambda|\le C_1 e^{-h_\Lambda t}$, where one may take $C_1=[\rho(0)/M^2+a_0^{-2}+(4C/5h_\Lambda)^2/3]/(3h_\Lambda)$. Thus $a e^{-h_\Lambda t}$ and $b e^{-h_\Lambda t}$ approach finite positive constants. Put $x=(a^2b)^{1/3}$. The separate Maxwell conservation law gives
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(\rho_{\rm M}x^4)
=\frac23D(p_a^{\rm M}-p_b^{\rm M})x^4,\qquad
\left|\frac{d}{dt}\log(\rho_{\rm M}x^4)\right|\le\frac43|D|.
\tag{I.13n.l.8}
$$
It follows that $\rho_{\rm M}x^4$ converges to a finite positive constant with a logarithmic tail at most $16C e^{-h_\Lambda t}/(15h_\Lambda^2)$. Equation (I.13n.l.3) gives the exact phase law $\rho_{\rm ph}x^6=\mathrm{constant}$. The combined vacuum and matter mean equation-of-state parameter satisfies
$$
0<1+w_{\rm tot}
=\frac{(4/3)\rho_{\rm M}+2\rho_{\rm ph}}{\rho_\Lambda+\rho}
\le \frac{2\rho(0)}{\rho_\Lambda}e^{-h_\Lambda t}.
\tag{I.13n.l.9}
$$
The phase and triad stress has $w>1/3$ independently of the choice of $e$, $M$, $f_*^2$, and the allowed integer triple. Along either expanding symmetry direction, the redshift formula below is invertible on a compact emission interval and gives a finite-parameter $w(z)$ by substitution, using the actual two-scale redshift.

*Directional optical projection.* An affinely parametrized null geodesic on the cover of the product has conserved circle momentum $P_b$ and conserved sphere angular-momentum magnitude $P_a$. Its sphere projection lies on a great circle when $P_a\ne0$, by the sphere rotation symmetries. The comoving frequency is
$$
\omega(t)=\left(\frac{P_a^2}{a(t)^2}+\frac{P_b^2}{b(t)^2}\right)^{1/2},
\qquad 1+z=\frac{\omega(t_e)}{\omega(t_o)} .
\tag{I.13n.l.10}
$$
For a purely axial ray the two angular-diameter eigenvalues on the screen at emission are both
$$
d_{\mathrm{axis}}=a(t_e)a(t_o)\int_{t_e}^{t_o}\frac{b(t)}{b(t_o)a(t)^2}\,dt .
\tag{I.13n.l.11}
$$
To see this, normalize $\omega(t_o)=1$. A small angular perturbation of the observer direction into one unit sphere tangent makes the corresponding conserved sphere momentum $a(t_o)$ times that angle. On the axial ray $P_b=b(t_o)$, so dividing the linearized affine sphere velocity by $\omega=b(t_o)/b(t)$ and converting the emission coordinate change to physical distance gives (I.13n.l.11).

For a purely spherical ray the two eigenvalues, with a fixed screen orientation and before conjugacy, are
$$
d_{\mathrm{sphere},a}=a(t_e)\sin\!\left(\int_{t_e}^{t_o}\frac{dt}{a(t)}\right),
\qquad
d_{\mathrm{sphere},b}=b(t_e)b(t_o)\int_{t_e}^{t_o}\frac{a(t)}{a(t_o)b(t)^2}\,dt .
\tag{I.13n.l.12}
$$
The first is the separation of neighboring great circles launched with the same observation point and perturbed initial angle. For the second, the circle momentum is $b(t_o)$ times the angular perturbation and $\omega=a(t_o)/a(t)$ on the reference ray. Both derivations use a perturbation whose travel time changes only to second order, so differentiation at fixed emission time gives the screen Jacobi map. The product $d_{\mathrm{sphere},a}d_{\mathrm{sphere},b}$ gives its area, and their difference gives its directional shear. Before wrapping or a conjugate point these are physical angular-diameter observables of the selected source. The pressure anisotropy enters the anisotropic expansion through (I.13n.l.6). For instance, $p_b-p_a=0$ on the initial coframe datum and $\dot D(0)=a_0^{-2}>0$. Even at that datum, axial and spherical redshifts separate at second order in the emission lookback time.

The homogeneous law and optical distances belong to the common sewn source on the slab of Theorem I.13n.j. The future estimate is for its boundary equations. The development of the bulk for the entire future, the inhomogeneous galaxy and cluster projections, the observational local and early-universe residuals, and the remaining Definition I.13d ledgers retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nm"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nm-collisionless-thermal-sky-residual-of-the-sewn-source"></a>**Theorem I.13n.m (Collisionless Thermal-Sky Residual of the Sewn Source).** On an expanding solution of Theorem I.13n.l, put comoving, isotropic, spatially uniform test radiation with Planck occupation $f_e(\omega)=(\exp(\omega/T_e)-1)^{-1}$, $T_e>0$, on an emission cut $t_e$. Use units with Boltzmann's constant one and let the distribution propagate collisionlessly to a comoving observer at $t_o>t_e$ on the common sewn slab. If $\mu$ is the observed direction cosine along the circle, set
$$
r=\log\frac{b(t_o)/b(t_e)}{a(t_o)/a(t_e)}
=\int_{t_e}^{t_o}D(t)\,dt,\qquad T_a=T_e\frac{a(t_e)}{a(t_o)} .
$$
The spectrum in every direction is Planck with temperature
$$
\frac{T(\mu)}{T_a}=\big[1+(e^{2r}-1)\mu^2\big]^{-1/2}.
\tag{I.13n.m.1}
$$
The temperature extrema obey $T_{\max}/T_{\min}=e^{|r|}$, and the homogeneous sky distortion relative to $T_a$ is bounded by $e^{|r|}-1$. The monopole and leading quadrupole have closed expressions or uniform error bounds.

*Propagation and angular moments.* Collisionless transport preserves occupation along each null bicharacteristic. In the orthonormal frame of the observer, the conserved sphere and circle momenta have magnitudes $a(t_o)\omega_o\sqrt{1-\mu^2}$ and $b(t_o)\omega_o|\mu|$. Apply (I.13n.l.10) at the emission cut and substitute the resulting frequency in $f_e$. This proves (I.13n.m.1) for all directions even if the ray winds, because the preparation is uniform on the cut. The extrema follow at $\mu=0$ and $|\mu|=1$.

Let $u=e^{2r}-1$, and let $\overline T$ denote the angular average of the temperature. Then
$$
\frac{\overline T}{T_a}=\int_0^1\frac{d\mu}{\sqrt{1+u\mu^2}}
=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{arsinh}(\sqrt u)/\sqrt u,&u>0,\\
1,&u=0,\\
\arcsin(\sqrt{-u})/\sqrt{-u},&-1<u<0 .
\end{cases}
\tag{I.13n.m.2}
$$
For $P_2(\mu)=(3\mu^2-1)/2$, put $q_2=5\int_0^1P_2(\mu)T(\mu)/T_a\,d\mu$. All odd angular coefficients vanish. The exact quadrupole bound is
$$
\left|q_2+\frac23r\right|
\le \frac{5}{3\sqrt3} e^{|r|}r^2 .
\tag{I.13n.m.3}
$$
Indeed for $g=T/T_a$ and $s=e^{2r}\mu^2/(1+(e^{2r}-1)\mu^2)$, one has $g_r=-s g$, $g_{rr}=(3s^2-2s)g$, and $0\le s\le1$. Thus Taylor's theorem gives $|g-1+r\mu^2|\le e^{|r|}r^2/2$. Now use $\mu^2=(1+2P_2)/3$, $\int_0^1P_2^2=1/5$, and $\int_0^1|P_2|=2/(3\sqrt3)$. Equation (I.13n.l.7) supplies an independent dynamical angular budget
$$
|r|\le \frac{4C}{5h_\Lambda^2}
\left(e^{-h_\Lambda t_e}-e^{-h_\Lambda t_o}\right)
\tag{I.13n.m.4}
$$
on the controlled expanding branch. For $t_e=0$ and small positive $t_o$, the anisotropy is nonzero because $D(0)=0$ and $\dot D(0)=a_0^{-2}>0$.

This gives an exact homogeneous free-propagation component of the early-universe projection using the same two-scale geometry and no angular calibration data. The preparation is a supplied test distribution. Recombination, inhomogeneous perturbations, and the certified observational $\Pi_{\mathrm{CMB}}$ interval of Definition I.13d retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nn"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nn-local-newton-tidal-coefficient-on-the-sewn-branch"></a>**Theorem I.13n.n (Local Newton Tidal Coefficient on the Sewn Branch).** Take the homogeneous cut of Theorems I.13n.i–I.13n.j, with its positive conformal constraint operator, and add a small comoving, gauge-neutral boundary dust probe. For a nonnegative smooth reference density $\bar\rho_d$ supported in a geodesic ball $B_s(y)$ of the reference spatial metric $\bar h$, write $m=\int_Y\bar\rho_d\,dV_{\bar h}$. There are exact common sewn data and smooth short-time developments for small nonnegative probe amplitude $\epsilon$, whose actual dust rest mass on the cut is $\epsilon m$. Let $\mathcal E_{ij}=R^{(4)}_{i0j0}$ in physical orthonormal frames with time axis normal to the cut, and compare frames using the conformal identification. For $r=d_{\bar h}(x,y)$ and $2s\le r<r_0$, the exterior derivative satisfies
$$
\left|\partial_\epsilon\mathcal E(x)\big|_0
-\bar\nabla_x^2\left(-\frac{G_0m}{r}\right)\right|
\le G_0m\big(C_1r^{-2}+C_2s r^{-4}\big),\qquad
G_0=\frac{1}{8\pi M^2}.
\tag{I.13n.n.1}
$$
Here $r_0>0$ and the finite constants are fixed by the reference cut and its coefficients. This determines the local Newton tidal normalization by geodesic deviation.

*Constrained source family.* Retain the reference auxiliary electric data $\bar E^I=\bar E^I_0$, auxiliary magnetic fields zero, phase charge form, magnetic bias and triple $(m_{\rm wind},n,k)$. Use $h=\phi^4\bar h$, $K=\tau h/3$ and the physical dust density $\rho_d=\epsilon\phi^{-6}\bar\rho_d$ with dust velocity the future unit normal on the cut. Its cut momentum and pressure vanish, and the choice of conformal power gives the asserted physical rest mass. The Hamiltonian equation of Theorem I.13n.i adds the term $-2M^{-2}\epsilon\bar\rho_d\phi^{-1}$. Its invertible derivative gives a smooth $\phi_\epsilon$ and exact common constraint data by the implicit function theorem. If $\psi=\partial_\epsilon\phi_\epsilon|_0$, then
$$
(-\bar\Delta+\mu^2)\psi=\frac{\bar\rho_d}{4M^2},\qquad
\mu^2=\frac18\left[-4\bar R+
2M^{-2}(8\rho_{\rm M,0}+12\rho_{\rm ph,0})\right]>0.
\tag{I.13n.n.2}
$$
The auxiliary Maxwell and phase initial stresses remain isotropic in their physical frames, with $\rho_{\rm M}=\phi^{-8}\rho_{\rm M,0}$ and $\rho_{\rm ph}=\phi^{-12}\rho_{\rm ph,0}$. For the Lorentzian development add the equations $U^a\nabla_aU^b=0$, $\nabla_a(\rho_d U^a)=0$ for the neutral dust, taking the velocity smoothly over the full cut including the vacuum part. The local Cauchy system for Einstein with dust and Maxwell includes the wave equations of the neutral phase as an additional normally hyperbolic block. Its principal terms are the same wave, geodesic transport and continuity operators, and the phase coupling adds its first-derivative stress and lower-order connection terms. The local Cauchy theorem applies on a short slab before any dust caustic, with the velocity fixed smoothly also where the density is zero. The boundary scalar remains source free. Its collar ansatz and the compactly supported Gauss correction in Theorem I.13n.j apply to the new boundary history since the phase charge form and relative magnetic data on the cut are unchanged. The boundary dust, phase, and Maxwell stresses are conserved in the stated solution family. See Choquet-Bruhat and Friedrich (2006).

*Tidal tensor.* For the curvature sign of (I.13n.l.5), the traced Gauss equation gives
$$
\mathcal E_{ij}={}^{(3)}R_{ij}+(\operatorname{tr}K)K_{ij}-(K^2)_{ij}
-{}^{(4)}R_{ij}.
$$
On the exterior cut ${}^{(4)}R_{ij}$ is a scalar multiple of the orthonormal metric by stress isotropy and Einstein's equation. Both extrinsic curvature terms are also pure trace. Hence the trace-free tidal tensor equals the trace-free spatial Ricci tensor. Its trace is ${}^{(4)}R_{00}=M^{-2}(\rho_{\rm M}+2\rho_{\rm ph})-\Lambda$ in the exterior. The conformal Ricci variation at $h=\phi^4\bar h$, in the conformally identified physical frames, therefore gives
$$
\partial_\epsilon \mathcal E\big|_0
=-2(\bar\nabla^2\psi)^{\rm tf}
-4\psi({}^{(3)}\bar R)^{\rm tf}
-\frac{8\rho_{\rm M,0}+24\rho_{\rm ph,0}}{3M^2}\,\psi\,\bar h .
\tag{I.13n.n.3}
$$
In this formula ${}^{(3)}\bar R$ inside the trace-free operator is the spatial Ricci tensor. On the exterior $\bar\Delta\psi=\mu^2\psi$, so the trace removal in its first term changes $-2\bar\nabla^2\psi$ only by a bounded coefficient times $\psi$.

*Local residual.* For $-\bar\Delta+\mu^2$ on the smooth compact three-manifold write its Green kernel near the diagonal as $G_\mu(x,z)=(4\pi d_{\bar h}(x,z))^{-1}+R_\mu(x,z)$, where $R_\mu$ is bounded and $|\bar\nabla_x^2 R_\mu|\le C d_{\bar h}(x,z)^{-2}$. To obtain these bounds, use the cutoff inverse-distance parametrix. Its residual source and its first spatial derivatives have sizes $O(d^{-1})$ and $O(d^{-2})$, by the smooth normal-coordinate expansion of the metric and its volume density. The residual is uniformly bounded in $L^2$ in dimension three. Invertibility gives a uniform $W^{2,2}$ bound and thus a uniform continuous bound for the remainder. Interior scaled Schauder estimates on balls of radius comparable to $d$, using these residual estimates, give the stated Hessian bound. All constants are uniform near the compact diagonal. Integrating (I.13n.n.2) yields $|\psi(x)|\le C m/(M^2r)$. Also the Hessian of $d_{\bar h}(x,z)^{-1}$ is smooth away from the diagonal, with first source derivative $O(r^{-4})$ when $d_{\bar h}(z,y)\le s\le r/2$. This follows by differentiating the smooth squared geodesic distance within the common normal radius. The difference between its integrated Hessian and $m\bar\nabla^2_x(r^{-1})$ is consequently bounded by $Cm s r^{-4}$. Multiplying by $-2/(4M^2)$ and the singular coefficient $1/(4\pi)$ gives the coefficient in (I.13n.n.1). The remainder, together with the terms proportional to $\psi$ in (I.13n.n.3), gives $G_0m C_1r^{-2}$ after reducing $r_0$ if needed. The result holds for every stated nonnegative packet without a shape fit.

The geodesic-deviation equation of freely falling neighboring observers uses $-\mathcal E$. In the scale window $s/r\to0$, $r\to0$, the error is small compared with the leading Newton tidal magnitude $G_0m/r^3$. This is a local, linear-in-amplitude initial tidal projection of exact source histories. The sustained quasistatic field, the Equation I.4 response, and the observational local-gravity residual of Definition I.13d retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13no"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13no-local-newton-and-optical-shear-match-for-a-common-dust-probe"></a>**Theorem I.13n.o (Local Newton and Optical Shear Match for a Common Dust Probe).** Use the exact released-dust histories of Theorem I.13n.n. At an exterior point $x$, take the future cut normal $u$ and a unit spatial direction $v$, with screen $S=v^\perp$. Identify physical orthonormal frames across the probe family as in that theorem. For the affine-normalized null bundle launched along $u+v$, let $C_S$ be its initial optical tidal matrix in the convention $\mathcal D''=-C\mathcal D$ of Theorem I.13n.k. With $\Phi(x)=-G_0m/r$ as in (I.13n.n.1),
$$
\left|(\partial_\epsilon C_S|_0)^{\rm tf_S}
-2\bigl(\bar\nabla^2\Phi|_S\bigr)^{\rm tf_S}\right|
\le G_0m\bigl(C_3r^{-2}+C_4s r^{-4}\bigr),\qquad 2s\le r<r_0 .
\tag{I.13n.o.1}
$$
The exterior optical trace has the exact response
$$
\operatorname{tr}_S(\partial_\epsilon C_S|_0)
=-\frac{(32/3)\rho_{\rm M,0}+24\rho_{\rm ph,0}}{M^2}\,\psi(x),
\tag{I.13n.o.2}
$$
where $\psi$ is the solution of (I.13n.n.2). Both readouts are normalized by the same action and baryonic input as the timelike tidal response.

*Cut curvature and optical shear.* The screen matrix has entries $C_{AB}=R^{(4)}_{A(u+v)B(u+v)}$. The mixed terms vanish by Codazzi since $K=\tau h/3$ has spatially constant $\tau$. The spatial Gauss identity gives $R^{(4)}_{\mathrm{AvBv}}=R^{(3)}_{\mathrm{AvBv}}+(\tau/3)^2\delta_{AB}$ in physical frames. In three dimensions $R^{(3)}_{\mathrm{AvBv}}=R^{(3)}_{AB}+(R^{(3)}_{vv}-R^{(3)}/2)\delta_{AB}$. The timelike tidal tensor is $\mathcal E_{AB}=R^{(3)}_{AB}+\lambda(x)\delta_{AB}$ for a scalar $\lambda$ by the traced Gauss equation and isotropic cut stresses. Thus the screen trace-free part of $C_S$ equals twice that of $\mathcal E|_S$ on the family. Taking the derivative gives (I.13n.o.1) by (I.13n.n.1). For the trace, Einstein's equation along $u+v$ gives $\operatorname{tr}_S C_S=M^{-2}((4/3)\rho_{\rm M}+2\rho_{\rm ph})$ in the exterior. The vacuum term vanishes in the null contraction. The conformal weights $\phi^{-8}$ and $\phi^{-12}$ give (I.13n.o.2).

*Finite light-bundle readout.* Let $\ell>0$ be the affine length with the observer normalization of Theorem I.13n.k. For the screen Jacobi map $\mathcal D_\epsilon$ with initial data $(0,I)$, smooth dependence of the metric, null geodesic and optical equation on $\epsilon$ gives
$$
-6\ell^{-3}\,\partial_\epsilon\mathcal D_\epsilon(\ell)\big|_0
=\partial_\epsilon C_S\big|_0+O(\ell).
$$
Indeed $\mathcal D_\epsilon'''(0)=-C_\epsilon(0)$, and the fourth affine derivative of $\partial_\epsilon\mathcal D_\epsilon$ is bounded on a common short ray segment by the differentiated Jacobi equation. The bound is uniform on a fixed compact exterior annulus and a compact set of screen directions for the stated family. The trace and trace-free part of this differential give the two readouts with the additional finite optical-length error.

This short-ray lensing projection belongs to the common released-dust history. The accumulated deflection by a stationary galaxy or cluster and the full lensing projection of Definition I.13d retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13np"></a>
