<a id="theorem-i13np-cluster-density-sign-and-spectral-residual-on-the-sewn-cut"></a>**Theorem I.13n.p (Cluster Density Sign and Spectral Residual on the Sewn Cut).** Take the released-dust preparation of Theorem I.13n.n with the homogeneous coframe, fixed phase charge form, and retained pure-trace extrinsic curvature. The constraint and development argument of that theorem applies to every smooth dust density profile $f\ge0$ with nonzero mass $m=\int_Y f\,dV_{\bar h}$. For every sufficiently small amplitude $\epsilon>0$, the proper boundary phase-plus-triad density is strictly below its zero-probe value at every point of the cut. The phase-plus-triad contribution to optical Ricci focusing also strictly decreases in every initial null direction. Its total proper energy on the cut decreases by an exact first-order mass coefficient. The density differential is a negative multiple of a normalized positive resolvent kernel. These signs rule out equality with the positive cluster density law of Equation I.7 on this preparation whenever that law has a nonzero baryonic weight. They also give a positive error floor after mean subtraction for the normalized $q=0$ comparison below.

*Finite-amplitude sign.* Denote the reference matter densities by $\rho_{\rm M,0}>0$ and $\rho_{\rm ph,0}\ge0$, and the local positive inverse length in (I.13n.n.2) by $\mu$. On this preparation the conformal factor $\phi_\epsilon$ solves
$$
-8\bar\Delta\phi_\epsilon+F_0(\phi_\epsilon)
=2M^{-2}\epsilon f\,\phi_\epsilon^{-1},
\qquad
F_0(z)=\bar R z+(2\tau^2/3-2\Lambda)z^5
-2M^{-2}(\rho_{\rm M,0}z^{-3}+\rho_{\rm ph,0}z^{-7}).
$$
The reference constraint gives $F_0(1)=0$, and the strict elliptic condition gives $F_0'(1)=8\mu^2>0$. Since $\phi_\epsilon\to1$ uniformly, $c_\epsilon=\int_0^1F_0'(1+t(\phi_\epsilon-1))\,dt$ is strictly positive for small $\epsilon$. The function $u=\phi_\epsilon-1$ satisfies
$$
(-8\bar\Delta+c_\epsilon)u=2M^{-2}\epsilon f\,\phi_\epsilon^{-1}.
$$
The minimum principle gives $u\ge0$. Its strong form and connectedness give $u>0$ everywhere because the right-hand side is not identically zero. The proper density and the source part of optical Ricci focusing are
$$
\rho_{\rm DS}(\epsilon)=\rho_{\rm M,0}\phi_\epsilon^{-8}+\rho_{\rm ph,0}\phi_\epsilon^{-12},\qquad
\mathcal F_{\rm DS}(\epsilon)
=M^{-2}\bigl((4/3)\rho_{\rm M,0}\phi_\epsilon^{-8}
+2\rho_{\rm ph,0}\phi_\epsilon^{-12}\bigr).
$$
The focusing expression holds in the orthonormal affine normalization of Theorem I.13n.k. The retained cut stress is isotropic, so the sign is independent of the null direction. Both expressions decrease strictly. On the exterior the dust has no direct stress, so the same focusing decrement is the change of the full optical Ricci trace there. The proper energy of the phase and triad also decreases since
$$
E_{\rm DS}(\epsilon)
=\int_Y(\rho_{\rm M,0}\phi_\epsilon^{-2}+\rho_{\rm ph,0}\phi_\epsilon^{-6})\,dV_{\bar h},
\qquad
E_{\rm DS}'(0)
=-\frac{2\rho_{\rm M,0}+6\rho_{\rm ph,0}}{4M^2\mu^2}\,m .
\tag{I.13n.p.1}
$$
Here the dust rest mass is $\epsilon m$ and the volume factor $\phi_\epsilon^6$ is included before taking the derivative. Integrating (I.13n.n.2) gives $\int_Y\psi\,dV_{\bar h}=m/(4M^2\mu^2)$, proving the exact coefficient. Smoothness of the constraint family gives a finite $O(\epsilon^2)$ residual for each fixed smooth input.

*Spectral projection and residual.* Define $P_\mu=\mu^2(-\bar\Delta+\mu^2)^{-1}$. Its Green kernel is symmetric and strictly positive off the diagonal by the maximum principle, and $P_\mu1=1$. On $Y=S^2_R\times S^1_L$ it is rotation and circle-translation invariant, with spherical and circle harmonic multipliers
$$
p_{\ell j}=\frac{\mu^2}{\ell(\ell+1)/R^2+j^2/L^2+\mu^2}.
$$
The full density differential for the reference-volume input $f$ is
$$
D_f\rho_{\rm DS}=-\gamma P_\mu f,\qquad
\gamma=\frac{8\rho_{\rm M,0}+12\rho_{\rm ph,0}}{4M^2\mu^2}>0.
\tag{I.13n.p.2}
$$
The proper density is the local scalar measured by the normal observer, and (I.13n.p.1) records its separate physical-volume integral. A comparison with Equation I.7 uses its background-subtracted baryonic weight on the actual preparation. For each nonnegative admissible weight $f (|\nabla\Phi_b|/g_*)^q$ with nonzero integral, a nonnegative normalized convolution with $A_{\rm PM}>0$ gives a nonnegative density of positive mass. The sign comparison applies as well to its normalized-kernel counterpart on $Y$. The response in (I.13n.p.2) is strictly negative and has reference-volume integral $-\gamma m$. Thus matching its sign requires a change of source or of the cluster prescription. The strict finite-amplitude result gives the same sign discrepancy for the comparison with the zero-probe density on this family.

For a mean-subtracted $q=0$ comparison on $Y$, put $f_0=f-\langle f\rangle_Y$. Let $\mathcal K$ have a symmetric, nonnegative, normalized kernel, and let $A\ge0$ be an amplification. The normalized integral operator is an $L^2$ contraction by Jensen's inequality and symmetry, fixes constants, and preserves the mean. Choose a real harmonic $w$ of eigenvalue $\lambda>0$ with $\|w\|_2=1$, and use $f=f_*(1+\delta w)$ with a positive constant $f_*$ and a nonzero $\delta$ small enough that $f\ge0$. For every such $\mathcal K$ with $\langle w,\mathcal K w\rangle\ge0$, one has
$$
\left\|-\gamma P_\mu f_0-A\mathcal K f_0\right\|_2
\ge f_*|\delta|\,\frac{\gamma\mu^2}{\lambda+\mu^2}.
\tag{I.13n.p.3}
$$
Indeed taking the inner product against $w$ gives two terms of the same sign under the stated modal condition. This condition holds for positive spectral kernels such as the heat and resolvent families.

A concentrated profile gives an error floor for every nonnegative normalized kernel, regardless of its harmonic coefficients. Write $V_Y=\operatorname{vol}_{\bar h}(Y)$ and choose $f$ of mass $m$ supported in $B_{r/2}(y)$. On $\mathcal A_r=\{x:r\le d_{\bar h}(x,y)\le2r\}$, the Green kernel estimate in Theorem I.13n.n implies $P_\mu f\ge \mu^2 m/(20\pi r)$ for sufficiently small $r$. Indeed $d_{\bar h}(x,z)\le 5r/2$ for $z$ in the support, and the bounded kernel remainder allows at least half of the singular term for a common small radius. Positivity and normalization of $\mathcal K$ give $\mathcal K f_0\ge-m/V_Y$, while $P_\mu f_0=P_\mu f-m/V_Y$. For a fixed finite $A\ge0$, take also $r\le\gamma\mu^2V_Y/(40\pi(\gamma+A))$. Then throughout $\mathcal A_r$,
$$
\left|-\gamma P_\mu f_0-A\mathcal K f_0\right|
\ge \frac{\gamma\mu^2 m}{40\pi r}.
\tag{I.13n.p.4}
$$
The $L^2$ lower bound is this value times $\operatorname{vol}_{\bar h}(\mathcal A_r)^{1/2}$. Thus any fixed finite amplification fails equality on the full smooth positive profile family even with mean subtraction. The amplitude can be taken sufficiently small for the chosen profile, so the cut constraint construction remains valid.

For each fixed nonzero $f$, the strict finite-amplitude cut inequalities have a positive margin by compactness. The developments of Theorem I.13n.n and smoothly continued observers preserve these signs on a common sufficiently short time interval by continuity, with the interval allowed to depend on the preparation and amplitude. The equal-time spatial response is obtained by solving the cut constraints. The stationary galaxy and cluster observables, including physical merger histories, retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nq"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nq-exact-mean-subtracted-cluster-kernel-test-on-the-sewn-cut"></a>**Theorem I.13n.q (Exact Mean-Subtracted Cluster Kernel Test on the Sewn Cut).** Use the released-dust data of Theorem I.13n.p. Denote by $V$ the reference volume, by $\mathcal P_0$ the projection to constants, and by $P_\mu$ and $\gamma>0$ the normalized resolvent and coefficient in (I.13n.p.2). For $q=0$, consider every fixed finite $A\ge0$ and every probability kernel $\mathcal K$ preserving the normalized reference measure. A probability kernel here maps each point to a probability measure on the cut and acts by integration. Symmetry, smoothness and positivity of the harmonic coefficients are unnecessary. No such $A\mathcal K$ gives the actual mean-subtracted density differential on all nonnegative smooth profiles. For $A>0$, the unique signed, constant-preserving candidate that could do so is
$$
\mathcal K_* =\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{A}\right)\mathcal P_0-\frac{\gamma}{A}P_\mu .
\tag{I.13n.q.1}
$$
This signed kernel is symmetric, has total weight one in each row, and has strictly negative density sufficiently close to the diagonal. More generally on any prescribed smooth compact connected cut with a positive symmetric normalized Green kernel $p$ for the response $-\gamma P$, a probability kernel of this form exists exactly when $p$ is essentially bounded by $(1+A/\gamma)/V$ with respect to the unnormalized reference volume. Thus a bounded smoothing kernel can pass at sufficiently large $A$, while the local inverse-distance singularity of this sewn branch excludes every finite $A$. On the sewn product cut the optimal uniform error over smooth profiles $0\le f\le1$ is attained by an explicit probability kernel at every finite gain.

*Identification on the full profile class.* Every smooth zero-mean function $w$ is obtained from a nonnegative smooth input by adding a sufficiently large positive constant. Since the measured output is $-\gamma P_\mu(I-\mathcal P_0)f$, agreement on the nonnegative input class therefore forces $\mathcal K w=-(\gamma/A)P_\mu w$ for all such $w$ when $A>0$. Constant preservation fixes the complementary one-dimensional block. The resulting identity on smooth functions identifies the signed row measure almost everywhere, by a countable dense family of smooth functions in the uniform norm. For $A=0$ take any nonconstant smooth profile and use injectivity of the resolvent on its nonzero zero-mean part. The normalized candidate (I.13n.q.1) has the row density $[1+\gamma/A]/V-(\gamma/A)p_\mu(x,z)$. Its positivity criterion is exactly the stated upper bound. A positive density with this bound has row integral one and preserves the reference measure because the Green kernel is symmetric. The inverse-distance term $p_\mu(x,z)=\mu^2/(4\pi d(x,z))+O(1)$ from Theorem I.13n.n violates the bound on a positive-measure neighborhood of the diagonal at every finite $A$. The criterion uses the actual baryonic density derivative and the same reference volume on both sides.

*Sharp uniform error for bounded input profiles.* Put
$$
h_A(x,z)=\frac{A+\gamma}{V}-\gamma p_\mu(x,z),\qquad
N_A=\int_Y (h_A(x,z))_-\,dV_z ,
\tag{I.13n.q.2}
$$
where the negative part is nonnegative. Product homogeneity makes $N_A$ independent of $x$, since $P_\mu$ commutes with the transitive product isometry group. The normalized reference-volume density of $A\mathcal K_*$ is $h_A$, and its row mass is $A$. The error on a general profile is the row measure $h_A(x,z)dV_z-A\mathcal K(x,dz)$ applied to that profile. This row has total mass zero. For every $x$, the negative mass is at least $N_A$ because $A\mathcal K$ is a positive measure. For a signed regular measure of total mass zero on a compact space, the supremum of the absolute integral over smooth $0\le f\le1$ is precisely its negative mass. Indeed compact and open approximations to a negative Hahn set and a smooth cutoff between them approximate that mass arbitrarily well. To apply this with the essential supremum over $x$, take a countable family dense in the smooth test class for the uniform norm. The row measures have a common finite total variation bound, so the supremum over that family equals the row-wise optimum. The essential supremum and this countable supremum commute. The resulting lower bound is therefore valid for $\sup_{0\le f\le1}\|(-\gamma P_\mu-A\mathcal K)(I-\mathcal P_0)f\|_\infty$.

For the upper bound use the row density $(h_A)_+/(A+N_A)$ as the probability kernel. Its row mass is one, it is symmetric, and it preserves the reference measure. The denominator is positive even at $A=0$ because the actual resolvent is nonconstant. The signed error row has negative part $(h_A)_-dV_z$ and positive part $N_A(h_A)_+dV_z/(A+N_A)$. Thus the infimum of the uniform error over all admitted kernels equals $N_A$ and is attained. In particular, with $c_*=\gamma\mu^2/(4\pi)$,
$$
N_A=\frac{2\pi}{3}\,c_*^3\frac{V^2}{(A+\gamma)^2}
\bigl(1+O((A+\gamma)^{-1})\bigr)\qquad(A\to\infty).
\tag{I.13n.q.3}
$$
To see this, the smooth Green density away from the diagonal is bounded. In a fixed normal ball, $\gamma p_\mu(x,z)=c_*/r+O(1)$ uniformly, with $r=d(x,z)$. The negative region is contained in a ball of radius $O((A+\gamma)^{-1})$. With $T=(A+\gamma)/V$, the negative-part integral is bounded between the integrals of $(c_*/r-(T+C))_+$ and $(c_*/r-(T-C))_+$ for a fixed $C$, each with normal-coordinate volume factor $1+O(r^2)$. The Euclidean integral at threshold $T'$ is $4\pi\int_0^{c_*/T'}(c_*/r-T')r^2\,dr=2\pi c_*^3/(3T'^2)$. This proves the expansion and its coefficient from the same Newton singularity as the tidal readout.

*One common total-variation witness.* There is a positive constant $c$ depending only on the reference cut and $\mu$ such that the following bound holds for every $A\ge0$. Choose a radius $r>0$ within the common normal-coordinate radius and small enough that
$$
r\le\frac{\gamma\mu^2 V}{40\pi(\gamma+A)} .
\tag{I.13n.q.4}
$$
Use a nonnegative smooth profile $f$ of mass $m>0$ supported in $B_{r/2}(y)$. On the annulus $\mathcal A_r=\{x:r\le d(x,y)\le2r\}$ the uniform Green estimate of Theorem I.13n.p gives $P_\mu f\ge\mu^2 m/(20\pi r)$. For any probability kernel, $\mathcal K(f-\mathcal P_0 f)\ge-m/V$. Thus the error, as an unnormalized signed density on this annulus, obeys
$$
-\gamma P_\mu(I-\mathcal P_0)f-A\mathcal K(I-\mathcal P_0)f
\le-\frac{\gamma\mu^2m}{40\pi r} .
\tag{I.13n.q.5}
$$
Integrating the absolute value on $\mathcal A_r$, whose volume is at least a fixed multiple of $r^3$, gives total variation norm at least $c\gamma m r^2$. The same bound applies when the comparison also subtracts its output mean, since measure preservation makes that mean zero. The witness depends on the admitted gain bound and the common geometry and works uniformly over the probability-kernel class. By differentiability of the actual dust family, for each fixed witness the finite-amplitude density comparison with a linear $q=0$ law has error at least $c\gamma m r^2\epsilon/2$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$. Here the nonlinear remainder is the sewn-cut density remainder in the same reference volume. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13nr"></a>

<a id="theorem-i13nr-all-exponents-in-the-mean-subtracted-released-dust-cluster-test"></a>**Theorem I.13n.r (All Exponents in the Mean-Subtracted Released-Dust Cluster Test).** Use the released sewn dust preparation of Theorems I.13n.n–I.13n.q, with reference volume $d\bar V$, $\mathcal P_0$ the reference mean projection and $P_\mu$ the positive normalized Green operator in (I.13n.p.2). Specify the background-subtracted baryonic acceleration port as the reference-cut Poisson readout of the actual transported baryonic mass form. Thus for a fixed smooth profile $f\ge0$ and source amplitude $\epsilon>0$, solve
$$
-\bar\Delta\Phi_{b,\epsilon}=4\pi G_0\epsilon(I-\mathcal P_0)f,\qquad
\mathcal P_0\Phi_{b,\epsilon}=0,\qquad
a_{b,\epsilon}=|\bar\nabla\Phi_{b,\epsilon}|_{\bar h}.
\tag{I.13n.r.1}
$$
The overall sign of the potential does not affect this acceleration. In this same reference comparison, take any fixed $g_*>0$, finite gain $A\ge0$, real exponent $q$, and probability kernel $\mathcal K$ preserving $d\bar V/V$. Use the weight one at $q=0$ and otherwise the weight $(a_{b,\epsilon}/g_*)^q$ against the transported baryonic mass. Compare the mean-subtracted result with the actual proper boundary phase-plus-triad density change evaluated in the reference labels. The complete classification is as follows.

1. For $q>-3$ there are admitted nonconstant smooth nonnegative profiles. For every real $q$ in this range, the comparison fails on the full admitted class at small amplitudes, and cannot match its first derivative in amplitude. At every $q\ne0$ this failure holds on each fixed nonconstant admitted profile. At $q=0$ the kernel exclusion and the sharp gain-dependent optimal residual are those of Theorem I.13n.q.
2. For $q\le-3$ there is no nonzero smooth nonnegative profile of finite weighted mass for the stated Poisson port.
3. For each $q\ne0$ and a fixed nonconstant admitted profile, one can use the same two source amplitudes $\epsilon,2\epsilon$ for every admitted kernel and gain. If the normalized discrepancy at amplitude $\delta$ is the $L^1(d\bar V)$ discrepancy divided by $\delta$, their maximum satisfies
   $$
   \max_{\delta\in\{\epsilon,2\epsilon\}}\frac{
   \left\|(I-\mathcal P_0)[\rho_{\rm DS}(\delta)-\rho_{\rm DS}(0)]
   -A\mathcal K(I-\mathcal P_0)\bigl[\delta f(a_{b,\delta}/g_*)^q\bigr]\right\|_{L^1(d\bar V)}
   }{\delta}
   \ \ge\
   \frac{|2^q-1|}{1+2^q}\,\gamma\,\|P_\mu(I-\mathcal P_0)f\|_{L^1(d\bar V)}
   -C_f\epsilon
   \tag{I.13n.r.2}
   $$
   for sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$. Here $C_f$ is independent of $A$ and $\mathcal K$. This remains a uniform obstruction even if a kernel and gain are chosen for the two-amplitude test, provided the same ones are used at both amplitudes.

*Physical mass and the readout measure.* The dust data are $h_\epsilon=\phi_\epsilon^4\bar h$ and $\rho_d(\epsilon)=\epsilon\phi_\epsilon^{-6}f$. The product $\rho_d(\epsilon)dV_{h_\epsilon}$ is exactly $\epsilon f\,d\bar V$ on the same cut. Thus (I.13n.r.1) uses the physical mass in the fixed reference geometry, rather than identifying the proper density scalar with the density relative to the reference volume. The Poisson subtraction is fixed by its zero mode, with inverse on the remaining spectrum. It is a specified cut observable, not an added force in the sewn equations. In particular the metric and phase evolution remain those of the released source. The comparison output is measured in the reference labels and projected by the fixed $\mathcal P_0$, as in Theorem I.13n.q. The result concerns this fixed reference-geometry acceleration port. A nonlinear or time-dependent prescription for the baryonic acceleration is a different response test.

Let $a_f=|\bar\nabla\Phi_{b,1}|_{\bar h}$, where $\Phi_{b,1}$ denotes the solution of the reference linear equation with unit source amplitude. By that equation $a_{b,\epsilon}=\epsilon a_f$ exactly. For $q<0$ require the gradient to be nonzero almost everywhere for the physical baryon mass and the weighted density to be integrable, as in Equation I.7. Put $F_q[f]=f(a_f/g_*)^q$, with zero value where $f=0$ and weight one at $q=0$. On the admissible class the weighted density relative to the reference volume is $\epsilon^{1+q}F_q[f]$. The measure-preserving probability kernel acts on $L^1$ with norm at most one and commutes with $\mathcal P_0$. These follow by integration of the pointwise triangle inequality and the two normalization identities. Thus the same formulas apply even when $F_q[f]$ is unbounded near critical points.

*Admissible exponents on the compact cut.* For a nonzero $f$ the mean $\mathcal P_0f$ is positive. If $\Phi_{b,1}$ is constant then $f$ is constant and positive, and the negative-exponent comparison is undefined on its entire baryonic support. Otherwise choose a maximum $x_0$ of the smooth potential. There $\bar\Delta\Phi_{b,1}\le0$, so $f(x_0)\ge\mathcal P_0f>0$. Smoothness gives $|\bar\nabla\Phi_{b,1}(x)|\le C\,d_{\bar h}(x,x_0)$ on a normal ball. For $q<0$ this bounds $f(a_f/g_*)^q$ below by a positive multiple of $d_{\bar h}(x,x_0)^q$ at points where it is defined, after shrinking the ball to keep $f$ positive. Its integral diverges when $q\le-3$ by the three-dimensional volume element. If the gradient vanishes on a set of positive baryonic mass instead, the stated nonzero-gradient condition already fails.

For $-3<q<0$ use a smooth Morse potential on the product cut, for example $\nu^3+\cos\theta$, where $\nu^3$ is the height on the unit sphere and $\theta$ the circle angle. Its critical points are the products of the poles and the two critical circle points, and the Hessian at each is nonsingular. Thus its gradient is comparable to the distance there. Set $f=c-(4\pi G_0)^{-1}\bar\Delta(\nu^3+\cos\theta)$ with $c$ large enough to make $f$ strictly positive. Its mean is $c$, so (I.13n.r.1) gives this potential at unit source amplitude. The finite critical set has zero baryonic mass, and all the power singularities are integrable in three dimensions at these exponents. The same nonconstant positive $f$ is admissible for $q\ge0$. This proves nonvacuity for every stated exponent.

*Two-amplitude separation.* On the same prepared dust family put $R_f=-\gamma P_\mu(I-\mathcal P_0)f$. Theorems I.13n.n and I.13n.p give the uniform cut expansion at fixed $f$,
$$
(I-\mathcal P_0)[\rho_{\rm DS}(\delta)-\rho_{\rm DS}(0)]
=\delta R_f+O_f(\delta^2)
\quad\text{in }L^1(d\bar V).
\tag{I.13n.r.3}
$$
For nonconstant $f$ the norm of $R_f$ is positive by injectivity of $P_\mu$ on the zero-mean part. For each $\epsilon$, write $U_\epsilon=A\epsilon^q\mathcal K(I-\mathcal P_0)F_q[f]$. The two first-order normalized comparisons have residuals $R_f-U_\epsilon$ and $R_f-2^qU_\epsilon$ up to $O_f(\epsilon)$. Their linear combination
$$
2^q(R_f-U_\epsilon)-(R_f-2^qU_\epsilon)=(2^q-1)R_f
$$
proves (I.13n.r.2) by the triangle inequality. The remainders come entirely from the source expansion and are independent of the kernel and gain. For a single fixed kernel and gain, the same distinction follows directly: at $q>0$ the normalized comparator tends to zero, and at $q<0$ it either diverges in norm or is identically zero. None has limit $R_f\ne0$. For $q=0$ apply Theorem I.13n.q on the unchanged amplitude normalization. This exhausts the displayed Equation-I.7 exponent choice for the specified comparison on the released cut. The measured density differential itself remains the signed Green response of that cut. A stationary or merger projection and a replacement cluster observable have their own tests. $\square$

<a id="theorem-i13o-a-varied-preferred-clock-action-with-the-registered-static-response"></a>**Theorem I.13o (A Varied Preferred-Clock Action with the Registered Static Response).** Use signature $(-,+,+,+)$, $x^0=ct$, fixed $G,c,\Lambda>0$, $a_0=c^2\sqrt\Lambda/8$, the rate-modulus convention $\beta_\chi=1$, and the $n=3/2$ static branch of Theorem I.13c.5. Fix its admitted amplitude $A>0$ and define
$$
\nu(y)=1+A(1-e^{-y^{-3/2}}),\quad h(y)=y\nu(y),\quad
k=h^{-1},\quad F(x)=\int_0^x k(s)\,ds,\quad \mu(x)=k(x)/x.
\tag{I.13o.1}
$$
Retain the strict branch $h'(y)>0$ for all $y>0$, including the populated $A=7$ member. The zero extensions of $F,\mu$ are those of Theorem I.13c.5. For a smooth clock $T$ with timelike gradient set
$$
Q=\sqrt{-g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu T\partial_\nu T},\quad
u_\mu=-\partial_\mu T/Q,\quad q_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}+u_\mu u_\nu,\quad
a_\mu=u^\nu\nabla_\nu u_\mu,\quad z=\sqrt{a_\mu a^\mu},
\tag{I.13o.2}
$$
The scalar $\nu(y)$ is the static enhancement; $u_\mu$ is the clock unit vector. Define
$$
f(z)=\Lambda+\frac{2a_0^2}{c^4}F(c^2z/a_0)-z^2,\qquad
\chi(z)=\frac{f'(z)}{2z}=\mu(c^2z/a_0)-1,
\quad\chi(0)=-\frac A{1+A}.
\tag{I.13o.3}
$$
The source is the explicitly varied action
$$
S=\frac{c^3}{16\pi G}\int\sqrt{-g}\,[R-2f(z)]\,d^4x+S_m[g,\psi].
\tag{I.13o.4}
$$
Here $S_m$ is the same registered minimally coupled diffeomorphism-invariant matter action in every consumed projection, with its on-shell stress and any endpoint/controller flux included. Variations have compact support in a smooth $Q>0$ domain. This construction uses the preferred-foliation architecture of Blanchet and Marsat (2011) and its dynamical-clock extension discussed by Flanagan (2023); the exponential static function and the calculations below are fixed by (I.13o.1), rather than by a different MOND law.

The action supplies a covariant conserved clock response, reproduces the same static nonrelativistic functional, and has the lensing, nonstationary source, relative linear CMB and exact geodesic-clock projections proved below. The last projection is conditional on its actual caustic-free reference tube; it is not a nonlinear evolution theorem for arbitrary clock initial data.

**Proof. I. Smooth extension and metric/clock variation.** Put $b_0=1+A$. The function $y e^{-y^{-n}}$, extended by zero at $y=0$, is smooth and flat there, so $h(y)=b_0y$ plus a flat remainder. Extend $h(y)=b_0y$ for negative $y$ near zero. The smooth inverse theorem at $h'(0)=b_0>0$ gives $k(x)=x/b_0$ plus a flat remainder and $F(x)=x^2/(2b_0)$ plus a flat remainder. Composing that remainder with $\sqrt X$ remains smooth and flat at $X=0$: each derivative is a finite sum of flat derivatives at $\sqrt X$ times inverse powers of $X$, which flatness dominates. This proves the smooth radial acceleration function at zero needed in (I.13o.4), rather than inferring it from the $C^1$ assertion of Theorem I.13c.5 alone. Keeping $T$ fixed while varying the inverse metric gives
$$
\delta u_\mu=\tfrac12u_\mu u_\alpha u_\beta\delta g^{\alpha\beta},\qquad
\delta f=\chi a_\alpha a_\beta\delta g^{\alpha\beta}+2\chi a^\mu\delta a_\mu.
\tag{I.13o.5}
$$
The first term is the direct inverse-metric variation of $a^2$ and must be retained. Vary $a_\mu=u^\nu\nabla_\nu u_\mu$, including the connection, integrate those terms once, and use $u\cdot a=0$ and hypersurface orthogonality. The field equation is
$$
G^{\mu\nu}+f g^{\mu\nu}+2u^\mu u^\nu\nabla_\rho(\chi a^\rho)-2\chi a^\mu a^\nu
=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_m^{\mu\nu}.
\tag{I.13o.6}
$$
Keeping the independently fixed $\Lambda$ on the gravitational side, the actual response tensor is
$$
T_C^{\mu\nu}=\frac{c^4}{8\pi G}
[-(f-\Lambda)g^{\mu\nu}-2u^\mu u^\nu\nabla_\rho(\chi a^\rho)+2\chi a^\mu a^\nu].
\tag{I.13o.7}
$$
Its anisotropic term is included; $c^4z^2/G$ has energy-density units. For a clock variation with the metric fixed,
$$
\delta u_\mu=-q_\mu{}^\nu\partial_\nu\delta T/Q,\quad
\delta a_\mu=\delta u^\nu\nabla_\nu u_\mu+u^\nu\nabla_\nu\delta u_\mu,\quad
B_\nu=\chi a^\mu\nabla_\nu u_\mu-\nabla_\mu(\chi a_\nu u^\mu).
$$
Integration by parts gives the explicit clock equation
$$
\nabla_\rho(q^{\rho\nu}B_\nu/Q)=0.
\tag{I.13o.8}
$$
For $S_C=-c^3(8\pi G)^{-1}\int\sqrt{-g}(f-\Lambda)d^4x$, set $E_T=(\sqrt{-g})^{-1}\delta S_C/\delta T$. The off-shell diffeomorphism identity is $\nabla_\mu T_C^{\mu\nu}=cE_T\partial^\nu T$. Thus (I.13o.8) and the actual matter equations give $\nabla_\mu(T_m^{\mu\nu}+T_C^{\mu\nu})=0$. The unit constraint was solved by the varied $T$; no externally fixed vector was substituted.

**II. Static reduction and lensing on the same lapse.** In the weak-static domain $|\Phi|/c^2\ll1$, $r\ll\Lambda^{-1/2}$, use $N=1+\Phi/c^2+O(c^{-4})$, $h_{ij}=(1-2\Psi/c^2)\delta_{ij}+O(c^{-4})$ and an aligned clock. For pressureless matter and the retained vanishing homogeneous boundary slip, the leading spatial equation gives $\Psi=\Phi$ and $z=|\nabla\Phi|/c^2$. After the Einstein spatial constraint, the two terms are
$$
-\frac{|\nabla\Phi|^2}{8\pi G},\qquad
-\frac{c^4(f-\Lambda)}{8\pi G}
=-\frac{a_0^2F(|\nabla\Phi|/a_0)}{4\pi G}+\frac{|\nabla\Phi|^2}{8\pi G}.
$$
The quadratic pieces cancel, giving exactly at this nonrelativistic order
$$
S_{\mathrm{NR,static}}=-\int dt\,d^3x
\left[\frac{a_0^2}{4\pi G}F(|\nabla\Phi|/a_0)+\rho_b\Phi\right],\qquad
\nabla\cdot[\mu(|\nabla\Phi|/a_0)\nabla\Phi]=4\pi G\rho_b.
\tag{I.13o.9}
$$
This is the same nonspherical static boundary problem of Theorem I.13c.5, not a second Newtonian force. It inherits the accepted spherical/sheet coefficient at $\beta_\chi=1$. Finite-$c$ residuals require their actual source, domain and window; exactness at this order does not make the static metric an exact relativistic solution.

All probes couple to the same metric. Their weak-static projections are
$$
\boldsymbol\alpha=\frac1{c^2}\int\nabla_\perp(\Phi+\Psi)\,dz
=\frac2{c^2}\int\nabla_\perp\Phi\,dz,\quad
\rho_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\Delta\Phi}{4\pi G},\quad
\rho_C=-\frac1{4\pi G}\nabla\cdot[(\mu-1)\nabla\Phi].
\tag{I.13o.10}
$$
For the exterior point-mass branch, $L_0^2=GM/a_0$ and
$$
\rho_C(r)=\frac{3AM}{4\pi L_0^3}e^{-(r/L_0)^3},\qquad
\alpha(b)=\frac{4GM}{c^2b}[1+A W(b/L_0)],
\quad W(s)=\int_0^\infty\frac{1-e^{-s^3(1+t^2)^{3/2}}}{(1+t^2)^{3/2}}\,dt.
\tag{I.13o.11}
$$
The ideal point-source increment is integrable, has total mass $AM$, is Cartesian $C^2$ but not $C^3$ at the origin, and contributes no extra $\delta$ mass there because the high-acceleration enhancement tends to zero. Positivity and dominated convergence give $W(0)=0$, $W(\infty)=1$ and strict increase for $s>0$. To certify the integral, set $z=s^3(1+t^2)^{3/2}$: its integrand is $s^3(1-e^{-z})/z$, with $z$ derivative proportional to $(z+1)e^{-z}-1<0$. Left/right rectangle sums on $[0,T]$ bracket it, and the omitted tail is at most $1/(2T^2)$. Equation (I.13o.11) is the ideal leading-order point-source projection; an actual finite ray and finite-$c$ residual retain the stated window and domain requirements. The light ray samples all radii, so its force factor cannot be replaced by the enhancement at $b$ alone. General static clusters use the same convex boundary solution, then (I.13o.10); this nonlinear map is not identified with a fixed positive convolution, and general nonspherical effective-density signs are retained.

**III. Nonstationary source and initial charge.** In the slow-motion limit put $T=t+\pi/c^2$, where $\pi$ has units $\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$, and define
$$
\Xi=\Phi-\dot\pi+\tfrac12|\nabla\pi|^2,\qquad v_C=-\nabla\pi,\qquad
S_{\mathrm{NR}}=-\int dt\,d^3x\left[
\frac{|\nabla\Phi|^2+c^4(f(|\nabla\Xi|/c^2)-\Lambda)}{8\pi G}+\rho_b\Phi\right].
\tag{I.13o.12}
$$
Varying $\Phi$ and $\pi$ yields
$$
\Delta\Phi=4\pi G(\rho_b+\rho_C),\qquad
\rho_C=-\frac1{4\pi G}\nabla\cdot[\chi(|\nabla\Xi|/c^2)\nabla\Xi],\qquad
\partial_t\rho_C+\nabla\cdot(\rho_Cv_C)=0.
\tag{I.13o.13}
$$
Indeed $\delta\Xi=-\partial_t\delta\pi+\nabla\pi\cdot\nabla\delta\pi$ and $\delta S_C=-\int\rho_C\delta\Xi$ give the last equation by integration by parts. For a smooth flow $\dot X=v_C(X,t)$,
$$
\rho_C(t,X(t,q))\det D_qX(t,q)=\rho_C(0,q).
\tag{I.13o.14}
$$
All boundary flux is part of this transport law. A zero initial response remains zero on a smooth no-inflow domain. The stationary $\pi=0$, $\Xi=\Phi$ halo instead has initial charge $AM$; in an isolated no-flux domain that charge is conserved. These different preparations cannot be spliced into one zero-charge formation history merely because their parameters agree. They may be separately predeclared protocols of the same action. Equations (I.13o.12)–(I.13o.14) prescribe a merger map once the actual coupled initial/boundary data and smooth solution domain are supplied; they alone neither continue through a caustic nor determine merger offsets.

**IV. Homogeneous and relative linear CMB projections.** On every homogeneous aligned-clock Bianchi-I background, $a_\mu=0$, $f=\Lambda$, $T_C=0$ and the clock current is zero. Thus the independently supplied ordinary worldline/controller matter and Einstein–$\Lambda$ equations are unchanged, including their existing response coefficient; in FLRW the additional source has $\rho_C=p_C=0$ and the vacuum is strict $w=-1$. At first order, only the divergence term in (I.13o.7) contributes:
$$
\delta T_C^{\mu\nu}=\delta\rho_C^{\mathrm{energy}}u^\mu u^\nu,\quad
\delta p_C=\delta j_C=\delta\pi_{C,\mathrm{anis}}=0,\quad
\partial_t\delta\rho_C^{\mathrm{energy}}+3H\delta\rho_C^{\mathrm{energy}}=0,
\tag{I.13o.15}
$$
$$
\delta\rho_C^{\mathrm{energy}}=-\frac{c^2}{4\pi G}\chi_0a_{\mathrm{FLRW}}^{-2}\Delta\Xi,
\quad\chi_0=-\frac A{1+A},\qquad
\delta\rho_{C,k}^{\mathrm{energy}}(t)=\delta\rho_{C,k}^{\mathrm{energy}}(t_0)
\left[\frac{a_{\mathrm{FLRW}}(t_0)}{a_{\mathrm{FLRW}}(t)}\right]^3.
\tag{I.13o.16}
$$
The background acceleration and response vanish, so this first-order source is gauge invariant. In particular the static Poisson enhancement cannot be substituted for it at recombination.

Fix an independently admitted reference FLRW background with the same $G,\Lambda$, matter/photon actions, collision coefficients, gauge, observer and initial time; fix a compact regular conformal-time interval with scale factor bounded away from zero and a registered mode set, or a normed domain where its linear evolution is unique. Let $X_i$ be constraint-compatible reference data and $U_{\mathrm{ref}}$ its solution operator. Embed the data by retaining $X_i$ and setting $\delta\rho_C(\eta_i)=0$, $\Delta\Xi(\eta_i)=0$. For each nonzero mode choose the clock by $\Xi=0$, equivalently $\dot\pi=\Phi$ in cosmic-time normalization. Integration bounds $\pi$ by its initial size plus the reference lapse integral; on the finite interval sufficiently small perturbations with bounded derivatives preserve a timelike clock. The homogeneous relabeling mode creates no linear stress. Equation (I.13o.16) gives $\delta T_C=0$ at all times. Uniqueness therefore gives
$$
P U_{\mathrm{clock}}J=U_{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{clock}}J=\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{clock}}J\Sigma_iJ^*\mathcal R_{\mathrm{clock}}^*
=\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ref}}\Sigma_i\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ref}}^*
\tag{I.13o.17}
$$
for every admitted positive initial covariance $\Sigma_i$ for which the maps exist. Here $P$ discards the clock, while $\mathcal R=\mathcal L U$ uses the same photon/observer map: $\delta I(n)=\int q^3\delta f_\gamma(\eta_o,x_o,q,n)dq$, $\Theta=\delta I/(4I_{\mathrm{background}})$, $a^T_{\ell m}=\int Y_{\ell m}^*\Theta\,d\Omega$, and the same spin-two projections of $Q\pm iU$ define $E/B$. Line-of-sight propagation, recombination and linear scattering are included in the fixed $U$. Thus the entire linear temperature/polarization covariance and cross-covariance have zero relative residual without a covariance refit. This is relative equality, not observational adequacy of the reference. Zero linear charge does not imply zero nonlinear charge. A generic finite-amplitude Taylor remainder would require actual second-derivative bounds $M_{\mathrm{clock}},M_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and is at most $\epsilon^2(M_{\mathrm{clock}}+M_{\mathrm{ref}})\|X_i\|^2/2$ only when those bounds hold.

**V. Exact nonlinear geodesic-clock reference embedding.** Let $(g_{\mathrm{ref}},\psi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ be an exact solution of the same Einstein–$\Lambda$–matter/photon reference action. Fix an initial spacelike surface and its future unit normal. On an actual domain where $E:(s,q)\mapsto\exp_q(sn_q)$ is smooth and injective with nonzero differential, set $T(E(s,q))=s$ in $x^0$ length units. Gaussian normal coordinates give $Q=1$, a geodesic $u$ and $a_\mu=0$. Substitution into the already varied equations gives $T_C=B_\nu=0$ exactly. Consequently
$$
(g_{\mathrm{ref}},\psi_{\mathrm{ref}})\longmapsto
(g_{\mathrm{ref}},\psi_{\mathrm{ref}},T_{\mathrm{geodesic}})
\tag{I.13o.18}
$$
is an exact solution embedding on that tube. It preserves all metric/matter/photon observables, source and actual apparatus clocks; $T$ is an added field, not a rescaling of those clocks. The relative nonlinear residual is $[0,0]$. Applying the same registered geometric construction outcome by outcome to an ensemble preserves the full observable distribution and covariance.

Local tube existence follows from the geodesic ODE, orthogonality and inverse function theorem, uniformly on a compact initial piece. A longer finite observation slab requires its actual normal-map injectivity, positive lower Jacobian, metric regularity and spatial boundary coverage. A compact regular aligned FLRW slab supplies such a tube. A sufficiently small $C^2$ neighborhood retains it by geodesic/Jacobi smooth dependence when injectivity and boundary conditions persist; numerical bounds for an unspecified inhomogeneous domain are not inferred. No caustic continuation is used. This exact branch has zero full response charge, whereas the stationary halo has charge $AM$. Distinct predeclared initial data may share the action and parameters without claiming one isolated common formation history. ∎

<a id="theorem-i13p-constrained-preferred-clock-principal-response-and-its-finite-band-boundary"></a>**Theorem I.13p (Constrained Preferred-Clock Principal Response and Its Finite-Band Boundary).** Retain the static functions of Theorem I.13o, or the admitted $n>1$ branch $\nu(y)=1+A(1-e^{-y^{-n}})$ of Theorem I.13c.5 with $h'>0$. Add real constant dimensionless parameters $b,\ell$ by
$$
S=\frac{c^3}{16\pi G}\int\sqrt{-g}
[R-2f(z)-bK_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}-\ell K^2]d^4x+S_m,
\quad K_{\mu\nu}=q_\mu{}^\rho\nabla_\rho u_\nu,\quad K=K_\mu{}^\mu,
\tag{I.13p.1}
$$
where $f(z)=\Lambda_b+2a_0^2F(c^2z/a_0)/c^4-z^2$ and $a_0$ remains independently fixed. The explicit frozen-principal constraint reduction below implies that no nondegenerate member has positive tensor kinetic energy, positive scalar kinetic energy and positive radial scalar gradient energy on the entire original static-source domain. This is a classification of this two-constant two-derivative family, not of every covariant completion. Every fixed finite unstable mode still has the actual time-retarded kernel and quantitative bounds below.

**Proof. I. The varied constraint system and anisotropic Hessian.** In clock-adapted coordinates $a_i=D_i\log N$, $u$ is the normal and, up to the Einstein boundary term,
$$
S_g=\frac{c^3}{16\pi G}\int N\sqrt h
[{}^3R+pK_{ij}K^{ij}-qK^2-2f(|D\log N|)]d^4x,
\quad p=1-b,\quad q=1+\ell,\quad d=3q-p=2+b+3\ell,\quad e=q-p=b+\ell.
\tag{I.13p.2}
$$
Static aligned fields have $K_{ij}=0$, so these constants leave the static reduction unchanged. At a point of a smooth static background with $a_i=z e_i$, $z>0$, $|e|=1$, a lapse variation $v=\delta N/N$ has principal part $\delta a_i=\partial_i v$. Since $f_z=2z(\mu-1)$ and $f_{zz}=2(k'-1)$,
$$
\mathsf A_{ij}:=-\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial a_i\partial a_j}
=2(1-\mu)(\delta_{ij}-e_ie_j)+2(1-k')e_ie_j,
\quad k'=1/h',
\tag{I.13p.3}
$$
$$
\alpha_\parallel=2(1-1/h'(y)),\qquad
\alpha(\theta)=2\left[1-\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\nu(y)}-\frac{\cos^2\theta}{h'(y)}\right],
\quad x=h(y).
\tag{I.13p.4}
$$
The radial Hessian identity $(f_z/z)(I-ee^T)+f_{zz}ee^T$ proves (I.13p.3). Where $h'<1$, the transverse coefficient is positive, the parallel coefficient negative, and the oblique symbol vanishes at $\cos^2\theta=h'(\nu-1)/(\nu-h')\in(0,1)$. Constraint inverses must therefore be checked for each retained finite direction; the parallel formula is not used at a zero oblique symbol.

Freeze principal coefficients and use $h_{ij}=e^{2\zeta}\delta_{ij}$, $N=1+v$, $N_i=\partial_iB$, with the spatial scalar longitudinal metric component gauged away but lapse and shift still varied. Dots in this calculation mean $\partial_{x^0}$. For a nonzero parallel wave number the quadratic form, suppressing the common positive $c^3/(16\pi G)$, is
$$
L_2=-3d\dot\zeta^2+2d\dot\zeta\Delta B-e(\Delta B)^2
+2|\nabla\zeta|^2-4v\Delta\zeta+\alpha_\parallel|\nabla v|^2.
\tag{I.13p.5}
$$
Indeed $K_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\dot\zeta-\partial_i\partial_jB$ gives $K_{ij}K_{ij}=3\dot\zeta^2-2\dot\zeta\Delta B+(\partial_i\partial_jB)^2$ and $K^2=9\dot\zeta^2-6\dot\zeta\Delta B+(\Delta B)^2$; Fourier transformation or periodic/decaying integration equates the last two integrated squares. Also $\sqrt h{}^3R=e^\zeta[-4\Delta\zeta-2|\nabla\zeta|^2]$, including the lapse–curvature cross term. Curvature, acceleration-gradient and background-stress lower derivatives have not been declared zero; they are outside this frozen principal form. At this order the metric/shift terms remain rotationally isotropic and the acceleration appears only through $\mathsf A_{ij}\partial_i v\partial_jv$, so other Fourier directions have (I.13p.5) with $\alpha(\theta)$ in place of $\alpha_\parallel$.

For $e\ne0$ and $\alpha\ne0$, both constraints and their substitution give
$$
\Delta B=(d/e)\dot\zeta,\quad v=-2\zeta/\alpha,\quad
L_{2,\mathrm{red}}=A_K\dot\zeta^2-B_K|\nabla\zeta|^2,
\quad A_K=2pd/e,\quad B_K=2(2-\alpha)/\alpha.
\tag{I.13p.6}
$$
Thus positive tensor kinetic energy requires $p>0$, and positive scalar kinetic energy requires $d/e>0$. The physical speed ratios are
$$
s_T^2=1/p,\qquad s_\parallel^2=B_K/A_K
=\frac{e(2-\alpha_\parallel)}{pd\alpha_\parallel}
=\frac e{pd(h'(y)-1)}.
\tag{I.13p.7}
$$
For the same conserved frozen linear stress, let $\rho=T^{00}$, $S=\sum_iT^{ii}$, $T_{LL}=\widehat k_i\widehat k_jT^{ij}$. Its actual coupling is $-\rho v+T^{0i}\partial_iB+S\zeta$, multiplied by $16\pi G/c^4$ in (I.13p.5). Conservation gives $\partial_0^2\rho=-|k|^2T_{LL}$. The sourced constraints are
$$
v=-2\zeta/\alpha+\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\frac\rho{\alpha|k|^2},\qquad
B=-\frac d{e|k|^2}\partial_0\zeta+
\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\frac{\partial_0\rho}{e|k|^4}.
$$
Substitute and integrate the mixed $\partial_0\rho\,\partial_0\zeta$ term by parts. In physical seconds,
$$
\ddot\zeta+c^2s^2|k|^2\zeta=f_k,\qquad
f_k=\frac{8\pi G}{A_Kc^2}\left[S+2\rho/\alpha-(d/e)T_{LL}\right].
\tag{I.13p.8}
$$
This fixes the same-stress $G,c$ normalization; a unit reduced force is not renamed unit baryonic mass. A curved nonzero background requires the connection–background-stress terms of its linearized Ward identity before a full finite-wavelength claim.

**II. Radial sign interval and its exact limits.** Put $u=y^{-n}$. Then
$$
h'=1+A[1-(1+nu)e^{-u}].
\tag{I.13p.9}
$$
For $n>1$, $r(u)=e^u-1-nu$ has $r(0)=0$, negative derivative at zero, strictly increasing derivative and tends to infinity. It has exactly one further zero $u_c>0$. Thus $h'<1$ precisely on $0<u<u_c$, equivalently $y>u_c^{-1/n}$, inside the retained $h'>0$ branch. On that interval $\alpha_\parallel<0$, $2-\alpha_\parallel>0$. If $p>0$ and $A_K>0$, then $B_K<0$; choosing $A_K<0$ instead makes the scalar kinetic energy negative. The zero or singular cases $A_K=0$, $e=0$, $p=0$, $d=0$, $\alpha=0$ are not covered by division in (I.13p.6).

For $n=3/2$ the minimum occurs at $u=1/3$, $y=3^{2/3}$, with
$$
h'(3^{2/3})=1+A[1-\tfrac32e^{-1/3}].
\tag{I.13p.10}
$$
At $A=7$ it is positive and below one. The point occurs outside a point mass at $r/L_0=3^{-1/3}$, or a sufficiently small positive baryonic core, and may be chosen with $GM/(c^2r)\ll1$, $r\ll\Lambda^{-1/2}$. The obstruction is therefore present on a weak-static patch. The transition $y=1$ has $h'(1)=1+A[1-5/(2e)]>1$; $y\le1$, the transition sheet and point-mass rays with impact at least $L_0$ give nonempty regular local domains, without covering all high-acceleration sources. As $y\to0$, $\alpha_\parallel\to2A/(1+A)\in(0,2)$. The actual benchmark $b=0$, $\ell=1/3$ has $p=1,d=3,e=1/3$, $A_K=18$, $s_T=1$ and $s_\parallel^2\to1/(9A)$, giving scalar speed $c/\sqrt{63}$ at $A=7$.

**III. Finite-mode retardation and the uncut Sobolev boundary.** For the retained nonzero parallel Fourier modes of this frozen principal model, stable modes have $G_k(t)=1_{t\ge0}\sin(cs|k|t)/(cs|k|)$. For $s_\parallel^2=-\gamma_u^2<0$, the actual time-retarded kernel is
$$
G_k(t)=1_{t\ge0}\frac{\sinh(c\gamma_u|k|t)}{c\gamma_u|k|},\quad
|G_k(t)|\le t e^{c\gamma_u K_{\max}t},\quad
|\dot G_k(t)|\le e^{c\gamma_u K_{\max}t}
\tag{I.13p.11}
$$
for $0<|k|\le K_{\max}$, $0\le t\le T$. Zero-data forcing obeys $|\zeta_k(t)|\le(t^2/2)e^{c\gamma_u K_{\max}t}\sup|f_k|$; the homogeneous solution is $\zeta_k(0)\cosh(c\gamma_u|k|t)+\dot\zeta_k(0)\sinh(c\gamma_u|k|t)/(c\gamma_u|k|)$. Thus every fixed finite band has a retarded solution with its amplification/precision cost. Without cutoff, normalized single-mode initial data at increasing frequencies grow as $\cosh(c\gamma_u|k|T)$, beyond any polynomial derivative allowance. No continuous retarded Cauchy map between fixed-order spatial Sobolev spaces exists at positive time for this frozen principal model; the same construction applies to polynomially bounded localized forcing.

This conclusion does not exclude an analytic, finite-mode or independently realized regulated domain. Conversely the displayed finite-band kernels do not construct an invariant nonlinear covariant cutoff: nonlinear $F$ and constraint products create outside-band frequencies, and Fourier projection is neither automatically local nor stress conserving. A full regulated solution needs its actual constraint-preserving dynamics, auxiliary resources and error bounds. The degenerate minimal member $b=\ell=0$ has $e=0$; its shift constraint is $\dot\zeta=0$ at this order, while its true nonrelativistic clock-density equation is (I.13o.13), not (I.13p.7). Additional fields, acceleration-dependent couplings, non-hypersurface-orthogonal vectors, disformal matter metrics, higher spatial derivatives and nonlocal terms are different families.

**IV. Shared homogeneous normalization and the distinct norm-term modification.** Put $s=1+(b+3\ell)/2=d/2$. The flat homogeneous equations of this same action are
$$
sH^2=\Lambda_b c^2/3+8\pi G\rho_m/(3c^2),\qquad
s\dot H=-4\pi G(\rho_m+p_m)/c^2.
\tag{I.13p.12}
$$
Keeping bare $\Lambda_b=\Lambda$ yields vacuum curvature $\Lambda/s$. Defining $\Lambda_b=s\Lambda$ instead preserves the physical vacuum but leaves matter coupling $G/s$; this is an explicit action-parameter relation, not an independent fit. The homogeneous trace-free equation has coefficient $p=1-b$. At a fixed isotropic release slice with unchanged actual stress difference $\Delta\Pi=R(k_x-k_y)$, its tidal response is
$$
\mathcal A_{xy}(0)=\frac{8\pi G}{c^2}\frac{R(k_x-k_y)}{2p}
=\mathcal A_{xy}^{\mathrm{Einstein}}(0)/p.
\tag{I.13p.13}
$$
Here $R,k_x,k_y$ describe that fixed matter preparation, not a new fitted clock parameter. Preserving a nonzero already registered response coefficient and ruler therefore forces $b=0$ in this family. Keeping the entire original homogeneous Einstein equation at the same bare $G,\Lambda$ requires $b+3\ell=0$. Under that condition a nondegenerate healthy low-gradient scalar with $p>0$ needs $b>0$, hence $s_T=1/\sqrt{1-b}>1$. If same-metric cone containment is an independently consumed premise, these requirements cannot all coexist. With $b=0$ imposed by the original nonzero tidal coefficient, the unchanged-homogeneous member is the degenerate $b=\ell=0$ clock. No universal cone-containment or identical-initial-history requirement is added.

A norm modification is different: adding $+2\mathcal K(Q)$ to the action bracket with $\mathcal K(Q)=m_{\mathcal K}^2(Q-1)^2$, $Q$ normalized to one on the reference clock, gives $Q=1-\Phi/c^2+O(c^{-4})$ in aligned stationarity. Its added nonrelativistic term is $+m_{\mathcal K}^2\Phi^2/(8\pi G)$, changing the static equation to
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mu\nabla\Phi)+m_{\mathcal K}^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho_b.
\tag{I.13p.14}
$$
It therefore introduces a new scale and does not preserve the exact static functional; a finite small-correction claim needs its own window and residual. Expansion/shear terms instead vanish on static aligned fields. These distinct modifications are also distinguished in Blanchet and Skordis (2024); no empirical CMB success of another response function is transferred to the fixed exponential branch. ∎

<a id="corollary-i13p1-a-complete-rational-124-mode-constraint-and-retarded-amplification-certificate"></a>**Corollary I.13p.1 (A Complete Rational 124-Mode Constraint and Retarded-Amplification Certificate).** In the frozen principal system of Theorem I.13p choose $A=7$, $n=3/2$, $y=3^{2/3}$, $b=0$, $\ell=1/3$, and align the background acceleration with the third spatial axis.
